items.description: Yacht rock (codified late-1970s through mid-1980s as a sub-strand of West-Coast AOR pop-rock with foundations in Steely Dan Aja 1977 establishing the jazz-and-R&B-extended-chord vocabulary and Doobie Brothers post-Michael-McDonald-arrival 1976 Takin' It to the Streets establishing the smooth-pop-rock idiom; flowering 1978-1984 through Toto IV 1982, Christopher Cross Christopher Cross 1979, Hall and Oates Voices 1980, Kenny Loggins Footloose era, Boz Scaggs Silk Degrees 1976, Michael McDonald solo era; the genre name itself is retrospective, coined in 2005 by JD Ryznar and Hunter Stair for their web-series mockumentary documenting the genre), the late-1970s through mid-1980s smooth-West-Coast-AOR pop-rock subgenre. Defined by jazz-and-R&B-derived chord vocabulary (extended chords, modal-interchange, secondary-dominants, distinguishing yacht-rock from contemporaneous straight-rock's I-IV-V foundation), polished West-Coast studio production aesthetic (the Sound City / Capitol / A&M Studios production approach with extensive overdub-and-arrangement layering, prominent Rhodes-electric-piano and string-machine pad work), session-musician virtuosity foreground (the Wrecking Crew / TOTO / Bernard Edwards-and-Nile Rodgers-and-Steve-Lukather-era LA session-pool studio-band sound), male-lead-vocal-and-multi-tracked-harmony arrangement (the smooth-and-clear lead-vocal delivery with prominent multi-tracked-harmony backing, distinguishing yacht-rock from contemporaneous rough-edged-rock), mid-tempo (typically 90-130 BPM) groove foundation, and adult-contemporary-romance-and-introspection lyric content. Distinguished from preceding 1970s soft-rock (James Taylor, Carole King) by R&B-and-jazz-foregrounding production aesthetic vs folk-rock acoustic-guitar foreground; distinguished from contemporaneous adult-contemporary AOR (Foreigner, Journey) by R&B-derived chord vocabulary vs straight-rock harmonic foundation; distinguished from later smooth-jazz (its lineage successor) by rock-band-foreground vs jazz-instrumental-soloist foreground.

items.name: Emo
items.lineage: Mid-1980s through present post-hardcore-derived confessional rock — codified through Rites of Spring (Rites of Spring 1985 on Dischord Records), Embrace, Sunny Day Real Estate (Diary 1994), Texas Is the Reason, the Promise Ring, and Mineral codifying the second-wave emo aesthetic; later mainstreamed through Jimmy Eat World (Bleed American 2001), Dashboard Confessional, and the Drive-Thru / Vagrant Records scene
items.description: Emo (codified mid-1980s onward through DC-and-Midwest-and-late-1990s American post-hardcore scenes; first wave 1985-1990 in DC-hardcore scene through Rites of Spring 1985 establishing the emotionally-confessional lyric foregrounding within hardcore-punk foundation, with Embrace 1985 and Beefeater extending the lineage; second wave 1993-2001 Midwest-emo through Sunny Day Real Estate Diary 1994, Cap'n Jazz Analphabetapolothology, Mineral Power of Failing 1997, American Football American Football 1999, The Promise Ring 30° Everywhere 1996, Texas Is the Reason Do You Know Who You Are? 1996 establishing the Midwest-emo intricate-clean-guitar-arpeggio + dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song-architecture vocabulary; third wave 2000-2008 mainstream-crossover through Jimmy Eat World Bleed American 2001, Dashboard Confessional The Places You Have Come to Fear the Most 2001, My Chemical Romance Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge 2004, Fall Out Boy From Under the Cork Tree 2005 bringing emo to mainstream-radio prominence; fourth wave 2008-onward revival including The World Is a Beautiful Place & I Am No Longer Afraid to Die, Modern Baseball, and 2020s-onward contemporary emo continuation), the mid-1980s through present-day post-hardcore-derived rock subgenre defined by emotionally-confessional lyric content and dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song architecture. Defined by emotionally-confessional lyric content (first-person confessional lyric register addressing depression, anxiety, romantic-heartbreak, social-alienation themes — the genre-defining lyric-content orientation that distinguishes emo from pop-punk's adolescent-romance content and from hardcore-punk's political-content), dynamic-quiet-loud-quiet song architecture (the Midwest-emo song-form alternating intricate clean-guitar-arpeggio quiet sections with full-band distorted-power-chord loud sections, distinguishing emo from straight-pop-punk's sustained-distortion approach), intricate clean-guitar-arpeggio textural work (the Midwest-emo math-rock-influenced finger-tapped-and-arpeggiated clean-electric-guitar vocabulary), vocal-delivery alternating between sung-melodic-introspection and shouted-cathartic-emotional-release (often called the emo-scream technique), and song-forms ranging from short pop-emo verse-chorus to extended Midwest-emo through-composed architecture. Distinguished from preceding hardcore-punk by emotional-confessional lyric foregrounding vs political-content foregrounding; distinguished from contemporaneous pop-punk by introspective-confessional lyric register vs pop-punk's extroverted-adolescent register and clean-guitar-arpeggio textural foreground vs pop-punk's sustained-distortion approach; distinguished from later screamo by song-melodic-foregrounding vs screamo's scream-and-noise-dominated approach.

items.name: Kansas City swing
items.lineage: 1930s-40s Kansas City African-American big-band swing tradition (Count Basie, Bennie Moten, Mary Lou Williams, Lester Young, Charlie Parker) built on blues-frame riff-foreground structure and head arrangements rather than pre-written scores
items.description: Kansas City swing (codified 1928-1942 across African-American Kansas-City-and-Oklahoma-City-and-territory-band performance circuits; emerging through Bennie Moten's Kansas City Orchestra 1923-1935 establishing the KC-territorial-band format; flowering through Count Basie Orchestra 1935-onward following Basie's 1929 joining of Moten and 1935 establishment of his own band, Andy Kirk and the Twelve Clouds of Joy with Mary Lou Williams arranger-and-pianist; parallel territory-band development through Jay McShann Orchestra 1939-1942 launching Charlie Parker's career; the 18-and-12-Street and Vine area of Kansas City as the performance-circuit hub with the Reno Club, Sunset Club, Subway Club, and the Hey-Hay Club hosting the jam-session culture that defined the genre; tradition fades after the 1942-1944 Pendergast-era political crackdown on KC nightlife and the AFM recording-strike), the 1930s-1940s African-American Kansas-City-regional swing-era jazz subgenre. Defined by twelve-bar-blues frame foundation (distinguishing KC-swing from contemporaneous New-York-and-Chicago swing's AABA-Tin-Pan-Alley-standards foundation), riff-based head arrangement (the KC riff-foreground arrangement-and-composition vocabulary where simple-but-memorable repeated brass-and-reed phrases form the song-foundation, distinguishing KC-swing from sectional-and-arrangement-foreground big-band approach), prominent blues-and-shouting-vocal foreground (Joe Turner, Jimmy Rushing, Big Joe Williams as KC-shouter exemplars), extended solo-feature-and-jam-session culture (the KC late-night jam-session tradition where the head-arrangements provided a frame for extended improvisational soloing — the cutting-contest culture that produced Charlie Parker), Bennie-Moten / Walter Page-foundational walking-bass and Jo-Jones-hi-hat-foreground drum-foundation (distinguishing KC swing-rhythm-section from contemporaneous swing-feel approaches). Distinguished from contemporaneous New-York-Harlem big-band swing by blues-frame foregrounding and riff-based arrangement vs Tin-Pan-Alley-standards foundation; distinguished from preceding 1920s African-American jazz by swing-eighth-feel and walking-bass rhythm-section foundation; distinguished from later bebop (which it directly fed through Charlie Parker via Jay McShann) by big-band-format vs small-combo-format. Lineage forward feeds bebop (Charlie Parker emerges from KC and McShann), early-R&B (KC-shouters Jimmy Rushing and Joe Turner directly bridge swing-blues-shouting and post-war R&B), and through them the broader post-war jazz-and-R&B continuum.
exemplars: Andy Kirk and the Twelve Clouds of Joy

items.name: Thai classical (piphat)
items.lineage: Thai court-and-temple piphat tuned-percussion ensemble tradition in seven-equal-temperament tuning — codified through the Ayutthaya-era (1351-1767) royal court repertoire and continuing through the Bangkok Rattanakosin period; the piphat ensemble centered on the ranat-ek and ranat-thum xylophones, khong wong large gong-circle, and pi-nai oboe, performing the great repertoire of Phra Aphai Mani, naphat ceremonial works, and dance accompaniment for khon and lakhon
items.description: Thai classical music (codified across centuries of Thai court-and-temple tradition with documented continuous performance practice from the Ayutthaya Kingdom 1351-1767 establishing the piphat ensemble repertoire; standardized through the Rattanakosin Kingdom 1782-onward Bangkok-court-music tradition and the 1934 establishment of the Department of Fine Arts which formalized the modern Thai classical performance pedagogy; performance contexts include royal-court ceremonial-music, Buddhist-temple ritual-music, classical-theater accompaniment for khon masked-dance-drama and lakhon classical-dance-drama, and modern concert-hall performance), the Thai court-and-temple classical-music tradition centered on piphat tuned-percussion-ensemble repertoire. Defined by piphat ensemble arrangement (the six-or-seven-instrument tuned-percussion-and-wind ensemble: ranat ek lead xylophone playing the foreground ornamental-melodic line, ranat thum lower xylophone playing the supporting melodic-line, khong wong yai large gong-circle playing the reference-melody foundation, khong wong lek small gong-circle playing the higher-octave-variant, pi nai quadruple-reed oboe playing the wind-melodic-foreground, taphon barrel-drum and klong-thad-pair-of-drums providing the rhythmic-foundation, ching small-finger-cymbal providing the timekeeping-foundation), heptatonic-equidistant tuning system (the Thai-classical tuning that divides the octave into seven roughly-equal intervals rather than Western-twelve-tone-equal-temperament or the just-intonation tuning of many other Asian classical traditions, giving Thai classical its distinctive harmonic-character), heterophonic compositional logic (multiple instruments playing the same underlying melody with each instrument adding its own characteristic ornamental variation — distinguishing Thai-classical from European-polyphony and from many other Asian classical traditions), three-part-piece compositional structure (the Thao three-tempo-variation form where the same melodic-frame is performed at three different tempos: slow, medium, fast), and chamber-mahori-ensemble variant adds saw-three-string-bowed-fiddles, chakhe long-zither, and khlui flute for indoor-and-court chamber performance. Distinguished from Cambodian pinpeat (its closest lineage neighbor) by tuning-system specificity and instrumental-variant differences; distinguished from Javanese-and-Balinese gamelan by Thai-specific tuned-percussion-and-wind composition vs Indonesian-specific bronze-gong-and-metallophone composition; distinguished from Burmese hsaing-waing by Thai-specific ensemble instrumentation and repertoire vs Burmese-specific drum-and-gong-circle ensemble.
exemplars: Department of Fine Arts (Krom Silpakorn) ensembles

items.name: Hard bop
items.lineage: 1953-1965 Blue Note / Prestige-canon African-American jazz movement extending bebop with extended blues, gospel-quoting melody, and elongated solo space — the defining post-bop vocabulary, with Lee Morgan, Wayne Shorter, Horace Silver, Art Blakey Jazz Messengers, Hank Mobley, Kenny Drew, Cannonball Adderley among the era practitioners
items.description: Hard bop (codified 1953-1965 East-Coast-and-Detroit-and-LA jazz subgenre extending bebop with blues-and-gospel-derived melodic vocabulary; emerging through Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers 1954-onward, Horace Silver Trio and quintet 1953-onward, Clifford Brown / Max Roach Quintet 1954-1956, Cannonball Adderley Quintet 1959-1965; flowering 1958-1964 through Blue Note label catalog of Lee Morgan The Sidewinder 1963, Hank Mobley Soul Station 1960, Wayne Shorter Speak No Evil 1964, Joe Henderson Page One 1963, Jimmy Smith Back at the Chicken Shack 1960; tradition merges into post-bop and modal jazz mid-1960s), the post-bebop jazz subgenre fusing bebop's harmonic-rhythmic complexity with R&B-and-gospel-derived groove and melodic accessibility. Defined by blues-and-gospel-derived melodic vocabulary (the funky-blues-shouted-and-call-and-response melodic-line work distinguishing hard-bop from cooler-pole bebop), prominent rhythmic-groove foreground (the harder-driving back-beat-and-shuffle feels with prominent ride-cymbal-and-tom-and-snare drum-foreground work, often Art Blakey-derived "Press Roll" and "shouting" drumming style), expanded harmonic vocabulary (turnarounds, II-V-I substitutions, blues-frame extensions), small-group format (typical quintet of trumpet-tenor-piano-bass-drums or sextet adding alto-or-trombone), and song-form built on AABA standards-and-original-compositions with head-solos-head architecture. Compositional approach: written-melody-foreground "head" tunes (distinguishing hard-bop from the standards-and-blues-frame foundation of earlier bebop), with original-composition tradition emerging through Horace Silver, Wayne Shorter, Lee Morgan, Joe Henderson establishing the hard-bop-canon repertoire. Recording approach: Blue Note, Prestige, Riverside labels with Rudy Van Gelder engineering, ribbon-mic and condenser capture, light tape compression. Distinguished from preceding bebop by harder-rhythmic-groove-foreground and blues-gospel-melodic vocabulary; distinguished from contemporaneous cool-jazz by intensity-and-blues-foregrounding vs cool-jazz's restraint-and-classical-influence; distinguished from later modal-jazz (its lineage successor) by chord-changes-foreground vs modal-vamp-foreground. Lineage forward feeds modal-jazz (Coltrane, Davis Modal era), soul-jazz (the organ-trio extension), funk-jazz, and through them the broader 1960s-and-1970s mainstream jazz continuum.
exemplars: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

items.name: Swing-era jazz orchestra
items.lineage: 1935-1955 American big-band swing tradition (Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Benny Goodman, Glenn Miller, Tommy Dorsey, Stan Kenton) with 14-18 piece ensembles built around saxophone-trumpet-trombone choirs supported by piano-bass-drums rhythm section
items.description: Big band swing (codified 1935-1945 across Kansas City, New York, Chicago, and Los Angeles ballroom circuits), the 16-piece-plus arranged ensemble that defined the swing era of American popular music. Defined by sectional architecture (4-5 saxes, 3-4 trumpets, 3-4 trombones, rhythm section of piano-bass-guitar-drums), tightly-notated arrangements with brief 8-or-16-bar improvised solo features for individual players, the call-and-response between brass and reed sections that gives the music its push, swing-eighth note rhythmic feel, dance-tempo focus (most charts 110-180 BPM), and a regional house-band ecosystem. Distinguished from Dixieland by section-not-collective-improvisation and arranged-not-head-form charts; distinguished from later bop combos by ensemble size and arrangement-foreground; distinguished from territory-band Western swing by absence of fiddle-and-pedal-steel.

items.name: Bebop
items.lineage: 1944-1955 small-group jazz vocabulary codified by Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, Max Roach, Kenny Clarke — rapid chord changes, virtuosic melodic improvisation, complex rhythmic displacement, intimate quintet-sextet format displacing swing-era big bands
items.description: Bebop (1944-1949 New York Harlem and 52nd Street, with Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Bud Powell, and Thelonious Monk as primary architects), the small-combo, fast-tempo, harmonically dense jazz that emerged in after-hours Minton's Playhouse jam sessions as a deliberate musician's-music separation from swing-era dance-band culture. Defined by the head-solos-head form on the standards repertoire (32-bar AABA show-tune chord progressions, blues), tempos pushed past 250 BPM, harmonic substitutions (tritone subs, ii-V-I extensions, altered dominants), virtuosic bebop-vocabulary improvisation built on chord-arpeggios with chromatic passing tones, instrumentation of trumpet-saxophone front-line over piano-bass-drums rhythm section, and a small-ensemble (combo) format replacing the big-band's section-based arrangement. Distinguished from earlier swing by tempo, harmonic density, and small-combo intimacy; distinguished from later hard bop by absence of blues-and-gospel grounding; distinguished from cool jazz by hot intensity and East Coast lineage.

items.name: Modal jazz
items.lineage: Late-1950s onward jazz subgenre dispensing with rapid bebop chord-changes in favor of static modal frameworks — Miles Davis Kind of Blue (1959), Coltrane Impressions and the McCoy Tyner / Elvin Jones quartet years, Bill Evans modal trio voicings, Wayne Shorter, Herbie Hancock
items.description: Modal jazz (codified 1958-1965 through Miles Davis's Kind of Blue and John Coltrane's My Favorite Things and A Love Supreme establishing the works), the jazz subgenre built on improvisation over modes rather than chord-progressions. Defined by improvisation over a tight set of slowly-changing modes (each section of a piece sits on a single mode for 8-32 bars rather than moving through chord-changes every 1-2 bars), the dorian-and-phrygian-and-mixolydian and other church-mode foundation enabling extended melodic exploration without the harmonic-vocabulary obligations of bebop chord-changes-improvisation, sparser rhythm-section comping (piano-and-bass leaving more space for soloist), foregrounded sustained-pedal-tone bass lines, and longer solo durations enabled by the modal latitude. Distinguished from bebop by mode-not-chord-changes foundation; distinguished from later free jazz by retention of explicit-tonal center and metric pulse; distinguished from cool jazz by modal-not-arrangement focus.

items.name: Free jazz
items.lineage: 1960-onward avant-garde jazz dispensing with fixed harmony and steady meter — Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, Albert Ayler, late John Coltrane (Ascension 1965, Meditations 1965), Pharoah Sanders, Sun Ra Arkestra; ESP-Disk, Impulse!, BYG-Actuel, and Strata-East labels
items.description: Free jazz (1959 onward, codified through Ornette Coleman's Atlantic recordings — particularly The Shape of Jazz to Come and Free Jazz: A Collective Improvisation — and parallel work by Cecil Taylor, Albert Ayler, and the Chicago AACM collective in the 1960s-70s), the radical-improvisation jazz lineage rejecting fixed harmonic structure. Defined by absence of pre-determined chord progressions and meter, collective real-time improvisational creation where multiple players develop musical material simultaneously, atonal melodic vocabulary drawing from extended jazz vocabulary, dissonance, and microtonal pitch-bend, instrumentation extending the standard jazz combo (saxophone-trumpet-piano-bass-drums) with double-bass-and-bass-clarinet doubles and percussion-amalgam set-ups, and performance contexts ranging from loft-jazz NYC scene to European avant-garde festival circuit. Distinguished from bebop by abandonment of chord-changes structure; distinguished from later electric-fusion by acoustic-instrument commitment; distinguished from Cecil-Taylor's solo-piano lineage by ensemble-foreground.

items.name: Fusion
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1970s jazz-rock hybrid genre electrifying jazz instrumentation and incorporating rock rhythms, funk grooves, modal harmonic language, and extended improvised form — codified through Miles Davis (In a Silent Way 1969, Bitches Brew 1970), Weather Report (Heavy Weather 1977), Mahavishnu Orchestra (Inner Mounting Flame 1971), Return to Forever, Herbie Hancock (Head Hunters 1973)
items.description: Jazz fusion (codified 1969 onward through Miles Davis's In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew sessions, and the diaspora into Mahavishnu Orchestra, Weather Report, Return to Forever, Headhunters, and the Chick Corea / Herbie Hancock electric era), the jazz subgenre that introduced electric instruments, rock/funk back lines, and synthesizers into jazz vocabulary. Defined by electric-bass replacing upright in the rhythm section, electric piano (Rhodes, Wurlitzer) and synthesizer (Moog, ARP, Oberheim) replacing or supplementing acoustic piano, electric guitar with pedal-effects-and-distortion adopted as front-line voice alongside saxophone-and-trumpet, rock-and-funk derived 16th-note rhythmic foundation replacing swing-eighth feel, and long-form improvisational performance with extended modal-and-vamp sections. Distinguished from earlier electric jazz by post-1969 timestamp and rock-and-funk back-line; distinguished from later smooth-jazz by retention of jazz-improvisational ambition; distinguished from progressive rock by jazz-not-rock instrumental sensibility.

items.name: Soul jazz
items.lineage: 1955-1975 jazz subgenre built on tonewheel-organ trio (organ-guitar-drums) with R&B / gospel-rooted melodic vocabulary — Jimmy Smith, Jack McDuff, Jimmy McGriff, Lonnie Smith, Big John Patton, the Blue Note organ-trio canon
items.description: Soul jazz (codified mid-1950s through 1970s African-American organ-trio-and-quartet jazz subgenre emerging from Jimmy Smith's 1956 Blue Note debut establishing the Hammond-B3-with-Leslie-speaker tonewheel-organ-foreground format, with parallel development through Brother Jack McDuff, Jimmy McGriff, Lou Donaldson, Stanley Turrentine, Hank Crawford, Charles Earland, and the Prestige and Blue Note label catalogs through the late 1960s; tradition extends through 1970s with Lonnie Smith, Larry Young, and Cherry Mountain era), the organ-trio jazz subgenre fusing hard-bop jazz vocabulary with R&B-and-gospel sensibility. Defined by Hammond-B3 tonewheel-organ-foreground arrangement (the bass-pedal-and-keyboard configuration where the organist plays both bass-pedal-foundation and chord-and-melodic-line work simultaneously, eliminating the need for a separate upright-bass player), Leslie-speaker rotary-modulation cabinet treatment (the signature swirling-modulated tonewheel-organ texture), electric-guitar (often hollow-body archtop like Gibson L-5 or ES-175) and drum-kit completing the trio (or quartet with added saxophone-or-trumpet horn voice), blues-and-gospel-derived melodic vocabulary applied to jazz harmonic frame (12-bar blues forms, modal-vamps, gospel-derived chord progressions), groove-foreground orientation with mid-tempo shuffle-and-straight-eighth feels, and song-forms built on AABA standards-and-blues-frames suitable for extended organ-trio jam treatment. Recording approach: Blue Note, Prestige, Verve labels with Rudy Van Gelder engineering, ribbon-mic distant capture of organ-and-Leslie-cabinet, drums in live-room with overheads, light tape compression. Distinguished from contemporaneous hard-bop by organ-foreground vs piano-or-trumpet foreground and R&B-derived groove vs swing-eighth feel; distinguished from later jazz-funk by 1950s-60s recording-era apparatus and hard-bop harmonic vocabulary preserved; distinguished from white-American organ pop (Booker T. and the MG's soul-instrumental tradition) by African-American jazz-tradition lineage and improvisational ambition. Lineage forward feeds 1970s jazz-funk (Lonnie Smith, Larry Young), 1990s organ-trio revival (John Scofield, Joey DeFrancesco), and through them the broader contemporary organ-trio jazz continuum.

items.name: Jazz manouche
items.lineage: 1930s Paris Romani-French string-led jazz-swing tradition combining American swing harmonic vocabulary with Eastern European Romani melodic-and-virtuoso-soloist tradition — codified through the Quintette du Hot Club de France (Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli, 1934 onward) and continuing through Romané musical-family transmission across European Romani communities into the present
items.description: Gypsy jazz / jazz manouche (codified 1934 onward through Quintette du Hot Club de France with Django Reinhardt and Stéphane Grappelli, with continuous tradition through to present and contemporary Belgian-and-French jazz-manouche scene), the hot-club string-led swing jazz tradition. Defined by string-only instrumentation (rejecting saxophone-and-trumpet front-line of mainstream swing in favor of two-or-three acoustic guitars and violin), comping-guitar pompe rhythmic technique (the gypsy-jazz signature where rhythm-guitar plays a percussive chord-stroke pattern with mute-and-release providing the steady eighth-note pulse), lead guitar and violin trading virtuosic improvisations using bebop-precursor harmonic-language and Romani-music melodic vocabulary, double-bass walking-bass foundation, repertoire of standards and original jazz-manouche compositions, and small-club performance contexts in Parisian clubs and global gypsy-jazz festival circuit. Distinguished from straight swing by absence of horn-front-line and presence of pompe-comping-guitar foundation; distinguished from later bossa nova by swing-eighth feel rather than batida; distinguished from Romani folk traditions by jazz-improvisation orientation.
exemplars: Quintette du Hot Club de France

items.name: Late Romantic symphonic
items.lineage: Western orchestral classical music tradition spanning the Classical period (Haydn, Mozart symphonic forms ca. 1760-1800), Romantic period (Beethoven through Mahler, ca. 1800-1910), and twentieth-century continuation — characterized by the standardized symphony orchestra ensemble of strings-winds-brass-percussion, the multi-movement symphony, concerto, and tone-poem forms, and the conductor-led-large-ensemble performance model
items.description: Symphonic / orchestral classical (codified mid-18th century onward through pre-Classical and Classical-era symphonic development, with continuous tradition through Beethoven's mature symphonies, Romantic-and-late-Romantic continuation, 20th-century modernist and postmodernist works, and contemporary continuation through to present), the large-orchestra notated tradition. Defined by full-orchestra ensemble (typically 60-100+ musicians across string, woodwind, brass, percussion, and harp sections), through-composed sonata-form, theme-and-variations, fugal, and other classical compositional forms, full dynamic range from intimate-pianissimo soloistic passages to fortissimo-tutti climaxes, no improvisation in classical practice (every note specified in score), repertoire spanning Classical core canon (Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven), Romantic continuation (Brahms, Bruckner, Mahler), 20th-century modernist (Stravinsky, Bartók, Shostakovich), and contemporary new-music continuation, and concert-hall performance contexts with subscription-orchestra institutional framing. Distinguished from chamber music by ensemble size; distinguished from opera by absence of vocal-and-stage component (or, in operas, the orchestral-pit-foundation of opera); distinguished from band music by string-section foundation rather than wind-band.

items.name: String quartet
items.lineage: Western chamber music tradition for two violins, viola, and cello, codified by Haydn in his sixty-eight quartets (1762-1803) — the form's most consequential codifiers include Mozart (the six Haydn quartets), Beethoven (the sixteen quartets including the late opp. 127-135), Schubert (Death and the Maiden), Bartók (six quartets), Shostakovich (fifteen quartets), and continuing through contemporary composers
items.description: String quartet (codified mid-18th century onward through Joseph Haydn's pioneering quartet-composition work establishing the genre, with continuous tradition through Mozart-and-Beethoven mature classical era, Romantic and 20th-century continuation, and contemporary continuation through to present), the four-voice contrapuntal chamber-music tradition. Defined by ensemble configuration of two violins, viola, and cello (the string-quartet voicing producing four-part contrapuntal texture), through-composed compositional architecture (no improvisation — every note specified in score), dynamic range from intimate-pianissimo to symphonic-fortissimo despite four-instrument ensemble size, repertoire spanning Classical and Romantic core canon, 20th-century modernist and postmodernist continuation, and contemporary new-music premiere venue, and concert-hall and chamber-music-society performance contexts. Distinguished from larger string-orchestra by ensemble size and absence of section-doubling; distinguished from string-quintet (with second viola or second cello) by configuration; distinguished from earlier 17th-century viol consort by Classical-period codification and modern-violin-family instrumentation.

items.name: Baroque period-instrument
items.lineage: 1600-1750 European art-music period encompassing the development of opera (Monteverdi Orfeo 1607), the concerto grosso (Corelli), the cantata and fugue (Bach), the oratorio (Handel), and the harpsichord and early-fortepiano keyboard repertoire — characterized by figured-bass continuo practice, contrapuntal compositional technique, ornamental melodic style, and the moderate-pitch (A=415 Hz typical) tuning convention
items.description: Baroque-period European art music (ca. 1600-1750, framed by Monteverdi's L'Orfeo at the start and J.S. Bach's death at the end), the codified European art-music tradition built on figured-bass continuo accompaniment, ornamented melodic lines, and the sonata-and-suite-and-fugue formal apparatus. Defined by basso continuo (bass line + chord-realizing keyboard or lute) underpinning treble melody, regional schools (Italian Corelli-Vivaldi violin tradition, French Couperin-Rameau ornamental style, German Bach-Handel contrapuntal mastery), Baroque-tuned period instruments (gut-strung violins, valveless brass, single-action harpsichord, baroque oboe and bassoon, viol family), well-temperament and meantone tunings rather than equal-temperament, and dance-suite forms (allemande-courante-sarabande-gigue) alongside the developing concerto-and-sonata. Distinguished from Renaissance polyphony by figured-bass texture and tonal harmony emerging; distinguished from Classical period by ornamental extravagance and continuo retention.

items.name: Minimalist
items.lineage: Late-1960s onward American art-music movement characterized by repetitive cells, gradual processual change, sustained tonal centers, and rejection of post-Webern serialism — codified through La Monte Young (early drone works), Terry Riley (In C 1964), Steve Reich (Music for 18 Musicians 1976, Music for Mallet Instruments Voices and Organ), Philip Glass (Music in Twelve Parts 1971-74, Einstein on the Beach 1976), and continuing through John Adams (Shaker Loops 1978)
items.description: American art-music tradition of process-driven gradual transformation: phasing patterns slipping out of unison, additive ostinato accumulation, drone-based hyper-extended tonality, cyclical structures playing out over 30-plus-minute timescales. Tonal-but-non-functional harmonic vocabulary; mantric repetition as compositional engine.

items.name: Gagaku
items.lineage: Japanese imperial court music tradition codified during the Nara and Heian periods (eighth through twelfth centuries CE) drawing on Tang Chinese, Korean, and indigenous Japanese ceremonial-court repertoire — preserved continuously through the Imperial Household Music Department (Kunaichō Gakubu) lineage in Tokyo, with characteristic ensemble of shō mouth-organ, hichiriki double-reed, ryūteki transverse flute, biwa lute, koto zither, kakko drum, and shōko gong
items.description: Gagaku (codified 8th-9th century Japan through importations from Tang-dynasty China, with continuous Imperial Court Music Office (Gakubu) transmission lineage to present), the Japanese imperial court music tradition preserving the oldest continuously-performed orchestral tradition in the world. Defined by the cluster-chord shō mouth-organ (a 17-pipe free-reed organ producing sustained dissonant chord-pads), hichiriki double-reed pipe (small loud-and-nasal melodic instrument), ryūteki transverse flute (alternative melodic voice), shō-and-hichiriki-and-ryūteki together forming the standard wind core, biwa lute and koto zither providing pitched accompaniment, kakko small barrel-drum and taiko large drum providing metric foundation, breath-defined slow tempi where phrase-pace follows wind-instrument breath rather than tempo-grid, and the ryo-and-ritsu mode systems organizing pitch material. Distinguished from later Japanese folk and popular musics by court-classical preservation lineage; distinguished from Chinese imperial music by Japanese-specific developmental trajectory.
exemplars: Music of the Imperial Court (Smithsonian Folkways)

items.name: Beijing opera (jingju)
items.lineage: Late-18th-century onward Chinese jingju classical theatrical tradition with the jinghu-led civilian orchestra and luogu martial percussion
items.description: Beijing opera / jingju (codified late-18th-century Qing-dynasty Qianlong court 1790-onward through the consolidation of Anhui-and-Hubei regional opera traditions imported into the imperial capital, with golden-era 1840s-1949 commercial-Beijing-and-Shanghai theater circuit and post-1949 People's Republic-of-China state-supported preservation through Mei Lanfang Beijing Opera Company and parallel state institutions; tradition continues into present-day China and overseas-Chinese communities though commercial centrality has diminished against modern entertainment), the Chinese classical theatrical music tradition that synthesizes stylized vocal-aria singing with martial-arts-derived stage movement, painted-face role-types, and a tightly-codified percussion-and-melodic-string orchestra. Defined by four role-types (sheng for male roles with dignified vocal-and-gestural vocabulary; dan for female roles often performed by male performers using falsetto vocal technique; jing for painted-face male roles with distinctive heavy-makeup visual identity and forceful vocal delivery; chou for clown roles with comic-vocal-and-physical idiom), the wenchang civilian-music ensemble core (jinghu small-bowed-fiddle as the lead melodic voice carrying aria-line, erhu second-bowed-fiddle as harmonic-melodic foil, yueqin moon-shaped lute providing rhythmic-and-harmonic foundation, occasional pipa pear-shaped lute and sanxian three-string lute filling out the texture), the wuchang martial-music percussion ensemble (luogu — daluo large gong, xiaoluo small gong, naobo cymbals, ban wooden clapper, bangu single-headed drum — providing martial-scene-and-fight-scene rhythmic foundation and structural punctuation throughout the performance), highly stylized vocal performance featuring extended aria-lines (xipi mode for lighter and brighter material, erhuang mode for slower-and-darker material), pentatonic-and-heptatonic Chinese tonal vocabulary with characteristic third-and-sixth scale-degree microtonal-inflection, and four-and-eight-bar phrase structures organizing aria material. Repertoire spans hundreds of plays drawn from Chinese historical-and-mythological narrative tradition (Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin, The Drunken Concubine, Farewell My Concubine, Crossroads). Distinguished from preceding Kunqu opera (the Ming-dynasty classical-theatrical antecedent) by less-literati-classical and more-popular-and-commercial register; distinguished from Cantonese-opera-yueju by Mandarin-language vocal practice versus Cantonese-language and by Beijing-court-court-cultural-center heritage versus Pearl-River-Delta-and-Hong-Kong-southern-coast cultural geography. Lineage forward feeds modern xiqu (Chinese-opera-tradition broadly), 20th-century Chinese huaju spoken-drama (which absorbed and reacted against Beijing-opera conventions), and a wide range of contemporary Chinese-language theatrical and cinematic adaptations.

items.name: Cantonese opera (yueju)
items.lineage: Mid-19th-century onward Pearl-River-Delta Cantonese yueju operatic tradition centered on Guangdong, Guangzhou, and Hong Kong — codified through the 19th-century touring red-boat troupes (hongchuan) and the early-20th-century Hong Kong commercial recording era — characterized by literary-Cantonese sung text, gaohu-fiddle-and-percussion accompaniment, and the male / female / clown role types of jingju adapted to Cantonese language and aesthetic
items.description: Cantonese opera / yueju (codified mid-19th-century Pearl-River-Delta and Hong Kong communities, with continuous tradition through 20th-century Hong Kong commercial entertainment industry and post-1949 mainland Guangzhou state-preservation programming), the Cantonese-language classical theatrical music tradition that operates as the southern-Chinese parallel to Beijing-opera-jingju's northern-court tradition. Defined by Cantonese-language vocal performance (versus Beijing opera's Mandarin), three-and-four-character role-type system parallel to but distinct from jingju's four-character system, melodic ensemble centered on yueqin moon-lute, erhu bowed-fiddle, and gaohu high-bowed-fiddle, percussion ensemble parallel to but smaller than jingju's luogu, repertoire spanning Cantonese-specific historical-and-mythological narrative material plus translated jingju repertoire, and Hong Kong-cinema 20th-century crossover that brought Cantonese-opera vocal stylings into popular-cinema soundtrack culture. Distinguished from jingju by Cantonese-language and Pearl-River-Delta cultural geography; distinguished from Cantonese-pop (Cantopop) by classical-theatrical-not-popular-mainstream framework.

items.name: Hindustani classical
items.lineage: North Indian classical raga tradition organized through the gharana (lineage-school) transmission system across Gwalior, Agra, Patiala, Kirana, Atrauli-Jaipur, Indore, Mewati, Benares gharanas — codified through V.N. Bhatkhandes 10-thaat system in the early 20th century, 20th-century lineage Ustad Bismillah Khan (shehnai), Ravi Shankar (sitar), Vilayat Khan (sitar), Ali Akbar Khan (sarod), Pandit Bhimsen Joshi (Kirana vocal), Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia (bansuri)
items.description: Hindustani classical music (codified 13th-15th century onward through Sufi-Hindu syncretic court traditions in Delhi, Lahore, Agra, and Lucknow, with the gharana family-disciple lineage system organizing transmission from 18th century onward), the North Indian classical tradition. The instrumental configuration is sitar lead, tabla rhythmic accompaniment, and tanpura drone-strings. Defined by raga-based modal melody (each raga a specific melodic-grammar with characteristic phrases, ascending-and-descending scales, and emotional-association), tanpura drone establishing the tonic and fifth as foundation, elaborate microtonal ornamentation (meend pitch-bending glides, gamak rapid oscillation, andolan slow vibrato, kan grace-note embellishment), and tabla percussion supplying the tala metric cycle (most commonly teental 16-beat, jhaptal 10-beat, ektal 12-beat). Other soloist instruments and vocal styles (sarod, bansuri, voice-led khayal, dhrupad, thumri) carry their own distinct sub-traditions in the codex. Distinguished from Carnatic by Persian-Sufi-and-Mughal influence, raga-elaboration-foreground over composition-foreground, and tabla-not-mridangam percussion; distinguished from Indian filmi by classical-not-pop framing.

items.name: Hindustani classical (sarod-led)
items.lineage: North Indian sarod tradition centered on the Maihar gharana of Allauddin Khan (1862-1972, the patriarch who taught both his son Ali Akbar Khan and his son-in-law Ravi Shankar) and the Senia Bangash gharana of the Bangash family (Hafiz Ali Khan, Amjad Ali Khan) — the sarod is the fretless metal-fingerboard plucked-lute derivation of the Afghan rabab brought to Hindustani classical from the 18th-19th centuries
items.description: Hindustani classical music with sarod as the soloist (codified through the Maihar gharana lineage from Allauddin Khan in early-20th century, with Ali Akbar Khan, Amjad Ali Khan, and the Bangash gharana extending the form into late-20th and twenty-first century concert practice). The configuration is sarod lead, tabla rhythmic accompaniment, and tanpura drone-strings. Defined by sarod fretless-fingerboard sustained-glide ornamentation (the meend pitch-bending characteristic of all Hindustani melodic instruments but especially fluid on sarod), metal-string-and-skin-resonator construction giving a darker timbral signature, plucked attack with a coconut plectrum (mizrab), raga-based modal elaboration following the standard Hindustani alap-jor-jhala-gat unfolding, tabla rhythmic accompaniment supplying the tala metric cycle, and tanpura drone establishing tonic-and-fifth foundation. Distinguished from the sitar-led Hindustani branch by darker fretless timbre, shorter-sustain plucked attack, and absence of the sympathetic-string shimmer; distinguished from the rudra Dhrupad branch by faster tempo elaboration and concert-not-temple framing.

items.name: Garage rock
items.lineage: Mid-1960s American teenage-band rock-and-roll tradition characterized by raw production, basic three-chord songwriting, and amateur-virtuoso instrumental performance — codified through the original garage-rock canon documented on Nuggets (Lenny Kaye compilation, 1972): The Sonics, The Standells, ? and the Mysterians, The Seeds, Count Five, The Electric Prunes, with the form serving as the protopunk template
items.description: Garage rock (codified 1963-1968 through US suburban-amateur rock-band scene, with revival traditions in the late-70s, late-80s, and 2000-onward), the 1960s amateur-band rock subgenre defined by raw production. Defined by raw production aesthetic (often single-take direct-to-tape recording in basement-or-amateur-studio contexts), distorted electric-guitar lead and rhythm, simple two-or-three-chord vamps and three-or-four-chord verse-chorus structures, snotty-attitude vocal delivery often by amateur-projection-untrained voices, and song-content of teenage-romantic-frustration-and-rebellion themes. Bands often regional-amateur (the Nuggets compilation documented hundreds of such regional 45s). Distinguished from contemporary British Invasion by US-not-UK origin and amateur-not-professional production; distinguished from later punk by less-political-stance and less-aggressive aesthetic ceiling; distinguished from psychedelia by absence of mind-expansion lyrical-and-arrangement apparatus.

items.name: Psychedelic rock
items.lineage: Mid-late 1960s through early 1970s rock genre informed by hallucinogenic-drug culture and Indian classical music influence — codified through The Beatles (Revolver 1966, Sgt Pepper 1967, Magical Mystery Tour 1967), The Jimi Hendrix Experience (Are You Experienced 1967, Axis Bold as Love 1967, Electric Ladyland 1968), Pink Floyd (the Syd Barrett era The Piper at the Gates of Dawn 1967), 13th Floor Elevators, Jefferson Airplane, the Grateful Dead (their early San Francisco psychedelic era), the Doors
items.description: Psychedelic rock (codified 1965-1969 in San Francisco, London, and Los Angeles psychedelic-counterculture scenes, with golden era 1966-1968 establishing the sound), the mid-1960s rock subgenre incorporating drones, modal harmony, and tape effects. Defined by drone-and-modal harmonic foundation (sustained tonic-pedal foundations with modal-rather-than-functional harmonic motion, drawing on Indian classical and folk-revival modal vocabulary), tape effects including reverse-tape, varispeed-tape, and Mellotron sampled-string textures, sitar and other Indian instruments adopted as adopted-instrument color, extended improvisational song-sections (often 5-15 minutes of extended jamming), and lyrical content addressing mind-expansion, drug-experience, and altered-consciousness subjects. Production aesthetic moved toward studio-as-instrument with experimental panning, EQ, and effects-processing. Distinguished from straight rock by drone-and-modal foreground; distinguished from later progressive rock by absence of jazz-fusion-and-classical-virtuosity orientation; distinguished from acid rock (its rougher cousin) by retention of pop-song-form structure.
exemplars: Pink Floyd — Piper at the Gates of Dawn

items.name: Hard rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1980s UK and US hard rock canon codified through Led Zeppelin (Led Zeppelin II 1969 anchoring the heavy-blues-derived foundation), Deep Purple (Machine Head 1972), Black Sabbath (the heavier sludge-pioneering wing), Aerosmith (the US blues-rock crossover), Van Halen (Eddie Van Halens technical-guitar virtuoso revolution from 1978 onward), AC/DC (the Australian-Scottish stripped-down hard rock canon, Back in Black 1980)
items.description: Hard rock (codified late-1968 through 1973 in the UK and US, descending from blues-rock and psychedelic-rock and crystallizing through Cream-Hendrix-Led-Zeppelin-Deep-Purple-Black-Sabbath-Mountain-Grand-Funk lineage), the amplified blues-rock subgenre. Defined by fifth-interval riff vocabulary (the I-V power-chord shape replacing earlier blues-rock's full triadic chord-voicings), shouted-and-wailed high-projection vocal delivery often with blues-rock-derived melismatic ornamentation, concussive bass-drum-and-snare backbeat with prominent fills and tom-foreground percussion, distorted Marshall-stack guitar tone (Big Muff and pre-amp gain-stage saturation), song-forms built on extended verse-chorus with riff-based bridge sections, and tempos around 100-130 BPM. Distinguished from psychedelic-rock by absence of mind-expansion lyrical apparatus and tighter song-form; distinguished from heavy metal (which descends from it) by retention of blues-rock vocabulary and absence of tritone occult-and-dissonant material; distinguished from punk by virtuosic-not-amateur instrumental aesthetic.

items.name: Surf rock
items.lineage: Early-1960s southern California instrumental rock genre built on reverb-drenched single-coil-guitar lead lines and the wet-spring-reverb-tank sound — codified through Dick Dale (Surfer's Choice 1962, Misirlou), The Ventures (Walk Don't Run 1960), The Surfaris (Wipe Out 1963), The Chantays (Pipeline 1963), and the surfing-subculture commercial scene around Hermosa Beach and the South Bay
items.description: Surf rock (codified 1961-1964 across Southern California instrumental-rock scene with Dick Dale establishing the genre through 1961-onward Del-Tones recordings and parallel development through The Ventures, The Surfaris, The Chantays, The Trashmen, and The Beach Boys vocal-surf branch; brief golden era 1962-1964 before the British-Invasion eclipse of late 1964), the early-1960s Southern-California instrumental-rock subgenre defined by spring-reverb-saturated electric-guitar foreground and Eastern-Mediterranean-derived modal melodic vocabulary. Defined by the spring-reverb-tank guitar tone (Fender Reverb Unit produced 1961-onward giving the wet-cavernous surf-guitar timbre — Dick Dale collaborated with Leo Fender on the development), single-coil Fender Stratocaster or Jazzmaster guitar bias (the bright cutting attack appropriate for the staccato-melodic surf vocabulary), tremolo-arm whammy-bar vibrato as melodic ornament technique, fast-picked single-note alternating-pick lines (Dick Dale's alternating-picking technique adopted from his Lebanese-American heritage and applied to oud-derived modal melodic scales — Misirlou as the example of the Eastern-Mediterranean modal source material), driving shuffle-or-straight-eighth drum patterns with prominent ride-cymbal and floor-tom emphasis, electric-bass walking-or-syncopated lines, occasional saxophone-foreground for vocal-surf and instrumental-jam material, and song-forms built on tight 2-to-3-minute single architecture suitable for AM-radio-and-jukebox-distribution. Distinguished from contemporaneous early British-Invasion rock by instrumental-not-vocal foreground and surf-specific guitar-tone-and-melodic vocabulary; distinguished from rockabilly by reverb-saturation-and-tremolo-vibrato sonic signature and faster-tempo material; distinguished from later 1980s-onward surf revival (Dick Dale's 1980s Pulp Fiction comeback, Man or Astro-Man? etc.) by original-1960s-period innocence-and-novelty character vs revival-era pastiche-and-historicism. Lineage forward into instrumental-rock continuum (The Ventures established the format that fed Joe Meek and beat-instrumental UK lineage), spy-and-James-Bond film-music idiom (John Barry borrowed surf-guitar timbres for the 1962 Dr. No theme), and through them the broader instrumental-guitar-rock vocabulary.

items.name: Arena rock
items.lineage: 1970s-1980s American stadium-rock genre crafting anthemic compositions for large-venue performance — codified through Boston (Boston 1976), Foreigner (Foreigner 1977), Journey (Escape 1981), Styx (Paradise Theatre 1981), REO Speedwagon (Hi Infidelity 1980), Kansas (Leftoverture 1976), and continuing through Bon Jovi (Slippery When Wet 1986) and Heart
items.description: American mid-major rock idiom optimized for stadium and arena performance contexts (1976-1992 commercial peak). Pyramid-vocal arrangement (lead-plus-stacked-harmony refrains designed for crowd singalong), guitar-driven anthemic choruses, gated-and-reverb-saturated drum production, synth-string-pad orchestration as cinematic-uplift signature. Recording infrastructure: late-Sound-City-A-room and equivalent multi-room flagship studios, SSL E-and-G consoles paired with Neve outboard, EMT 140 plate reverbs, AMS digital delays. Distinct from hard-rock by chorus-as-priority songwriting and pop-radio-friendly production polish; distinct from AOR by stadium-energy intensity rather than studio-introspection register.

items.name: Hair metal
items.lineage: Sunset Strip glam-metal commercial 1980s American hard-rock subgenre characterized by virtuoso lead-guitar, anthemic choruses, glamorous androgynous stage presentation, and ballad-and-banger album construction — codified through Mötley Crüe (Shout at the Devil 1983), Ratt (Out of the Cellar 1984), Poison (Look What the Cat Dragged In 1986), Bon Jovi (Slippery When Wet 1986), Def Leppard (Hysteria 1987), Whitesnake (Whitesnake 1987), Warrant, Cinderella
items.description: Glam-metal commercial-major idiom centered on the Los Angeles Sunset Strip scene (1983-1991 commercial peak). Distinguished from earlier NWOBHM and contemporaneous thrash by ballad-and-anthem songwriting priority over riff-and-aggression, by visual-glam presentation, and by full integration into MTV-era commercial-pop production aesthetics. Trademark sonic markers: high-gain stack guitar tone (Marshall JCM800-and-similar), gated reverb on snare, layered backing-vocal "gang-chorus" choruses, ballad-format secondary singles. Recording infrastructure shared with arena-rock: SSL-Neve flagship-studio tracking, plate-and-digital-reverb spatial palette, late-analog tape mastering.
exemplars: Poison — Open Up and Say... Ahh! (1988)

items.name: Album-oriented rock
items.lineage: Late-1970s polished mainstream rock genre crafted for FM-radio rotation, characterized by smooth productions, melodic hook-foregrounded songwriting, and adult-contemporary instrumental polish — codified through Toto (Toto IV 1982), Foreigner (4 1981), REO Speedwagon (Hi Infidelity 1980), Boston, Journey, Asia, Survivor (Vital Signs 1984), with the form serving as the late-1970s and 1980s commercial-rock mainstream
items.description: Late-1970s-and-1980s American mainstream rock idiom optimized for the FM-album-radio format. Distinguished from arena-rock by introspective-or-craftsmanly studio register over stadium-energy intensity, by jazz-and-R&B-derived harmonic vocabulary (extended chords, modulation, and chromatic voice-leading uncommon in three-chord rock), and by session-musician virtuosity foregrounded in arrangements. AOR studio practice: meticulous overdub stacking, audiophile attention to vocal placement and reverb depth, frequent use of session woodwind and string overdubs. Recording infrastructure overlaps with arena-rock and hair-metal but with a less-aggressive mix philosophy.
exemplars: The Doobie Brothers — Minute by Minute (1978)

items.name: Heartland rock
items.lineage: Late-1970s through 1980s American populist working-class rock genre with social-realist lyrical content addressing economic decline, blue-collar life, and small-town America — codified through Bruce Springsteen (Born to Run 1975, The River 1980, Born in the USA 1984), Bob Seger (Night Moves 1976), John Mellencamp (Scarecrow 1985), Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers (Damn the Torpedoes 1979), and continuing through Steve Earle
items.description: American populist rock idiom (1979-1995 commercial peak) drawing from country-and-folk songwriting traditions and Dylan-era narrative-lyric authorship while using mainstream-rock instrumentation and production. Lyrical preoccupations with working-class-American themes (industrial-decline, small-town life, military service, romantic-and-economic disillusionment) distinguish heartland-rock from contemporaneous arena-rock and AOR by lyrical-content register rather than production-infrastructure. Tonewheel organ and harmonica are signature instrumental colors. Recording-aesthetic-shared with arena-rock and AOR but typically with less-polished vocal production and more-prominent live-tracking room sound.
exemplars: Bruce Springsteen — Born in the U.S.A. (1984)

items.name: Doom metal
items.lineage: Doom metal as broad genre family descended from the Black Sabbath template — covering traditional doom (Pentagram, Saint Vitus, Candlemass), funeral doom (the slowest variant, 30-40 BPM, Mournful Congregation, Esoteric, Skepticism), the Electric Wizard / Cathedral UK occult-doom canon, and stoner-doom (psychedelic-sub-elements through Sleep, Electric Wizard, Bongripper) — distinct from the New Orleans sludge-and-hardcore axis covered by sludge metal and distinct from the sustained-tone minimalism covered by drone metal
items.description: Doom metal (1970 onward, with first-wave English heavy-blues-rock origin through Black Sabbath's eponymous 1970 debut and a 1980s second-wave codification through Saint Vitus, Pentagram, and Trouble), the slow-tempo downtuned-and-sustained heavy metal subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed down to 60-80 BPM with sustained chord-and-riff durations stretching past five minutes, downtuned guitars (D-standard, drop-C, drop-B) producing thicker low-end heaviness, vocal delivery alternating clean-melodic with growled (subgenre-dependent), heavy reverb-and-fuzz guitar tone preserving extended sustain, lyric and visual themes of occult, mortality, and existential dread, and song-form built on slow riff-progression rather than verse-chorus pop structure. Subgenres include traditional doom (clean vocals, heavy-blues), funeral doom (extreme slowness past 40 BPM), and stoner doom (psychedelic sub-elements). Distinguished from heavy metal by tempo; distinguished from drone metal by retention of song-form structure rather than sustained-tone minimalism; distinguished from sludge metal by absence of hardcore-punk-derived aggression and New Orleans regional lineage; distinguished from black-metal atmospheric by absence of blast-beat foundation.

items.name: Black metal
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward extreme metal subgenre characterized by tremolo-picked treble-guitar, blast-beat drumming, false-fold ventricular shriek vocal, lo-fi production aesthetic, and anti-Christian thematic vocabulary — codified through the Norwegian second wave: Mayhem (De Mysteriis Dom Sathanas 1994), Burzum (Filosofem 1996), Darkthrone (Transilvanian Hunger 1994), Emperor (In the Nightside Eclipse 1994), Immortal
items.description: Black metal (1990 onward, the Norwegian second-wave centered on Bergen and Oslo 1991-1996 establishing the sound after first-wave precursors in the 80s), the high-tempo extreme metal subgenre defined by treble-heavy production aesthetic and shrieked vocals. Defined by tremolo-picked tonal-modal riffs (single-note-rapid-repetition figures outlining minor-key chord-tones), blast-beat drumming alternating bass-drum-and-snare at extreme tempo, deliberately raw lo-fi production with treble-foreground and bass-cut so the entire mix sits in the upper register, shrieked or rasped vocal delivery far above conversational pitch, lyrics treating Norse mythology, anti-Christian polemic, and nature-mysticism, and corpse-paint and forest-photoshoot visual codification. Distinguished from death metal by treble-not-low-mid emphasis and shrieked-not-growled vocal; distinguished from doom by tempo and aggression; distinguished from atmospheric black metal by raw-rather-than-reverb-washed production.

items.name: Punk
items.lineage: Mid-1970s underground rock movement reasserting amateur three-chord rock against progressive-rock complexity, with simplified song-form, aggressive vocal delivery, and anti-establishment thematic content — codified through the New York scene (Ramones, Television, Patti Smith, the Voidoids) and the UK scene (Sex Pistols Never Mind the Bollocks 1977, The Clash 1977, Buzzcocks, The Damned), spreading worldwide through the late-1970s as a distinct underground commercial-and-DIY scene
items.description: Punk rock (codified 1975-1979 in New York City Bowery scene, London Sex-Pistols-and-Clash-and-Damned scene, and Los Angeles Germs-and-X-and-Black-Flag scene), the stripped-down 4/4 rock at high tempo subgenre. Defined by stripped-down 4/4 rock foundation (rejection of progressive-rock-and-arena-rock virtuosity in favor of basic-band economy), tempos pushed to 140-180 BPM, three-chord changes and simple verse-chorus structure under 3 minutes, shouted-and-sung vocal delivery often with deliberately-amateur projection, deliberately-crude production aesthetic embracing fidelity-imperfection as feature, lyric content addressing political-rebellion, generational-disaffection, and confrontational subjects, and DIY-distribution-and-fanzine ecosystem. Distinguished from earlier garage rock by post-1975 timestamp and political-stance foreground; distinguished from later hardcore punk by retention of song-form economy at 140-180 BPM rather than 200+ BPM extreme; distinguished from new wave by anti-pop-craft stance and absence of synth-pop-and-art-rock vocabulary.

items.name: Post-punk
items.lineage: Late-1970s through early-1980s underground rock movement extending punk's rejection of rock-tradition conventions through more harmonic-and-rhythmic experimentation, dub-and-disco bass-and-rhythm sensibility, and intellectualized lyrical content — codified through Wire (Pink Flag 1977), Joy Division (Unknown Pleasures 1979), Gang of Four (Entertainment! 1979), The Fall, Public Image Ltd (Metal Box 1979), Magazine, Talking Heads (Remain in Light 1980)
items.description: Post-punk (codified 1977-1984 in UK and US, descending from punk and crystallizing through Wire, Joy Division, Public Image Ltd, Gang of Four, Talking Heads, and the broader art-rock-departure-from-punk movement), the post-1977 art-rock departure from punk. Defined by angular-bass-led grooves where bass-foundation often becomes the song's melodic-foreground rather than a rhythm-section foundation, dissonant chord voicings and modal-and-atonal harmonic vocabulary departing from punk's three-chord-vocabulary, treble-heavy guitar tone with chorus-and-flanger effects, processed and treated drum-sounds (often emphasizing snare and floor-tom over kit-foundation), lyrical content addressing political-and-philosophical subjects rather than punk's nihilist-confrontational stance, and song-form often extended beyond punk's 2-3-minute economy with experimental structural ambition. Distinguished from punk by art-music ambition and rejection of three-chord-vocabulary; distinguished from new wave by darker mood and absence of pop-craft commercial orientation; distinguished from gothic rock by absence of romantic-melodrama-and-occult lyrical apparatus.

items.name: Shoegaze
items.lineage: UK underground guitar-pop genre that emerged 1988-1991 — named for the bands characteristic stage posture of staring down at effect-pedal boards rather than engaging the audience; codified through My Bloody Valentine (Loveless 1991, the wall-of-guitars masterpiece tracked over 2 years across 19 studios with Kevin Shields perfectionism), Slowdive (Just for a Day 1991, Souvlaki 1993), Ride (Nowhere 1990), Lush, Chapterhouse, the Pale Saints; built on dense overlapping guitar tracks with reverb / delay / tremolo / flanger / phaser processing and buried-in-mix vocals
items.description: Shoegaze (codified 1989-1992 UK with My Bloody Valentine's Loveless and Slowdive's Souvlaki establishing the sound, with second-wave revival 2000s-onward continuing through to present), the wall-of-sound guitar-music subgenre. Defined by pedal-effected layered guitars (heavy use of fuzz, chorus, flanger, phaser, and reverb-pedal stacking creating dense-distorted ambient-textural guitar layers), buried vocals (vocal performance mixed below the guitars in a hushed-near-whispered delivery, often with overlapping male-and-female harmony), retention of melodic content underneath the wash (despite wall-of-sound aesthetic, songs maintain pop-melodic foundation), midtempo song-tempos around 90-130 BPM with non-aggressive drum-pattern, and song-form retaining verse-chorus structure stretched-and-textured. Distinguished from straight dream pop by greater wall-of-sound distortion-and-density; distinguished from noise-rock by retention of pop-melodic foreground; distinguished from later post-rock by retention of vocal-and-song-form structure.

items.name: Alternative rock
items.lineage: Late-1980s through early-2000s American independent-label guitar-rock genre that crossed over to mainstream radio after the Nirvana breakthrough — the umbrella covering the underground-to-mainstream trajectory distinct from grunge (Pacific Northwest specific), shoegaze (UK MBV-derived), noise rock (narrower experimental scope), and emo (post-hardcore confessional). Codified through the Pixies (Surfer Rosa 1988, Doolittle 1989, Bossanova 1990, the soft-loud-soft dynamic Cobain cited as Nevermind template), Sonic Youth (Daydream Nation 1988, Goo 1990, Dirty 1992 produced by Butch Vig), R.E.M. (Murmur 1983, Reckoning 1984, Document 1987, Out of Time 1991 commercial breakthrough, Automatic for the People 1992), Pavement (Slanted and Enchanted 1992, Crooked Rain Crooked Rain 1994, Wowee Zowee 1995), Dinosaur Jr. (Youre Living All Over Me 1987, Bug 1988, Green Mind 1991), Hüsker Dü (Zen Arcade 1984, New Day Rising 1985, Candy Apple Grey 1986), the Replacements (Let It Be 1984, Tim 1985, Pleased to Meet Me 1987), Modest Mouse (The Lonesome Crowded West 1997, The Moon and Antarctica 2000), Built to Spill (Perfect From Now On 1997, Keep It Like a Secret 1999), Yo La Tengo (Painful 1993, I Can Hear the Heart Beating as One 1997), Guided by Voices (Bee Thousand 1994, Alien Lanes 1995), Wilco (Being There 1996, Yankee Hotel Foxtrot 2002, the post-alt-country reinvention), the Breeders (Last Splash 1993), Throwing Muses, the Lemonheads, the Flaming Lips (The Soft Bulletin 1999), Weezer (Blue Album 1994, Pinkerton 1996). Built around electric guitar as primary lead — single-coil Fender-derived for jangly REM/Pavement chime, humbucker Gibson-derived for Pixies/Dinosaur Jr full-bodied roar — drums dry and unpolished in deliberate contrast to 80s arena-rock gated-reverb production, bass clean and melodic carrying counter-lines rather than locking to kick, vocals untrained and conversational or shouted rather than belted, lyrics interior-and-oblique rather than anthemic-and-universal, song structures hewing to verse-chorus but with quirks of extended noise interludes, soft-loud-soft Pixies dynamics, sudden key-asymmetric bridges, dropped-time outros. Production approaches centered on independent labels (Matador, Merge, Sub Pop, SST, Twin/Tone, Touch and Go, Drag City, Kill Rock Stars) with budget constraints producing the genre characteristic dry-and-direct sound antagonistic to the polished mainstream rock production of the same era. Recurring producers Steve Albini (electric-and-acoustic-pair drum micing, ambient-room aesthetic, anti-compression), Butch Vig (the Smart Studios Madison Wisconsin sound), Brian Paulson, Brad Wood. The genre dissolved into the broader indie-rock continuum by mid-2000s as the underground-mainstream distinction collapsed
items.description: Alternative rock (codified late-1980s through early-2000s American independent-label guitar-rock scene that crossed over to mainstream radio after Nirvana 1991, the umbrella spanning the underground-to-mainstream trajectory through Pixies, Sonic Youth, R.E.M., Pavement, Dinosaur Jr., Hüsker Dü, the Replacements, Modest Mouse, Built to Spill, Yo La Tengo, Wilco, Weezer, the Breeders, the Flaming Lips, and Guided by Voices), the independent-rock genre that became the dominant mainstream-rock idiom 1991-2000. Defined by guitar-foreground arrangement spanning single-coil-Fender-derived jangle (R.E.M., Pavement chime) and humbucker-Gibson-derived full-bodied roar (Pixies, Dinosaur Jr.), dry-and-unpolished drum production in deliberate contrast to 80s arena-rock gated-reverb aesthetic, clean-and-melodic bass carrying counter-lines rather than locking to kick, untrained-conversational-or-shouted vocal delivery, interior-and-oblique lyric content, and verse-chorus song architecture with Pixies-derived soft-loud-soft dynamic shape. Independent-label production infrastructure (Matador, Merge, Sub Pop, SST, Twin/Tone, Touch and Go, Drag City, Kill Rock Stars) producing the genre-characteristic dry-and-direct sound antagonistic to mainstream rock polish; recurring producers Steve Albini (electric-and-acoustic-pair drum micing, ambient-room aesthetic, anti-compression), Butch Vig (Smart Studios Madison sound), Brian Paulson, Brad Wood. Distinguished from grunge by broader scope (not Pacific-Northwest specific); distinguished from shoegaze by US-not-UK origin and song-over-texture orientation; distinguished from noise rock by mainstream-radio crossover; distinguished from emo by absence of post-hardcore confessional lyric stance. Dissolved into broader indie-rock continuum by mid-2000s as the underground-mainstream distinction collapsed.

items.name: Grunge
items.lineage: Seattle Pacific Northwest alternative-rock genre that emerged in the late 1980s and went global in 1991 — codified through Nirvana (Nevermind 1991, the commercial breakthrough produced by Butch Vig), Pearl Jam (Ten 1991), Soundgarden (Badmotorfinger 1991, then Superunknown 1994), Alice in Chains (Facelift 1990, Dirt 1992), Mudhoney (the Sub Pop founding band), Screaming Trees, Tad — built on a fusion of hardcore punk aggression and Sabbath-style heavy-blues-derived guitar tone
items.description: Grunge (codified 1985-1995 Seattle and broader Pacific Northwest, with first-wave Sub Pop label era and second-wave major-label commercial breakthrough through Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, and Alice in Chains), the late-1980s/early-1990s hybrid of punk, hardcore, and metal. Defined by Sabbath-derived heavy-blues-rock riff vocabulary translated through hardcore-punk-and-college-rock sensibility, alternation between quiet verse and loud chorus dynamic structure (the soft-loud signature established by the Pixies and adapted), distorted-fuzz-pedal electric-guitar tone (Big Muff fuzz, MXR Distortion+), apathetic-or-distressed vocal delivery, lyric content of generational disaffection, depression, and Pacific-Northwest-suburban-malaise, and college-rock-and-indie-label production aesthetic transitioning into major-label commercial sound 1991 onward. Distinguished from straight metal by punk-and-college-rock lineage; distinguished from hardcore punk by retention of heavy-blues-rock guitar; distinguished from Britpop by US-not-UK origin and darker-and-grungier aesthetic.

items.name: Chicago house
items.lineage: Mid-1980s Chicago club-music genre developed at the Warehouse and Music Box clubs through Frankie Knuckles, Ron Hardy, and the early Trax Records and DJ International record-label catalogs — characterized by 120-128 bpm four-on-the-floor kick, drum-machine programming, sampled-and-looped disco-and-soul vocal hooks, and the form's explicit Black-and-Latino-queer-club origins (1984-1988)
items.description: Chicago house (1981-1989 Chicago, founded at Frankie Knuckles's Warehouse club residency and codified through Larry Heard, Marshall Jefferson, and Adonis production output on Trax and DJ International labels), the foundational electronic dance music genre. Defined by Roland TR-909 and TR-808 four-on-floor drum-machine foundation, syncopated TR-909 hi-hat-and-clap on the offbeats, simple synth bass lines either programmed in TB-303 or on monophonic synths, soulful or near-spoken vocal samples and live vocal hooks, song form built on extended sectional vamps for DJ-mixing rather than pop-song verse-chorus, and tempos around 118-128 BPM. Originated at Black gay clubs as a successor scene to disco. Distinguished from disco by drum-machine-not-orchestral-rhythm-section foundation and DJ-mix-form construction; distinguished from Detroit techno by warmer Chicago-rooted soul-vocal foreground and deeper retention of black-gospel-and-soul harmonic vocabulary; distinguished from acid house by absence of TB-303 lead foreground.

items.name: Detroit techno
items.lineage: Mid-1980s Detroit electronic dance music genre developed by the Belleville Three (Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson) drawing on Kraftwerk's electronic vocabulary, Parliament-Funkadelic's Afrofuturist aesthetic, and Chicago house's rhythmic foundation — codified through Cybotron (Clear 1983), Model 500, Rhythim Is Rhythim (Strings of Life 1987), Inner City (Big Fun 1988), and the labels Metroplex, Transmat, KMS
items.description: Detroit techno (codified 1985-1990 through the Belleville Three — Juan Atkins, Derrick May, Kevin Saunderson — and the Cybotron precursor work, with second-wave Underground Resistance lineage 1990 onward), the Detroit-originated mechanical-funk electronic music genre. Defined by drum-machine four-on-floor foundation (TR-909 kicks, TR-808 hats and claps, TR-606 snares), synthesizer-derived bass lines and lead lines drawing from Kraftwerk-Yellow-Magic-Orchestra futurist palette, atmospheric synth-pad layers and processed sound effects, song-form built on long sectional vamps for DJ-mixing, futurist-sci-fi lyrical content (when vocals appear), and tempos around 125-140 BPM. Production lineage emerging from black Detroit producers' response to disco's death and Reagan-era Rust-Belt deindustrialization. Distinguished from Chicago house by mechanical-not-soulful aesthetic and futurist-not-disco lineage; distinguished from European techno by warmer Detroit funk-and-soul traces; distinguished from acid house by absence of TB-303-foreground.

items.name: Acid house
items.lineage: Late-1980s Chicago and UK club-music genre built on the squelchy resonant filter sweep of the Roland TB-303 bass-synth (originally a 1981 commercial failure rediscovered by DJ Pierre and Phuture) — codified through Phuture (Acid Tracks 1987), Sleezy D (I've Lost Control 1986), the UK Second Summer of Love rave-scene breakthrough (1988-1989), 808 State, A Guy Called Gerald (Voodoo Ray 1988)
items.description: Acid house (1985-1989 Chicago, 1988-1992 UK), the house subgenre defined by the resonant-filter-modulated bass lines of the Roland TB-303 sequencer-synthesizer used outside its intended bass-accompaniment role. Defined by the iconic squelching saw-wave 303 line under 909 four-on-floor and 808 hi-hats, vocal samples and yelps over otherwise instrumental grooves, hardware-live-improvised filter and resonance sweeps as the central performance gesture, and tempos around 120-130 BPM. Originated in Chicago warehouse parties (DJ Pierre and Phuture’s Acid Tracks the codifying record) and exploded as the 1988 Second Summer of Love sound of UK acid-house clubs and rave culture. Distinguished from Chicago house by 303 prominence and acid-trip aesthetic; distinguished from Detroit techno by warmer Chicago-rooted groove and song-form remnants over Detroit’s machine-funk severity.

items.name: Peak-time techno
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward European hard-techno subgenre crafted for peak-time large-club and outdoor festival rotation, characterized by 130-140 bpm driving four-on-the-floor, aggressive sub-bass, hypnotic loop-based arrangement, and minimal melodic content — codified through Berlin's Berghain-orbit producers (Marcel Dettmann, Ben Klock, Surgeon, Function), the Ostgut Ton label, and the broader European hard-techno festival circuit
items.description: Peak-time techno (codified 1990s onward through Berlin's Tresor and London's Lost club residencies, with continuous tradition through to present), the hard-fast club-floor techno subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed to 135-145 BPM, heavy-and-distorted four-on-floor kick foundation designed for large-club sound-system impact, minimal melodic content (often single-note or two-note bass-line patterns and minimal synth-stab phrases, with the kick-drum and percussion carrying primary musical weight), industrial-and-acid-derived synth textures, sparse arrangement maximizing dance-floor energy, and song-form built on long sectional vamps with build-up-and-drop construction designed for DJ-set programming. Distinguished from Detroit techno by harder-and-faster aesthetic and absence of soul-vocal-and-funk-traces; distinguished from gabber by sub-180 BPM ceiling and absence of distorted-clipped kick; distinguished from minimal techno by maximalist big-room aesthetic over restraint.

items.name: Dub techno
items.lineage: Berlin dub-techno subgenre codified by Basic Channel and Chain Reaction (founded 1993 by Moritz von Oswald and Mark Ernestus, at the Hardwax record store / Kreuzberg techno-scene infrastructure) — fuses Detroit techno-foundational vocabulary with King Tubby-derived dub mixing aesthetic; recordings: Basic Channel Phylyps Trak 1993, Maurizio Domina 1995, Porter Ricks Biokinetics 1996
items.description: Dub techno (1993-1997 Berlin and Cologne, codified through Basic Channel and Rhythm & Sound's pseudonymous releases on their own labels), the techno subgenre fused with Jamaican dub processing. Defined by Maurizio-and-Mark-Ernestus deep-chord-pad foundations processed with long delay-and-reverb tails creating phasing chord stabs that extend across 4-8-bar phrases, filtered hi-hats with slow filter-sweep modulation, four-on-floor kick foundation around 120-130 BPM, near-absence of melody beyond the chord stabs, and album-length sustained-mood sequencing. Production lineage emerging from German techno's encounter with Jamaican dub via Rhythm & Sound's collaborations with Jamaican vocalists. Distinguished from straight techno by chord-pad-foreground over kick-and-percussion-foreground; distinguished from minimal techno (which it influenced) by warmer harmonic palette; distinguished from dub by techno-not-reggae rhythmic foundation and absence of song-form.

items.name: Jungle and drum-and-bass
items.lineage: Early-1990s UK breakbeat-bass continuum genre developed in the British rave scene through the chopping and pitching-up of the Amen break (the seven-second drum break from The Winstons' Amen Brother 1969) over reggae-and-dub sub-bass foundations — codified through Goldie (Timeless 1995), Roni Size (New Forms 1997), LTJ Bukem (Logical Progression 1996), 4hero, and continuing through drum-and-bass as the genre's late-1990s commercial evolution
items.description: Jungle (codified 1992-1996 UK rave-and-hardcore evolution, descending from breakbeat-hardcore and crystallizing through Goldie, A Guy Called Gerald, Roni Size, and 4 Hero), the 160-180 BPM breakbeat-driven UK electronic music. Defined by chopped-and-resequenced Amen breakbeat samples (the James-Brown-Funky-Drummer and Winstons-Amen drum-break source samples chopped into new rhythmic configurations) at extreme tempo, heavy reggae-derived sub-bass foundation underneath the fast breakbeats producing the jungle-specific dual-tempo feel (fast breaks over slow sub), ragga vocal samples (chopped-and-pitched samples from Jamaican dancehall sources providing vocal textural elements), and song-form built on long sectional progression with dub-style breakdown sections. Distinguished from later drum-and-bass (often considered the same genre split in two) by retention of ragga-and-reggae vocal and dancehall-aesthetic emphasis; distinguished from breakbeat-hardcore by post-1992 sub-bass foreground; distinguished from gabber by UK-not-Dutch lineage and absence of distorted-kick foundation.

items.name: Ambient
items.lineage: Long-form atmospheric electronic-music genre codified by Brian Eno from 1975 onward — Discreet Music 1975, then the Ambient series Ambient 1: Music for Airports 1978 establishing both the genre name and the founding aesthetic of music as functional environment-shaping; extended through Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks 1983 with Daniel Lanois and Roger Eno, Harold Budd collaborations, the modern continuation through Stars of the Lid, William Basinski (The Disintegration Loops 2002), Tim Hecker, Grouper
items.description: Ambient music (1978 onward, the Brian Eno Music for Airports framing crystallizing a tradition of attention-optional sonic environment design that traces back to Erik Satie’s 1917 furniture music). Defined by long-form (often 20+ minute) static or slowly-evolving textures, minimal or absent metric pulse, designs that reward both close attention and distracted ambient hearing equally, dense reverb-and-delay processing of source materials so original instruments become diffuse pads, and a deliberate refusal of song-form, climax, or melody-as-figure. Subgenres include dark ambient (heavier drones, industrial sources), space music (synthesizer-derived cosmic palette), and ambient-drone (overtone-extended sustained pitches). Distinguished from new-age by absence of healing-claim framing and rhythmic-pulse accompaniment; distinguished from drone-metal by lack of distortion and metal-derived gestures; distinguished from minimalism by absence of pattern-process foreground.
exemplars: Aphex Twin — Selected Ambient Works Vol. II

items.name: IDM and experimental electronic
items.lineage: Early-1990s onward experimental-electronic genre intentionally constructed for headphone listening rather than club-dance use, characterized by complex broken-beat programming, glitchy textural sound design, and the post-acid-house compositional ambition — codified through Aphex Twin (Selected Ambient Works 85-92 in 1992, Richard D. James Album 1996), Autechre (Tri Repetae 1995), Boards of Canada (Music Has the Right to Children 1998), Squarepusher, the Warp Records Artificial Intelligence series
items.description: IDM / Intelligent Dance Music (codified 1992 onward, named for the Hyperreal IDM mailing list and crystallizing through Warp Records' Artificial Intelligence series — Aphex Twin, Autechre, Black Dog Productions, B12), the listening-rather-than-dancing electronic music genre.
