Defined by 2/4 syncopated meter (the milonga-rhythm: a habanera-derived dotted-eighth-and-sixteenth-and-eighth pattern that gives the genre its propulsive forward-motion and that fed directly into tango's rhythmic foundation), faster tempo than tango (typically 90-130 BPM milonga vs 60-90 BPM tango), payada-troubadour-and-folklore-rural lyric tradition (the milonga lyric content of rural-pampas-life, gaucho-mythology, payada-improvised-poetic-duels distinguishing milonga from tango's urban-port-melancholic content), guitar-foreground instrumentation (the milonga-rural arrangement of voice + classical-guitar with optional bandoneón, violin, and contrabass for urban-milonga; distinguished from tango's bandoneón-foreground orquesta-típica arrangement), strophic song-form structure typical of folk-ballad tradition. Distinguished from tango by faster-tempo and rural-folkloric content vs tango's slower-tempo and urban-melancholic content, and by guitar-foreground vs bandoneón-foreground arrangement; distinguished from contemporaneous nueva canción by absence of explicit political-ideological content; distinguished from later folklore-argentino subgenres (chacarera, zamba) by 2/4 syncopated milonga-rhythm vs 6/8 chacarera-or-zamba rhythm.

items.name: Samba
items.lineage: Brazilian Rio carnival and samba-canção tradition, codified through the early-twentieth-century Rio favelas and the 1917 first-recorded-samba "Pelo Telefone" — through Cartola, Noel Rosa, and Ataulfo Alves codifying samba-canção lyric tradition, then Pixinguinha as the orchestrating bandleader, with samba-de-roda Bahian roots and samba-enredo carnival-school evolution
items.description: Samba (codified 1917 onward through Donga's Pelo Telefone — first samba commercial-recorded — with the Estácio neighborhood Carioca samba and the post-1928 escola-de-samba carnival-school institutional development establishing the genre), the Brazilian dance music tradition. Defined by surdo-tamborim-cuíca-pandeiro-tantã percussion battery (the bateria — the samba-school percussion-ensemble core), syncopated cuíca whoops (the friction-drum-instrument's signature sound), surdo bass-drum providing the heart-beat foundation pattern, syncopated 2/4 metric organization with second-and-fourth beat emphasis (samba's defining off-beat feel), call-and-response between lead-vocalist (puxador) and chorus, lyric content drawing on Carioca-Rio-de-Janeiro neighborhood subjects, and Carnival-procession performance context. Distinguished from later bossa nova by absence of intimate-vocal-and-jazz-harmony orientation; distinguished from samba-jazz fusion by retention of Carnival-percussion foundation; distinguished from Brazilian MPB by direct samba-tradition lineage rather than samba-fusion-with-rock-and-folk.

items.name: Pagode
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro 1980s-onward backyard urban-samba subgenre with small-roda informal performance setting — codified through Beth Carvalho discovering and promoting the Cacique de Ramos sambistas, Zeca Pagodinho’s rise from that scene to mainstream stardom (Pagode do Zeca 1986 onward), and Almir Guineto and Jovelina Pérola Negra — characterized by the tantã, banjo-cavaco, and repique-de-mão small-ensemble instrumentation
items.description: Pagode (codified 1978-onward Rio de Janeiro urban-samba subgenre defined by samba-school small-group informal-roda performance practice; emergence through the 1978 Cacique de Ramos roda-samba scene led by Bezerra da Silva and Almir Guineto, with parallel development through Fundo de Quintal collective establishing the pagode-roda format; flowering through 1980s recordings of Fundo de Quintal, Beth Carvalho, Almir Guineto, Jorge Aragão; 1990s commercial-pagode mainstream-crossover through Raça Negra, Os Travessos, Soweto, and the broader pagode-romântico subgenre extension toward pop-radio audience; tradition continues through 2000s-onward continuation including Exaltasamba, Sorriso Maroto, Thiaguinho, and contemporary pagode-and-samba revival), the Rio de Janeiro 1970s-onward urban-samba subgenre defined by samba-school small-group informal-roda performance practice. Defined by small-group roda performance practice (the pagode-roda informal-circle performance context with musicians sitting around a table playing for each other and small audience, distinguishing pagode from the larger bateria-and-procession samba-school format), small-ensemble instrumentation foundation (the pagode-roda instrumentation: cavaquinho providing harmonic-and-rhythmic foundation, surdo handheld for bass-beat foundation, pandeiro for percussion, tantã handheld-drum providing the genre's signature low-tone-and-high-tone alternation pattern, voice-and-classical-guitar for melodic foreground, distinguishing pagode from samba's larger bateria ensemble), 2/4 samba-meter with prominent tantã-handheld-drum rhythm pattern, vocal-lead-with-chorus-backing arrangement (often with multiple voices trading lead role within the roda format), lyric content centered on Rio neighborhood life, samba-school internal politics, love and friendship themes, and informal-celebratory orientation (distinguishing pagode from samba-de-enredo competitive Carnival-school format). Distinguished from traditional samba by smaller ensemble-format and informal-roda performance context vs procession-and-bateria format; distinguished from later samba-rock and samba-jazz fusion by retention of acoustic-and-percussion foundation; distinguished from pagode-romântico 1990s commercial subgenre by retention of roda-aesthetic vs pop-radio production approach.

items.name: Bossa nova
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro 1958-1965 chamber-samba intimate-vocal tradition — codified through João Gilberto’s Chega de Saudade (1959) defining the genre’s syncopated guitar batida, Antônio Carlos Jobim’s compositions, Vinícius de Moraes’s lyrics, and the Stan Getz / João Gilberto Getz/Gilberto (1964) international crossover; characterized by close-miked whispered-vocal aesthetic, jazz-chord harmonic vocabulary, and Zona Sul apartment-recording origin
items.description: Bossa nova (1958-1965 Rio de Janeiro, particularly the Ipanema-Copacabana intimate-club scene), the Brazilian intimate-samba derivative that fused samba rhythmic foundation with cool-jazz harmonic vocabulary. Defined by the João Gilberto guitar-pattern (steady-thumb-bass with offbeat-syncopated upper-string strums producing the bossa-nova batida rhythm), breath-quiet conversational vocal delivery without operatic projection, jazz-derived extended-chord harmony (major-7s, minor-9s, altered dominants moving through ii-V cycles), studio-recording-not-Carnival context, and Portuguese-language lyrics about Rio beach life and saudade-romantic longing. Brief golden-era 1958-1965 ended with the bossa-jazz US export and tropicália's break with intimate aesthetic. Distinguished from samba batucada by indoor-intimate scale and removal of percussion-ensemble foreground; distinguished from MPB by pre-1965 timestamp and specific batida-pattern signature.

items.name: Choro
items.lineage: Brazilian instrumental urban-popular-music tradition originating 1870s-onward in Rio de Janeiro from European salon-dance (polka, schottische, waltz, mazurka) re-rhythmicized through Afro-Brazilian syncopation (especially habanera-derived). The canonical regional-choro ensemble: solo lead (flute, clarinet, or mandolin), seven-string guitar (violão-de-sete) providing baixaria walking-bass-line, six-string guitar accompanying-harmony, cavaquinho four-double-course soprano-guitar rhythmic-strum, and pandeiro frame-drum-with-jingles. The repertoire layers virtuosic compositional pieces (often modulating through multiple keys with rapid 16th-note arpeggios) with roda-de-choro participatory jam-session-tradition. Three historical phases: foundational late-19th-century, golden-age 1920s-1940s, and bossa-nova-and-modern-revival 1950s-onward.
items.description: Choro (1870s onward, originating in Rio de Janeiro through the fusion of European salon-dance forms with African-Brazilian rhythmic feel, with golden ages 1880-1930 and 1970s-onward revival), the Brazilian instrumental virtuoso form that prefigured samba and bossa nova. Defined by lead melodic instrument (flute, clarinet, bandolim, cavaquinho, or wind instrument) playing fast melodic lines over harmonic accompaniment from seven-string guitar (violão de sete cordas, the choro-instrument with a low-B string for bass-line walking), six-string guitar, and pandeiro tambourine. Repertoire built on rondo-form ABA-with-modulating-trio compositions in 2/4, with conversational call-and-response solo improvisation between players in the regional choro-circle. Distinguished from samba by absence of Carnival-procession context and instrumental-not-vocal foreground; distinguished from Brazilian classical by improvisational expansion of composed material; distinguished from American Dixieland by 7-string-guitar-and-bandolim instrumentation and Brazilian-rather-than-New-Orleans rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Afrobeat
items.lineage: West African 1970s polyrhythmic horn-driven big-band genre fusing Yoruba highlife, jazz, and James Brown funk — codified by Fela Kuti at his Shrine club in Lagos with Tony Allen on drums (Afrika 70 and Egypt 80 ensembles), characterized by extended jam-form arrangements, political-protest lyrics, and the dense polyrhythmic interlock that became the genre signature
items.description: Afrobeat (1968-1979 Lagos, Nigeria), the funk-jazz-Yoruba hybrid that fused American James Brown rhythm-section vamping, post-bop horn voicings, traditional Yoruba rhythmic structures, and pidgin-English political polemic. Defined by extended one-chord vamps stretching past 15 minutes, a two-drummer rhythm section playing complementary patterns over conga and shekere, multi-horn arrangements with call-and-response between lead and section, electric-guitar palm-muted choke-strums on the upbeat, and a singer-bandleader delivering lyric verses over recurring choral hooks. Distinguished from highlife by anti-pop length and political register; distinguished from American funk by Yoruba rhythm foundation and horn-section weight; distinguished from Afro-Cuban by Lagos-not-Havana lineage and lack of clave.

items.name: Ska and rocksteady
items.lineage: Jamaican ska (1959-1965, fast-tempo guitar-upbeat horn-section-foregrounded dance music) and its slower-tempo derivation rocksteady (1965-1968) — codified at Studio One, Treasure Isle, and Federal through the Skatalites (Tommy McCook, Don Drummond, Roland Alphonso, Lloyd Knibb, the ska house band), Prince Buster, Toots and the Maytals, the Wailers (early-period), Alton Ellis (Get Ready Rocksteady), Ken Boothe, the Heptones; preceded reggae and remains foundational to the broader Jamaican popular music lineage
items.description: Ska and rocksteady (codified 1962-1968 Jamaica, with ska-era 1962-1965 establishing the up-tempo upbeat-emphasis sound through Studio One and Treasure Isle productions, transitioning into rocksteady 1966-1968 with slower tempo and harmony-vocal foreground), the pre-reggae Jamaican music tradition. Defined by uptempo upbeat-emphasis (the ska-chop-strum on beats 2 and 4 with kick-and-snare-foreground groove producing the genre's signature feel), horn sections (saxophone, trumpet, trombone) playing call-and-response with the rhythm-section, R&B-derived harmony and song-form structures (American R&B records were the immediate source material for early Jamaican producers), tempos around 130-140 BPM in ska-era, slowing to 90-100 BPM in rocksteady-era, and lyric content addressing Jamaican social-and-political subjects. Distinguished from later reggae by faster tempo and absence of one-drop drumming; distinguished from American R&B (its source) by Jamaican-rhythmic-displacement and Kingston-production-context; distinguished from later 2-tone ska revival by pre-1970 Jamaican origin.

items.name: Tuvan throat singing (khoomei)
items.lineage: Tuvan Republic (Russian-Federation Southern-Siberia, ethnically and linguistically Turkic-Mongolic) throat-singing tradition with five canonical styles — khöömei middle-register-resonance, sygyt high-isolated-whistle-overtone, kargyraa low-deep-undertone-style, borbangnadyr rolling-modulated-overtone, ezenggileer rhythmic-broken-overtone (horse-riding-mimetic). Distinct from the parallel Mongolian khoomei lineage despite the shared ethnographic-Turkic-Mongolic heritage; Tuvan technique tends toward higher-pitched sygyt isolation versus Mongolian deeper kharkhiraa. Embedded in nomadic herder-pastoralist work-song repertoire and in shamanic-trance ritual practice. The 1990s-onward post-Soviet international-touring exposure (initial European-and-American world-music-circuit) catalyzed contemporary-revival and academic-research interest.
items.description: Tuvan throat-singing / khoomei tradition (continuous tradition centuries-onward across Tuva (Russian Federation autonomous republic), Mongolia, and adjacent Inner-Mongolian-Chinese steppe pastoralist regions, with Soviet-era folkloric documentation and post-1990s international visibility through ensembles like Huun-Huur-Tu and Tuva Ensemble), the Tuvan/Mongolian overtone-singing tradition. Defined by single-voice production of fundamental-and-harmonic simultaneously (the throat-singing-technique where one vocalist produces a low fundamental tone and a clear-pitched overtone simultaneously, the overtone selected and varied across the harmonic series to produce melody above the drone), regional sub-styles (khoomei mid-throat baseline-style; sygyt high-whistle-overtone-foreground; kargyraa subbass-growl deep-fundamental-foreground; borbangnadyr rolling vocal-trill style; ezenggileer rhythmic-modulation cycle-style), morin khuur horsehead-fiddle and igil two-string spike-fiddle accompaniment, repertoire addressing pastoral-and-spiritual subjects, and ceremonial-and-festival performance contexts at naadam festivals and family gatherings. Distinguished from Mongolian long-song by overtone-foundation rather than melismatic-vocal-foundation; distinguished from Inuit throat-singing (katajjaq) by individual-not-paired performance and Mongolian-Tuvan source.

items.name: Sardinian polyphony (cantu a tenore)
items.lineage: Sardinian a cappella four-voice polyphonic tradition — cantu a tenore (male four-voice with bassu, contra, mesa voche, and boche solo lead) and cantu a chiterra (vocal-with-guitar shepherd song), preserved through the village traditions of Bitti, Nuoro, and Logudoro, with the Tenores di Bitti Mialinu Pira ensemble as the canonical late-twentieth-century preservation lineage
items.description: Sardinian male-quartet polyphony / cantu a tenore (codified pre-Christian onward through Sardinian shepherd-and-rural-community vocal tradition, with continuous tradition through to present), the Sardinian male-quartet polyphonic singing tradition. Defined by four-male-voice quartet performance with assigned vocal roles (boche — lead solo voice carrying the melodic-and-textual material; mesu boche — second voice supporting the lead; bassu — guttural-bass voice producing the characteristic deep-throat-rasp foundation; contra — guttural-counter-voice harmonizing with bassu), characteristic guttural-throat-resonance vocal aesthetic in bassu and contra parts (the cantu-a-tenore-distinct deep-throat technique), repertoire of traditional Sardinian poetic texts addressing rural-shepherd life, religious themes, and historical-narrative material, and unaccompanied vocal performance in informal community gatherings, religious processions, and folkloric-festival circuits. Distinguished from Corsican polyphonic singing by Sardinian-specific guttural-bass-and-contra technique; distinguished from other Mediterranean polyphonic traditions by unique four-voice-with-guttural-pair configuration; distinguished from later Sardinian folk-revival ensembles by traditional-unaccompanied form.

items.name: Mbalax
items.lineage: Senegalese popular-music genre codified by Youssou NDour from 1979 onward — Wolof-language vocal foreground over Senegalese sabar polyrhythmic drum-battery foundation extended with electric guitar, electric bass, keyboards, and saxophone; figures Youssou NDours Super Étoile de Dakar band (Set 1990), Baaba Maal, Thione Seck, Omar Pene, Ismael Lo, Cheikh Lo
items.description: Mbalax (codified 1970s onward in Senegal and Gambia through Youssou N'Dour, Étoile de Dakar, and Orchestra Baobab establishing the modern Senegambian dance genre), the Senegambian dance music genre. Defined by sabar drum ensemble at the percussive core (multiple goblet-and-cylindrical sabar drums of different pitches playing interlocking polyrhythmic patterns), griot-derived ornamented vocal performance with extended melismatic decoration, multiple electric guitars (often 2-3) playing interlocking riffs in conversational call-and-response, electric bass providing low-end foundation, optional brass-section horn arrangements, and Wolof-and-French language vocal lyrics addressing romantic-and-social-commentary subjects. Distinguished from straight Senegambian griot acoustic music by electric-band instrumentation and dance-music orientation; distinguished from soukous by Senegambian-not-Congolese lineage and sabar-percussion-foreground; distinguished from West African mande tradition by Wolof-not-Mandinka linguistic-and-cultural framing.

items.name: Jùjú
items.lineage: Yoruba Nigerian popular music genre codified through Tunde King (1930s palm-wine-derived early juju), Ayinde Bakare (1940s commercial founder), IK Dairo (1960s-1970s Decca West African phase), and King Sunny Adé (1976-onward international breakthrough through Island Records and the 1982 album Juju Music) — built on Yoruba dundun talking-drum battery, electric-guitar interlocking patterns, and Yoruba-language praise-singing for celebrations
items.description: Juju (codified 1930s-1940s Lagos through Tunde King's pioneering recordings, with golden era 1960s-1980s through King Sunny Adé and Ebenezer Obey lineage), the Yoruba popular dance music genre. Defined by talking drum (gangan/dundun) and bata percussion lineage at the rhythmic core, multiple electric guitars (often 3-5 in larger juju ensembles) playing in conversational interlocking-melodic-line texture (each guitarist plays a distinct rhythmic-melodic part, all of which lock together as a composite groove), pedal-steel guitar (King Sunny Adé's distinctive innovation), Hawaiian-derived bottleneck-slide work, and Yoruba-language vocal lyrics addressing praise-singing, social commentary, and Christian-or-syncretic religious themes. Performance contexts: Yoruba weddings, parties, and concert tours. Distinguished from fuji (the parallel Yoruba Muslim percussion-vocal tradition) by Christian-or-secular framing and electric-guitar foreground; distinguished from highlife by Yoruba-not-Akan lineage and talking-drum centrality; distinguished from afrobeat by song-form-and-dance-music orientation over extended-vamp political-polemic.

items.name: Fújì
items.lineage: Yoruba-Nigerian Muslim popular music genre codified through Sikiru Ayinde Barrister (1965-onward founder), Ayinde Kollington (Wasiu Ayinde Marshal Kollington Ayinla, then KWAM-1 / King Wasiu Ayinde Marshal), Pasuma Wonder, Saheed Osupa — derived from the Yoruba Muslim were tradition (pre-dawn Ramadan religious-rousing songs) extended into secular celebration music, with the dundun talking-drum battery expanded to 6-8 drummers and percussion-only acoustic instrumentation (no electric instruments)
items.description: Fuji (codified late-1960s through early-1970s in Lagos and Yoruba southwest Nigeria by Ayinde Barrister and Kollington Ayinla as a Yoruba Muslim alternative to apala and were music), the Yoruba Muslim percussion-vocal tradition. Defined by the talking drum (gangan or dundun pressure-drum producing the Yoruba-language tonal-mimicking sound) and bata two-headed drum at the core of dense polyrhythmic percussion ensemble, sakara frame-drum and shekere gourd-rattle providing additional layers, lead vocal performance by the singer-bandleader (the fuji bandleader is the genre-central role) delivering Yoruba-language verses on praise-singing, social commentary, and Islamic moral-themes, call-and-response with chorus, and electric guitar and accordion sometimes adopted for modernized fuji. Performance contexts: Yoruba Muslim wedding, naming-ceremony, and social-occasion. Distinguished from juju music (the parallel Yoruba Christian/secular tradition) by Islamic-religious framing and percussion-foreground over guitar-foreground; distinguished from apala (its predecessor) by post-1965 timestamp and modernized instrumentation.

items.name: Hiplife
items.lineage: Ghanaian hip-hop-highlife fusion codified through Reggie Rockstone Asante (the New York-Ghana cross-Atlantic founder, 1994 album Makaa Maka), Obrafour, VIP, Tic Tac, Sarkodie (the modern hiplife-into-Afrobeats crossover bridge), then extended into the contemporary Ghanaian hiplife / azonto / Afrobeats hybrid
items.description: Hiplife (codified 1994 onward in Accra Ghana through Reggie Rockstone's pioneering Ghanaian-language hip-hop recordings, with successor waves through the 2000s), the Ghanaian fusion of highlife with hip-hop. Defined by programmed beats drawing on hip-hop production conventions (sample-based or drum-machine-programmed) but retaining traditional highlife rhythmic feel (the highlife two-bar offbeat-emphasis pattern integrated into hip-hop programming), Akan-Twi-and-English code-switching MC vocal verses, melodic-sung hook chorus sections often by guest singers, and instrumentation including programmed kick-and-snare, optional live percussion (congas, shaker), and synth-pad and bass programming. Tempos around 100-120 BPM. Distinguished from straight Ghanaian hip-hop by retention of highlife rhythmic and melodic conventions; distinguished from highlife by hip-hop-MC vocal foreground over horn-section call-and-response; distinguished from later afrobeats (Nigerian, distinct genre) by Ghanaian-not-Nigerian centrality and direct highlife-derivation.

items.name: Afrobeats (Naija)
items.lineage: Nigerian (with Ghanaian and broader West African parallel development) urban popular music genre that emerged in the 2000s and went global from 2017 onward through Burna Boy (Pan-African genre-fusion), Wizkid (the Drake collaboration Come Closer 2017, then the 2020 album Made in Lagos), Davido, Tems, Tiwa Savage, Rema, Asake — distinguished from Fela Kutis original 1970s Afrobeat by 30-40 BPM faster tempo, digital production foundation, hip-hop-influenced song structure, and broader pop-radio commercial register
items.description: Modern Nigerian/Ghanaian popular music; mid-tempo programmed beats with West African rhythmic DNA, melodic Afro-pop singing in Pidgin and English. Distinct from 1970s Lagos Afrobeat (singular, with no s).

items.name: Makossa
items.lineage: Cameroonian (Douala / Bantu coastal) popular music genre codified by Manu Dibango from 1972 onward (Soul Makossa, the international breakthrough that established the genre name in the global pop vocabulary) — built on a fusion of Douala traditional drumming, jazz horn-section vocabulary, and Cameroonian Catholic-mission church music; tracked extensively at Paris Pathé-Marconi studios for European distribution and recurring back to Yaoundé and Douala studios
items.description: Makossa (codified 1972 onward in Cameroon, with Manu Dibango's Soul Makossa as the international-breakthrough crystallizing record and continuing Cameroonian pop tradition through to present), the Cameroonian dance music genre. Defined by prominent bass-guitar walking lines (the makossa bassline being the genre's rhythmic-and-melodic signature, with strong syncopated bass-pattern phrases driving the song forward), brass-section punctuation (saxophone, trumpet, trombone) playing horn-stabs over the rhythm, electric-guitar lead and rhythm parts, sung lyrics in Duala (Sawa-language coastal Cameroon) and French, congas and percussion adding layered rhythmic feel, and tempos around 110-130 BPM with characteristic offbeat-emphasis groove. Distinguished from soukous by Cameroonian-not-Congolese lineage and bass-line-foreground over guitar-line-foreground; distinguished from highlife by Cameroonian-coastal-not-Ghanaian lineage and characteristic bass-line; distinguished from Afrobeat by song-form pop-tempo over extended-vamp.

items.name: Soukous
items.lineage: Congolese fast-tempo dance derivation of Congolese rumba, codified through Tabu Ley Rochereau, Sam Mangwana, Papa Wemba (Viva la Musica band), Pepe Kalle, Kanda Bongo Man (the mid-1980s Paris-recorded breakthrough), Diblo Dibala — characterized by the structural chanson-then-sebene form with sebene section accelerated to 130-180 BPM and the mi-solo / mi-composé interlocking-guitar foreground
items.description: Soukous (codified 1960s onward Kinshasa Democratic Republic of the Congo, descending from Congolese-rumba lineage and crystallizing through Franco's TPOK Jazz and Tabu Ley Rochereau's African Fiesta as foundational figures), the Congolese rumba descendant. Defined by two-and-three-guitar interlocking sebene patterns (the soukous-specific multi-guitar texture where 2-3 electric guitars play distinct rhythmic-melodic parts that lock together as a composite groove, with the sebene the up-tempo dance-break section becoming the genre's structural focus), subtle percussion rather than aggressive-drumming (Congolese soukous percussion stays in supporting rhythmic foundation rather than foregrounded), French-and-Lingala vocal performance often by lead-vocalist with chorus call-and-response, electric-bass providing low-end foundation, and tempos around 110-140 BPM with characteristic offbeat-emphasis groove. Distinguished from later ndombolo by intensified-sebene-foreground and post-1995 timestamp; distinguished from earlier Congolese rumba by faster tempo and electric-band instrumentation; distinguished from West African mande tradition by Congolese-not-Mande lineage.

items.name: Congolese rumba
items.lineage: 1940s-1960s Congolese-Kinshasa-and-Brazzaville Cuban-rumba-influenced urban dance music — codified through Joseph Kabasele (Grand Kallé) and African Jazz (Indépendance Cha-Cha 1960, the de facto anthem of Congolese independence) and Luambo Makiadi (Franco) and OK Jazz; built on the GV series Cuban son 78 records that came to the Congo through Belgian colonial trade in the 1930s-40s, then reinterpreted through Congolese guitar-and-voice ensembles into a distinct genre
items.description: Congolese rumba (codified mid-1940s through 1960s in Léopoldville-Kinshasa and Brazzaville urban dance-bar circuits, with Joseph Kabasele's African Jazz and Franco Luambo's OK Jazz as foundational ensembles, and the genre crystallizing through 1948-onward 78rpm and later vinyl recordings on Loningisa, Esengo, Surboum African-Jazz, and Pathé-Marconi labels), the urban Congolese popular-music tradition that descends from Cuban son and rumba records arriving via Belgian and French shipping routes (the GV-series of 78rpm Cuban discs sold in Léopoldville from the 1930s onward) crossbred with local Lingala-and-French-language song tradition. Defined by clean electric-guitar-foreground arrangement organized around the mi-solo (mid-range melodic guitar) and sebene (rhythmic-lead guitar) interplay (this two-guitar interlocking foundation predates and seeds the later soukous tradition), call-and-response Lingala-and-French vocal practice with lead-singer-and-chorus arrangement, light Latin-derived percussion (maracas, hand-claves, occasional congas), upright-bass moving to electric-bass through the era, accordion appearing on early-1950s recordings before fading, and dance-tempo 4/4 cyclic-vamp rhythmic foundation (the Cuban 3-2 clave often retained as underlying rhythmic structure though not always foregrounded). Distinguished from Cuban-rumba antecedent by Lingala-and-French vocal language, African-tonal-vocabulary integration, and electric-band-not-acoustic instrumentation; distinguished from later soukous descendant by slower tempos, less-foregrounded sebene-section emphasis, and pre-1965 timestamp; distinguished from highlife by Congolese-Cuban-rumba lineage versus Ghanaian-palm-wine-guitar lineage. Lineage forward feeds soukous (the same musicians and ensembles literally evolved the form), ndombolo, and the broader African-pop electric-guitar tradition extending through Tabu Ley Rochereau, Papa Wemba, Koffi Olomide, and current Congolese-pop artists.
exemplars: Joseph Le Grand Kallé Kabasele and African Jazz
Franco Luambo Makiadi and OK Jazz

items.name: Ndombolo
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward Congolese fast-tempo dance derivation of soukous codified through Wenge Musica Maison Mère (the breakthrough), JB Mpiana, Werrason, Koffi Olomide, Awilo Longomba — characterized by accelerated tempo (180+ BPM in the sebene section), heavy-percussion-foregrounded mix, and the namesake ndombolo hip-shaking dance form
items.description: Ndombolo (codified 1995 onward in Kinshasa Democratic Republic of the Congo as an up-tempo dance descendant of soukous, with international diffusion through 2000s Pan-African pop circuits), the up-tempo Congolese dance music subgenre. Defined by intensified sebene section as the structural focus (the sebene is the up-tempo instrumental dance-break section originally a feature of soukous song-form, in ndombolo it becomes the genre's primary aesthetic event), multiple electric guitars in interlocking-melodic-line conversation (typical 2-3 guitars playing distinct rhythmic-melodic parts that lock together as composite groove), electric bass providing low-end foundation, drum kit and congas providing rhythmic foundation, vocal performance often by lead-vocalist with chorus call-and-response, and characteristic high-tempo around 130-150 BPM. Distinguished from straight soukous by post-1995 timestamp and intensified-sebene-foreground; distinguished from earlier Congolese rumba by faster tempo and dance-floor-functional sebene structure; distinguished from West African ndombolo-influenced pop by Kinshasa-Congolese centrality.

items.name: Taarab
items.lineage: East African Swahili-coast genre (Zanzibar, coastal Tanzania, coastal Kenya, Comoros) fusing Arab maqam-system melody, Indian classical raga vocabulary, and Bantu-Swahili language poetry into large-ensemble wedding-and-celebration music; codified through Siti binti Saad (1928 HMV-Bombay first commercial recordings, the mother of taarab), Bi Kidude (1910-2013, Zanzibars longest-living taarab matriarch), the Culture Musical Club (founded 1958), and Black Star Musical Club
items.description: Taarab (codified 19th century onward in Zanzibar coastal Swahili-Arab cultural-mixing zones, with continuous tradition through to present and parallel Mombasa, Comoros, and broader East-African-coast lineages), the Swahili-coast tradition fusing Arab maqam ornamentation, Indian melody, and African coastal feel. Defined by oud and qanun (Arab-classical adopted instruments) providing melodic-instrumental foundation, frame-drum and dumbek percussion supplying rhythmic foundation, accordion and violin sometimes adopted for modernized taarab, lead-vocal performance with characteristic Swahili-Arab-melismatic ornamentation, repertoire of poetic-vocal songs in Swahili-language addressing romantic-melancholy and social-commentary subjects, and performance contexts spanning intimate gathering, wedding-celebration, and concert-stage. Distinguished from straight Arab classical by Swahili-language and Indian-Ocean coastal-cultural framing; distinguished from broader East African popular music by Arab-classical-derived instrumental and ornamental vocabulary; distinguished from later Tanzanian popular music by retention of taarab-traditional ensemble and repertoire focus.

items.name: Chimurenga
items.lineage: Zimbabwean liberation-struggle music genre codified by Thomas Mapfumo from 1973 onward (chimurenga is the Shona word for struggle, used to refer to the Second Chimurenga liberation war 1966-1979 against Rhodesian white minority rule); built on translating Shona mbira interlocking-cycle repertoire (kushaura and kutsinhira patterns from the religious mbira dzavadzimu tradition) into the electric-band context with electric guitars playing the mbira parts
items.description: Chimurenga (1973 onward, codified through Thomas Mapfumo and Blacks Unlimited's groundbreaking electric-mbira recordings during the late-Rhodesian liberation war), the Zimbabwean popular music form translating Shona mbira polyrhythm and modal phrasing onto electric guitar. Defined by interlocking electric-guitar lines that mimic the two-mbira interlocking patterns of traditional Shona dande and matepe music (the kushaura lead-pattern interlocking with the kutsinhira response), electric bass replacing the deep mbira manacles' bass register, drum kit replacing hosho gourd-rattle pulse, Shona-language vocal lyrics frequently coded protest content during the war and post-independence political commentary thereafter, and tempos around 110-130 BPM with characteristic 12/8 cyclical metric organization. Distinguished from traditional acoustic mbira music by electric-band instrumentation and pop-song format; distinguished from South African mbaqanga by Zimbabwean-not-South-African political-cultural context and mbira-derived rather than marabi-derived melodic vocabulary; distinguished from sungura by political-protest focus and chimurenga-as-name-as-stance.

items.name: Kwaito
items.lineage: South African post-apartheid (1994-onward) township urban dance music codified through Boom Shaka, Brenda Fassie (her late-career kwaito turn), Trompies, M_du Masilela, Arthur Mafokate, TKZee — slower-tempo (90-110 BPM) derivation of house music with Zulu and Tsotsitaal language vocals and characteristic shouted-and-rapped delivery; precursor to the post-2010 amapiano genre
items.description: Kwaito (codified 1990 onward in post-apartheid Soweto and Johannesburg through Arthur Mafokate, Boom Shaka, and TKZee establishing the genre, with golden era 1994-2002), the South African post-apartheid mid-tempo electronic dance genre. Defined by slowed house-tempo beats around 100-110 BPM (markedly slower than international house's 120-130), chanted-and-rapped township-vocals in Zulu-Xhosa-Sotho-Tswana code-switching with English, programmed kick-and-snare with prominent off-beat percussion, sample-based or repurposed-house-track foundations, and lyric content addressing post-apartheid township life, romantic-relationships, and youth-culture references. Distinguished from house by tempo and township-vocal foreground; distinguished from later amapiano by pre-2010 timestamp and absence of log-drum sub-bass; distinguished from gqom by retention of melodic-vocal centrality and slower tempo.

items.name: Gqom
items.lineage: South African Durban-Zulu late-2000s minimal-bass dance subgenre, codified through Naked Boys, DJ Lag, Citizen Boy, and Rudeboyz starting circa 2010 — characterized by repetitive 4/4 sub-bass-driven drum patterns at 120-130 BPM, sparse hi-hats, vocal chants in isiZulu, and the deliberately dark / minimal aesthetic distinguishing it from house and amapiano
items.description: Gqom (2010 onward, codified through Durban township producers DJ Lag, Citizen Boy, and the Goon Squad collective), the Durban warehouse-and-taxi-rank electronic dance music genre. Defined by tempos around 120-130 BPM, broken-and-syncopated drum patterns where kick-and-snare placement avoids four-on-floor regularity (the broken nature giving the genre its signature angular feel), minimal harmonic content (often single-note or two-note bass lines with sparse melodic decoration), prominent sub-bass pressure designed for taxi-rank speaker-system playback, vocal samples and chants in Zulu and Xhosa code-switching, and a distribution ecosystem through WhatsApp and Bluetooth sharing rather than traditional commercial release. Distinguished from amapiano by tempo and aggressive-rather-than-laid-back posture; distinguished from kwaito by post-2010 timestamp and absence of melodic-vocal-foreground; distinguished from house by broken-rather-than-four-on-floor rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Amapiano
items.lineage: South African Pretoria-Johannesburg late-2010s house-jazz hybrid characterized by deep log-drum sub-bass figures, jazzy keys, and slowed 110-115 BPM tempo — codified through Kabza De Small, DJ Maphorisa, Mas Musiq, MFR Souls, and Vigro Deep from 2017 onward, exploding internationally 2020-2023
items.description: Amapiano (2012 Pretoria-Soweto onward), the South African house descendant that fused Johannesburg deep-house piano stabs, kwaito’s mid-tempo groove, and a distinctive sub-bass log-drum (the marimba-like patch synthesized on FL Studio that became the genre’s signature element). Defined by 110-115 BPM tempos, jazz-house Rhodes and piano vamps over four-on-floor kicks, vocal hooks delivered in Zulu/Xhosa/English code-switching, the percussive log-drum bass pattern that drives the groove instead of a synth bass, and a strong DJ-edit/blend culture distributed via streaming and WhatsApp. Distinguished from gqom by mid-tempo polish over gqom’s 130-BPM aggression; distinguished from kwaito by greater piano-jazz harmonic ambition and post-2015 timestamp; distinguished from deep house by the log-drum and African-language vocals.

items.name: Maskandi
items.lineage: Zulu South African male-vocal-and-guitar tradition that emerged in the mid-20th century from rural KwaZulu-Natal migrant-labour culture — characterized by the izibongo praise-poetry vocal opening, the maskandi guitar style with characteristic open-chord strumming and finger-picking patterns, and Zulu-language lyrical content addressing rural-urban migration, romantic longing, and traditional social commentary; figures Phuzekhemisi, Ihhashi Elimhlophe, Bhekumuzi Luthuli, Mfaz Omnyama
items.description: Maskandi (codified 1930s-1950s onward in KwaZulu-Natal South Africa as Zulu rural-urban migrant-laborer music, with continuous tradition through to present), the Zulu picking-guitar tradition. Defined by izibongo praise-poetry vocal performance (the traditional Zulu praise-poetic-narrative-recitation form translated into musical context), picked-acoustic-or-electric-guitar accompaniment in Zulu-traditional fingerpicking style with characteristic rolling-arpeggiated patterns, optional concertina or accordion lead voice, electric-bass and percussion in modernized maskandi, vocal lyrics in Zulu addressing migrant-laborer subjects, social commentary, and praise-narrative content, and performance contexts spanning rural-and-urban Zulu communities and South African modern-traditional festival circuits. Distinguished from mbube and isicathamiya (the parallel Zulu a-cappella choral traditions) by guitar-instrumental foreground; distinguished from later mbaqanga by retention of solo-guitar-and-vocal format; distinguished from straight Zulu traditional music by guitar-modernization and izibongo-praise-poetry foregrounding.

items.name: Isicathamiya
items.lineage: 1920s-onward Zulu South African male a-cappella vocal-group tradition (the name derives from the Zulu word cathama, to tread softly) that developed among Zulu migrant labourers in the Johannesburg mining hostels — codified through Solomon Linda Mbube 1939 recording (the recording that became The Lion Sleeps Tonight after a tortured rights-acquisition history), Ladysmith Black Mambazo (founded 1960 by Joseph Shabalala, the internationally famous group through their Paul Simon Graceland 1986 collaboration), and the broader Friday-night isicathamiya competition circuit in Johannesburg
items.description: Isicathamiya (codified 1920s-onward in KwaZulu-Natal and Witwatersrand-Johannesburg South African mining-hostel weekend competition circuit, with Solomon Linda's 1939 Mbube Gallo Studios recording of the song that became The Lion Sleeps Tonight establishing the "mbube" subgenre name and the broader genre crystallizing through 1940s-1960s competition tradition; later international codification through Ladysmith Black Mambazo founded 1964 and Paul-Simon-collaboration 1986 Graceland-album breakthrough), the Zulu South African a-cappella male-vocal-group tradition. Defined by tightly-choreographed close-harmony eight-to-fifteen-voice male ensemble with bass-led foundation (the low-bass voice carrying the harmonic and rhythmic foundation while upper voices provide tightly-arranged harmonic counterpoint), call-and-response leader-and-chorus vocal arrangement (the leader presents melodic line; chorus answers with harmonic response), unaccompanied a-cappella performance practice (no instrumental accompaniment in the form, though some modern recordings add piano or light percussion), choreographed footwork and gestures performed in synchronized ensemble (the "isicathamiya" name etymology suggests "tip-toe" — the dance practice of moving softly to avoid disturbing mining-hostel sleeping-quarters), repertoire combining Christian-Zulu-language sacred material with secular-Zulu courtship-and-praise themes, and competition-tradition performance context (groups compete at all-night Saturday-night-into-Sunday-morning mining-hostel and community-hall events for cash prizes and social recognition). Cultural origin in Zulu rural-traditional choral practice (amahubo war-songs, izibongo praise-poetry, ingoma dance-songs) translated into urban-mining-hostel context where Zulu migrant laborers preserved cultural identity through weekend musical competition. Distinguished from preceding rural Zulu choral tradition by tighter ensemble-choreography and competition-format performance practice; distinguished from contemporary maskandi by a-cappella-not-guitar instrumentation; distinguished from later mbaqanga by absence of instrumental backing and pre-electric era foundation. Lineage forward feeds Ladysmith Black Mambazo international gospel-and-pop crossover, the 1986 Paul Simon Graceland-album collaboration that brought the genre to global attention, and the broader Zulu a-cappella tradition continuing into present-day township and competition contexts.
exemplars: Solomon Linda — Mbube (1939, the original recording of the song that became "The Lion Sleeps Tonight")

items.name: Gnawa
items.lineage: Moroccan Sufi-trance ceremonial tradition with West-African Bambara-Soussi-Hausa-Songhai lineage tracing to sub-Saharan enslaved peoples brought to Morocco — codified through the lila ceremony with master-musician maâlem leading sintir-bass-lute and qarqaba-iron-castanets ensemble; canonical lineage through Mahmoud Guinia (Marrakech), Mustapha Baqbou, and the Essaouira Gnaoua festival (founded 1998) as the genre’s international showcase
items.description: Gnawa (transmitted from West African Bambara, Soussi, Hausa, and Songhai sub-Saharan traditions via the trans-Saharan slave trade into Morocco from the 16th-19th centuries, with three discrete production contexts the codex must keep separated: ethnographic mono field recordings on portable Ampex 601 to quarter-inch tape from the 1950s-1990s including Paul Bowles's 1959 Library of Congress / Rockefeller Foundation expedition and Philip Schuyler's UCLA-based recordings; festival-multitrack mobile recordings from Festival Gnaoua Essaouira post-1998; and the Axiom-school canon — Bill Laswell with Richard Horowitz and engineer Billy Youdelman recording Gnawa Music of Marrakesh: Night Spirit Masters in 1990 in the Marrakesh medina, then Laswell with Pharoah Sanders and Maleem Mahmoud Ghania recording The Trance of Seven Colors in 1994 in Essaouira), the Moroccan Sufi trance-ceremonial tradition of West African slave descendants. Defined by sintir / guembri / hajhouj three-string bass-lute played by the maâlem (master) — camel-skin soundboard, goat-gut or heavy-monofilament-nylon strings, drone+octave+fourth tuning (D-D-G or C-C-F), galvanized-metal sersara buzzer with hanging rings as a NON-OPTIONAL element of the instrument's identity — qarqaba large iron castanets played in the Gnawa closed-clang style (cymbals held shut between hits, NOT the Tunisian open-ring) by 6-20 chorus players, tbel double-headed processional drum used in the outdoor aâda introductory procession, lead-vocal-and-responsorial-chorus pattern in Moroccan Darija Arabic with preserved Bambara/Soussi/Hausa/Songhai loanwords from West African ancestors, repertoire organized around the seven mlouk suite progression (white Bouhala, black Sidi Mimoun, blue Moussa-Bahriya, red Hamadcha, yellow Lalla Mira, green Moulay Abdelqader, multi Aisha Qandisha) with each color carrying specific scalar/rhythmic identity and trance function, all-night lila ceremony tempo-acceleration arc from 80-110 BPM opening to 140+ BPM trance peak in 12/8 polyrhythm (sintir slow 3+3 against qraqeb fast 6 or 12), and stone-and-plaster medina-room natural-slapback acoustic. CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION: Gnawa is NOT Jajouka. The Master Musicians of Jajouka featuring Bachir Attar — recorded by Bill Laswell on Akai A-DAM 12-track digital tape at Jajouka village November 8-10 1991, mixed at The Hit Factory NYC, mastered by Howie Weinberg — is the Jbala Sufi-trance tradition, a fundamentally-different ensemble despite shared Moroccan-Sufi-trance category — distinct instruments and ritual practice from gnawa proper. Distinguished from Sufi qawwali by sub-Saharan-not-Arab-classical foundation; distinguished from West African source traditions by Moroccan-Maghrebi context.
exemplars: Maleem Mahmoud Ghania with Pharoah Sanders — The Trance of Seven Colors (Axiom 1994)

items.name: Rapso
items.lineage: Trinidadian chantwell spoken-word over soca-derived rhythm bed — codified through Brother Resistance (Lutalo Masimba) and the Network Riddum Band starting late 1970s, then Brother Marvin and the broader 3 Canal collective bringing rapso into Trinidad’s carnival mainstream; characterized by oratorical-political rapso-flow delivery over Caribbean percussion-and-electronic-instrument production
items.description: Rapso (1979-onward Port of Spain, codified through Brother Resistance / Lutalo Masimba and Brother Shortman / Everard Romany founding the Network Riddum Band in 1979; Port of Spain tracking 1979-1985 at studios including Sea-Sand, KH Studios under Kenny Phillips, and Semp Studios; Network Riddum Band rehearsal space and offices destroyed by police June 1983; 1986 onward continued at the Brent Black Music Co-Op in Harlesden NW London with Rapso Take Over album, Brother Resistance opening the Uprising Culture House on All Saints Road in Notting Hill; early-1990s Caribbean-UK-hybrid era with co-producer Martin "Mice" Raymond and the 1991 Touch De Earth Wid Rapso transition to dancehall-and-synth production; sound engineer Robin Foster at Network Riddum Band, fellow Queen's Royal College alumnus of Brother Resistance), the Trinidadian chantwell spoken-word tradition over soca-derived rhythm bed. Defined by chantwell-spoken-word baritone delivery rooted in Trinidadian griot tradition (NOT American hip-hop flow despite the "rap" surface), Trinidadian English with Creole interjections and African-derived percussive consonants, soca-derived drum kit at rapso-distinctive 95-115 BPM (the tempo separator from soca at 130+ and dancehall at 70-85), low-mid-emphasis electric bass NOT dancehall-sub locking with kick, Trinidadian iron engine-room percussion (struck brake-drum or iron pipe on every quarter or every eighth) distinct from Cuban cowbell and Brazilian agogô, occasional Indo-Trinidadian tassa drum on pan-African/pan-Caribbean material, double-tenor or guitar steel pan in accompaniment role (rarely lead tenor solo), Stratocaster-style single-coil clean rhythm guitar on offbeats with reggae-influenced skank at faster pulse, soca-derived brass section stab figures, 1980s synth palette (Yamaha DX7 FM soca-bell, Roland Juno-60/106 pads, Korg M1 post-1988, Casio CZ-series as Trinidad-accessible option), politically-pointed call-and-response chorus, dub-influenced tape echo (Roland Space Echo RE-201 / Echoplex) on vocals on a subset of tracks, predominantly major-key I-IV-V or I-V-vi-IV harmony, minor-key on protest material. Direct lineage: 1971 Lancelot Layne "Blow 'Way" → Cheryl Byron's calypso-tent dub poetry → Brother Resistance codification. CRITICAL DISAMBIGUATION: Rapso's Port-of-Spain context is NOT Brooklyn Bed-Stuy Charlie's Records / Rawlston Recording Studio (Rawlston Charles's Neve-mixer-equipped facility above his Brooklyn record store, with engineer Franklyn Grant, which recorded the Sparrow/Kitchener/Shadow/David Rudder/Charlie's Roots calypso-soca diaspora canon). Distinguished from calypso by slower tempo and simpler harmonic palette; distinguished from soca by 95-115 BPM vs 130+ and spoken-word vs sung; distinguished from dancehall by 95-115 BPM vs 70-85, soca-derived rhythm bed vs Jamaican-dancehall riddim, and absence of Jamaican-dancehall-DJ-flow.
exemplars: Brother Resistance — Roots of de Rapso Riddum
Brother Resistance — Touch De Earth Wid Rapso

items.name: Raï
items.lineage: Algerian popular-music genre that emerged in Oran in the 1970s as modernization of older raï bedoui (rural bedouin praise-poetry) — codified through the Cheb generation of the 1980s: Cheb Khaled (the king of raï, his 1992 Didi the international breakthrough), Cheb Mami, Cheb Hasni (assassinated 1994 during the Algerian civil war), Chaba Fadela, Cheb Hamid
items.description: Raï (codified 1920s onward in Oran Algeria as bedouin meddahat-foundation rural tradition, transformed in 1980s Oran into pop-raï through the cassette-tape-distribution scene and Cheb Khaled-and-Cheb Mami crystallizing era), the Algerian secular vocal tradition. Defined by bedouin meddahat melodic-and-modal roots (the original rural rai derived from sung-poetic meddahat tradition delivered by ould-meddah singer-poets at celebration gatherings), 1980s pop transformation introducing synthesizer-and-electric-band instrumentation (Casio synthesizers, electric guitar, electric bass, drum-machine programming) replacing traditional gallal-drum and gasba-flute ensemble, vocal performance often by male and female singers with characteristic melismatic-North-African ornamentation, lyric content addressing romantic-and-social-taboo subjects (drinking, romance outside marriage, secular-against-religious-conservative tension), and Arabic-and-French code-switching. Distinguished from Algerian classical chaabi by Oran-not-Algiers regional lineage and pop-rather-than-classical framing; distinguished from Moroccan chaabi by Algerian-specific industry; distinguished from later raï-rap and raï-fusion by 1980s pop-raï-specific era.

items.name: Andalusī nūba
items.lineage: Moroccan-Maghrebi Andalusi classical music tradition (al-ala / musique andalouse) descended from the 11-12th century cultural heritage of Muslim-ruled Iberian Andalusia, brought to North Africa with the post-1492 Iberian Muslim and Jewish expulsion and preserved in Fez, Tetouan, Tangier, Rabat — codified through 11 surviving nūba multi-section suites in the Moroccan corpus (sister lineages: Algerian gharnati, Tunisian malouf)
items.description: Andalusi nuba (codified ca. 9th century Córdoba, transmitted through Maghrebi conservatory schools 1492 onward in Fez, Tetouan, Tlemcen, Algiers, and Tunis), the multi-movement classical suite descended from medieval Al-Andalus court music. Each nuba is built on one of the eleven surviving ṭubūʿ (modal-melodic frameworks comparable to maqam but with distinct Maghrebi inflection), structured as a fixed sequence of five movements progressing from slow free-rhythm istikhbar through metric mizan sections at increasing tempos. Standard ensemble: ʻud, rabāb (bowed lute), kamanjah (violin held vertically), qanun, nay, darbuka, and a unison vocal chorus. Distinguished from Mashriqi (Egyptian/Levantine) takht ensemble by Maghrebi-Andalusi mode-system and codified-suite-not-tarab-improvisation form; distinguished from Sufi sama by court-classical context and absence of dhikr framing.

items.name: Tarab (Arab East classical)
items.lineage: Arab East (Egyptian, Levantine, Syrian, Iraqi) classical-vocal art-music tradition built on the takht ensemble (oud, qanun, ney, riq, kamancheh, with violin section added in the 20th-century Egyptian extension) accompanying a virtuoso vocal soloist performing elaborated maqam-system vocal-form on classical Arabic poetry; figures include Mohammed Abdel Wahab, Sayed Darwish, and the post-WWII era anchored by Umm Kulthum and Abdel Halim Hafez
items.description: Arab tarab (codified late-19th to mid-20th century in Cairo, Beirut, and Aleppo with roots in earlier Ottoman and Andalusi practice), the Arab classical aesthetic ideal centered on the singer-and-takht-ensemble interaction that produces deep emotional rapture (tarab — the affective state itself names the genre). Defined by the takht ensemble (oud, qanun, nay, riq, sometimes violin), maqam-based modal performance with extended improvised vocal ornamentation (mawwal, layali), stretch-form arrangements where a single song expands across forty-plus minutes through audience-call-and-response cycles, and the foregrounded singer-improvising-melodically-on-a-pre-composed-text relationship that defines Egyptian Golden Age tradition. Distinguished from later Arabic pop by length, instrumentation, and improvisation; distinguished from Andalusi nuba by Mashriqi maqam system and tarab affective focus over Maghrebi codified-suite form.

items.name: Persian dastgāh
items.lineage: Iranian classical-music tradition built on the radif (the repertoire body codified by the late-19th-century Mirza Abdollah and Aqa Hossein Qoli families) organized into 7 principal dastgāhs (Shur, Mahour, Homayoun, Segāh, Chahargāh, Rastpanjgāh, Nava) and 5 secondary avaz (subsidiary modal systems); 20th-century lineage: Ali-Naqi Vaziri, Ruhollah Khaleqi, Mohammad-Reza Shajarian (vocal), Hossein Alizadeh (tar), Kayhan Kalhor (kamancheh)
items.description: Persian dastgāh (codified 17th-19th century Iran with continuous tradition through to present, transmitted through master-disciple lineage and the radif memorized-repertoire pedagogy), the Persian classical music modal system. Defined by the seven dastgāh (Shur, Mahur, Homayun, Segah, Chahargah, Nava, Rast-Panjgah) and five āvāz (subordinate modes — Abu Ata, Bayat-e Tork, Afshari, Dashti, Bayat-e Esfahan), each containing characteristic gusheh (melodic-mode subsections) that performers traverse during performance, the radif (traditional repertory of fixed gusheh memorized by every classical musician) as raw material for improvisation rather than fixed-performance repertoire, instrumentation centered on tar and setar (long-neck plucked-lutes), santur (hammered dulcimer), kamancheh (spike-fiddle), ney (end-blown flute), and tombak (goblet-drum), and vocal-foreground performance with extensive tahrir (yodel-ornament) decoration. Distinguished from Arab maqam by Persian-specific dastgāh-and-radif system and characteristic tahrir vocal-ornament; distinguished from Hindustani classical by absence of taal-cycle metric foundation in non-metric sections; distinguished from Turkish makam by Persian linguistic-and-cultural framing.

items.name: Turkish makam (classical)
items.lineage: Ottoman-Turkish classical music tradition (Klasik Türk müziği) descended from the Ottoman court tradition and Mevlevi (Sufi whirling-dervish) ceremonial repertoire, organized through the makam modal system (~600 documented makams, ~150 in active use) and the usul (rhythmic-cycle) system; figures: Itri (1640-1712), Hammamizade İsmail Dede Efendi (1778-1846), and the modern recording-era voices Münir Nurettin Selçuk, Safiye Ayla, Zeki Müren
items.description: Turkish makam classical / Ottoman classical (codified Ottoman-era onward, with foundational theoretical writings by Ali Ufki and Dimitrie Cantemir 17th-18th century establishing the makam-and-usul system, and continuous tradition through Republican-Turkey-era reform and contemporary Turkish-classical practice), the Ottoman court classical music tradition. Defined by makam modal system (over 200 makamat — modal frameworks each with characteristic intervals, melodic phrases, and emotional-association — much more elaborate than Arab-maqam or Persian-dastgah), usul rhythmic cycles (specific time-cycle patterns ranging from short 2-beat to extended 28-beat structures), fasıl suite-form organizing performance around a single makam through fixed-form composition-categories (peshrev instrumental opening, beste vocal middle, sharki vocal aftermath, saz semaisi instrumental conclusion), takım classical-orchestra ensemble (ud, kanun, ney, kemençe, tanbur as instruments), and vocal-foreground performance with extensive melismatic-Turkish-vocal-ornament. Distinguished from Arab maqam by Turkish-specific elaborated mode-system and Turkish-language texts; distinguished from Persian dastgah by usul-rhythmic-cycle foundation and fasıl-suite-form structure; distinguished from later Turkish-classical-pop and Turkish-folk by court-classical-tradition framing.

items.name: Ghazal
items.lineage: Persian-Urdu (and Pashto, Bengali, Hindi) classical lyric-poetry vocal song-form built on the rhyming-couplet ghazal poetic structure originated in 7th-century Arabic poetry, refined in 13th-century Persian poetry (Rumi, Hafez), and developed into a vocal-musical canon through the Mughal-era courts; Indian subcontinental ghazal singers: Begum Akhtar, Mehdi Hassan, Ghulam Ali, Jagjit Singh, Farida Khanum
items.description: Ghazal (codified 7th century Persian classical poetry tradition, transmitted through Mughal India 13th-19th century into Hindustani classical and semi-classical performance, with continuing tradition in Pakistan and India), the lyric-poetic vocal tradition of Persian-Urdu literary culture. Defined by ghazal poetic structure (5-15 couplets with shared rhyme-and-refrain scheme — radif ending all couplets with the same word, qafia matching internal rhyme, all couplets independent in meaning), couplets on love-and-longing thematics (mystical-divine love often shading into earthly romantic love through deliberate ambiguity), sung melismatically over harmonium-and-tabla accompaniment in light-classical or filmi-derived settings, performance contexts spanning private mehfil (poetry-and-music gathering), public concert, and film soundtrack, and vocal delivery prioritizing sung-poetic-recitation expressiveness over operatic projection. Distinguished from Hindustani khayal classical by lyric-poetic-foreground over raga-elaboration-foreground; distinguished from qawwali by smaller ensemble (no chorus or party) and lyric-poetic-not-Sufi-devotional framing.

items.name: Dhrupad
items.lineage: The oldest surviving North Indian classical vocal genre, dating from the 12-13th centuries and preserved through the Dagar Bani (Dagar family lineage, the modern dhrupad school) and the Bishnupur and Talwandi sub-traditions; characterized by an extended alap (40+ minutes free-meter), the dhamar / chautal / sultal metric sections with pakhawaj accompaniment, and the use of rudra veena, surbahar, or sursingar as alternative melodic instruments to vocal
items.description: Dhrupad (codified 13th-15th century in Northern Indian temple and court traditions, with the four banis schools — Dagarvani, Khandarvani, Gauharvani, Nauhar — preserving the lineage through to present-day Banaras, Mathura, and family-disciple gharana transmission), the oldest extant Hindustani vocal genre. Defined by the four-section composition structure (sthāyī, antarā, sañcārī, ābhōga), extensive ālāp opening section using non-semantic vocal syllables (ri-ta-na-na-tom — the dhrupad-specific syllable sequence) to expose the raga before the composition begins, dhamar (14-beat) or chautal (12-beat) tala for the metric composition section, accompaniment from pakhawaj two-headed barrel-drum and tanpura drone-strings, all-male vocal performance often as duet of brothers or master-disciple pair, and a temple-and-court repertoire centered on devotional Krishna-and-Shiva-praise themes. Distinguished from later khayal by older origin, dhrupad-syllable ālāp, and pakhawaj-not-tabla accompaniment; distinguished from Carnatic by Hindustani lineage and dhamar-tala focus.

items.name: Thumrī
items.lineage: Hindustani semi-classical romantic vocal genre originating in mid-19th-century Lucknow under the patronage of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah, codified through the Banaras (Varanasi) and Lucknow gharana lineages — typically setting Brij Bhasha romantic poetry to elaborated raga performance, with the female-vocal lineage of Begum Akhtar, Gauhar Jaan, Siddheshwari Devi, Girija Devi (the 20th-century thumri-and-tappa voice from the Banaras gharana)
items.description: Thumri (codified 19th century onward in Lucknow Awadh-court tradition of North India, with successive lineages through Banaras, Punjab, and Patiala gharanas establishing regional schools of thumri practice, and continuous tradition through to present), the Hindustani semi-classical romantic vocal genre. Defined by freer raga-treatment than strict-classical khayal (the thumri-specific approach of treating raga as flexible-emotional-foundation rather than strict-melodic-grammar, allowing modulation between related ragas mid-piece), expressive bhāva-led ornamentation (each phrase shaped to convey specific emotional inflection, the bhāva-led performance aesthetic), vocal-foreground performance with sarangi or harmonium melodic-accompaniment and tabla rhythmic-accompaniment, repertoire addressing romantic-Krishna and viraha (separation-from-lover) thematic material with text in Brajbhasha or Hindi-Urdu, and performance contexts spanning courtesan-tradition (the thumri's original setting in tawaif kotha-salon culture) and modern-classical concert. Distinguished from khayal by greater raga-flexibility and emotional-bhāva-foreground over abstract-raga-development; distinguished from ghazal by raga-foundation over ghazal-poetic-form structure; distinguished from later filmi by direct-classical-tradition lineage despite shared romantic-emotional vocabulary.

items.name: Carnatic vocal
items.lineage: South Indian classical vocal tradition organized around the 72-melakarta scale system codified by Venkatamakhin in 1620 and the kriti-composition canon of the early-19th-century Trinity (Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, Syama Sastri); 20th-century lineage M.S. Subbulakshmi, D.K. Pattammal, M.D. Ramanathan, T.N. Krishnan, Semmangudi Srinivasa Iyer, T.R. Mahalingam
items.description: Carnatic vocal (codified ca. 14th century through Purandara Dasa and crystallized 17th-19th century through the trinity of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri in Thanjavur and Madras), the South Indian classical vocal tradition centered on composed kriti repertoire decorated with manōdharma improvisation. Defined by lead vocal performance of fixed kritis (composed three-section pallavi-anupallavi-charanam pieces in specific raga and tala) with extensive improvisation appendages: ālāpana free-rhythm raga-exposition before the composition, niraval melodic-textual elaboration on a single line, kalpana svaras solfège-syllable-based melodic improvisation, and the climactic ragam-tanam-pallavi extended-form virtuosic display. Standard accompaniment: violin (carnatic style, held on chest), mridangam two-headed drum, ghatam clay pot, kanjira tambourine, and tanpura drone-strings; performance language spans Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Sanskrit, and Malayalam. Distinguished from Hindustani khayal by composition-foreground over raga-elaboration-foreground; distinguished from temple kriti and javali by concert-not-temple performance context.

items.name: Carnatic instrumental
items.lineage: South Indian classical instrumental tradition spanning veena (Saraswathi veena, the South Indian fretted long-neck lute), Carnatic violin (held in vertical Carnatic posture, codified by Baluswami Dikshitar in the early 19th century), bansuri flute (Carnatic flute is distinct from Hindustani in tuning), nadaswaram (temple double-reed), mandolin (U. Shrinivas adaptation), and even saxophone (Kadri Gopalnath South Indian classical saxophone), all interpreting the same 72-melakarta-and-kriti repertoire as the vocal tradition
items.description: Carnatic instrumental (codified ca. 14th century through Purandara Dasa's pedagogical foundation and crystallized 17th-19th century through the Tamil Nadu trinity of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri), the South Indian classical instrumental tradition treating melodic instruments as gāyaki ang — singing-style — to elaborate compositions originally written for voice. Defined by veena (large fretted plucked-lute), violin (held on the chest with the scroll resting on the foot, played by a sitting performer), bansuri or flute, mandolin, and saxophone among other adopted instruments, performing compositions across the kriti-varnam-tillana repertoire with manōdharma improvisation (ālāpana free-rhythm exposition, niraval melodic-textual decoration, kalpana svaras solfège-based melodic improvisation), accompanied by mridangam two-headed drum, ghatam clay pot, kanjira tambourine-frame, and morsing jaw-harp percussion. Distinguished from Hindustani by composition-foreground over raga-elaboration-foreground and Tamil-Telugu-Kannada-Malayalam compositional language; distinguished from Carnatic vocal by absence of vocal text and gāyaki-ang melodic-mimicry of vocal phrasing.

items.name: Bhajan
items.lineage: Pan-Indian Hindu devotional song tradition setting Sanskrit, Hindi, Braj Bhasha, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil and other Indian-language devotional poetry by Surdas, Mirabai, Tulsidas, Tukaram, Kabir, the Alvar saints — performed in temple-and-domestic-shrine contexts across regional Hindu sub-traditions; modern voices Anup Jalota, Jagjit Singh (the late ghazal-bhajan crossover canon), and the Pushti Marg haveli sangeet tradition
items.description: Bhajan (early-medieval onward, codified through the bhakti devotional movement 12th-17th century across North India and now performed in temple, ashram, and home-puja contexts globally), the Hindu congregational devotional song form built on responsorial structure between lead singer and group. Defined by harmonium drone-and-melody accompaniment, dholak two-headed barrel-drum metric pulse, optional manjira hand cymbals, lead-vocal-and-call-and-response group answer pattern across cycles of 4-8 measures, lyrics in Hindi-Sanskrit-Marathi-Bengali-Gujarati or other regional languages addressing deities (Krishna, Rama, Shiva, Devi, Hanuman), and increasing tempo and intensity across the bhajan as devotional fervor builds. Distinguished from kirtan by smaller-scale and home/temple-rather-than-procession context; distinguished from Carnatic kriti by congregational-not-classical performance and bhakti-not-temple-art-music framing.

items.name: Kīrtan
items.lineage: Indian devotional call-and-response congregational singing tradition with two principal branches: Hindu kirtan (Vaishnava Bengali kirtan tradition tracing to Chaitanya Mahaprabhu in 15th-century Bengal, performed at Krishna temple courtyards with khol drum and karatala cymbals; Maharashtrian abhang kirtan tradition tracing to Tukaram and Eknath; the broader Hare Krishna ISKCON tradition extending Bengali Vaishnava kirtan globally) and Sikh kirtan (shabad kirtan of the Guru Granth Sahib at gurdwaras worldwide)
items.description: Kirtan (codified medieval period through the bhakti devotional movement, with continuous tradition in Sikh gurdwara, Vaishnava temple, and contemporary Western kirtan-revival contexts), the call-and-response devotional chant practice central to Sikh and Vaishnava bhakti devotional practice. Defined by mantric repetition (the kirtan-distinct practice of repeating a mantra or short devotional phrase across many cycles, building intensity and tempo), call-and-response between lead-singer and group, harmonium drone-and-melody accompaniment, tabla and mridanga two-headed drum percussion, and lyrical content of divine name (Naam) repetition, Krishna-praise verses, or Sikh shabad scriptural quotation depending on tradition. Performance contexts span temple service, ashram practice, and public satsang gathering. Distinguished from bhajan by greater emphasis on mantra-repetition over verse-narrative; distinguished from Sikh shabad kirtan (a specific subset using Guru Granth Sahib scripture) by broader bhakti applicability; distinguished from secular Indian devotional pop by direct ritual function.

items.name: Bhangra (modern)
items.lineage: Modern bhangra — the post-1980s British-Asian diaspora extension of the originating Punjab village male-harvest-dance tradition into urban electronic pop format, codified through Bally Sagoo, Apache Indian, Malkit Singh, Bally Jagpal, the Punjabi MC dance-floor crossover era (the 1998 Mundian To Bach Ke that found its global breakthrough through Jay-Z 2003 remix), and the broader UK-Punjab Sangeeta / Multitone label catalogs
items.description: Modern bhangra (originating from Punjabi Vaisakhi-festival harvest dance music, transformed 1980s-1990s into a UK-Punjabi-diaspora pop genre, now globally distributed), the Punjabi pop-fusion genre that retains traditional dhol-and-tumbi instrumentation alongside electronic dance-music production. Defined by the dhol double-headed barrel-drum playing the chaal pattern (the genre's rhythmic signature), tumbi single-string melodic instrument or dhad waist-drum melodic role, robust bilingual Punjabi-English vocal hook, four-on-floor or chaal-pattern programmed kick alongside the dhol, and a performance context spanning Punjabi wedding dance floor, UK club, and Bollywood film soundtrack. UK production lineage hybridized with hip-hop, reggae, and house. Distinguished from traditional folk bhangra by electronic production and pop-song format; distinguished from filmi by direct-from-Punjab-festival-folk lineage.

items.name: Hindi filmi (Bollywood)
items.lineage: Hindi-language Bombay film-song playback tradition codified 1940s-onward, with first-wave golden-age 1940s-1960s through Naushad (Mughal-e-Azam 1960, the template-setting orchestrated-classical-folk-fusion music director), S.D. Burman (Pyaasa 1957, Aradhana 1969), Shankar-Jaikishan (Awaara 1951, Sangam 1964), Madan Mohan, Roshan, Salil Chowdhury; second-wave funk-fusion era 1970s-1980s through R.D. Burman (Hare Rama Hare Krishna 1971, Sholay 1975, the bossa-and-disco-and-funk-fusion auteur), Laxmikant-Pyarelal, Kalyanji-Anandji, Bappi Lahiri (the disco-filmi specialist); third-wave 1990s-onward through A.R. Rahman (Roja 1992, Bombay 1995, Dil Se 1998, Slumdog Millionaire 2008 global Oscar breakthrough), Vishal-Shekhar, Pritam, Amit Trivedi; the canonical playback singer lineage of Lata Mangeshkar (1929-2022, the 30000-song discography defining the female playback voice from 1948 onward), Mohammed Rafi (1924-1980, the male romantic-and-classical voice), Asha Bhosle (1933-, the cabaret-and-folk-versatile voice), Mukesh, Kishore Kumar (the 1970s comic-and-romantic voice and R.D. Burman collaborator), Manna Dey, Hemant Kumar
items.description: Hindi filmi / Bollywood (codified 1940s-onward as the Hindi-language Bombay film-industry song-playback tradition, the dominant popular-music form across the Indian subcontinent and South Asian diaspora for over seven decades). Defined by the playback-singer model (songs pre-recorded in studio by professional playback singers — Lata Mangeshkar, Asha Bhosle, Mohammed Rafi, Kishore Kumar, Manna Dey, Mukesh — then lip-synced by film actors on screen, the singing and acting professions fully separated), the music-director composer-arranger role (the named auteur figure who conceived the song and led the studio orchestra), large-orchestra arrangements combining Indian-classical melodic instruments (sitar, tabla, harmonium, bansuri, dholak, santoor, shehnai) with Western symphonic strings, brass, and woodwinds (50-100 musicians tracked live in the Mumbai filmi studios — Mehboob 1954, Famous Studios Tardeo 1948, Empire, Film Centre, Rang Mahal), raga-derived melodic ornamentation (drawing from Hindustani classical vocabulary but compressed into verse-chorus pop song-form), Western functional harmony imposed under the Indian melodic foreground, and bilingual lyric content (Urdu poetic-ghazal register in the golden-age era, Hindi pop-vernacular by the 1970s onward). Music-director lineage: Naushad (Mughal-e-Azam 1960, Mother India 1957 — the template-setting orchestrated-classical-folk-fusion auteur), S.D. Burman (Pyaasa 1957, Aradhana 1969), Shankar-Jaikishan (Awaara 1951, Sangam 1964), Madan Mohan, Roshan, Salil Chowdhury (the golden-age 1940s-60s anchors); R.D. Burman (Hare Rama Hare Krishna 1971, Sholay 1975, the 1970s funk-bossa-disco-fusion auteur), Laxmikant-Pyarelal (Bobby 1973, Karz 1980), Kalyanji-Anandji, Bappi Lahiri (Disco Dancer 1982); A.R. Rahman (Roja 1992, Bombay 1995, Dil Se 1998, Slumdog Millionaire 2008 global Oscar breakthrough), Vishal-Shekhar, Pritam, Amit Trivedi (1990s-onward third wave). Distinguished from Hindustani classical by song-form architecture and Western-harmony foundation rather than raga-elaboration discipline; distinguished from bhangra by orchestrated-pop arrangement rather than dhol-foregrounded festival format; distinguished from Sufi qawwali by secular-cinema context rather than dargah devotional setting; distinguished from regional Indian film music (Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Malayalam parallel canons) by Hindi-language scope and Bombay industrial centrality.

items.name: Shidaiqu (Shanghai Mandarin jazz-pop)
items.lineage: Pre-revolutionary Shanghai Mandarin popular jazz-and-pop song tradition codified 1927-1949, the foundational stratum of Chinese-language popular music — Li Jinhui (1891-1967, the father of Chinese popular music, composer of the seminal 1927 song Drizzle / Maomao Yu often cited as the first shidaiqu) establishing the genre by fusing Western jazz-band orchestration with Mandarin-language vocal melodic vocabulary at his Bright Moon Song-and-Dance Troupe in Shanghai; the seven great singing stars (qida ge xing) era of the 1940s through Zhou Xuan (1918-1957, the Golden Voice, the canonical female playback voice through When Will You Return / He Ri Jun Zai Lai 1937 and Shanghai Nights / Ye Shanghai 1947), Bai Hong, Yao Lee, Bai Guang, Li Xianglan (Yamaguchi Yoshiko, the Japanese-Manchurian crossover voice), Wu Yingyin, Gong Qiuxia; composer-arranger lineage Chen Gexin (Rose Rose I Love You 1940), Yao Min (Zhou Xuan collaborator), Li Houxiang; production infrastructure of the EMI Pathé / Pathé Records Shanghai studios on Hengshan Road and Great China Records on the French Concession (the dominant pre-revolutionary recording labels for Mandarin popular music); ended abruptly with the 1949 Communist takeover when shidaiqu was banned in Mainland China as "yellow music" / huang se yinyue (pornographic music) and many singers and composers fled to British Hong Kong where the tradition continued under the Pathé Hong Kong umbrella through Yao Lee and Pan Wan-ching late careers, seeding the later Mandopop and Cantopop traditions of the 1970s-onward
items.description: Shidaiqu (codified 1927-1949 as the pre-revolutionary Shanghai Mandarin popular jazz-and-pop tradition, the foundational stratum of all subsequent Chinese-language popular music), the Shanghai-jazz-pop fusion genre. Defined by the founding-composer Li Jinhui (1891-1967, the father of Chinese popular music, conducting the Bright Moon Song-and-Dance Troupe in Shanghai from 1927 onward and writing the seminal Drizzle / Maomao Yu often cited as the first shidaiqu), the seven great singing stars (qida ge xing) lineage of the 1940s Shanghai cabaret-and-recording scene — Zhou Xuan (1918-1957, the Golden Voice through When Will You Return 1937 and Shanghai Nights 1947), Bai Hong, Yao Lee, Bai Guang, Li Xianglan, Wu Yingyin, Gong Qiuxia — the composer-arranger lineage Chen Gexin (Rose Rose I Love You 1940, later translated and recorded by Frankie Laine 1951), Yao Min, Li Houxiang, the Western-jazz-band orchestration imported through the Shanghai International Settlement nightclub-and-cabaret scene (trumpet, saxophone, piano, double bass, drum kit foreground) hybridized with Chinese melodic-vocabulary and occasional Chinese-instrument color (erhu, pipa), Mandarin-language vocal-melodic vocabulary applied over Western functional harmony, and recording infrastructure of the EMI Pathé / Pathé Records Shanghai studios on Hengshan Road and the Great China Records studios on the French Concession. Ended abruptly with the 1949 Communist takeover that classified shidaiqu as yellow music / huang se yinyue and banned the genre in Mainland China; the tradition continued in British Hong Kong through Pathé Hong Kong (Yao Lee and Pan Wan-ching late careers) and seeded the 1970s-onward Mandopop and Cantopop traditions. Distinguished from later Mandopop by pre-revolutionary Shanghai origin and acoustic-jazz-band orchestration rather than Taiwan-Mainland-Hong-Kong 70s-onward production; distinguished from contemporaneous Shanghai jazz instrumentals by Mandarin-language vocal-foreground; distinguished from Western jazz of the same era by Chinese melodic-vocabulary and Mandarin lyric content.
exemplars: Zhou Xuan — When Will You Return
Yao Lee — Rose Rose I Love You

items.name: Gǔqín
items.lineage: Chinese seven-string scholar-zither solo tradition with documented written scores (jianzipu tablature-notation) dating from the Han-dynasty (206 BCE-220 CE) onward, making it the oldest continuously-notated musical tradition. Constructed of paulownia-tung-wood top and zi-wood bottom with thirteen mother-of-pearl hui position-markers and silk or steel-nylon strings. The repertoire layers Wei-Jin-and-Tang dynasty meditative-philosophical pieces with Song-Yuan-and-Ming court-and-scholar-amateur literati compositions, performed solo in studio-and-garden settings as a wenrenhua scholar-painting-music-poetry integrated-art-form practice. Microtonal sliding (yin-and-rou portamento), harmonics (fan-yin), and silent-finger gestures comprise the canonical performance vocabulary.
items.description: Guqin (continuous tradition pre-Han onward across Chinese literati culture, with extant repertoire of approximately 3000 pieces preserved through Ming-Qing-era handbook codifications and continuous master-disciple transmission to present), the seven-string Chinese zither solo tradition of literati culture. Defined by the qin instrument itself (a 4-foot horizontal long-zither with seven silk-or-modern-nylon strings, no movable bridges — the strings rest on a fixed nut and are stopped by the player's left hand on the unmarked but indicated playing surface), meditative-sparse performance aesthetic (the guqin tradition explicitly opposes virtuosic-display-foregrounded performance, instead prizing contemplative-restrained gesture and silent-pause-as-musical-element), microtonal sliding ornamentation (the guqin specialty of slow-glissando left-hand techniques producing extensive pitch-bend decoration), tablature notation specific to the guqin (distinct from Chinese ensemble notation, indicating finger-position and technique rather than pitch directly), and solo-or-small-chamber performance contexts in literati gardens, scholar's studios, and contemporary concert settings.
