items.name: Latin Rituale Romanum exorcism recitation
items.lineage: The Latin exorcism recitation is the imprecatory liturgy of the Roman Catholic Rituale Romanum, whose exorcism section (De exorcizandis obsessis a daemonio) was codified in 1614 and revised in 1999. Performed by a priest with the bishop's mandate, it interleaves psalmody, Gospel readings, and the imperative deprecatory-and-imperative formulae addressed directly to the demon ('Exorcizo te, immundissime spiritus'). Delivery is forceful heightened Latin declamation in a resonant church interior, punctuated by the sign of the cross and sprinkling of holy water. The rite is documented in the Rituale itself and in the Church's liturgical-law tradition.

items.name: Korean muga shamanic ritual narrative
items.lineage: Muga are the sung and chanted ritual songs of the Korean mudang (shaman), performed within the kut ceremony to invoke, entertain, and petition the spirits (gods, ancestors, and the dead). Regional forms range from the hereditary tradition of the southwestern seseummu to the possession-based gangsinmu of the north, and the repertoire encompasses invocation, narrative epic (such as the Bari Gongju abandoned-princess myth), and divination speech, all accompanied by janggu and other percussion. Muga is widely regarded as a root source of pansori epic singing and of shinawi and sinawi-derived instrumental music. It is documented through twentieth-century field recordings and the scholarship of Korean folklorists and is designated within the Important Intangible Cultural Property system.

items.name: Mongolian böö shamanic invocation
items.lineage: Böö mörgöl is the indigenous shamanism of the Mongols and neighboring Buryat and Darkhad peoples, in which the böö (shaman) invokes and embodies spirits (ongod) to heal, divine, and mediate with the sky-father Tengri and the master-spirits of place. The ritual voice combines invocatory calls (duudlaga), praise and summoning of the ongod, and glossolalic utterance during trance, historically accompanied by the frame drum (khengereg) and jingling costume. Suppressed under the twentieth-century socialist state, the tradition has seen a strong post-1990 revival across Mongolia and Buryatia. It is documented through ethnographic fieldwork and recordings of Inner Asian shamanic practice.
items.description: Böö mörgöl is the indigenous shamanism of the Mongols and neighboring Buryat and Darkhad peoples, in which the böö (shaman) invokes and embodies spirits (ongod) to heal, divine, and mediate with the sky-father Tengri and the master-spirits of place. The ritual voice combines invocatory calls (duudlaga), praise and summoning of the ongod, and glossolalic utterance during trance, historically accompanied by the frame drum (khengereg) and jingling costume. Suppressed under the twentieth-century socialist state, the tradition has seen a strong post-1990 revival across Mongolia and Buryatia. It is documented through ethnographic fieldwork and recordings of Inner Asian shamanic practice.

items.name: Sami noaidi drum-journey joik-chant
items.lineage: The noaidi was the shaman of the Sami peoples of northern Fennoscandia, who entered trance to travel to the spirit worlds — for healing, hunting-luck, and mediation with the dead — often falling into ecstatic stillness while helpers sang. The rite combined the runebomme (frame drum, whose membrane bore a painted cosmological map read with a vuorbi pointer) with joik, the characteristically non-lexical, circular Sami vocal genre. Christian missionary campaigns from the seventeenth century onward suppressed the drums and demonized joik, and much is reconstructed from missionary accounts, confiscated drums, and later joik documentation. The associated joik tradition survives strongly and is documented in extensive twentieth-century field recordings.

items.name: Navajo Blessingway (Hózhǫ́ǫ́jí) recitation
items.lineage: Blessingway (Hózhǫ́ǫ́jí) is the central ceremony of the Diné (Navajo), a rite for restoring and maintaining hózhǫ́ (beauty, harmony, balance) used at childbirth, marriage, girls' puberty (Kinaaldá), and to sanctify life-passages, rather than to cure illness. Led by a hataałii (singer/medicine person) in the hogan over one or two nights, it consists of long fixed sequences of sung prayer and recited text recounting the emergence and the deeds of Changing Woman, learned through years of apprenticeship. The songs and prayers must be delivered in exact order and wording. The tradition is documented in the scholarship of Washington Matthews, Leland Wyman, and Father Berard Haile, and remains a living practice.

items.name: Nahua/Aztec flower-song (in xochitl in cuicatl) oratory
items.lineage: In xochitl in cuicatl ('flower and song') is the Nahua difrasismo for poetry and sung oratory, the elevated verbal art of the Aztec (Mexica) and wider Nahuatl-speaking world of central Mexico. The corpus survives chiefly in two sixteenth-century manuscripts, the Cantares Mexicanos and the Romances de los señores de la Nueva España, transcribed after the conquest and preserving pre-Hispanic and early-colonial song-poems on transience, war, and the divine, alongside the huehuetlahtolli oratory of the elders. In performance, poet-singers (cuicapicqueh) declaimed and sang these texts, historically to the huehuetl and teponaztli drums whose beat patterns are notated by syllables in the manuscripts. The tradition is reconstructed from these codices and the scholarship of Ángel María Garibay and Miguel León-Portilla.

items.name: Ethiopian debtera liturgical incantation
items.lineage: The debtera is the learned non-ordained cleric of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, trained for many years in the church schools to master the Ge'ez liturgy, the zema chant of Saint Yared, aquaquam liturgical dance, and qene sacred poetry. Beyond the sanctioned liturgy, debtera are also the authors and reciters of asmat prayers and protective magical scrolls (ketab), an esoteric incantatory practice invoking secret names of God and angels for healing and protection. Their liturgical voice moves in the three qenet modal families of Ethiopian chant. The tradition is documented in Ge'ez manuscript scholarship and ethnographies of Ethiopian Christianity, and is a sibling of the Coptic Egyptian rite.

items.name: Tibetan chöd rite (voice with damaru and kangling)
items.lineage: Chöd ('cutting') is a Tibetan Buddhist tantric practice systematized in the eleventh–twelfth centuries by the female adept Machig Labdrön, in which the practitioner symbolically severs ego-attachment by visualizing the offering of the body to spirits, often performed in charnel grounds and wild places. The sadhana is sung to characteristic melodic chant lines while the practitioner plays the damaru (double-headed hand drum) and the kangling (thighbone trumpet), whose blasts summon the guests to the feast. It crosses lineage boundaries (Nyingma, Kagyü, Gelug) and combines melodic yang-style chant with deep resonant vocalization. The tradition is transmitted through empowerment and practice-text lineages and documented in Tibetan liturgical manuscripts and modern ethnomusicology.

items.name: Palo Mayombe Kongo mambo ritual chant
items.lineage: Palo (Las Reglas de Congo), of which Mayombe is a principal branch, is the Afro-Cuban religion derived from Kikongo-speaking Bantu peoples of Central Africa, brought to Cuba under slavery and centered on the nganga (prenda) spirit-vessel and the dead (nfumbi). Its ritual songs, called mambos, are call-and-response chants in a Kikongo-derived liturgical language (habla congo) led by a soloist and answered by the chorus over Palo drums (ngoma) and iron, to summon, praise, and work with the mpungu forces and the spirits. Delivery is metrical, percussive, and communal, driving the ceremony toward possession. The tradition is documented in the ethnographic work of Lydia Cabrera (El Monte) and later scholars of Afro-Cuban religion.

items.name: Icelandic kvæði / þula recitation
items.lineage: Kvæði are the traditional chanted narrative poems of Iceland, most importantly the rímur — long metrical verse-cycles retelling sagas and romances — performed in the distinctive kvæðaskapur (rímnalag) manner of half-sung, half-spoken chanting on a narrow set of stemmur (tune-formulae). The þula is a related genre of catalog- or rigmarole-poem, often a strung list of names or lore chanted rhythmically, historically used within the home. These forms flourished from the late medieval period through the nineteenth century as Iceland's principal domestic evening entertainment (kvöldvaka). They are documented in extensive manuscript collections and in twentieth-century field recordings held by the Árni Magnússon Institute.

items.name: Kabuki tsurane declamation (aragoto)
items.lineage: Tsurane are the extended rhetorical set-speeches of the aragoto ('rough business') style of kabuki, the bravura acting mode created by Ichikawa Danjuro I in late-17th-century Edo and carried through the Ichikawa Danjuro line to the present. Delivered by the leading male-role actor in exaggerated, rhythmically pointed declamation, often as a boastful self-introduction punctuated by the mie pose and tsuke wooden clappers, the tsurane is stage-speech distinct from the sung nagauta and chanted gidayu music that accompany the play. Canonical examples occur in the 'Shibaraku' interlude and other Kabuki Juhachiban 'eighteen great plays' of the Ichikawa house. It is documented in the Kabuki-za and National Theatre of Japan performance records and the Shochiku theatrical archive.

items.name: Kyogen comic declamation
items.lineage: Kyogen is the comic spoken-theatre form performed as interludes between the solemn noh plays on the same stage, codified in Muromachi-period Japan (14th to 16th centuries) and transmitted through the Okura and Izumi hereditary schools. Its dialogue is delivered in a highly stylized, clearly projected declamation with fixed cadences and stock phrases such as the entrance line 'Kore wa kono atari no mono de gozaru', serving as the spoken counterpart to noh's chanted utai. Performers train from childhood in the family line, with the Nomura and Shigeyama families among the best-known modern lineages. It is documented in the repertories of the Nohgaku Performers' Association and UNESCO's Nogaku intangible-heritage inscription (2001/2008).

items.name: Noh kotoba spoken declamation
items.lineage: In noh, the classical masked music-drama codified by Kan'ami and Zeami in 14th-century Japan, kotoba denotes the spoken (rather than chanted) passages of the text, delivered in a heightened, slow, resonant declamation with a characteristically lowered larynx and darkened timbre. Kotoba alternates with the melodic utai chant and is set against the hayashi ensemble of flute and drums, but is itself stylized speech governed by the strict schools Kanze, Hosho, Konparu, Kongo, and Kita. It is transmitted through hereditary iemoto lineages and preserved in centuries of utaibon libretti. It is documented in the National Noh Theatre records and the Nogaku UNESCO inscription.

items.name: Shakespearean verse declamation
items.lineage: Shakespearean verse declamation is the stage delivery of English Renaissance blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, as developed in the London playhouses of the 1590s to 1610s and transmitted through four centuries of Anglophone theatre practice. Modern declamatory technique, associated with the Royal Shakespeare Company and conservatoires such as RADA, foregrounds the metrical line, caesura, and end-stopping while projecting to an unamplified house. The delivery is heightened spoken speech rather than song, though its scansion is metrically governed. It is documented in recorded stage and broadcast performances by actors such as John Gielgud, Laurence Olivier, and Ian McKellen.

items.name: Kutiyattam Sanskrit recitation
items.lineage: Kutiyattam is the Sanskrit temple theatre of Kerala in southwestern India, the oldest continuously performed classical theatre tradition of the subcontinent, staged in the kuttampalam theatres of Hindu temples and transmitted through the Chakyar and Nangyar hereditary performer families. Its recitation delivers Sanskrit and Prakrit verse in stylized, raga-based intonation with greatly elongated syllables, accompanied by the mizhavu copper drum, so that a single verse may be expanded across many hours of vachika (vocal) and angika (gestural) elaboration. The guru Ammannur Madhava Chakyar (1917-2008) is the emblematic 20th-century master. It is documented under UNESCO's intangible-cultural-heritage inscription (2001/2008) and in the Margi and Kerala Kalamandalam training institutions.

items.name: Wayang kulit dalang narration
items.lineage: In Javanese wayang kulit shadow-puppet theatre, the dalang (puppeteer-narrator) delivers the story through janturan and carita narration, heightened descriptive speech intoned over the soft grimingan shimmer of the gamelan, alternating with sulukan mood-songs and character dialogue across an all-night performance. The dalang is simultaneously narrator, voice of every character, conductor of the gamelan, and manipulator of the puppets, working within the court traditions of Surakarta and Yogyakarta in central Java. Ki Nartosabdho (1925-1985) is among the most celebrated 20th-century dalang. It is documented under UNESCO's Wayang intangible-heritage inscription (2003/2008).

items.name: Hat boi (tuong) declamation
items.lineage: Hat boi (also tuong) is the classical theatre of Vietnam, a heroic-historical stage form crystallized under the Nguyen court in central Vietnam (Binh Dinh province and the imperial capital Hue) in the 18th and 19th centuries. Its declamation delivers stylized, emphatic, tonally shaped stage-speech, loud and rhetorically pointed for warrior and loyal-minister roles, alternating with sung passages and set against a percussion-led ensemble dominated by the trong chau drum. It is distinct from the later southern reformed opera cai luong and from the northern comic-satirical cheo. It is documented in the repertories of the Vietnam Tuong Theatre and in Vietnamese Institute of Musicology field recordings.

items.name: Jingju yunbai stage-speech
items.lineage: In jingju (Beijing/Peking opera), which crystallized in the Qing capital after the 1790 arrival of the Anhui troupes, stage-speech falls into two registers: yunbai, a heightened stylized declamation using an archaic rhyme-speech pronunciation, and jingbai, closer to colloquial Beijing dialect used chiefly by clown (chou) and certain female roles. Both are delivered with bright, forward, tonally exaggerated projection, are role-type specific, and are set against the jinghu fiddle and percussion, as codified as the sung arias themselves. Actors train by role-type in academies descending from masters such as Mei Lanfang (1894-1961). It is documented in the China National Peking Opera Company records and extensive 20th-century recordings.

items.name: Commedia dell'arte lazzi delivery
items.lineage: Commedia dell'arte was the professional improvised masked comedy of Italy from the mid-16th to the 18th century, performed by touring troupes such as the Gelosi and Confidenti on temporary trestle stages in piazzas and courts. Lazzi are the codified comic bits, verbal set-pieces, puns, and rhetorical riffs delivered by the stock masks (Arlecchino, Pantalone, il Dottore, Brighella), declaimed with broad, projected, dialect-inflected exaggeration and improvised around a scenario (canovaccio) rather than a fixed script. The tradition is documented in surviving scenario collections such as Flaminio Scala's 'Il teatro delle favole rappresentative' (1611) and in the modern revival led by Giorgio Strehler's Piccolo Teatro di Milano.

items.name: Black gospel whooping sermon
items.lineage: African-American Baptist and Pentecostal folk-preaching tradition whose sermonic climax shifts from spoken prose into a metered, pitched chant known as whooping (also zooning or tuning-up), delivered in call-and-response with the congregation and frequently doubled by the Hammond organ. Documented from the earliest race-record sermons of Rev. J. M. Gates and Rev. J. C. Burnett in the 1920s through the mid-century recorded sermons of Rev. C. L. Franklin on Chess and Jewel. The chanted-preaching form and its formulaic building-blocks were analyzed by Bruce Rosenberg in The Art of the American Folk Preacher (1970). The preacher improvises within stock cadential formulas, accelerating and rising in pitch until the congregation's shouts and the organ carry the room.

items.name: Fire-and-brimstone revival sermon
items.lineage: Hortatory evangelical preaching of the American revival and camp-meeting tradition, marked by vivid imagery of judgment and hellfire delivered at high projected volume in rhythmic, accelerating cadences. Traces from the 18th-century Great Awakening (Jonathan Edwards's Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, 1741) through the 19th-century frontier camp meetings to the 20th-century tent-revival and radio evangelists such as Billy Sunday and Oral Roberts. The delivery relies on repeated exhortation, dramatic pauses, and congregational punctuation with cries of amen and hallelujah. It is a foundational strand of Protestant evangelical oratory in the United States.

items.name: Jewish maggid homiletic preaching
items.lineage: The derashah of the itinerant Ashkenazi preacher (maggid) of Eastern Europe, a homiletic sermon weaving Torah, Talmud, and midrash with moral exhortation, typically delivered in Yiddish with a distinctive study-chant cadence derived from the lernen (Gemara) shteyger. The form flourished from the 17th through 19th centuries; the Dubner Maggid (Jacob Kranz, d. 1804) was celebrated for his mashal parables, and the Maggid of Mezeritch was central to the spread of early Hasidism. The delivery moves fluidly between conversational speech and a rising, questioning recitative melody used to voice textual argument. It survives today in yeshiva drashot and Hasidic gatherings.

items.name: Islamic khutbah sermon
items.lineage: The formal Friday (jumuah) and Eid sermon delivered by the khatib from the minbar, a two-part homily of praise, Qur'anic citation, exhortation, and supplication codified from the earliest Medinan community. It is delivered in heightened, projected Arabic oratory that frequently cadences into maqam-inflected dua and quoted Qur'anic verse. The rhetorical structure — opening hamd and salawat, admonition, and closing prayer for the community — is preserved across the Sunni and Shia worlds. It stands alongside the adhan and tajwid recitation as a central genre of Islamic vocal practice, though speech-centered rather than fully melodic.

items.name: American political stump oratory
items.lineage: The campaign stump speech of United States electoral politics, from 19th-century torchlight-rally and Chautauqua oratory through populist and civil-rights platform styles to the modern televised rally. The name derives from candidates literally standing on tree stumps to address frontier gatherings. It is characterized by projected, persuasive delivery, memorable refrains and applause-lines, escalating cadence, and call-and-response engagement with the crowd. The genre spans a rhetorical continuum from plain conversational address to near-chanted, revival-inflected peroration.

items.name: Tobacco and livestock auctioneer chant
items.lineage: The rapid rhythmic auction cry, or bid-calling, of North American tobacco warehouses and livestock sale barns, alternating spoken numbers with sustained filler syllables held on a single pitch to keep bidding momentum. The style was carried into national awareness by the Lucky Strike radio advertisements featuring auctioneers L. A. Speed Riggs and F. E. Boone, whose Sold, American! tag became a catchphrase in the 1930s through 1950s. It is taught systematically at modern auction schools as a controlled breath-and-rhythm technique and is frequently cited as a vernacular precursor to the rhythmic speech-flow of rap. The chant balances legible numbers against a percussive stream of connective vocables.

items.name: Appalachian square-dance calling
items.lineage: The caller's rhythmic patter directing figures for old-time Appalachian square and big-circle dances, delivered in strict time over a string band of fiddle and banjo. It descends from Anglo-Celtic and French quadrille calling adapted in the southern mountains, where the caller became an improvising rhythmic voice rather than a mere prompter. The running-set dancing that underlies it was documented by Cecil Sharp during his 1916 to 1918 Appalachian fieldwork, and figures such as Bascom Lamar Lunsford institutionalized the practice through the Asheville Mountain Dance and Folk Festival from 1928. Calls are locked to the reel's meter, blending fixed figure-names with spontaneous filler.

items.name: Māori whaikōrero oratory
items.lineage: The formal oratory of the marae ātea (forecourt) in Māori ceremonial encounter (pōwhiri) in Aotearoa/New Zealand, performed by male speakers (kaikōrero) following the women's karanga. A whaikōrero is structured through a formulaic opening (tauparapara), recitation of whakapapa (genealogy), acknowledgement of the dead and the living, and the matter at hand, and is typically sealed by a sung waiata supported by the speaker's group. It is a primary vehicle of mana, whakapapa, and tikanga Māori, transmitted orally from senior orators to successors. Both an art of memory and of improvised response, it draws freely on proverb (whakataukī) and chanted passages.

items.name: Hawaiian haʻa ancestral chant
items.lineage: Sacred Hawaiian chant (oli) performed in the low, bent-knee haʻa posture reserved for akua and ancestors, encompassing genealogical (koʻihonua) and name (mele inoa) chants that transmit lineage and cosmology. The style is marked by sustained, measured vocal delivery and stylized ornaments such as the ʻiʻi trill, and was traditionally taught within the hula hālau under a kumu hula. The corpus and its performance practice were documented in Nathaniel B. Emerson's Unwritten Literature of Hawaii (1909) and in the later scholarship of Mary Kawena Pukui. Chant carried genealogy, prayer, and place-lore as authoritative oral record in pre-literate Hawaiʻi.

items.name: Audiobook narration
items.lineage: Solo long-form literary narration tradition rooted in the 1932 American Foundation for the Blind / Library of Congress talking-book program for blind readers and in the 1952 founding of Caedmon Records, whose Dylan Thomas reading of A Child's Christmas in Wales is the commonly cited commercial origin point. It grew through the Books on Tape cassette-rental era of the 1970s-80s into the Audible-era digital industry, with the narrator working alone in a dry, heavily damped close-miked booth, sustaining a consistent voice, pacing, and character palette across many hours of finished audio. Canonical narrators include Jim Dale and Stephen Fry (the US and UK Harry Potter cycles respectively), George Guidall, and Barbara Rosenblat.

items.name: Documentary voiceover
items.lineage: Authoritative scripted narration read over documentary picture, descending from 1930s-40s newsreel narration such as Westbrook Van Voorhis's reads for The March of Time into postwar television nature and history documentary. Canonical exemplars include David Attenborough's intimate-authoritative BBC natural-history narration (Life on Earth, 1979, through the Planet Earth series), David McCullough's narration of Ken Burns's The Civil War (1990) and Peter Coyote's later Burns work, and Morgan Freeman's March of the Penguins (2005) as the popular touchstone of the warm 'voice of God' register. The performer reads alone to picture in a dry, treated studio, balancing measured pacing and low, resonant delivery against the score and location-sound bed.

items.name: Old-time radio announcer
items.lineage: American network-radio announcer style of the 1930s-50s NBC and CBS era, delivered in projected, precisely articulated diction — often the cultivated Mid-Atlantic ('transatlantic') accent taught in period broadcast and elocution training — into RCA 44 and 77 ribbon microphones. Staff and program announcers such as Don Wilson (The Jack Benny Program), Harry von Zell, Ken Carpenter, and Milton Cross (the Metropolitan Opera broadcasts) defined the register across variety-show openings, drama introductions, station identifications, and live commercial reads; Orson Welles's 1938 Mercury Theatre on the Air 'War of the Worlds' broadcast famously exploited the authority this announcer voice carried. The sound is inseparable from the period transmission chain: ribbon mic, tube electronics, and bandwidth-limited live AM air or transcription disc.

items.name: Golden-age radio drama
items.lineage: American network radio drama of the 1930s-1950s: full-cast actors performing live-to-air around ribbon microphones in large broadcast studios, with foley artists creating door slams, footsteps, and storms in real time and organ or orchestra cues stitching scenes together. The canonical exemplar is Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre on the Air, whose 'The War of the Worlds' broadcast (CBS, 30 October 1938) demonstrated the form's power, alongside Norman Corwin's poetic productions and long-running series such as Suspense and The Shadow. A parallel BBC radio drama tradition continued in Britain after American network drama faded with television in the late 1950s. Actors worked the mic distance itself as a dramatic instrument, stepping in for intimacy and off-axis for exits.

items.name: Podcast conversation
items.lineage: Long-form conversational talk distributed as on-demand internet audio, emerging with RSS audio enclosures in the mid-2000s and codified as a two-plus-voice close-mic form by shows like Marc Maron's WTF (2009) and The Joe Rogan Experience (2009). The signature sound is each speaker on their own close dynamic microphone (the Shure SM7B became the emblematic choice) in a dry treated room, mixed in a DAW and delivered as compressed digital files. Remote 'double-ender' recording, where each participant captures their own local track over an internet call, became standard practice in the 2010s and expanded the form globally. Unscripted turn-taking conversation, running one to three-plus hours, is the defining performance mode.

items.name: Sports play-by-play commentary
items.lineage: Live-event narration born on 1920s American AM radio, with KDKA Pittsburgh's 1921 boxing and baseball broadcasts and NBC's Graham McNamee establishing the announcer role. The mid-century canon runs through Red Barber and Mel Allen in baseball, Foster Hewitt's 'He shoots, he scores!' in Canadian hockey, and Vin Scully's 67 seasons with the Brooklyn and Los Angeles Dodgers (1950-2016). The craft is fully improvised real-time description whose pitch, tempo, and volume escalate with game action, delivered from a booth headset microphone riding above continuous crowd roar. The form spread worldwide, with national schools such as the melismatic 'gooooal' call of Latin American football commentary.

items.name: Numbers-station shortwave broadcast
items.lineage: Cold War-era shortwave espionage broadcasts, active from the 1950s onward and still transmitting (Cuba's HM01 continues today): flat monotone read or machine-generated numeral groups sent to field agents for one-time-pad decryption. Stations announce themselves with repeating interval signals such as the 'Lincolnshire Poacher' folk-tune ident and the 'Swedish Rhapsody' music box, then recite number groups at a fixed metronomic pace before signing off. The aesthetic — affectless voice buried in shortwave carrier hiss, heterodyne whistles, and fading — was canonized by The Conet Project (Irdial-Discs, 1997), a four-CD anthology of off-air recordings that made the genre a touchstone for experimental musicians. Operating agencies almost never acknowledge the stations, and their purpose is known largely through espionage trials and defector accounts.

items.name: Shipping forecast cadence
items.lineage: The Met Office marine weather bulletin broadcast on BBC radio since the mid-1920s, read in a measured, deliberately calm cadence over long wave for mariners around the British Isles. The forecast names its 31 sea areas in a fixed roughly clockwise order — Viking, North Utsire, South Utsire, Forties, Cromarty, Forth, Tyne, Dogger, Fisher, German Bight and onward — within a strict word limit, so the litany's rhythm barely varies from bulletin to bulletin. The 0048 Radio 4 broadcast, preceded by the light-orchestral tune 'Sailing By', has become a secular bedtime liturgy for British listeners far beyond its maritime audience, its cadence quoted by poets and musicians alike. Delivery is neutral continuity-announcer speech: unhurried, evenly stressed, pitch-flat, with terminal falls closing each area's report.

items.name: ASMR whisper and trigger audio
items.lineage: Internet-native whisper-and-trigger audio form that coalesced on YouTube around 2009-2010; Jennifer Allen coined the term 'autonomous sensory meridian response' in 2010 to name the tingling relaxation response the recordings aim to elicit. Performers whisper directly into binaural microphone rigs (dummy-head and 3Dio ear-shaped arrays) and foreground mouth sounds, tapping, scratching, and prop crinkles as the primary sonic content, panned for close in-ear headphone listening. Canonical early channels include GentleWhispering (Maria Viktorovna) and WhispersRed (Emma Smith), with the form professionalizing across YouTube and streaming platforms through the 2010s.

items.name: Guided meditation
items.lineage: Recorded spoken instruction guiding a listener through relaxation and meditation practice, descending from 1970s self-help relaxation cassettes and the secular-mindfulness turn led by Jon Kabat-Zinn, whose Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction program (University of Massachusetts, 1979) circulated body-scan recordings as core practice material. Delivery is slow, low-register, and deliberately under-projected, with long structured silences left between instructions. The 2010s app era — Headspace with Andy Puddicombe, Calm with Tamara Levitt — turned the form into a mass studio-produced voice genre.

items.name: Hypnotic induction
items.lineage: Clinical and stage tradition of spoken hypnotic induction descending from Franz Mesmer's eighteenth-century salons through James Braid, the Manchester surgeon who coined 'hypnotism' in the 1840s, into twentieth-century American practice. Milton H. Erickson developed conversational, indirect induction while Dave Elman codified rapid inductions for physicians; both styles rely on monotone, descending-cadence suggestion delivery, progressive-relaxation deepeners, and counted descents. From the 1970s onward the form also became a mass-market audio genre through self-hypnosis cassettes and later digital downloads.

items.name: Stand-up comedy
items.lineage: American solo comic form descending from vaudeville and Borscht Belt monologists through 1950s-60s nightclub soloists like Mort Sahl and Lenny Bruce, who replaced setup-punchline joke telling with personal, conversational material. The craft is built in comedy clubs — The Improv (New York, 1963) and The Comedy Store (Los Angeles, 1972) anchoring the club boom — where a comic works a single handheld microphone against live crowd response, honing timing across nightly sets. Richard Pryor's and George Carlin's early-1970s live albums fixed the recorded canon of the form.

items.name: Poetry slam / performance poetry
items.lineage: Competitive performance-poetry format created by Chicago poet Marc Kelly Smith, who launched the Uptown Poetry Slam at the Green Mill jazz club in 1986 after workshopping the format at the Get Me High Lounge. Poets perform original memorized work within a time limit, scored by randomly selected audience judges, and the format spread through New York's Nuyorican Poets Cafe and the National Poetry Slam (from 1990). Delivery favors rhythmic build, anaphora, and projected direct address, drawing on Beat reading culture, Black Arts spoken word, and hip-hop cadence; Saul Williams and HBO's Def Poetry Jam carried the style to wide audiences.

items.name: Greek tragedy chorus declamation
items.lineage: Choral declamation of Athenian tragedy, 5th century BCE, performed by a chorus of twelve (later fifteen under Sophocles) in the circular orchestra of the Theatre of Dionysus during the City Dionysia festival. The chorus of the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides moved between spoken dialogue, chanted anapestic recitation for entrances (parodos) and exits, and fully sung strophic odes accompanied by the aulos, with strophe and antistrophe mirrored in dance. No notated choral music survives beyond fragments, so modern practice is scholarly reconstruction, staged today in surviving open-air stone theatres such as Epidaurus, where unison declamation projected without amplification remains the defining sound.

items.name: Victorian melodrama narration
items.lineage: Heightened declamatory stage narration of 19th-century British melodrama and pantomime, the dominant popular theatre of Victorian London houses such as the Adelphi and Drury Lane. The form takes its name from melos plus drama: spoken text delivered over and between orchestral incidental-music cues, with 'melos' stings underscoring villain entrances, agitatos for chases, and tremolando strings beneath emotional speeches, so the narrator-actor's projected, rhetorically exaggerated delivery is timed against the pit. Dion Boucicault's plays and Henry Irving's celebrated vehicle The Bells (1871) exemplify the style, and the earliest sound recordings of veteran Victorian-trained actors preserve its swooping, oratorical cadence.

items.name: Manchu shamanic seance chant
items.lineage: Trance-seance chant of Manchu and related Tungusic peoples of Manchuria (northeast China) and adjacent Siberia — the culture from whose language the word 'shaman' (saman) entered Western usage. In the seance the shaman invokes clan and wild spirits in pulsed chanted verse driven by a hand-held frame drum and jingling waist bells, building toward possession-trance, with assistants answering the shaman's calls in fixed responses. Domestic clan rites were codified under the Qing dynasty in an imperially commissioned 18th-century ritual code, while the ecstatic wild-spirit seances survived in village practice; S. M. Shirokogoroff's Psychomental Complex of the Tungus (1935) remains the canonical ethnographic documentation.

items.name: Yoruba dùndún surrogate speech
items.lineage: Surrogate-speech practice of the Yoruba dùndún hourglass tension-drum family of southwestern Nigeria, in which the lead ìyá ìlù drummer squeezes the drum's lacing cords to glide pitch across the three tone levels of spoken Yoruba, literally 'talking' proverbs (òwe), oríkì praise epithets, and Ifá verses to listeners who decode the drummed speech. Drumming is the hereditary craft of àyàn lineages, who trace their art to the drum ancestor-spirit Àyàngalú, performing at royal courts, festivals, and ceremonies since at least the era of the Oyo empire. Akin Euba's monograph Yoruba Drumming: The Dùndún Tradition (1990) is the canonical scholarly study, and the idiom feeds directly into the talking-drum roles of jùjú and fújì popular music.

items.name: Proto-rap spoken word
items.lineage: Militant Black Arts Movement poetry declaimed over conga vamps in late-1960s and early-1970s New York, the most-cited direct ancestor of rap MCing. The Last Poets formed in Harlem in 1968 and their self-titled 1970 debut set traded, chanted verses over hand percussion, while Gil Scott-Heron's 'The Revolution Will Not Be Televised' first appeared on Small Talk at 125th and Lenox (Flying Dutchman, 1970) with only congas behind the voice; the Watts Prophets carried the parallel West Coast strand. The delivery is rhythmically locked to the drum pulse but spoken rather than sung, with group members answering the lead line in call-and-response, and the records circulated through Black radio and community networks into the record crates of the first Bronx DJs.

items.name: Tamil filmi / Kollywood playback
items.lineage: Tamil-language Madras (Chennai) film-song playback tradition — the Kollywood parallel canon that the catalog's hindi_filmi record explicitly scopes out — codified by Ilaiyaraaja from his 1976 debut score Annakili onward across roughly 1000 films, hand-orchestrated at a rate of about one song per session and tracked on the Madras cinema-industry scoring stages at Prasad, AVM and Gemini; the defining innovation is the fusion of Tamil village folk idiom (gaana, villuppattu, therukoothu and the nadaswaram-thavil temple-and-wedding repertoire) and Carnatic melakarta-raga melody with Western symphonic orchestration, functional harmony and genuine written counterpoint, heard on Mullum Malarum (1978), Sindhu Bhairavi (1985), Punnagai Mannan (1986), Mouna Ragam (1986) and Nayakan (1987), and carried into concert form on his own How To Name It? (1986) and Nothing But Wind (1988); preceded by the Tamil music-director generation of M.S. Viswanathan and K.V. Mahadevan (1950s-1970s); voiced by the playback axis of S.P. Balasubrahmanyam (1946-2020, some 40000 recorded songs across Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Hindi) and S. Janaki (1938-), with P. Susheela, Malaysia Vasudevan, Vani Jairam and K.J. Yesudas; the core era closes with A.R. Rahman's Roja (1992), whose sampler-and-sequencer bedroom-studio method displaced the live-orchestra scoring stage and reset Tamil film sound for the 1990s. Distinct from hindi_filmi in language, industrial base (Madras rather than Bombay), Carnatic rather than Hindustani melodic source, and single-auteur rather than music-director-rotation production economy
items.description: Tamil filmi / Kollywood playback (Madras/Chennai, core era 1976-1992), the Tamil-language film-song playback canon of the South Indian cinema industry and the largest of the regional Indian film-music traditions that Bombay-centred Hindi filmi explicitly excludes. Defined by the same playback-singer division of labour as Hindi filmi (songs cut in studio by career playback voices, lip-synced on screen by actors) applied to a different musical substrate: Carnatic melakarta-raga melody and Tamil village folk idiom — gaana, villuppattu, therukoothu, koothu rhythm, and nadaswaram-and-thavil temple-and-wedding material — set under Western symphonic orchestration with functional harmony and real written counterpoint, a 40-to-60-piece string-and-wind orchestra sectioned across a multitrack film-scoring stage rather than tracked live-to-disc. Codified almost single-handedly by Ilaiyaraaja (1943-), who from his debut score Annakili (1976) wrote roughly 1000 film scores, notated every part himself, and worked at Prasad, AVM and Gemini studios in Madras at a pace of about one song per session: Mullum Malarum (1978), Sindhu Bhairavi (1985), Punnagai Mannan (1986), Mouna Ragam (1986), Nayakan (1987), with the parallel concert projects How To Name It? (1986) and Nothing But Wind (1988) making the Bach-and-Tyagaraja synthesis explicit. Predecessor music directors M.S. Viswanathan and K.V. Mahadevan established the Tamil playback orchestra in the 1950s-60s; the singer canon runs through S.P. Balasubrahmanyam (1946-2020, roughly 40000 songs in five languages, the defining male playback voice of the era) and S. Janaki (1938-), with P. Susheela, Malaysia Vasudevan, Vani Jairam and K.J. Yesudas. The era ends with A.R. Rahman's Roja (1992), whose sampler, sequencer and multitracked-vocal method retired the live scoring-stage orchestra. Distinguished from hindi_filmi by Tamil language, Madras rather than Bombay industrial base, Carnatic rather than Hindustani raga source, and a single-auteur rather than rotating-music-director production economy — hindi_filmi's own scope note names the Tamil, Telugu, Bengali and Malayalam canons as out of its bounds, and this record fills that gap; distinguished from Carnatic classical by three-minute song form, fixed notated arrangement and absence of manodharma improvisation; distinguished from Tamil folk song by studio orchestra, professional playback voice and cinema-commercial transmission.

items.name: French touch / filter house
items.lineage: Parisian filter-house tradition running from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s, built from disco, funk and soul loops lifted off vinyl into an Ensoniq ASR-10 or Akai sampler and reshaped by resonant band-pass and low-pass filter sweeps, phasing and heavy kick-keyed pumping compression, the filter gesture itself carrying the arrangement — codified through Motorbass (Philippe Zdar and Étienne de Crécy, Pansoul 1996), de Crécy's Super Discount (1996) and the Solid label, Thomas Bangalter and Daft Punk (Da Funk on Soma 1995, Homework 1997, Discovery 2001) and Bangalter's Roulé label (Spinal Scratch 1995, Trax on da Rocks 1995-1997), Alan Braxe (Vertigo 1997), Stardust's Music Sounds Better With You (Roulé 1998, Bangalter with Braxe and Benjamin Diamond over a Chaka Khan Fate loop), Cassius (Zdar with Hubert "Boom Bass" Blanc-Francard, the album 1999 in 1999), Bob Sinclar (Gym Tonic 1998), Alex Gopher (The Child 1999), Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo's Crydamoure, and Modjo (Lady Hear Me Tonight 2000, over Chic's Soup for One); an apartment-studio culture with no tracking room and no live band, summing sampled loops through a colored analog desk to DAT and cutting the club 12-inch at Paris lacquer houses
items.description: French touch, the Paris filter-house tradition (codified 1995-2001 and commercially peaking 1998-2001 around Thomas Bangalter's Roulé label, Étienne de Crécy and Alex Gopher's Solid, Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo's Crydamoure, and the Virgin-backed Source imprint). Defined by a four-on-the-floor house frame at roughly 118-130 BPM carrying a two-to-eight-bar disco, funk or soul loop sampled off vinyl rather than replayed, with the loop's extended seventh-and-ninth harmony inherited from 1970s Philadelphia and New York disco left intact as the entire chord progression; by resonant band-pass and low-pass filter sweeps opened and closed by hand across that loop so the filter, not new material, produces the build and the drop; by aggressive bus compression keyed to the kick, giving the audible ducking pump that is the style's fingerprint; by phaser, flanger and retained vinyl saturation and hiss as timbre; and by vocoder and talkbox toplines in the later Daft Punk and Modjo phase. Landmark records are Motorbass's Pansoul (1996), de Crécy's Super Discount (1996), Daft Punk's Homework (1997), Alan Braxe's Vertigo (1997), Stardust's Music Sounds Better With You (1998) and Modjo's Lady (Hear Me Tonight) (2000). Distinguished from Chicago house by its sampled-loop rather than drum-machine-programmed foundation and its French disco-crate source material; distinguished from contemporaneous American filtered disco house (Masters at Work, Armand Van Helden) by the tight Paris label network and by the extremity of the filter-and-pump gesture; distinguished from later nu-disco and future funk by predating them and by its analog apartment-studio chain rather than in-the-box revivalism.
exemplars: Stardust — Music Sounds Better With You (1998)

items.name: Urbano latino
items.lineage: Pan-Hispanic commercial umbrella consolidated around 2015-2020 across the Miami-San Juan-Medellín label axis (Rimas, Sony Latin, Universal Music Latino) as reggaetón, Latin trap and dancehall-pop merged into one radio-and-streaming format — 88-96 BPM dembow or halftime trap grids, TR-808 sub-glides, Auto-Tuned Spanish hooks doubled in stacked thirds, minor-key four-chord synth loops, and sung-rapped verses over near-identical percussion programming regardless of subgenre origin
items.description: Urbano latino is the industry-level category that absorbed reggaetón, Latin trap, dembow and Spanish-language dancehall into a single commercial format after 2015, driven by streaming playlisting rather than a single scene. Its sonic signature is a fully in-the-box build: a programmed dembow or trap kit, a sub-heavy 808 line carrying the harmony, four-bar minor loops, and heavily tuned lead vocals stacked into wide hook choruses. It differs from reggaetón proper by not committing to the dembow pattern, and from Latin trap by keeping the melodic pop chorus as the structural centre.

items.name: Música mexicana (modern regional umbrella)
items.lineage: Streaming-era umbrella term adopted around 2020-2023 for the whole modern regional-Mexican field — banda sinaloense, norteño-sax, sierreño, mariachi-pop and corridos tumbados marketed together out of Culiacán, Guadalajara and Los Angeles by labels such as Rancho Humilde, Street Mob and Fonovisa — unified by 2/4 polka and 3/4 vals frames, tuba or tololoche bass on the downbeat with bajo sexto offbeats, twin-trumpet or requinto lead lines, and plain-toned chest-voice duet singing in close thirds
items.description: Música mexicana is the 2020s marketing-and-scene label under which banda, norteño, sierreño and tumbado acts are grouped, after regional Mexican music became one of the fastest-growing streaming categories in the US. Sonically it retains the polka and vals metric backbone, the tuba-or-tololoche downbeat, bajo sexto or requinto chording, and unadorned paired vocals, but is now tracked to a modern loudness-normalized digital chain rather than the mid-century Mexico City orchestral chain. It is broader than banda sinaloense or norteño alone, and distinct from Tejano in retaining the Mexican rather than Texan instrumentation and diction.

items.name: Permanent wave
items.lineage: Retroactive streaming-derived category for the durable Anglo-American alternative-rock mainstream of roughly 1991-2010 — the post-Nevermind radio format built by Nirvana, Radiohead, Foo Fighters, Muse and Coldplay — characterized by mid-tempo 90-140 BPM 4/4 backbeats, quiet-verse/loud-chorus dynamics driven by pedal switching between clean single-coil arpeggios and saturated humbucker power chords, close-miked dry drums, and unornamented mid-range male lead vocals doubled at the chorus
items.description: Permanent wave names the alternative-rock lineage that stayed on mainstream rock radio continuously from the early 1990s onward, absorbing grunge, Britpop and post-Britpop stadium rock into one long-lived format. The sound is a four-piece band tracked in a large commercial room to a late-analog or hybrid digital chain: dry backbeat kit, clean-to-distorted guitar dynamic contrast, root-motion bass, and a plainly recorded lead voice carrying an anthemic chorus. It is broader and more radio-oriented than grunge, and less abrasive than noise rock or 1980s American indie, from which it inherits its verse-chorus dynamic device.
exemplars: Coldplay — A Rush of Blood to the Head

items.name: Sierreño
items.lineage: Acoustic trio format from the Sierra Madre Occidental (Sinaloa, Durango, Chihuahua) that spread through Southern California Mexican-American communities in the 1990s-2000s — requinto or twelve-string lead guitar picking the melody, second guitar strumming the 2/4 polka or 3/4 vals rhythm, and tuba or tololoche walking the bass, under two unornamented chest voices in parallel thirds narrating corridos at 90-130 BPM with no drum kit at all
items.description: Sierreño is the stripped acoustic corrido format of the western Sierra Madre, built on a requinto or twelve-string lead line, a strummed rhythm guitar, and a tuba or tololoche bass, with no percussion. Two voices sing in close parallel thirds with flat, conversational delivery, letting the narrative text dominate. It differs from norteño by dropping the accordion and drum kit, and from banda by replacing the whole brass ensemble with a single bass horn and guitars — a sparseness that made it the direct acoustic template for corridos tumbados.
exemplars: Los Plebes del Rancho de Ariel Camacho

items.name: Mellow gold
items.lineage: Soft-rock AM-radio format of roughly 1970-1980 centred on Los Angeles session infrastructure (Wrecking Crew successors, Sunset Sound, Village Recorder) and singer-songwriter labels Asylum and A&M — mid-tempo 70-110 BPM 4/4 with brushed or lightly damped kit, warm compressed electric bass, Rhodes and acoustic guitar beds, extended seventh and ninth harmony borrowed from jazz-pop, string or horn sweetening, and close-miked conversational lead vocals with tight background stacks
items.description: Mellow gold is the smooth, adult-oriented soft-rock mainstream of the 1970s, produced largely in Los Angeles by session players and multitrack-era engineers for AM and early FM formats. Its markers are restrained dynamics, warm tape-compressed low end, Rhodes and acoustic guitar textures, jazz-inflected extended chords, and intimate lead vocals surrounded by carefully blended harmony stacks. It is quieter and more harmonically sophisticated than mainstream 1970s rock, and more band-oriented and less orchestral than easy listening or countrypolitan.

items.name: Corridos tumbados
items.lineage: Fusion codified in 2019-2020 by Natanael Cano and the Rancho Humilde label in Los Angeles and Hermosillo, grafting trap-rap phrasing, cadence and lyric attitude onto the sierreño acoustic trio — requinto lead over strummed rhythm guitar and tuba or tololoche bass at 70-100 BPM, sometimes with added 808 sub and trap hi-hat rolls, and rapped-sung nasal lead vocals with light Auto-Tune narrating contemporary narco and flex themes
items.description: Corridos tumbados emerged around 2019 when young Sonoran and Los Angeles artists kept the sierreño acoustic instrumentation but adopted trap vocal cadence, slang and occasionally 808 sub-bass and hi-hat rolls. The result is a hybrid where a requinto still carries the melodic hook and a tuba still marks the bass, but the vocal is delivered in loose rapped-sung phrases with mild pitch correction rather than the squared-off ballad diction of the traditional corrido. It is distinguished from plain sierreño by that vocal rhythm and production, and from Latin trap by keeping acoustic strings and horn bass as the primary instrumentation.

items.name: Reggaetón colombiano
items.lineage: Medellín-centred variant that took over the reggaetón mainstream between 2010 and 2020 through producers Sky Rompiendo, Ovy on the Drums and Mosty working with J Balvin, Maluma and Karol G — softening the Puerto Rican dembow into a lighter 90-96 BPM pattern with brushed shaker and rim-click layers, foregrounding major-key or bright-minor synth and plucked-guitar loops, and replacing hard rapped delivery with melodic paisa-accented crooning and airy stacked hooks
items.description: Reggaetón colombiano is the Medellín strain of reggaetón that displaced San Juan as the genre's commercial centre in the 2010s. Its producers thinned the dembow — quieter snare, more shaker and rim layers, more space — and built tracks around bright melodic loops and sung rather than rapped hooks, aiming at global pop radio. Against Puerto Rican reggaetón it is lighter, more major-key and more overtly pop; against urbano latino generally it stays committed to the dembow pulse rather than drifting toward trap.

items.name: Alt-Z
items.lineage: Streaming-era alternative pop category consolidated around 2018-2022 out of American and Anglo bedroom-production scenes (Billie Eilish and Finneas in Highland Park, Clairo, girl in red) — 80-110 BPM halftime or trap-derived programmed beats, sub-heavy 808 or synth bass, deliberately dry close-miked whisper-register lead vocals with audible breath and lip noise, sparse harmonic beds of detuned pads or muted guitar, and confessional first-person lyrics
items.description: Alt-Z is the Gen-Z alternative-pop format that grew out of home-studio production around 2018, defined more by vocal proximity and restraint than by any single rhythm. Tracks are typically built in a bedroom DAW: a sparse programmed beat, a dominant sub-bass, minimal harmonic filler, and a very close, very dry lead vocal sung near a whisper with breath deliberately left in the mix. It differs from mainstream pop in its low dynamic level and unpolished vocal texture, and from hyperpop in avoiding extreme processing and maximalist density.
exemplars: Billie Eilish — When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?

items.name: Indietronica
items.lineage: Indie-electronic hybrid formed circa 1999-2008 around Morr Music (Berlin), Ghostly International (Ann Arbor) and the early Postal Service axis — laptop-sequenced glitch and click percussion under live guitar, bass and analog synth, 100-130 BPM 4/4 grids with deliberately quantized micro-edits, soft untrained indie lead vocals mixed level with the beat, and sample-and-hold or granular textures used as counter-melody rather than effect
items.description: Indietronica names the turn-of-the-2000s meeting of indie-pop songwriting with laptop electronic production, associated with Morr Music, Ghostly and a cluster of American and German artists. Tracks keep verse-chorus song structure and a soft, untrained indie vocal, but the rhythm section is programmed — clicks, glitched fragments, drum machines — and synth textures replace much of the traditional band arrangement. It is more song-shaped than IDM and more electronically constructed than indie pop, sitting between the two rather than in either.
exemplars: Caribou — The Milk of Human Kindness

items.name: Rock en español
items.lineage: Spanish-language rock movement that matured across Mexico City, Buenos Aires, Santiago and Madrid in the 1980s and peaked commercially 1988-1998 through the Mexico City rock urbano scene and BMG/Sony Latin signings — post-punk and new-wave guitar textures and synth pads over 4/4 rock backbeats, frequent grafting of ska, cumbia, bolero and Andean rhythms onto rock instrumentation, and declamatory Spanish lead vocals carrying overtly political or urban-social lyrics
items.description: Rock en español is the Spanish-language rock mainstream that consolidated in Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Spain during the 1980s and became a continental commercial force in the 1990s. It combines post-punk and new-wave guitar and synth vocabulary with Latin American rhythmic borrowings — ska upstrokes, cumbia bass figures, bolero ballad forms — and a strongly declaimed Spanish vocal usually carrying social or political content. It differs from Anglo alternative rock in that rhythmic hybridity and lyrical register, and from Latin alternative in being more straightforwardly rock-band-shaped.

items.name: K-pop boy group
items.lineage: Seoul idol-agency format codified from the mid-1990s (SM Entertainment's H.O.T., 1996) and industrialized through SM, YG, JYP, Big Hit and HYBE — multi-member male ensembles performing 100-130 BPM hybrid tracks that cut between rap verses, sung pre-choruses and a hook-dense chorus, over EDM, trap or new-jack-swing programming, with dense multitracked unison-and-harmony vocal stacks, sharp English-Korean code-switching, and arrangements written to synchronized choreography
items.description: The K-pop boy group is a production format as much as a genre: a trained multi-member male ensemble recording songs assembled by international writing camps and finished in Seoul agency studios. Tracks are structurally restless, switching between rap, sung melody, chant-like hooks and a post-chorus dance break, and are mixed with very dense stacked vocals against club-derived programming. Compared with K-pop girl-group production it leans harder on rap sections and low-end weight, and compared with Western boy bands it uses far more abrupt sectional contrast and hip-hop vocabulary.

items.name: Agronejo
items.lineage: Brazilian sertanejo substrain named in the late 2010s around Goiás and Mato Grosso agribusiness culture and its rodeo-festival circuit — mid-tempo 90-120 BPM sertanejo universitário arrangements of viola caipira, acoustic guitar, accordion and full drum kit, with major-key parallel-third duet singing, big live-DVD stadium mixes, and lyrics explicitly celebrating farm, cattle, pickup-truck and rural-proprietor identity
items.description: Agronejo is the agribusiness-identified branch of Brazilian sertanejo that took shape in the late 2010s on the Centre-West rodeo and agro-festival circuit. Musically it is sertanejo universitário — viola caipira and acoustic guitar over a full pop-country rhythm section, sung in the traditional two-voice parallel-third duet — but its repertoire is thematically dedicated to farming, cattle, machinery and rural wealth, and much of its canon is released as arena live recordings rather than studio albums. It differs from sertanejo raiz by its electrified pop-country arrangement and from sertanejo universitário generally only in lyrical program and festival context.

items.name: Trap argentino
items.lineage: Buenos Aires trap scene that grew directly out of the El Quinto Escalón freestyle battle plaza (Parque Rivadavia, 2012-2017) and turned professional 1017-1019 through Duki, Bizarrap and Neo Pistea — 130-150 BPM halftime trap grids with rolled hi-hats and long 808 glides, dark minor-key synth loops, heavy Auto-Tune on rioplatense-accented Spanish, and lunfardo battle-rap diction carried over from freestyle into melodic song forms
items.description: Trap argentino is the Buenos Aires branch of Spanish-language trap, unusual in having grown out of a live freestyle-battle culture — El Quinto Escalón — rather than a studio scene, which left its lyricism sharper and more competitive than most urbano. Productions are bedroom-DAW trap: halftime kick placement, triplet hi-hat rolls, long detuned 808 glides, spare minor synth motifs, and saturated Auto-Tune on a distinctly rioplatense accent. It is distinguished from Puerto Rican Latin trap by that accent and lunfardo vocabulary, and from reggaetón by rejecting the dembow pattern outright.

items.name: UK Dance
items.lineage: British commercial dance-pop consolidated in London and Manchester from the late 2000s as garage, house and drum-and-bass producers crossed into the singles chart — Duke Dumont, Disclosure, Rudimental, Gorgon City, Sigala and Chase & Status codifying a 120-128 BPM four-on-the-floor (or 174 BPM liquid D&B) template built on filtered piano-and-organ house stabs, sidechained sub-bass, chopped garage-swing hi-hats and a full-throated guest topline sung rather than rapped.
items.description: UK dance is the British radio-facing wing of club music, formed in the late 2000s when the country's garage and house undergrounds were absorbed into the pop singles market. It is defined by a swung or shuffled hi-hat grid inherited from 2-step, hard sidechain pumping under piano and organ stabs, and a soul-trained guest vocalist carrying a full verse-chorus song form rather than a looped sample. Against American EDM it is warmer and more song-shaped, with less white-noise buildup and drop architecture; against deep house it is faster, brighter and structurally conventional.

items.name: Adult Standards
items.lineage: American mid-century popular-song repertoire — the Tin Pan Alley and Broadway catalogue as sung by post-swing crooners in New York and Hollywood between roughly 1946 and 1965, codified by Sinatra's Capitol concept albums with Nelson Riddle and Gordon Jenkins: 32-bar AABA and ABAC forms at ballad-to-medium-swing tempos, lush string-and-reed orchestration with muted brass punctuation, brushed kit and walking bass, and a conversational baritone delivery that treats lyric diction and rubato phrasing as the primary expressive instrument.
items.description: Adult standards is the postwar performance culture built around the American songbook, cut live to tape in large New York and Hollywood rooms with a singer standing in front of a full arranged orchestra. Its sonic signature is a tube-condenser close vocal riding over strings, muted brass and brushed drums, with the arrangement's dynamic swell rather than percussion carrying the song's shape. It differs from big-band swing in that the band accompanies rather than competes, and from later easy listening in that the vocalist's rhythmic liberties and lyric-reading remain the point.
exemplars: Frank Sinatra — In the Wee Small Hours
Ella Fitzgerald — Sings the Cole Porter Song Book
Nat King Cole — Love Is the Thing

items.name: Post-Teen Pop
items.lineage: North American and British mainstream pop of the 2010s made by artists who graduated out of teen-idol machinery into adult authorship — Ariana Grande, Selena Gomez, Demi Lovato, Halsey and Shawn Mendes working with Max Martin, Ilya Salmanzadeh and Ryan Tedder — built at 90-110 BPM on trap-derived hi-hat rolls and 808 sub-bass under sparse keyboard-and-plucked-synth beds, with stacked, heavily comped, lightly retuned vocal arrangements and whisper-to-whistle-register dynamic staging replacing the four-on-the-floor of prior teen pop.
items.description: Post-teen pop names the 2010s style of former teen-market singers whose records absorbed hip-hop and R&B rhythm while keeping pop song architecture. Sonically it is spare and vocal-forward: 808 sub-bass and rolled trap hi-hats under thin synth pads, with the majority of the frequency spectrum given over to a dense, multitracked lead vocal carrying melisma and register shifts. Compared with the boy-band and bubblegum pop it descends from, it is slower, harmonically flatter, less chorus-band-driven and far more dependent on vocal production as the arrangement itself.

items.name: Grupera
items.lineage: Mexican regional-popular style formed in Michoacán, Sinaloa and Nuevo León across the late 1970s and 1980s and codified by Los Bukis, Bronco, Los Temerarios and Los Yonic's — small self-contained 'grupos' replacing the mariachi and banda ensembles with electric bass, drum kit, electric guitar and layered polyphonic synthesizer, playing rancheras, cumbias and romantic baladas at 90-130 BPM under a plaintive lead tenor with close-harmony backing and openly sentimental lyric content.
items.description: Grupera emerged in provincial Mexico in the late 1970s as touring dance groups downsized from horn-and-string ensembles to a synthesizer-led combo that one van could carry. The defining sound is a bright polyphonic-synth pad and lead line doubling the melody over a simple kit-and-electric-bass ranchera or cumbia pulse, with a high, emotionally unguarded male lead and thirds-harmony backing vocals mixed close. It is distinguished from banda sinaloense by the absence of a brass section, from norteño by the demotion of the accordion to a colour rather than the lead, and from bolero by its dance-floor tempo.
exemplars: Los Bukis — Me Volví a Acordar de Ti
Los Temerarios — Mi Vida Eres Tú

items.name: OPM (Original Pilipino Music)
items.lineage: Filipino popular song codified in Manila from the mid-1970s through the Metro Manila Popular Music Festival and the work of Ryan Cayabyab, Freddie Aguilar, APO Hiking Society and later Eraserheads and Rivermaya — Tagalog-language verse-chorus writing over a Western pop-rock and soft-rock instrumentation of piano, clean electric guitar, electric bass and kit at 70-120 BPM, with wide-interval, high-tessitura melodies engineered for full-throated belting and dense stacked backing harmony inherited from the country's choral and vocal-group culture.
items.description: OPM is the umbrella term for Tagalog-language popular songwriting that emerged in Manila during the 1970s as a deliberate nationalist alternative to imported Anglo-American pop. Its recordings favour piano or acoustic guitar foundations, restrained kit, sweetened string-machine or synth pads, and above all a soaring belted lead vocal with wide leaps and sustained high climaxes, supported by tight multi-part backing harmony. It differs from Cantopop and J-pop in its rock-band rather than orchestral-arranger foundation, and from Anglo soft rock in its melodic reach and its lyric register of direct sentiment.

items.name: Boy Band
items.lineage: Manager-assembled male vocal-group pop running from Motown-era harmony acts through New Kids on the Block, and codified between 1993 and 2001 by Backstreet Boys and NSYNC recording with Denniz PoP and Max Martin at Cheiron Studios Stockholm — four or five non-instrumentalist singers trading lead lines over a 90-110 BPM programmed R&B-swing or four-on-the-floor track of sampled kit, slap-and-sub bass, sawtooth pad stacks and orchestral-hit punctuation, with block-harmony choruses and a mandatory unaccompanied a-cappella breakdown.
items.description: The boy band is a production format rather than a scene: a vocal-only male group whose records are assembled by a writer-producer team around traded solo lines and massed block harmony. The Cheiron-era template that fixed the sound uses gated programmed drums, a compressed synth bass on the octave, layered saw pads, and an unusually loud, dry, heavily doubled vocal stack sitting well above the track. It separates from 1960s girl groups by its programmed rather than live rhythm section, and from post-teen pop by its density, faster tempos, and reliance on group harmony over a single star vocalist.

items.name: Stomp and Holler
items.lineage: Anglo-American indie-folk revival style of roughly 2008-2015 — Mumford & Sons, The Lumineers, Of Monsters and Men, Edward Sharpe and The Head and the Heart — built on strummed dreadnought guitar and clawhammer or rolled banjo at 100-140 BPM, a kick-drum-and-tambourine floor pulse played by the singers themselves, communal 'hey!' shouts and massed unison choruses, and a soft-verse-to-full-band-crescendo dynamic arc borrowed from post-rock and applied to acoustic instrumentation.
items.description: Stomp and holler is the arena-scaled acoustic revival that dominated Anglo-American festival billing around 2010, taking string-band instrumentation and playing it with rock dynamics. Its markers are a driving eighth-note strum, banjo used as a rhythmic texture rather than a soloing voice, a bass drum stomped on every beat, handclaps and gang shouts, and an arrangement that withholds the full band until an explosive final chorus. It is distinguished from bluegrass by the absence of instrumental soloing and high-lonesome modality, and from earlier indie folk by its sheer volume and communal chorus writing.
exemplars: Of Monsters and Men — My Head Is an Animal
Edward Sharpe and the Magnetic Zeros — Up from Below

items.name: Contemporary Christian Music
items.lineage: American evangelical pop-rock formed out of the late-1960s California Jesus Movement and Maranatha! Music, professionalized in Nashville through the 1980s by Amy Grant, Michael W. Smith and Steven Curtis Chapman, and re-founded in the 2000s as congregational 'modern worship' by Hillsong, Chris Tomlin and Bethel — 68-80 or 130-140 BPM, delay-drenched arpeggiated electric guitar over piano pads and four-on-the-floor kit, diatonic I-V-vi-IV loops in singable narrow-range keys, and a build-to-anthemic-bridge form designed for a congregation to join.
items.description: CCM is evangelical Protestant devotional music written and recorded to mainstream pop-rock production standards, centred on Nashville and, since the 2000s, on the megachurch worship-album pipeline. The characteristic sound is a washed, dotted-eighth-delay guitar figure over sustained piano and pad, an unhurried kit, and a lead vocal in a comfortable middle register singing four-chord diatonic loops with lyrics addressed in the second person to God. It parts from Black gospel in its avoidance of blue notes, melisma and call-and-response, and from Southern gospel in dropping quartet harmony for solo-plus-congregation texture.

items.name: Hip Pop
items.lineage: American crossover style of roughly 1998-2010 in which pop and R&B singers built records on hip-hop production and rap features — Nelly, Ne-Yo, Fergie, Gwen Stefani and Chris Brown working with The Neptunes, Timbaland, Jermaine Dupri and will.i.am — using 88-105 BPM programmed breakbeats, syncopated 808 and Moog sub-bass, staccato synth-and-keyboard riffs and chopped vocal samples under a sung hook, with a guest rapper occupying the middle-eight in place of an instrumental solo.
items.description: Hip pop describes the turn-of-the-millennium fusion in which chart pop adopted rap production wholesale while retaining a sung hook and verse-chorus structure. Its production hallmarks are dry, tightly quantized programmed drums with prominent handclap or snare on the backbeat, a melodic sub-bass line doubling the riff, spare percussive keyboard motifs, and an obligatory rapped guest verse. It differs from contemporary R&B in its harder, sparser rhythm-first arrangements and from hip-hop proper in that the rapper is a featured guest rather than the record's author and voice.
exemplars: Gwen Stefani — Love. Angel. Music. Baby.

items.name: Piano Rock
items.lineage: Anglo-American rock strain in which an acoustic or upright piano rather than electric guitar carries the riff and harmony, running from Little Richard and Jerry Lee Lewis through its 1970s codification by Elton John with Gus Dudgeon and Paul Buckmaster, Billy Joel and Randy Newman, and its 1990s-2000s revival by Ben Folds Five, Keane and The Fray — mid-tempo 90-130 BPM rock-band backing under octave-doubled left-hand bass patterns, gospel-derived suspended and inverted triads, hammered eighth-note chordal comping and an unguarded belted lead vocal.
items.description: Piano rock inverts the standard rock hierarchy by putting a struck-string keyboard at the front of the arrangement, with guitar reduced to colour or removed entirely. The recorded sound depends on a stereo-miked grand tracked live with the rhythm section in a large room, its low octaves reinforcing the bass and its right hand supplying both riff and pad, frequently with an added string arrangement. Compared with singer-songwriter piano ballads it keeps a full backbeat kit and rock dynamics; compared with boogie-woogie or barrelhouse it works from major-key pop and gospel voicings rather than twelve-bar blues.
exemplars: Elton John — Goodbye Yellow Brick Road
Ben Folds Five — Whatever and Ever Amen
The Fray — How to Save a Life

items.name: Metropopolis
items.lineage: Algorithmically named 2010s internet-era style of sleek electro-funk pop, made largely in home studios across Los Angeles, Auckland and Tokyo-facing online scenes and shaped by Tuxedo, Yumi Zouma, Anderson .Paak's polished side and the Japanese city-pop and French-touch revivalists — 100-118 BPM programmed or tightly played funk kit with a clean sixteenth-note hi-hat, slap or synth-octave bass, glassy FM electric-piano and chorused clean guitar chords, and a light, close, often processed or vocoded lead vocal singing over lush major-seventh and ninth harmony.
items.description: Metropopolis is a 2010s streaming-era category for glossy, urban-evoking synth pop that reworks late-1970s and 1980s boogie, city pop and French touch through modern in-the-box production. Its signature is warm FM electric-piano and chorused clean guitar over a soft-clipped funk drum programme and a melodic bass line, with reverb kept short and the mix polished, never lo-fi. It is more harmonically rich and slower than nu-disco, more song-based than future funk's sample-chop approach, and cooler and more restrained in vocal delivery than mainstream synth pop.
exemplars: Toro y Moi — Anything in Return

items.name: Europop
items.lineage: Continental European chart pop consolidated between the mid-1970s and the late 1990s through the Eurovision circuit, ABBA's Polar Studios records with Michael B. Tretow, Italo-disco, Stock Aitken Waterman's London hit factory and the Scandinavian and Benelux dance-pop of Ace of Base, Aqua and Dr. Alban — 118-140 BPM four-on-the-floor kick with offbeat eighth-note keyboard or hi-hat, unambiguous major-key diatonic progressions, English-as-second-language lyrics chosen for phonetic clarity, and glossy multi-tracked unison-and-thirds choruses.
items.description: Europop is the pan-continental commercial pop idiom that grew out of Eurovision, Schlager and Italo-disco and reached its peak in Scandinavian and Benelux studios between the 1980s and late 1990s. The sound is deliberately bright and frictionless: a hard four-on-the-floor kick with an offbeat keyboard stab, saturated polysynth and string-machine pads, a prominent melodic bass, and stacked, precisely tuned choral hooks sung in accented English. It differs from Anglo-American pop of the same period in its avoidance of blues inflection and its preference for major-key stepwise melody built for cross-language singability.

items.name: Urbano Español
items.lineage: Spanish-state urban music consolidated in Madrid, Barcelona and Sevilla from roughly 2015, when the trap generation around PXXR GVNG, Yung Beef and Bad Gyal and the flamenco-schooled work of Rosalía with El Guincho and C. Tangana with Alizzz fused Puerto Rican reggaetón and Atlanta trap with palmas, cante jondo melisma and copla lyric idiom — 90-100 BPM dembow or halftime trap grids, 808 sub-bass and rolled hi-hats layered against handclap compás, Andalusian-cadence guitar, and Auto-Tuned melismatic vocals in caló-inflected Castilian.
items.description: Urbano español is the Spanish-state branch of Latin urban music that emerged after 2015 by grafting Andalusian flamenco practice onto reggaetón and trap production. Its distinguishing feature is rhythmic bilingualism: an 808-driven dembow or halftime trap pattern running against, or dropping out entirely for, hand-clapped twelve-beat compás, with the vocal carrying flamenco melisma and quejío under Auto-Tune. It is separated from Puerto Rican reggaetón and Latin trap by that flamenco harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary, the Phrygian Andalusian cadence, and a Castilian rather than Caribbean lyric register.

items.name: Anison (anime song)
items.lineage: Japanese screen-tied popular song formed with television animation in Tokyo from 1963 (Tetsuwan Atomu) and industrialized as a distinct chart category from the late 1970s through Columbia, Nippon Animation and later King Records — brisk 130-180 BPM major-key song forms with a compulsory 90-second edit, brass-and-string sweetened rock rhythm section, wide-interval anthemic choruses sung in bright forward head-voice, and modulating final choruses that lift a semitone or a whole tone
items.description: Anison is the Japanese anime-song industry that grew out of 1960s television theme production and became a self-sustaining commercial genre by the 1980s, with dedicated singers (Ichiro Mizuki, Akira Kushida) and later idol and rock crossover acts. Sonically it is defined by the 90-second broadcast edit, a maximalist arrangement stacking distorted guitar, brass and synth strings under a very forward vocal, cadence-heavy harmony borrowed from kayōkyoku, and the truck-driver key change at the last chorus. It differs from general J-pop by its narrative obligation to a series and by the hyperactive tempo and near-symphonic density that fit a title sequence; it differs from Western cartoon themes by being released as chart singles by career recording artists.

items.name: Soundtrack (hybrid screen scoring)
items.lineage: Contemporary film, television and game underscore as codified in Los Angeles and London from the mid-1990s by Hans Zimmer's Media Ventures and its descendants — sample-library and live-orchestra hybrids built to picture in a DAW, ostinato-driven minor-modal cells at 100-140 BPM, sub-bass braams and processed percussion loops layered under divisi strings, cues locked to timecode with click and stem-delivered for the dub stage
items.description: Hybrid screen scoring is the dominant post-1995 practice of writing to picture in a sequencer with sampled orchestra, then overdubbing live players and processing the result as a production rather than a performance. Its markers are static harmony over pedal points, short repeating rhythmic cells that can be stretched to any cue length, heavily compressed low percussion, and synthetic sub-bass and reverse swells welded to string writing. It differs from traditional orchestral soundtrack in that the sound design and the notes are authored together and mixed in stems for the film dub, and it differs from concert art music in being subordinate to edit points and dialogue frequency space.

items.name: Orchestral Soundtrack (symphonic film score)
items.lineage: Symphonic screen music codified at the Hollywood studio orchestras between 1933 and 1960 by Max Steiner, Erich Korngold and Alfred Newman out of late-Romantic Viennese practice, revived in 1977 by John Williams — full 70-100 piece orchestra recorded live to picture on a scoring stage, leitmotivic theme-and-transformation writing, rubato cues conducted to streamers and punches, and brass-and-string tutti climaxes with harp and celesta coloration
items.description: The orchestral soundtrack is the symphonic underscore tradition established on the Hollywood scoring stages in the 1930s and renewed from Star Wars onward, written in full score and performed live by a conducted orchestra to projected picture. It is marked by leitmotif — named themes transformed in mode, orchestration and tempo across a film — chromatic late-Romantic harmony, and a tutti sound built around horns, divisi strings and a wide natural hall image captured with a Decca tree. Against hybrid scoring it uses no synthetic layer and derives its motion from harmonic development rather than looped cells; against concert symphonic writing it is cut into two- to four-minute cues shaped by dramatic timing rather than sonata argument.

items.name: R&B français
items.lineage: French-language contemporary R&B formed in Paris around 1996-2002 through Wallen, Matt Houston and the Secteur Ä and Alliance Ethnik orbits, revived after 2015 by Aya Nakamura and Dadju — mid-tempo 85-100 BPM programmed swing with Antillean zouk and coupé-décalé rhythmic inflection, layered close-harmony backing stacks, sung-rapped melisma over minor-seventh keyboard pads, and hooks alternating French, Nouchi and Lingala
items.description: R&B français is the francophone branch of contemporary R&B that took shape in Paris in the late 1990s alongside the rap scene it shares studios and features with, and that returned to dominance after 2015 with Aya Nakamura and Dadju. The sound keeps American R&B's stacked vocal harmony and extended minor-seventh harmony but sits it on Afro-Caribbean rhythm — zouk guitar figures, coupé-décalé hi-hat patterns, and a lighter kick than US productions — with lyrics moving fluidly between French, Lingala, Arabic and Antillean Creole. It is distinguished from US contemporary R&B by that rhythmic base and multilingual delivery, and from Afrobeats by its ballad-weighted song forms and heavier vocal layering.

items.name: Trap Triste (Latin melancholic trap)
items.lineage: Spanish-language melancholic trap crystallized in San Juan, Medellín and Madrid around 2016-2019 through Bad Bunny's early SoundCloud sides, Duki and Cazzu — 130-145 BPM half-time trap with rolled hi-hats and long 808 glides, minor-key detuned piano or guitar loops soaked in reverb, and heavily Auto-Tuned confessional vocals about heartbreak and dissociation delivered in a slurred, near-spoken register
items.description: Trap triste is the melancholic wing of Latin trap that surfaced on SoundCloud and YouTube between 2016 and 2019 across Puerto Rico, Argentina, Colombia and Spain.
