It differs from easy listening in that the song, not the mood, is the object, and from film scoring in that everything serves a sung verse-chorus form.

items.name: Popera (classical crossover)
items.lineage: Classical-crossover repertoire consolidated in Britain and Italy from the late 1980s — Sarah Brightman with Andrew Lloyd Webber, then Andrea Bocelli, Il Divo assembled by Simon Cowell in 2003, Katherine Jenkins and Josh Groban — pairing conservatory-trained operatic and legit-musical vocal production, sustained high tessitura and portamento, with pop ballad forms at 60-80 BPM, DAW-assembled orchestral and synth-orchestral beds, wide plate reverb and multitrack choir, sung largely in Italian and Spanish regardless of the singers' origins.
items.description: Popera is the late-twentieth-century commercial genre in which operatically or legit-trained voices sing pop ballads over orchestral backing, built for arena tours and television specials from the late 1980s onward. Sonically it is defined by an extremely close, heavily compressed lead vocal using operatic breath support and vibrato but no unamplified projection, a large orchestral bed that is usually a hybrid of recorded strings and sampled libraries, and a wet, long-tailed reverb field that suggests a hall the recording never occupied. It is separated from opera proper by its microphone-dependent technique, verse-chorus forms and lack of dramatic context, and from orchestral pop by its foregrounded classical vocal training and its digital rather than live-room production.

items.name: Psychedelic Pop
items.lineage: Studio-centred pop written under the influence of 1966-1969 psychedelia in London and Los Angeles — the Beatles of Revolver, the Beach Boys of Smile, the Zombies, the Left Banke, the Small Faces and Curt Boettcher's productions — retaining two-to-three-minute verse-chorus forms and close vocal harmony while adding modal and chromatic mediant harmony, Mellotron, harpsichord and sitar colour, backwards and varispeed tape, and heavy artificial double-tracking and chamber reverb on the voice.
items.description: Psychedelic pop is the melodic, song-form wing of the 1966-69 psychedelic moment: bands who kept the three-minute single and its harmony vocals but used the multitrack studio as a colouring instrument. The identifying features are unusual keyboard and world-instrument timbres (Mellotron flutes, harpsichord, sitar, tack piano), tape manipulation — reversed guitar, varispeed, flanging — chamber and plate reverb used to place sounds at different depths, and vocals doubled or ADT-treated into a glowing composite. It differs from psychedelic rock in avoiding extended jamming and volume as an end in itself, and from baroque pop in that its ornament is electro-acoustic and tape-based rather than orchestrally scored.

items.name: Space Age Pop
items.lineage: American instrumental mood music of roughly 1955-1965 written for the new stereo hi-fi market — Les Baxter, Martin Denny, Esquivel, Juan García Esquivel's RCA ping-pong stereo sessions and the Enoch Light Command Records catalogue — light Latin and lounge tempos of 80-130 BPM, exotic orchestration built on vibraphone, celesta, marimba, muted brass and theremin or Ondes Martenot, wordless cooing vocal choirs, abrupt stereo channel-to-channel effects and bird calls or percussion novelties used as arrangement punctuation.
items.description: Space age pop is the bachelor-pad instrumental mood music produced by American major labels through the stereo-demonstration boom of the late 1950s and early 1960s, closely overlapping exotica. Its identity is entirely orchestrational and technological: vibraphone, celesta, marimba and muted brass in place of a rhythm-section foreground, theremin or Ondes Martenot for the 'space' signifier, wordless choral oohs, and arrangements deliberately written so that motifs leap between the two stereo channels — Esquivel's hallmark — captured with wide tube-mic pairs at Capitol and Webster Hall. It differs from easy listening by its novelty-forward, futurist orchestration and from lounge jazz by being fully arranged with almost no improvisation.

items.name: Surf Pop (vocal surf)
items.lineage: Southern Californian vocal branch of the surf craze, 1962-1965, codified by Brian Wilson with the Beach Boys and by Jan Berry with Jan & Dean — mid-tempo 4/4 rock-and-roll at 130-165 BPM with a shuffling or straight backbeat, doo-wop and Four Freshmen-derived four- and five-part block harmony, falsetto lead, reverb-drenched single-coil guitar figures, honking sax, and Los Angeles session-player backing tracked live in small chamber-equipped rooms.
items.description: Surf pop is the sung counterpart to instrumental surf rock, made in Los Angeles between 1962 and 1965 for a teenage market built around beaches, cars and school. Its signature is dense, wide-voiced vocal harmony — jazz-choral block writing inherited from the Four Freshmen laid over a rock-and-roll rhythm section — with falsetto lead lines, spring- and chamber-reverbed guitar, and mono session tracking in small rooms fed to live echo chambers. It differs from instrumental surf, whose subject is the wet reverb guitar itself, by putting the voices in front, and from contemporaneous East Coast girl-group pop by its harmony-group rather than lead-and-answer construction and its Californian subject matter.

items.name: Traditional Pop Music
items.lineage: American and British mainstream popular song from roughly 1930 to 1955, built on Tin Pan Alley and Broadway 32-bar AABA writing by Berlin, Porter, Kern and Van Heusen, arranged for big band or lush string orchestra by Nelson Riddle, Gordon Jenkins and Axel Stordahl, and delivered by microphone-intimate crooners and torch singers at slow-to-medium swung or ballad tempos with legato phrasing, wide vibrato and conversational rubato.
items.description: Traditional pop is the pre-rock mainstream of the American and British record industry, roughly 1930 to 1955, in which professionally written 32-bar songs were sung over staff-notated big-band or string-orchestra charts. Its sound is defined by close-microphone crooning, legato phrasing with rubato, muted brass and sectional strings, and brushed drums kept low in the balance. Unlike the jazz vocal tradition it borrows repertoire from, the singer stays close to the written melody and the arrangement, not improvisation, carries the interest.

items.name: Vispop
items.lineage: Cebuano-language pop songwriting movement launched in Cebu City in 2013 by the Vispop compilation and competition series, codified by Kurt Fick, Jewel Villaflores and Kyle Wong, characterized by mid-tempo 80-110 BPM acoustic-guitar and piano ballads with unaffected conversational Bisaya vocals, simple diatonic loops and lightly programmed drums built entirely in home DAWs.
items.description: Vispop emerged in Cebu in 2013 as a deliberate campaign to make Cebuano a viable language for contemporary Philippine pop, organized around an annual songwriting competition and compilation album. The sound is deliberately plain: strummed acoustic guitar or piano, soft programmed or lightly played kit, minimal reverb, and a close, untrained-sounding lead vocal foregrounding the Bisaya lyric. It differs from Manila's Tagalog OPM mainstream chiefly in language, regional identity and its smaller, home-studio production scale.

items.name: Wonky Pop
items.lineage: British press-coined pop tendency of 2007-2010 centred on London club nights of the same name, associated with Mika, Alphabeat, Frankmusik and Little Boots, characterized by 110-130 BPM major-key synth and piano hooks, theatrical wide-interval falsetto vocals, glockenspiel and handclap ornament, abrupt key and tempo lurches, and knowingly camp arrangement borrowed from 70s glam and 80s synthpop.
items.description: Wonky pop was a short-lived UK label of the late 2000s for chart pop that used deliberately eccentric, off-kilter hooks and theatrical vocal delivery instead of the smooth R&B-derived idiom then dominant. Its markers are bright stacked synths, cabaret piano, falsetto leaps, handclaps and glockenspiel, and arrangements that change direction mid-song. Against straight synthpop revival it is more song-cycle theatrical and more harmonically restless, and against indie pop it is fully studio-constructed.

items.name: Boogie (Post-Disco)
items.lineage: New York and Los Angeles post-disco dance style of roughly 1979-1985, developed by Leon Sylvers III, Kashif and the Prelude and West End label rosters, characterized by 100-118 BPM four-on-the-floor grooves with slapped or synthesized bass ostinati, Linn and 808 drum programming layered over live kit, clipped funk guitar, Rhodes and DX-era keyboard stabs, and smooth multi-tracked group vocals on twelve-inch extended mixes.
items.description: Boogie is the electronic-leaning funk that filled the gap between disco's commercial collapse in 1979 and the rise of house, made largely for the twelve-inch single market. It is slower and sparser than disco, replaces the string orchestra with polysynth pads and brass patches, and foregrounds a melodic slap or synth bassline over drum-machine-and-kit hybrid programming. Compared with electro it keeps live players and sung song form; compared with disco it is drier, cooler and more machine-timed.

items.name: Dream House
items.lineage: Italian trance offshoot of 1995-1997 codified by Robert Miles, Gianni Bini and the DFC and Time labels, characterized by 130-140 BPM four-on-the-floor kicks with rolling offbeat bass, long reverbed piano arpeggio motifs as the lead hook, breathy wordless female vocal pads, extended filtered breakdowns and almost no rapping or verse structure.
items.description: Dream house, or dream trance, was an Italian commercial trance variant that peaked in 1996 with Robert Miles' Children. Its signature is a long, heavily reverbed diatonic piano arpeggio carrying the entire melodic weight over a 135 BPM kick and offbeat bass, with wordless vocal pads and multi-minute breakdowns. Against contemporary German trance it is softer, more consonant and piano-led rather than saw-lead driven, and against progressive house it is far more melodically explicit.

items.name: Space House
items.lineage: French and Belgian house variant of the mid-to-late 1990s associated with Alan Braxe, Stardust, I:Cube and the Roule and Versatile labels, characterized by 118-126 BPM disco-derived kicks, cosmic analogue synth arpeggios and phaser-swept pads over filtered loops, sustained vocoder or heavily processed vocal fragments, and slow-evolving one-chord builds owing more to 70s space disco than to Chicago tracks.
items.description: Space house is the cosmic wing of 1990s French touch, taking the filtered disco loop of the Paris scene and pushing it toward the wide analogue synth textures and vocoded voices of 1970s space disco. Tracks are long, largely instrumental, built on a single loop with slow filter and phaser motion rather than song sections. It is distinguished from mainstream filter house by its synthetic, non-sample-led pads and from Italo house by its cooler, more static harmonic language.

items.name: Scouse House
items.lineage: Liverpool and North West England hard-house offshoot of roughly 1997-2010, propagated through the 3 Beat and Clubland circuit and DJs such as Ultrabeat and Flip & Fill, characterized by 140-150 BPM four-on-the-floor kicks with the distinctive detuned 'donk' offbeat percussion hit, pitched-up female vocal hooks or reworked pop toplines, simple major-key sawtooth stabs and short breakdowns.
items.description: Scouse house, later known as bounce or donk, formed around Liverpool and the North West English club circuit from the late 1990s, spreading through cheap CD compilations and bedroom production software. Its defining element is the donk, a hard detuned offbeat percussive stab, set against a fast pounding kick and pitched-up vocal hooks lifted from pop or trance records. It is faster, more repetitive and far less harmonically ambitious than mainstream UK hard house, and openly proudly populist in its use of familiar melodies.

items.name: Progressive Breaks
items.lineage: UK and US crossover style of roughly 1996-2005 developed by Hybrid, BT, Way Out West and the Distinctive and Bedrock labels, characterized by 128-134 BPM chopped syncopated breakbeats replacing the four-on-the-floor kick, long filtered progressive-house pads, orchestral or cinematic string layers, sub-bass ostinati and eight-to-ten-minute arrangements built on extremely gradual DJ-friendly transitions.
items.description: Progressive breaks grafted the chopped breakbeat of UK big beat and nu-skool breaks onto the long-arc harmonic structures of progressive house, peaking commercially around 1999-2003. Tracks run long, layer sub-bass and evolving filtered pads over a shuffling non-four-to-the-floor drum edit, and often add cinematic string and choir samples. It is distinguished from nu-skool breaks by its slower emotional build and melodic content, and from progressive house purely by the drum programming.

items.name: Beach Music (Carolina)
items.lineage: Coastal Carolina dance-club repertoire that crystallized between the late 1940s and the mid 1960s along the Grand Strand and Myrtle Beach pavilions, built around jukebox R&B and vocal-group sides selected for the mid-tempo shag dance at roughly 110-130 BPM in a 12/8 or shuffled 4/4 with walking bass, honking tenor saxophone breaks, triplet piano and warm four-part male harmony behind a gritty lead.
items.description: Carolina beach music is defined less by a production style than by a dance and a listening community: mid-tempo rhythm and blues and vocal-group records adopted by white and Black beach crowds along the Carolina coast for the shag. Musically it favours shuffled 12/8 or relaxed 4/4 grooves, tenor sax solos, triplet piano and group harmony, and it later produced its own studio bands writing to that template. It is slower and more harmony-focused than northern soul, and warmer and less driving than Motown.
exemplars: General Johnson and the Chairmen of the Board

items.name: Modern Soul
items.lineage: British collector-scene term for the uptempo soul of roughly 1973-1982 that displaced 1960s stompers on the northern circuit, centred on Philadelphia, Detroit and independent West Coast productions, characterized by 105-120 BPM four-on-the-floor grooves with sixteenth hi-hats, sweetened string and flute arrangements, electric piano and clavinet, melodic bass lines and smooth multi-tracked lead and backing vocals.
items.description: Modern soul is a scene classification rather than a production centre: it names the smoother, faster 1970s soul records that UK northern soul DJs turned to once the supply of unheard 1960s sides ran thin. Sonically it means Philadelphia-style sweetening, Rhodes and clavinet comping, sixteenth-note hi-hat drive and layered vocal arrangements over a danceable four-on-the-floor. Against northern soul it is later, glossier and less percussively hard; against boogie it retains full live string and horn arrangements rather than synth substitution.

items.name: Northern Soul
items.lineage: English club movement of 1968-1981 centred on the Twisted Wheel, Wigan Casino and Blackpool Mecca and named by journalist Dave Godin, built on rare mid-1960s American soul 45s played at 120-135 BPM with insistent four-on-the-floor kick, driving eighth-note tambourine, punchy horn stabs, walking or pumping bass and urgently belted lead vocals over Motown-derived changes.
items.description: Northern soul is an English dancefloor canon assembled from obscure mid-1960s American soul singles, not a style produced by its own scene. The records selected share a hard four-on-the-floor kick, constant tambourine, brass punctuation and a high-energy vocal, generally cut fast and mono for jukebox impact. It is separated from Motown proper by rarity and tempo rather than technique, and from later modern soul by its rawer, harder-hitting rhythm sections.
exemplars: Frank Wilson - Do I Love You (Indeed I Do)
Dobie Gray - Out on the Floor
R. Dean Taylor - There's a Ghost in My House

items.name: Psychedelic Soul
items.lineage: American soul mutation of 1967-1973 codified by Norman Whitfield at Motown, Sly Stone in San Francisco and George Clinton's Funkadelic, characterized by extended one-chord vamps at 95-115 BPM, fuzz and wah electric guitar, phased and heavily reverberated mixes, layered congas and hand percussion, group-passed lead vocals trading lines, and socially pointed lyrics stretched across multi-part arrangements of six minutes or more.
items.description: Psychedelic soul emerged in the late 1960s when Black American producers absorbed the studio effects and long-form structures of psychedelic rock into soul and early funk. Its markers are fuzz and wah guitar, phasing and heavy plate reverb, dense conga-layered percussion, static modal vamps in place of chord-driven song form, and lead vocals passed around a group. It sits between the tight three-minute Motown single and full-blown funk, keeping soul harmony and vocal groups while adopting rock's textural experiment.
exemplars: The Temptations - Papa Was a Rollin' Stone

items.name: 2-Tone
items.lineage: English ska revival launched in Coventry in 1979 by Jerry Dammers' 2 Tone label and the Specials, Selecter, Madness and the Beat, characterized by 150-180 BPM upbeat offbeat guitar and organ chops, walking or bouncing electric bass, punk-derived driving kit with rimshot backbeat, terse horn lines and shouted or half-spoken multiracial vocals over lyrics about unemployment, racism and street violence.
items.description: 2-Tone was a two-year explosion of British ska revival built by racially mixed bands in the English Midlands and London around 1979-1981, taking the 1960s Jamaican ska upbeat and driving it at punk tempo and punk volume. The sound is fast offbeat guitar and organ, prominent melodic bass, a hard rock-derived backbeat and stabbing horns behind shouted vocals. It differs from original Jamaican ska in speed, distortion and aggression, and from punk in its Caribbean rhythmic core and horn arrangements.

items.name: Reggae Bultrón
items.lineage: Puerto Rican underground style of the mid-to-late 1990s San Juan marquesina and caserío scene, codified by DJ Nelson (Reggae Bultrón, 1997), DJ Playero and DJ Negro out of the earlier Playero mixtape series — Jamaican dancehall riddims (Dem Bow, Bam Bam) re-sequenced on hardware samplers at 90-100 BPM under Spanish-language duo toasting, with heavily gated kick-and-tresillo snare, sirens, gunshot stabs and cassette-generation hiss.
items.description: Reggae Bultrón is the mid-to-late-1990s Puerto Rican underground stage between Jamaican dancehall and fully formed reggaetón, named for DJ Nelson's 1997 compilation and grown out of the Playero and Noise mixtape culture of San Juan housing projects. Its sound is a looped Dem Bow tresillo pattern under aggressive Spanish-language dual-MC toasting, with sampler-chopped dancehall riddims, sirens and effect stabs, and the compressed, cassette-dubbed low end of underground distribution. It differs from Jamaican ragga by language and by the fixed Dem Bow loop replacing changing riddim beds, and from post-2004 reggaetón by its rawer mix, longer freestyle passages, and absence of pop songform.

items.name: Ragga
items.lineage: Jamaican digital dancehall style dating from the 1985 Sleng Teng riddim, codified by Wayne Smith, King Jammy, Steely & Clevie, Shabba Ranks and Buju Banton — Casio and drum-machine riddims at roughly 90-105 BPM with all-electronic kick, rimshot and bassline, no live band, and a hoarse, rapid-fire chatted DJ delivery in Jamaican Patois riding a single recycled riddim.
items.description: Ragga is the fully digital branch of Jamaican dancehall that opened with King Jammy's 1985 Sleng Teng riddim, the first reggae backing built entirely on a preset Casio rhythm rather than a studio band. Its markers are skeletal electronic drums, a synthesized bassline carrying almost all the harmony, one riddim voiced by dozens of DJs across competing labels, and a chatted, percussive vocal that sits between singing and speech. Compared to roots reggae it discards the one-drop live rhythm section and the mystical lyric register; compared to later 1990s dancehall it is thinner and drier, with less pop melody and less studio layering.
exemplars: Wayne Smith - Under Mi Sleng Teng

items.name: Raggamuffin
items.lineage: Late-1980s to early-1990s transatlantic development of digital dancehall between Kingston and Black British studios in Brent, Hackney and Birmingham, carried by Rebel MC, Asher D & Daddy Freddy, Tippa Irie, Papa San and Super Cat — 90-105 BPM computer riddims thickened with sampled breakbeats, sound-system sub-bass, and a fast, syllable-dense ragga chat cut to dubplate for clash use.
items.description: Raggamuffin is the late-1980s and early-1990s sound-system culture built on digital dancehall riddims, developed as much in Black British studios and pirate-radio circles as in Kingston. It keeps ragga's electronic riddim and chatted Patois vocal but adds sampled funk breaks, denser sub-bass mixed for large speaker stacks, and a dubplate-special economy of exclusive cuts made for clashes. It is distinguished from Jamaican ragga proper by its diaspora production values and breakbeat borrowing, and from the jungle that grew directly out of it by remaining at dancehall tempo rather than accelerating the break to 160 BPM.
exemplars: Asher D & Daddy Freddy - Ragamuffin Hip-Hop

items.name: Rocksteady
items.lineage: Jamaican style of roughly 1966-1968, formed at Studio One and Treasure Isle when ska's fast shuffle slowed to about 80 BPM in the hot summer of 1966 — codified by Alton Ellis (Get Ready Rock Steady), Hopeton Lewis, the Techniques and Duke Reid's productions, with the horn section receding, Jackie Jackson and Leroy Sibbles' melodic walking basslines moving to the front, guitar and piano on the offbeat skank, and close soul-harmony vocal trios.
items.description: Rocksteady is the short-lived Jamaican style that bridged ska and reggae between 1966 and 1968, made at Studio One and Duke Reid's Treasure Isle. Slowing the tempo to a loping mid-80s BPM freed the bass to play composed melodic figures rather than walking quarters, cut the horn arrangements back to occasional punctuation, and put American soul vocal-harmony writing at the centre. Against ska it is slower, sparser and bass-led; against the reggae that followed it lacks the one-drop kick displacement and the organ bubble, and its lyrics remain romantic rather than Rastafarian.

items.name: Afro-Punk
items.lineage: Black American hardcore and alternative-rock current running from Washington DC's Bad Brains (1977 onward) and Los Angeles' Fishbone and Living Colour through the 2003 Afro-Punk documentary and the Brooklyn festival scene it created — fast downstroked power chords and hardcore backbeats interleaved with reggae dub breaks, funk syncopation and gospel-shouted vocal delivery.
items.description: Afro-Punk names the Black presence in American hardcore and alternative rock, running from Bad Brains' 1977 DC beginnings through Fishbone and Living Colour and formalized as a scene by James Spooner's 2003 documentary and the Brooklyn festival that followed. Sonically it is hardcore's speed and downstroke attack repeatedly broken open by dub reggae passages, funk basslines and church-derived vocal power, so records swing between blast-tempo thrash and half-time skank inside a single song. It differs from straight hardcore punk in its rhythmic range and vocal virtuosity, and from funk-metal in that its roots are in the DIY punk circuit rather than the arena.

items.name: Anatolian Rock
items.lineage: Turkish style of roughly 1968-1976 formed around the Istanbul Golden Microphone contests and the Unkapanı record trade, codified by Erkin Koray, Cem Karaca with Moğollar and Kardeşler, Barış Manço and Selda Bağcan — türkü melodies and aksak meters set to fuzz guitar, Farfisa organ and rock drum kit, with bağlama or electrified saz doubling the line and free-rhythm modal introductions before the beat enters.
items.description: Anatolian rock emerged in Istanbul around 1968 when Turkish bands began setting village türkü repertoire and makam melody to Western rock instrumentation, a movement pushed by the Golden Microphone song contests and released on the Unkapanı 45 market. The result pairs fuzz guitar, combo organ and drum kit with saz, darbuka and asymmetric aksak meters, and keeps microtonal inflection and free-rhythm modal openings that no Anglo-American rock record would attempt. It differs from Western psychedelia by its melodic source material and pitch system, and from contemporaneous arabesk by retaining rock band format and a left-populist lyric stance.

items.name: British Invasion
items.lineage: British beat-group wave that broke in the United States in 1964 following The Beatles' Ed Sullivan appearance, produced largely at EMI Abbey Road, Decca and IBC on four-track — Liverpool and London bands recasting American R&B, Chuck Berry and Brill Building songwriting as compact two-to-three-minute guitar-bass-drums records at 120-150 BPM with tight two- and three-part harmony, tambourine backbeat and heavily limited mono mixes.
items.description: The British Invasion is the 1964-1967 wave of UK beat and R&B groups that took over the American charts after The Beatles' Ed Sullivan broadcast. Its records are short, mono, four-track productions built on jangling single-coil guitar, driving eighth-note bass, tambourine-reinforced backbeat and close vocal harmony, with American rhythm-and-blues repertoire filtered through English vocal accent and Tin Pan Alley songcraft. Set against the American rock and roll it borrowed from, it is tighter, more harmonically adventurous and more producer-shaped; set against the psychedelia that followed it, it is still constrained to dance-single length and form.
exemplars: The Beatles - A Hard Day's Night
The Rolling Stones - The Rolling Stones (1964)
The Kinks - You Really Got Me
The Animals - The House of the Rising Sun

items.name: Jam Bands (festival circuit)
items.lineage: North American touring scene consolidated in the 1990s around Phish, Widespread Panic, String Cheese Incident and moe., extending the Grateful Dead's practice — multi-night stands with rotating setlists, songs opened into twenty-minute modal or funk vamps with segues between them, mixed on a house desk and taped from the audience section for free trading.
items.description: The jam-band circuit is the 1990s-onward North American touring scene that formalized the Grateful Dead's improvisational live practice into an economy of multi-night runs, rotating setlists, destination festivals and tape trading. Musically the songs are frames: a written head gives way to extended modal, funk or bluegrass-derived group improvisation, often segued directly into the next tune without a stop, so a recording's value lies in a specific night rather than a studio master. It differs from studio rock in that the canonical documents are soundboard and audience tapes, and from jazz in retaining rock instrumentation, tonal vamps and song-length verse-chorus anchors.

items.name: Roots Rock
items.lineage: Late-1960s American reaction against psychedelia, formed around Woodstock and the Bay Area with The Band's Music from Big Pink (1968), Creedence Clearwater Revival and Bob Dylan's John Wesley Harding — moderate 90-120 BPM backbeats, unaffected guitar tones, piano and Hammond organ, gospel-derived group harmony and country, blues and R&B forms recorded with minimal overdubbing.
items.description: Roots rock is the late-1960s turn away from studio psychedelia toward older American forms, announced by The Band's Music from Big Pink and Dylan's John Wesley Harding and carried commercially by Creedence Clearwater Revival. Its markers are dry unprocessed guitar and drums, prominent acoustic piano and Hammond, rotating lead vocals with rough gospel-style harmony, and songwriting drawn from country, hymnody, blues and rockabilly rather than blues-rock virtuosity. It differs from country rock by leaning on rhythm-and-blues and gospel as much as on Nashville, and from the Americana that later descends from it by belonging to a mainstream rock market rather than an alt-country one.
exemplars: Creedence Clearwater Revival - Willy and the Poor Boys

items.name: Spazzcore
items.lineage: Mid-1990s chaotic-hardcore offshoot of American and Japanese powerviolence, named for the band Spazz and carried by Charles Bronson, Melt-Banana, The Locust and Arab on Radar — songs of ten to sixty seconds built on abrupt blast-beat to stop-time cuts, atonal dissonant guitar stabs, treble-heavy bass and shrieked or yelped vocals, recorded fast and cheap on DIY budgets.
items.description: Spazzcore is the mid-1990s chaotic wing of hardcore punk, taking its name from the California band Spazz and overlapping with powerviolence and noisecore. Tracks last seconds rather than minutes and are assembled from violent tempo cuts between blast beats and lurching half-time, atonal or chromatic guitar stabs instead of riffs, and vocals delivered as shrieks, yelps and barks; releases arrive as split seven-inches on tiny labels. It is distinguished from grindcore by its punk rather than metal lineage and its refusal of steady groove, and from noise rock by extreme brevity and hardcore tempo.

items.name: Surf Music
items.lineage: Southern California style of 1961-1965 spanning Dick Dale's Rendezvous Ballroom instrumentals and the vocal surf of The Beach Boys and Jan & Dean, recorded at Western, Gold Star and United in Los Angeles — reverb-tank guitar with fast alternate picking, saxophone honks, driving tom-and-snare shuffles at 140-180 BPM, and stacked falsetto-topped close harmony over car-and-beach lyrics.
items.description: Surf music is the Southern California scene of roughly 1961 to 1965, encompassing both the instrumental strain built on Dick Dale's outboard spring-reverb guitar tone and rapid tremolo picking and the vocal strain in which The Beach Boys and Jan & Dean stacked Four Freshmen harmony over the same beat. Records are short, bright and heavily echoed, with saxophone doubling, propulsive tom patterns and lyric worlds of beaches, waves and hot rods. It is broader than the instrumental surf-rock category alone, since it includes the vocal-harmony repertoire; against the British Invasion that displaced it, it is more chord-simple, more reverb-defined and more regionally specific.
exemplars: Dick Dale and His Del-Tones - Surfers' Choice

items.name: Tex-Mex
items.lineage: South Texas border music codified between the 1930s and 1960s in San Antonio and the Rio Grande Valley by Narciso Martínez, Valerio Longoria, Flaco Jiménez and Tejano bandleaders — the two-row diatonic button accordion carrying the melody over bajo sexto bass-and-chord accompaniment, tololoche or electric bass and drums, in polka, redova, huapango and ranchera-waltz meters with paired-voice duet singing in thirds.
items.description: Tex-Mex is the border music of South Texas, formed when German and Czech settler polka and waltz repertoire met Mexican song forms and was recorded commercially from the 1930s onward around San Antonio and the Rio Grande Valley. Its core is the diatonic button accordion playing ornamented single-line melody against the twelve-string bajo sexto's bass-and-chord pulse, with duet singing in parallel thirds and dance meters of polka, redova, huapango and vals ranchero. It differs from Mexican norteño mainly by its United States base and its later absorption of country and rhythm-and-blues instrumentation, and from orquesta Tejano by keeping the accordion-and-bajo core rather than a horn section.

items.name: Time Lord Rock
items.lineage: Doctor Who fan-music genre (Trock) begun in 2008 when Charlie McDonnell and Alex Day formed Chameleon Circuit and released through YouTube and DFTBA Records — bedroom-recorded pop-punk and acoustic power-pop at 120-160 BPM, close-miked doubled lead vocals over strummed acoustic and clean electric guitar, programmed or lightly played drums, and lyrics narrating specific episodes and characters.
items.description: Time Lord Rock, or Trock, is a small British-led fan genre of songs about Doctor Who, launched in 2008 by Chameleon Circuit and distributed through YouTube channels and DFTBA Records rather than conventional labels. Musically it is bedroom-produced acoustic power-pop and pop-punk with doubled untrained lead vocals well forward, simple diatonic progressions, programmed or minimally tracked drums, and dense narrative lyrics that assume episode knowledge. It differs from wizard rock, its nearest neighbour, only in source text; it differs from general indie bedroom pop in that the subject matter, not a sound, defines membership.
exemplars: Alex Carpenter / The Ministry of Magic

items.name: New Acoustic
items.lineage: US late-1970s acoustic-string idiom formed around David Grisman's San Francisco quintet and Tony Rice's Bay Area circle, codified on Grisman's 1977 'Dawg Music' sessions — bluegrass instrumentation (mandolin lead, flatpicked dreadnought, fiddle, five-string banjo, upright bass) played over jazz-derived changes, minor and modal keys, hemiola-laced 6/8 and odd-metre heads, extended solo choruses at 100-200 BPM with no vocals and no backbeat.
items.description: New Acoustic emerged in the San Francisco Bay Area in the late 1970s when David Grisman, Tony Rice, Darol Anger and Mike Marshall began playing bluegrass instruments over jazz harmony, gypsy-swing phrasing and Balkan-derived meters. The sound is entirely acoustic and almost entirely instrumental: close-miked mandolin and flatpicked guitar trading long improvised choruses over a walking upright bass, with wide dynamic shading and no drum kit. It differs from bluegrass proper in its absence of high-lonesome vocals and its use of extended chords and modulation, and from jazz in retaining flatpicked string attack and fiddle-tune formal structure.
exemplars: Strength in Numbers - The Telluride Sessions

items.name: Original Score (Film & Media)
items.lineage: Purpose-composed narrative underscore for film and television, codified in 1930s-40s Hollywood by Max Steiner, Erich Korngold and Bernard Herrmann and extended by Ennio Morricone, John Williams and Hans Zimmer — through-composed orchestral cues timed to picture at fixed frame-rates with click tracks, leitmotif recurrence, tempo and metre subordinated to onscreen action, and recording on a scoring stage against projected image.
items.description: Original score is music composed specifically for a moving image, established as a craft in Hollywood during the 1930s and continuously reinvented from Herrmann's astringent chamber writing through Morricone's timbral collage to Zimmer's hybrid orchestral-electronic textures. Its defining constraints are external: cues begin and end on picture cues, tempo is governed by click and streamer rather than musical shape, and orchestration serves dramatic function, so through-composed development and abrupt textural change are normal. It is distinguished from concert orchestral music by its dependence on synchronization and from the compiled soundtrack by being written rather than licensed.
exemplars: Ennio Morricone - Once Upon a Time in the West
Jonny Greenwood - There Will Be Blood

items.name: Chicano Rock
items.lineage: East Los Angeles Mexican-American rock and R&B scene of the late 1950s-60s, codified by Ritchie Valens, Thee Midniters, Cannibal & the Headhunters and the Whittier Boulevard dance-hall circuit — 12/8 shuffle ballads and mid-tempo 4/4 stompers built on doo-wop changes, honking tenor saxophone, Farfisa or Hammond organ, tremolo-heavy single-coil guitar, tight harmony vocals and Spanish-language interpolations of ranchera and huapango material.
items.description: Chicano rock formed in the barrios of East Los Angeles between the late 1950s and the late 1960s, where Mexican-American teenagers absorbed R&B, doo-wop and Latin dance rhythms and fed back ranchera melodies and Spanish lyrics. The characteristic record is a small-studio recording with plate-and-chamber reverb, a saxophone-and-organ front line, group harmony and either a rolling 12/8 ballad feel or a driving Latin-inflected backbeat. It differs from mainstream 1960s garage rock in its R&B horn vocabulary and Spanish-language repertoire, and from Tejano conjunto in using electric band instrumentation rather than accordion and bajo sexto.

items.name: Conjunto (Tejano)
items.lineage: South Texas-Rio Grande Valley border ensemble music formed circa 1930s from German-Czech dance repertoire, codified by Narciso Martinez and Santiago Jimenez Sr. and modernized by Valerio Longoria and Flaco Jimenez — diatonic button accordion carrying the melody over bajo sexto bass-and-chord accompaniment, later joined by tololoche or electric bass and trap drums, playing polkas, redovas, huapangos and 3/4 valses and rancheras at dance-hall tempos with paired-voice duet singing in thirds.
items.description: Conjunto is the working-class dance music of the Texas-Mexico border, crystallizing in the 1930s when Mexican-American accordionists adapted the polka and schottische repertoire left by Central European settlers. The core sound is a two-row diatonic accordion playing rapid melodic runs against the twelve-string bajo sexto, with a two-beat bass and a plain backbeat, supporting duet vocals sung in parallel thirds. It differs from orquesta Tejana in its small acoustic roster and rural associations, and from norteno across the river mainly in repertoire emphasis and the later adoption of drum kit and electric bass.

items.name: New Mexico Music
items.lineage: Hispano regional popular style of the upper Rio Grande valley, consolidated in Albuquerque and Espanola from the 1940s onward around Al Hurricane, Tiny Morrie and Baca Records — Spanish-language rancheras, valses, corridos and polkas fused with mid-century rock and roll rhythm section, twin-fiddle or violin lead inherited from the Hispano baile tradition, accordion or organ, and a shuffling 'Nuevo Mexicano' backbeat under lyric Spanish vocals.
items.description: New Mexico music is the Hispano popular tradition of the Rio Grande corridor north of El Paso, distinct from both Tejano and Mexican norteno because it descends from a colonial Spanish-speaking community that was never part of the twentieth-century border migration. Its records, largely cut for family-run Albuquerque labels from the 1950s on, pair the old baile fiddle repertoire and 3/4 vals with a rock-and-roll drum kit, electric guitar and organ under Spanish vocals. The fiddle rather than the accordion is the identifying lead voice, and the rhythmic feel leans toward a loping shuffle rather than the conjunto two-beat.

items.name: A Cappella (Contemporary Vocal)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied multi-voice arrangement of popular repertoire, established on US and UK college campuses from the mid-twentieth century and codified commercially by the Bobs, Take 6, the King's Singers' pop sets and post-2000 groups such as Pentatonix — four to sixteen voices covering bass line, chordal pads and lead, with vocal percussion supplying kick, snare and hi-hat, close-miked and multitracked, in strophic pop forms at 70-130 BPM.
items.description: Contemporary a cappella is the practice of rendering popular songs entirely with voices, grown from the collegiate glee and jazz-vocal-group traditions and standardized after the 1980s by groups that assigned voices to instrumental roles. Records are heavily produced: each part is close-miked and multitracked, vocal bass is often octave-shifted, and a beatboxer supplies the drum kit, so the finished sound is dense and studio-constructed rather than choral. It differs from barbershop in repertoire and equal-tempered pop harmony, and from choral music in its instrument-imitating arrangement and per-voice studio processing.

items.name: Barbershop Harmony
items.lineage: American close-harmony quartet singing of the 1890s-1920s revived and codified after 1938 by SPEBSQSA — four unaccompanied male or female voices with the melody in the second-from-top lead part, tenor harmonizing above, bass on roots and fifths and baritone filling the remaining chord tone, built on ringing dominant-seventh 'barbershop sevenths' tuned in just intonation, sung rubato with swipes, tags and an expanded-sound overtone effect.
items.description: Barbershop is unaccompanied four-part close harmony that arose in American vernacular singing around 1900 and was institutionalized by the amateur society movement from 1938. Its signature is the chain of dominant seventh chords tuned by ear to just intonation, which locks and produces audible difference tones, plus the practice of placing the melody in an inner voice so the tenor floats above it. It differs from doo-wop by its pre-electric repertoire, absence of a rhythmic bass vamp and flexible rubato phrasing, and from choral singing by its one-voice-per-part quartet texture.

items.name: Cantique
items.lineage: French-language devotional hymn tradition of France, Quebec, Brittany and Francophone Africa and the Caribbean, formalized in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century parish collections and diffused through nineteenth-century cantique books — strophic verse-and-refrain settings in duple or triple metre, sung in unison or simple parts by congregation and choir over harmonium or pipe organ, with syllabic text-setting in vernacular French rather than Latin.
items.description: The cantique is the vernacular French devotional song of Catholic worship, distinct from Latin liturgical chant and used for popular piety, processions, Christmas and Marian devotions from the seventeenth century onward. Musically it is plain and strophic: a memorable refrain alternating with narrative verses, sung syllabically by the whole assembly in unison or easy harmony, supported by harmonium or organ in a reverberant stone church. Its Breton and Quebecois branches preserve older modal melodies, and its African and Haitian branches add local percussion, but the defining marker across all of them is French-language congregational strophic singing rather than trained choral polyphony.
exemplars: Les Petits Chanteurs a la Croix de Bois

items.name: Gregorian Chant
items.lineage: Latin liturgical monophony of the Western church, synthesized from Roman and Frankish practice in the Carolingian empire during the eighth and ninth centuries and notated in neumes from circa 900, restored by the Solesmes monks in the nineteenth century — unaccompanied male or female unison voices, free unmeasured prose rhythm following the Latin text, eight-mode system, syllabic psalm tones through melismatic graduals and alleluias, sung antiphonally in resonant stone spaces.
items.description: Gregorian chant is the unaccompanied Latin monophony of the Roman rite, assembled under Frankish rule in the eighth and ninth centuries and preserved through neumatic and later square notation. Its defining traits are total absence of harmony and instruments, free prose rhythm governed by the accents of the Latin text, an eight-mode tonal framework, and long reverberation from the stone churches it was written for. It differs from Byzantine and Ambrosian chant in repertoire and modal theory, and from later polyphony in remaining strictly single-line even when sung by a large schola.
exemplars: Monks of Santo Domingo de Silos

items.name: Standards (Great American Songbook)
items.lineage: The core repertoire of Broadway and Tin Pan Alley songs written roughly 1920-1955 by Gershwin, Porter, Kern, Berlin and Arlen and adopted as the common ground of jazz performance — thirty-two-bar AABA and ABAC forms with functional ii-V harmony, sung with rubato verse and swung chorus by a vocalist over piano-bass-drums or big band, typically at ballad 60-80 BPM or medium swing 140-200 BPM, with the melody stated then improvised over.
items.description: The standards repertoire is the body of American popular songs from the interwar theatre and film industry that became the shared vocabulary of jazz musicians and cabaret singers. Performance practice is fixed by convention rather than notation: an optional out-of-tempo verse, a swung statement of the thirty-two-bar chorus, improvised choruses over the same changes, and a return to the head, all over ii-V-driven harmony that invites reharmonization. It differs from bebop originals in retaining the sung lyric and lyric-shaped melody, and from pop crooning in the expectation of substantial improvisation.
exemplars: Frank Sinatra - Songs for Swingin' Lovers

items.name: Yodel
items.lineage: Alpine herding-call vocal technique of Switzerland, Austria and Bavaria documented from the eighteenth century and paralleled in Georgian krimanchuli, Central African forest polyphony and American cowboy song — rapid repeated breaks between chest and falsetto register on nonsense syllables, often built on the natural harmonic series of the alphorn so that the eleventh partial sounds as the flattened 'alphorn fa', performed solo or in two- and three-voice juuzli over a held bass drone.
items.description: Yodeling is the deliberate rapid alternation between chest voice and falsetto, originating as a long-distance herding and signalling call in the Alps and retained as a musical genre in Swiss naturjodel and juuzli, Austrian and Bavarian jodler, and by transmission the American cowboy and early country yodel. Alpine yodel is tuned to the natural harmonic series rather than equal temperament, producing the characteristically sharp fourth degree, and is usually sung outdoors on open vowels with no fixed metre. It differs from ordinary falsetto singing in making the register break itself the ornament, and from the country yodel of Jimmie Rodgers in remaining wordless and untethered from song form.

items.name: African Heavy Metal
items.lineage: Continental African metal scenes formed from the late 1980s onward in Botswana, Angola, Kenya, Madagascar and South Africa, codified by Wrust, Skinflint, Overthrust and the Gaborone leather-cowboy subculture — NWOBHM and thrash templates at 120-190 BPM with downtuned humbucker guitars and double-kick drumming, but with Setswana, Swahili or Portuguese lyrics, local praise-song melodic contours and occasional talking drum or call-and-response chant layered over the riff.
items.description: African heavy metal names the metal scenes that took root across the continent from the late 1980s, most visibly the Botswana scene around Gaborone with its distinctive leather-and-stetson visual code, alongside Angolan, Kenyan, Malagasy and South African bands. Musically it is built on classic heavy metal and thrash riffing and double-kick drumming recorded on modest digital budgets, but repertoire and delivery draw on indigenous language, praise-singing phrase shapes and sometimes local percussion, giving vocal lines a chanted, communal contour uncommon in European metal. It differs from South African rock more broadly in its metal instrumentation and tempo, and from Western thrash in its lyrical language and its polyrhythmic and call-and-response inflections.

items.name: Apala
items.lineage: Yoruba Muslim percussion-and-praise genre of southwestern Nigeria, developed in the 1930s-40s to rouse the faithful after Ramadan fasting and codified commercially by Haruna Ishola and Ayinla Omowura from the 1950s onward — a talking-drum ensemble of omele and sakara frame drums with agidigbo thumb-piano bass, agogo bell and shekere, moving in fast Yoruba dance metre under a lead praise-singer and chorus trading proverb-laden call-and-response in tonal Yoruba.
items.description: Apala arose among Yoruba Muslims in southwestern Nigeria in the 1930s and 1940s as music for waking and entertaining worshippers during Ramadan, and became a commercial recording genre from the 1950s through Haruna Ishola and later Ayinla Omowura. Its sound is almost entirely percussion and voice: sakara and omele drums with a pressure-drum lead, the agidigbo lamellophone supplying a bass ostinato, plus rattle and bell, over which a lead singer delivers proverbs and praise names answered by a chorus. It differs from juju in refusing guitars and Western harmony, and from fuji, which grew directly out of apala's Ramadan were tradition, by retaining the agidigbo and a slower, more speech-weighted delivery.

items.name: Fújì Music (Yoruba Muslim percussion pop)
items.lineage: Yoruba Muslim popular style formalized in Lagos and Ibadan in the late 1960s–70s by Sikiru Ayinde Barrister and Ayinla Kollington out of wéré/ajísáàrì Ramadan wake-up music, built on interlocking dùndùn and sákárà drum batteries with omele accents at roughly 100–130 BPM, no guitars in its classical form, and a declamatory praise-singing lead answered by a chanting chorus over open-ended twenty-minute medleys.
items.description: Fújì emerged in Lagos in the late 1960s when Sikiru Ayinde Barrister expanded Ramadan wéré chanting into a full commercial percussion ensemble, and dominated Yoruba popular music through the 1980s and 90s. Its signature is a dense all-drum texture — dùndùn pressure drums bending speech-tone phrases, sákárà frame drums, ṣẹ̀kẹ̀rẹ̀ and omele — under a nasal, quasi-Qur'anic praise vocal with responsorial chorus, later augmented by synthesizer pads. Unlike jùjú, which is guitar-led and Christian-inflected, fújì keeps guitars out and foregrounds percussion, Islamic vocal melisma, and extended non-repeating praise medleys rather than song-form.

items.name: Sákárà (Lagos sakara-drum praise song)
items.lineage: Yoruba Muslim urban style of Lagos and Ijebu that crystallized in the 1920s–30s among Ilorin and Ijebu Muslim communities and was codified on 78s by Abibu Oluwa and Yusuf Olatunji, pairing a set of tuned clay-framed sákárà drums played with thin sticks against the gòjé one-string spike fiddle, at a slow-to-moderate walking pulse under a low, gravelly proverb-laden praise vocal with brief chorus refrains.
items.description: Sákárà formed in early twentieth-century Lagos as the music of Yoruba Muslim traders and artisans, and was the dominant recorded Yoruba Islamic idiom from the 1930s until fújì displaced it. The sound is sparse and speech-close: a chorus of tuned round clay-and-goatskin frame drums struck with sticks, the whining gòjé fiddle shadowing the vocal line, and a deep, slow praise voice quoting Yoruba proverbs and orílẹ̀ lineage poetry. Against fújì it is far slower, thinner in texture and older in repertory; against apala it is defined by the sákárà drum and fiddle rather than the àkúbà and agidigbo.

items.name: Kwela
items.lineage: South African township street music of the early 1950s, born on Johannesburg and Pretoria pavements and commercialized through Gallo by Spokes Mashiyane and the Lerole brothers, built on a bright pennywhistle lead improvising over a bouncing 4/4 marabi-derived I–IV–I(6/4)–V cycle at 130–160 BPM with strummed guitar, tea-chest or double bass, and a chugging offbeat.
items.description: Kwela arose in the early 1950s among township youth in Johannesburg and Pretoria who adopted the cheap German pennywhistle as a street instrument, and became South Africa's first international pop export with Spokes Mashiyane's records and the Lerole brothers' 'Tom Hark'. The sound is a single piercing six-hole whistle blown breathily and rhythmically over a four-chord marabi cycle carried by guitar and tea-chest bass, with the whistle player bending and overblowing in place of a singer. It differs from the mbaqanga and sax-jive that succeeded it in being almost entirely instrumental, whistle-led, and acoustic rather than electric and vocal-group based.
exemplars: Elias Lerole & His Zig Zag Jive Flutes

items.name: Rumba Lingala
items.lineage: The Lingala-language dance-song idiom of Léopoldville and Brazzaville from the late 1940s to the mid-1960s, codified by Joseph Kabasele's African Jazz and Franco's O.K. Jazz out of Cuban son records circulating on the GV series, setting sweet paired-tenor Lingala vocals over clean single-coil guitar arpeggios, clave-locked congas and a mid-tempo 4/4 that opens into an accelerating seben instrumental section.
items.description: Rumba Lingala names the first fully Congolese popular style, made in Léopoldville and Brazzaville studios owned by Greek and Portuguese merchants between roughly 1948 and 1965, and carried across the continent by Lingala's status as a lingua franca. Its markers are close-harmony male duet singing, an interlocking two- or three-guitar web derived from likembe and Cuban tres figuration, restrained conga and clave, and a lyrical first section that gives way to the faster seben over which the lead guitar rides. Compared with the later soukous of the 1970s–80s it is slower, softer, horn-led rather than synth-led, and keeps the seben brief rather than making it the whole record.
exemplars: Joseph Kabasele (Le Grand Kallé) & African Jazz

items.name: Maloya
items.lineage: Créole ancestor-worship and protest music of Réunion, descended from Malagasy and East African slave servis kabaré rites and revived from 1970 by Firmin Viry, Granmoun Lélé and Danyèl Waro, driven by the low roulèr bass drum, rattling kayamb tray-shaker and triangle in a slow-building 6/8-into-4 pulse under a hoarse solo call and unison Creole chorus response that accelerates across a single trance-length cycle.
items.description: Maloya is the ritual and protest music of Réunion's Créole descendants of enslaved Malagasy and African labourers, suppressed by French authorities into the 1970s and revived as an explicitly political idiom by Firmin Viry, Granmoun Lélé and Danyèl Waro before UNESCO listing in 2009. Its texture is entirely percussive and vocal: the seated roulèr laying a deep two-stroke bass figure, the kayamb hissing a continuous shuffle, hand clapping and a strained solo voice trading short Kreol phrases with a shouted chorus over a single cell that tightens and speeds toward trance. Séga, its island neighbour, is fast, sweet, secular and later took on guitars and horns, while maloya stays slow-starting, drum-only and tied to servis kabaré ancestor ceremony.

items.name: Séga (Mauritian creole dance song)
items.lineage: Creole dance song of Mauritius, Rodrigues and Réunion with slave-era roots, professionalized on record from the late 1950s by Ti Frère and Serge Lebrasse, built on the goatskin ravanne frame drum's driving triplet-inflected 6/8, the kayamb or maravanne rattle and triangle, a fast accelerando toward the closing 'séga tipik' break, and light strophic Kreol verses with call-and-response chorus.
items.description: Séga is the national dance music of Mauritius, descended from the music of enslaved Mozambican and Malagasy people and moved from beach and yard gatherings onto commercial records from the late 1950s. The core is the fire-tuned ravanne frame drum playing a rolling triplet pattern, the maravanne or kayamb shaker filling the offbeats, and short strophic Kreol verses about work, love and gossip, with the tempo pushed steadily upward until the closing frenzy. It is faster, lighter and more secular than Réunionnais maloya, and unlike maloya it readily absorbed guitar, bass and later horn sections into its 'séga moderne' recorded form.

items.name: Seggae
items.lineage: Mauritian fusion of séga and Jamaican roots reggae created in the mid-1980s by Kaya (Joseph Reginald Topize) and developed by Ras Natty Baby, laying the ravanne's triplet séga pulse across a reggae one-drop at 70–90 BPM with skanking offbeat guitar, dubwise bass, organ bubble and Kreol lyrics of Rastafari and Creole social grievance.
items.description: Seggae was invented in Mauritius around 1985 by Kaya, who set ravanne-driven séga rhythm over reggae's one-drop and Rastafari-inflected Kreol lyrics, and it became the island's protest idiom after his death in police custody in 1999 triggered nationwide riots. The records combine a reggae rhythm section — bubbling organ, chopped offbeat guitar, melodic bass — with the ravanne and maravanne still audible under the kit, and a rough, plain-spoken vocal delivery. It differs from Jamaican roots reggae in its Creole language, its triplet-leaning percussion layer, and from séga proper in its halved tempo and bass-forward mix.

items.name: Museve
items.lineage: Zimbabwean guitar-band dance style named by Simon Chimbetu in the late 1980s from his dendera branch of sungura, running a fast 4/4 at roughly 130–150 BPM with a rapid rolling snare-and-hi-hat kit pattern, two interlocking clean electric guitars trading cyclic mbira-derived riffs, walking bass and Shona narrative vocals in warm two- and three-part harmony.
items.description: Museve is the Zimbabwean dance-band idiom that split from sungura in the late 1980s, the label Simon Chimbetu applied to his Dendera Kings sound and which spread across Harare's studios through the 1990s. It is guitar-band music in which two clean electrics weave short repeating figures modelled on mbira interlocking patterns, over a fast kit groove with the snare rolling in near-continuous sixteenths, hosho shaker on top, and Shona lyrics of migrancy, morality and love sung in close harmony. Against Congolese soukous it is faster and drier with no horn section, and against chimurenga it uses the guitar-band frame rather than direct mbira transcription and political allegory.

items.name: Negro Spiritual (concert arrangement)
items.lineage: The arranged concert form of the African-American spiritual, created when the Fisk Jubilee Singers toured from 1871 and codified as a solo art song by Harry T. Burleigh from 1916 and later by Hall Johnson, William Dawson and Moses Hogan — setting plantation-era melodies in Western four-part harmony or voice-and-piano, in slow rubato-inflected strophes with dialect text, swelling dynamics and a trained legato delivery.
items.description: The concert spiritual is the notated, harmonized descendant of the oral plantation spiritual, launched by the Fisk Jubilee Singers' fundraising tours from 1871 and turned into a recital genre by Harry T. Burleigh's 1917 solo arrangements. It keeps the original melodies and dialect texts but places them in European functional harmony, sung with conservatory tone, controlled rubato and terraced dynamics, accompanied by piano or performed a cappella by a trained mixed choir. This is what separates it from the congregational spiritual it came from — fixed notation, no heterophony, no shout or foot percussion — and from twentieth-century gospel, which added rhythm section, improvised melisma and blue tonality.

items.name: Anison (Japanese anime theme song)
items.lineage: Japanese commercial song written for anime opening and closing titles, established as a distinct trade in the 1960s–70s by Columbia and Nippon Columbia sessions for Ichirou Mizuki and Isao Sasaki, characterized by a 90-second broadcast edit, declamatory belted male or bright female lead, marching or driving 4/4 at 130–170 BPM, brass-and-string sweetened rock backing, shouted title hooks and abrupt key-lifting final choruses.
items.description: Anison is the Japanese industry category for songs commissioned as anime title music, professionalized in the 1960s and 70s around specialist singers such as Ichirou Mizuki and Isao Sasaki and later around JAM Project and tie-in J-pop acts. Its constraints are formal: a tightly compressed 90-second broadcast cut, an immediate hook, a heroic full-throated belt often shouting the show's title, brisk march-derived 4/4 with brass stabs and string counterlines, and a modulation into the last chorus. It is distinguished from general J-pop less by harmony than by function and delivery — declamatory rather than intimate, structurally truncated, and built to survive a weekly title sequence.

items.name: Fann at-Tanbura
items.lineage: Afro-Gulf ritual and entertainment music of Bahrain, Kuwait and the Saudi Eastern Province, carried by communities descended from East African and Sudanese people from the nineteenth century, centred on the six-string tanbura lyre played over a slow-building 6/8 or compound cycle, the mangūr goat-hoof rattle belt shaken by a dancer, tār frame drums, hand clapping and a leader's call answered by a heavy unison male chorus.
items.description: Fann at-tanbura is the lyre-and-rattle music kept by Afro-Arab communities of the Arabian Gulf littoral, performed in dedicated dūr houses in Muharraq, Kuwait City and Qatif for healing, celebration and, historically, alongside the pearling economy. The tanbura, a large bowl lyre of East African descent, is strummed in a continuous ostinato while the mangūr — a belt of stitched goat hooves worn by a standing dancer — supplies a dry sizzling counter-rhythm, over which frame drums, clapping and antiphonal male chorus intensify across a long single cycle. It sits apart from other Gulf repertoires such as sawt or fijiri in retaining an explicitly African instrument and trance-oriented, spirit-related function.
exemplars: Dār tanbura troupes of Muharraq, Bahrain
Gulf recordings by Poul Rovsing Olsen

items.name: Fijiri
items.lineage: The pearl-divers' song of Bahrain, Kuwait and the eastern Arabian coast, performed since at least the nineteenth century by crews in shore-side dūr houses through the off-season, led by a nahhām soloist who improvises long melismatic maqām-based lines answered by a seated male chorus over hand claps, clay jahla water-jar drums struck with the palms, and frame drums in slow compound cycles of the ʿadsānī, bahrī and ḥaddādī suites.
items.description: Fijiri is the land-side music of Gulf pearl-diving crews, still maintained by heritage troupes in Muharraq and Kuwait long after the pearling economy collapsed in the 1930s. A nahhām lead singer delivers heavily ornamented, microtonally inflected free lines in maqām, answered by a tight seated chorus singing drone-like responses, while clapping, palm-struck clay water jars and frame drums mark a slow compound cycle that gradually accelerates; one performer often chest-slaps or sways to intensify the pulse. Unlike Atlantic sea shanties it is not sung at work but commemorates it, and unlike fann at-tanbura it uses no melodic instrument at all — the voice and the jahla carry everything.
exemplars: Dār Bin Hindi fijiri troupe, Muharraq
Bahraini nahhām recordings by Poul Rovsing Olsen
Kuwaiti fijiri ensembles of the Gulf heritage festivals

items.name: Khalījī (Gulf dance song)
items.lineage: Popular song of the Arabian Gulf states shaped from the 1950s onward by Kuwaiti and Bahraini radio and by Saudi singers such as Talal Maddah and Mohammed Abdu, setting Gulf dialect lyrics over the distinctive limping khalījī 2/4 and 6/8 patterns played on mirwās and ṭabl with hand claps, an oud-led maqām melody doubled by massed violins and qānūn, and an ornamented but relatively unforced solo vocal.
items.description: Khalījī is the shared popular idiom of Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the Emirates, consolidated through Gulf state radio orchestras from the 1950s and 60s and carried into pan-Arab stardom by Talal Maddah, Mohammed Abdu and later Abdallah Al Rowaished and Nawal. Its identifying feature is rhythmic: the syncopated Gulf patterns hit on paired mirwās hand drums and ṭabl with clapping, which pull against an otherwise Egyptian-style ensemble of oud, qānūn and unison violin section playing quarter-tone maqām lines. Against Egyptian ṭarab it is shorter-formed, faster and drum-forward; against the older sawt tradition it is orchestrated, notated in part, and built for broadcast rather than for the intimate ṣawt majlis.

items.name: Liwa (Swahili-Omani coastal dance)
items.lineage: Coastal Swahili dance-music of Zanzibar, Mombasa and the Omani-Gulf diaspora, carried by Hadhrami and Baluchi communities from the 19th century and maintained by neighbourhood liwa associations — a loud outdoor style built on a paired double-headed drum battery and shaker ostinato at brisk 4/4 processional tempo under the piercing continuous circular-breathed zumari (conical shawm), with call-and-response Swahili and Arabic chorus shouting over the drums.
items.description: Liwa is an outdoor drum-and-shawm dance tradition of the Swahili coast and the Omani Gulf, sustained by community associations in Zanzibar, Mombasa and Muscat since the 19th-century Indian Ocean trade era. Its sound is a dense, unbroken drum ostinato topped by the nasal, circular-breathed zumari and shouted responsorial refrains, with no melodic instruments in the European sense. Unlike taarab, the coast's other Arab-influenced idiom, liwa is loud, non-strophic, entirely percussion-led and played standing in the street rather than seated in a hall.

items.name: Onkyokei (Japanese onkyo improvisation)
items.lineage: Tokyo improvised-music movement crystallized around the Off Site venue circa 1998-2004 and codified by Otomo Yoshihide, Sachiko M, Toshimaru Nakamura and Taku Sugimoto — extremely quiet, near-static music of sine tones, no-input mixing-board feedback, contact-mic scrapes and long silences, with no pulse, no harmony and structure emerging from the acoustics of the room itself.
items.description: Onkyokei emerged in Tokyo's small improvisation venues around 1998, most associated with the Off Site space in Yoyogi. It works at the threshold of audibility: unmodulated sine tones, feedback held at the edge of self-oscillation in a mixing desk with nothing plugged in, tiny physical noises, and silences long enough to expose the room and the audience. It differs from European free improvisation in its refusal of gesture and virtuosity, and from ambient music in that it is performed live, unlooped and without harmonic bed.

items.name: Sawt (Gulf khaliji urban song)
items.lineage: Urban chamber song of Kuwait and Bahrain codified in the early 20th century by Abdullah al-Faraj and later Mohammed bin Faris and Dahi bin Walid — sung classical Arabic or Nabati verse over an oud in Gulf tuning, in the slow duple sawt arabi or the limping 6/8 sawt shami, with mirwas hand-drums, offbeat handclaps and the seated zafan dancer marking the cycle.
items.description: Sawt is the pearl-era chamber song of Kuwait and Bahrain, performed in the private samra gathering by a solo singer-oudist with mirwas drummers and clapping companions. The oud carries an improvised taqsim opening before the metered song, and the interlocking clap pattern against the drum cycle produces the characteristic Gulf lilt that neither Egyptian nor Levantine song shares. It is distinguished from later khaliji pop by its unamplified small-room texture, Nabati poetic texts and the seated solo zafan dance.

items.name: Chutney (Trinidad-Guyana Bhojpuri dance song)
items.lineage: Indo-Caribbean dance song of Trinidad and Guyana, grown out of Bhojpuri women's wedding repertoire and taken public in the 1960s-70s by Sundar Popo and Ramdew Chaitoe — fast duple dholak with the steel dhantal's ringing offbeat, harmonium doubling the vocal line, and Bhojpuri-Creole lyrics sung in a high nasal folk register at dance tempo.
items.description: Chutney formed among the descendants of Indian indentured labourers in Trinidad and Guyana, moving from the private matikor wedding ritual to public dance halls in the 1960s. The core sound is dholak and dhantal with harmonium and a nasal, ornamented Bhojpuri vocal, faster and more percussive than the folk repertoire it draws on. It is distinct from later chutney soca in keeping an acoustic Indian roster and Bhojpuri-language text rather than a soca rhythm section.

items.name: Chutney Soca
items.lineage: Trinidadian hybrid launched by Drupatee Ramgoonai's 1987 recordings and formalized by the Chutney Soca Monarch competition from 1996 — chutney's dholak and dhantal layered onto a 4/4 soca rhythm section of programmed kick, electric bass, brass stabs and synth, at carnival tempo around 130-150 BPM with English-Bhojpuri call-and-response hooks.
items.description: Chutney soca is the carnival-stage fusion of Indo-Trinidadian chutney with soca, dating from Drupatee Ramgoonai's late-1980s crossover records and institutionalized by the annual Chutney Soca Monarch. It keeps the dholak, dhantal and tassa but sets them over a soca kick pattern, synth brass and a big compressed mix built for outdoor fete sound systems. Against acoustic chutney it is louder, English-dominant and hook-driven; against mainstream soca it is marked by the Indian percussion layer and harmonium-derived melodic turns.

items.name: Compas (Haitian konpa dirèk)
items.lineage: Haitian dance style created by saxophonist Nemours Jean-Baptiste in 1955 as konpa dirèk — a slowed, straightened méringue at roughly 100-120 BPM with a steady tanbou-and-kick pulse, cowbell marking the beat, interlocking clean electric guitar arpeggios, a walking-to-riffing bass, and horn or synth sections trading with Creole lead vocal and chorus.
items.description: Konpa dirèk was launched by Nemours Jean-Baptiste's Ensemble Aux Calebasses in 1955 and became Haiti's national dance music, later reshaped in New York and Miami diaspora studios in the 1970s-80s. Its signature is an unhurried, unwavering duple groove with cowbell and tanbou, glassy chorded guitar and horn or synth pads under Creole vocals. Compared with Dominican merengue it is markedly slower and less brass-frantic, and compared with the older méringue it is straighter and band-driven rather than salon-based.

items.name: Méringue (Haitian salon and carnival)
items.lineage: Haiti's 19th-century national dance, formed in Port-au-Prince salons from contredanse and Afro-Haitian rhythm and elevated by Occide Jeanty, Ludovic Lamothe and later Issa el Saieh's big bands — a moderate 2/4 with a distinctive quintolet-inflected bass-drum figure, played by piano or wind band in its lente salon form and by carnival brass in the street.
items.description: Méringue is the older Haitian dance from which konpa was drawn, current from the mid-19th century in both a refined salon form for piano or chamber wind band and a rowdier carnival form for brass and tanbou. It is built on a lilting 2/4 with a syncopated bass-drum figure and European harmonic phrasing coloured by Afro-Haitian percussion. It is separated from Dominican merengue by tempo and drum roster, and from konpa by its notated, composer-led repertoire and lack of an electric rhythm section.

items.name: Carnatic kacheri (South Indian concert practice)
items.lineage: South Indian art-music concert format consolidated in Madras in the 1920s-30s around the Music Academy sabha, drawing on the Trinity's 18th-19th century kriti repertoire and Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar's programme template — raga alapana and kalpanaswara improvisation framing composed kritis, sung to tanpani drone with violin accompaniment, mridangam laying the tala and ghatam or kanjira joining for the tani avartanam percussion solo.
items.description: The Carnatic kacheri is the concert form of South Indian classical music as standardized in early-20th-century Madras: a graded sequence of composed kritis interleaved with alapana, niraval and kalpanaswara, resting on a constant tanpura drone and a 72-melakarta raga system. The violin shadows and answers the singer heterophonically while mridangam articulates the tala cycle, culminating in the tani avartanam. Against Hindustani practice it is far more composition-centred, faster in gamaka ornamentation, and organized around fixed tala cycles rather than extended unmetered alap.

items.name: Celtic Folk (pan-Celtic revival)
items.lineage: Pan-Celtic revival repertoire consolidated in Ireland, Scotland and Brittany from the mid-1960s by Planxty, The Bothy Band, Alan Stivell and Silly Wizard — dance tunes in Dorian and Mixolydian modes played in unison by fiddle, flute and pipes over bouzouki or guitar in modal open voicings, with bodhran driving reels and jigs and unaccompanied or lightly backed ballad singing between sets.
items.description: Celtic folk is the arranged, ensemble-based revival music that grew out of Irish, Scottish and Breton session traditions from the 1960s onward. It keeps the modal dance tunes and their cranned, rolled ornamentation but adds bouzouki and guitar backing, arranged tune sets, and studio recording, alternating instrumental sets with ballads. It is distinguished from unaccompanied sean-nós or a pub session by its fixed arrangements and harmonic accompaniment, and from Celtic rock by its acoustic roster and absence of a drum kit.
exemplars: Alan Stivell — Renaissance de la Harpe Celtique

items.name: Ode (ancient Greek sung ode)
items.lineage: Sung strophic poetry of archaic and classical Greece — Sappho's monodic lyric on Lesbos in the 7th century BC and Pindar's choral victory odes in the 5th — reconstructed from the Delphic hymns and Mesomedes fragments as syllabic melody in Pythagorean-tuned diatonic and enharmonic genera, voice doubled heterophonically by kithara or lyre with aulos, phrase shape governed by quantitative poetic metre rather than a drum pulse.
items.description: The ode was the sung lyric of ancient Greece, either monodic self-accompanied song or choral hymn performed at festivals and victory celebrations. Modern realizations rest on surviving notated fragments — the Delphic paeans, Seikilos, Mesomedes — and give a mostly syllabic, narrow-ambitus melody in Pythagorean intervals, sung with lyre or kithara doubling and aulos drone, its rhythm dictated by long and short syllables. It is separated from later Byzantine chant by its instrumental accompaniment and quantitative metre, and from any surviving folk lineage by being a scholarly reconstruction rather than a continuous practice.
exemplars: Atrium Musicae de Madrid — Musique de la Grèce Antique

items.name: Piphat (Thai-Khmer ceremonial ensemble)
items.lineage: Court and ritual ensemble of Siam and Cambodia, codified in the Bangkok Rattanakosin court from the late 18th century and standardized under Luang Pradit Phairoh's lineage — the pi nai shawm and ranat ek xylophone leading a stratified polyphony over khong wong gong-circle, with taphon and klong that drums and the ching hand-cymbals marking the colotomic cycle in a near-equidistant seven-tone tuning.
items.description: Piphat (Cambodian pinpeat) is the loud percussion-and-shawm ensemble of the Thai and Khmer courts, used for masked drama, shadow play, boxing and temple ritual. Each instrument elaborates the same underlying melody at its own density, producing a shimmering stratified heterophony over gong-punctuated cycles, in a tuning close to seven equal steps that sits outside Western intervals. It differs from the softer mahori and khruang sai ensembles by excluding strings in its core form and by its outdoor ceremonial volume.
exemplars: Royal Cambodian Pinpeat of the Royal University of Fine Arts

items.name: Polka (Central European dance)
items.lineage: Bohemian couple dance from the 1830s that swept European ballrooms within a decade and was carried by Czech, German and Polish emigrants to the American Midwest and Texas — a fast duple with the half-step hop figure, oom-pah bass from tuba or bass on beats one and three, off-beat chords, and a lead of clarinet, trumpet or accordion in bright parallel thirds.
items.description: The polka originated in Bohemia around 1830 and became a mass ballroom dance across Europe before emigrant communities replanted it in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Chicago and central Texas. Its constant marker is the fast 2/4 with a tuba or bass oom-pah and off-beat chording under paired clarinets, trumpets or accordion, harmonized in thirds over simple tonic-dominant progressions. Regional variants diverge sharply: Czech-style keeps brass and clarinet, Slovenian-style features button accordion and banjo, and the Texas-Czech line fed directly into conjunto and Tejano.

items.name: Worldbeat
items.lineage: Anglo-American pop hybrid of the mid-1980s built in flagship multitrack studios by Peter Gabriel, Paul Simon, David Byrne and Talking Heads — African and Latin percussion batteries and mbaqanga or soukous guitar figures set against gated drum sounds, Fairlight and sampled loops, fretless or high-life bass and layered guest vocalists, at mid-tempo 4/4 with tightly compressed studio polish.
items.description: Worldbeat names the mid-1980s wave of Western pop records that folded African, Caribbean and Latin rhythm sections and guest vocalists into high-budget studio production, from Graceland and So through Remain in Light's precedents. Sonically it is defined by dense layered percussion and interlocking guitar lines placed inside a gated, heavily compressed 1980s mix with samplers and synth pads. It is distinguished from the source traditions themselves by that studio construction and Anglophone songwriting, and from later world-music reissue culture by being new hybrid composition rather than curation.

items.name: Baila (Sri Lankan)
items.lineage: Sri Lankan Portuguese-Burgher dance song codified commercially in Colombo from the 1960s-70s by Wally Bastian and above all Maxwell Mendis and M.S. Fernando, then arena-scaled by Desmond de Silva and Anton Jones — built on a fast 6/8 kaffringha lilt over rabana frame-drum and conga, strummed acoustic and clean single-coil guitar, walking electric bass, accordion or organ fills, and a shouted-communal call-and-response chorus in Sinhala with the singer improvising rhyming verses.
items.description: Baila is Sri Lanka's Portuguese-creole party music, descended from the kaffringha and chikothi dances of the island's Afro-Portuguese Kaffir communities and turned into a national commercial idiom in Colombo between the 1960s and 1980s. Its signature is a headlong 6/8 shuffle carried by rabana frame drum and hand percussion, chordal guitar and bass, and a lead voice trading shouted rhyming couplets with a crowd chorus, often with topical or comic Sinhala lyrics. It is distinguished from Sri Lankan sarala gee and film-derived pop by its dance function, its Iberian rather than Indian rhythmic root, and its improvised verse-capping tradition.

items.name: Bhojpuri Lok Geet (village folk song)
items.lineage: Village song repertoire of the Bhojpuri-speaking belt of eastern Uttar Pradesh and western Bihar, documented from the nineteenth century and carried into print and recording by Bhikhari Thakur's Launda Nach theatre from the 1920s — seasonal and life-cycle cycles (kajri, chaita, sohar, vivah geet, birha, purbi) sung mostly by women in unison or by a male birha soloist, over dholak and naal with harmonium drone and manjira, in short strophic cycles at moderate walking tempo with nasal, high-tessitura, heavily portamento-laden delivery.
items.description: Bhojpuri lok geet is the pre-commercial folk song tradition of the Bhojpuri region of eastern India, organised around agricultural seasons (kajri for the monsoon, chaita for spring) and household ritual (sohar for birth, vivah geet for weddings), plus the male narrative form birha. Texture is thin and drone-anchored: dholak or naal keeping a tight kaharwa or dadra cycle, harmonium sustaining a tonic, and unison female voices in a narrow, ornamented, strongly portamento range. It differs from Bhojpuri pop, its commercial descendant, in having no fixed authorship, no electronic backing and no double-entendre hook economy, and from Hindustani classical in its short strophic cycles and absence of raga elaboration.
