The sound is relentlessly rhythmic: wet-tuned reeds, bellows shake, thumping left-hand basses and a frame drum keeping saltarello or tarantella time, with sung stanzas traded between dancers. It is faster, harder-driving and more harmonically fixed than the older zampogna pastorale it displaced in many villages.

items.name: Canzone Genovese
items.lineage: Ligurian urban song tradition of Genoa's old-town caruggi and osterie, formalized in the 19th-century dialect songbook repertoire and revived from the 1970s by Fabrizio De André and Gilberto Coscia, marked by Genoese-dialect texts on port life and emigration, moderate duple ballad tempi, guitar and mandolin accompaniment, and melodic lines shadowed by the parallel-third habits of local choral singing.
items.description: Canzone genovese is the sung poetry of Genoa in Ligurian dialect, a maritime cousin to canzone napoletana but darker, plainer and less operatic. Typical settings pair a lead voice with nylon-string guitar and mandolin over slow-to-moderate strophic forms, often shading into the parallel-third harmonizations of the city's trallalero choirs. Its modern canon runs through De André's dialect albums, which recast the tavern repertoire as literary song.
exemplars: Fabrizio De André – Crêuza de mä

items.name: Trallalero
items.lineage: Genoese male polyphonic tavern singing documented from the late 19th century in Liguria's port osterie, sung by squadre of five to nine men in fixed roles — falsetto contralto, tenor lead, baritone, guitar-imitating chitarra voice and a massed bass drone — in slow free-flowing strophic songs with close open-fifth harmony, nonsense 'tra-la-la' vocables, and no instruments at all.
items.description: Trallalero is the a cappella polyphony of Genoese working-men's drinking societies, sung standing in a tight circle in the osteria. Its signature is role specialization: a high male falsetto, a solo tenor, and a bass chorus sustaining a hummed drone, over which one singer performs the chitarra — a percussive vocal imitation of a strummed guitar with hand cupped over the mouth. That guitar-voice and the nonsense-syllable refrains separate it from Sardinian tenores and from Corsican paghjella.

items.name: Canto a Tenore
items.lineage: Sardinian pastoral quartet polyphony of the Barbagia and central highlands, attested for centuries and inscribed by UNESCO in 2005, built from the solo boghe delivering the poetic text while mesu boghe, contra and bassu sustain guttural throat-produced chords on nonsense syllables in a slow strophic cycle keyed to dance forms such as the ballu tundu.
items.description: Canto a tenore is four-man Sardinian polyphony in which three singers produce a deep, buzzing, harmonic-rich throat timbre — bassu and contra especially — as a living chord beneath a freely ornamented solo poet. Singers stand in a tight closed circle so the blend forms in the middle; tuning is just and beat-free rather than tempered. The bovine-sounding guttural production and the fixed four-role architecture make it immediately distinct from Corsican paghjella or Genoese trallalero.

items.name: Musica Sarda
items.lineage: The wider Sardinian island repertoire outside the tenores quartet — launeddas triple-clarinet dance music of the Campidano played with circular breathing over a continuous drone, organetto-led ballu sardu at fast duple tempi, sung gara poetica improvised poetic duels, and confraternity cuncordu chant — documented intensively from Giulio Fara's 1910s cylinders through Andreas Bentzon's 1960s launeddas fieldwork.
items.description: Musica sarda covers Sardinia's instrumental and non-tenore vocal traditions, whose emblem is the launeddas: three cane single-reed pipes played simultaneously by one musician using circular breathing, yielding an unbroken drone with two interlocking melodic voices across long suite-like nodas. Alongside it sit organetto and accordion ballu tundu dance sets and the confraternity polyphony of cuncordu. The island's archaic untempered intonation and endless-breath continuity set it apart from mainland Italian folk.

items.name: Fado Antigo
items.lineage: The oldest documented layer of Lisbon fado, formed in the 1830s-1860s among the Mouraria and Alfama underclass and associated with Maria Severa, using a small fixed set of traditional fado castiço strophic frameworks (fado corrido, fado mouraria, fado menor) over which singers set quatrains, accompanied only by guitarra portuguesa and viola in slow-to-moderate duple time with heavily rubato, unornamented but weighted vocal delivery.
items.description: Fado antigo, or fado castiço, is the pre-professional Lisbon repertoire: a handful of inherited chord-and-melody moulds onto which any singer could fit new verse, as opposed to the through-composed authored fado canção that dominated from the 1930s. Accompaniment is bare — guitarra portuguesa playing countermelody and the viola marking the bass and chords — and the singing pushes tempo elastically against it. Early shellac recordings and tavern practice preserve its rougher, less orchestrated character.

items.name: Guitarrada (Portuguese Guitar Instrumental)
items.lineage: Instrumental repertoire for the pear-shaped twelve-string guitarra portuguesa, codified in Lisbon and Coimbra from the 1920s by Armandinho and later Carlos Paredes, in which the fado accompanist becomes soloist — fan-shaped preservation of fado harmonic frames plus variações, played with fingernail plectra, dense tremolo and cascading triplet runs over viola de fado bass-chord accompaniment at variable rubato tempi.
items.description: Guitarrada is fado without the singer: the guitarra portuguesa, normally the accompanying countermelody instrument, takes the whole musical argument. Players use metal fingerpicks on twelve strings in six courses, producing a bright, sustaining, tremolo-heavy tone with rapid ornamental turns, backed by the plain nylon-string viola. Coimbra-school playing is more lyrical and modally coloured; Lisbon-school guitarrada stays closer to the dance-derived fado moulds.

items.name: Cante Alentejano
items.lineage: Unaccompanied male choral singing of Portugal's Alentejo plains, formed among landless agricultural labourers in the 19th century and inscribed by UNESCO in 2014, structured as a solo ponto who announces the line, an alto who ornaments a third above, and a slow-moving massed coro entering underneath in parallel thirds at a very slow free-pulse tempo with long held cadences and social-protest texts.
items.description: Cante alentejano is grave, slow, wholly a cappella group song from southern Portugal's wheat and cork country, sung by grupos corais of a dozen or more men (and, increasingly, women) with no conductor and no instruments. The texture is fixed: ponto states the phrase, alto floats a decorated line above, and the chorus fills in beneath, all in broad unmeasured phrases that swell and taper together. Its slowness and thick homophony are the opposite of the guitar-driven fado usually taken as Portugal's national voice.
exemplars: Grupo Coral Os Ceifeiros de Cuba
Grupo Coral e Etnográfico da Casa do Povo de Serpa
Grupo Coral Os Camponeses de Pias

items.name: Portuguese Folk (Música Popular Portuguesa)
items.lineage: The regional rural repertoire of mainland Portugal — Minho vira and chula, Beira and Trás-os-Montes dance tunes, Alentejo and Ribatejo song — collected systematically by Michel Giacometti and Fernando Lopes-Graça in the 1960s-70s and revived by Grupo de Acção Cultural and Brigada Victor Jara, marked by fast 6/8 and 2/4 dance metres, women's high open chest singing, adufe square frame-drum patterns, and plucked viola braguesa and cavaquinho accompaniment.
items.description: Portuguese folk outside fado is overwhelmingly rural, communal and dance-driven: the Minho's whirling vira and chula, Beira Baixa's adufe-accompanied women's songs, bagpipe and drum ranchos in the north-east. Small plucked instruments — viola braguesa, viola campaniça, cavaquinho — supply strummed chordal drive while frame drums and castanets carry the rhythm and singers use a bright, unrounded, high-set chest voice. It sits closer to Galician tradition across the border than to the urban Lisbon guitar tradition.
exemplars: Michel Giacometti / Lopes-Graça Antologia da Música Regional Portuguesa

items.name: Flemish Folk
items.lineage: Dutch-language folk tradition of northern Belgium, largely reconstructed during the 1960s-70s Vlaamse folkrevival by Wannes Van de Velde, Rum and Kadril from 18th-19th-century songbooks and surviving dance repertoire, featuring moderate-tempo strophic ballads and hoppe/schottische dance tunes carried by diatonic accordion, hurdy-gurdy, fiddle and doedelzak bagpipe over strummed guitar, with plain unornamented conversational singing in Antwerp dialect.
items.description: Flemish folk is a revival tradition: the living rural repertoire of Flanders had largely lapsed by 1900, so the modern style was rebuilt from printed song collections and continental dance tunes in the folk clubs of Antwerp and Leuven. The result is drone-inflected — hurdy-gurdy and bagpipe are prominent — but harmonically simple, with clear syllabic storytelling in dialect over accordion and guitar. It is drier and more literary than neighbouring Dutch levenslied and less tune-virtuosic than Irish session music, which it self-consciously borrowed from.

items.name: Dutch Folk
items.lineage: Folk and street-music tradition of the Netherlands, spanning 19th-century Amsterdam draaiorgel barrel-organ street repertoire, the Jordaan café levenslied, and the 1970s revival led by Fungus and Wolverlei working from Nynke van Hichtum and Boer collections — moderate duple-time waltzes and marches, accordion and harmonica lead, sentimental full-throated chest singing, and sing-along strophic choruses.
items.description: Dutch folk music is dominated by urban rather than rural forms: the mechanical street organ, whose loud reed-and-pipe arrangements set much of the popular repertoire, and the Amsterdam levenslied, sentimental sing-along songs of working-class neighbourhoods delivered in a broad, unrestrained chest voice. The 1970s revival added instrumental dance tunes and older ballads recovered from printed collections. Compared with Flemish folk it is plainer harmonically, more tightly metrical, and far more oriented toward mass singalong.

items.name: Volksmusik
items.lineage: German-Austrian-Swiss Alpine folk music codified in the 19th century and standardized for radio and television from the 1950s, built on Ländler and waltz in steady 3/4 and polka in 2/4, diatonic major harmony with prominent I-IV-V bass, steirische Harmonika or Schwyzerörgeli lead, zither and Hackbrett fills, brass bass, and close-harmony yodelling in the Jodler refrain.
items.description: Volksmusik is the Alpine dance and song tradition of Bavaria, Austria and German-speaking Switzerland, performed by small mixed ensembles of button accordion, zither, hammered dulcimer, clarinet and brass bass. Harmony stays firmly in major triads with an oom-pah bass, phrasing is squarely periodic, and vocal sections favour close thirds and the register-breaking yodel. The televised Musikantenstadl repertoire is its polished commercial face; the older Stubenmusi chamber style is quieter and less brass-heavy, and both are distinct from the schlager pop that borrowed its costumes.
exemplars: Slavko Avsenik und seine Original Oberkrainer

items.name: Neue Volksmusik
items.lineage: Alpine (Austrian, Bavarian, Swiss) reinvention of village folk music that crystallized around 1990-2005 with Hubert von Goisern's Alpinkatzen, the Upper-Austrian duo Attwenger, and later Herbert Pixner Projekt and Kofelgschroa — diatonic Steirische harmonica, zither and brass melodies from Ländler and Jodler repertoire set over rock drum kits, dub bass and hip-hop-derived loops at 90-140 BPM, with dialect singing and yodel refrains kept intact rather than smoothed out.
items.description: Neue Volksmusik emerged in the Austrian and Bavarian Alps in the early 1990s as a generation of trained folk players deliberately collided inherited Ländler, Jodler and Marsch material with rock, dub and dance production. The signature sound is a diatonic button accordion or zither carrying an unmistakably traditional tune while a drum kit, electric bass and studio processing supply the floor. Unlike heimat-style volkstümliche Schlager, which sanitizes folk into television pop, Neue Volksmusik keeps dialect diction, modal cadences and yodel breaks abrasive and regional.

items.name: Alpine Yodeling
items.lineage: Herding and signalling vocal practice of the Swiss, Austrian and Bavarian Alps documented from the 18th century onward and codified by 19th-century Jodlerklubs and the Eidgenössischer Jodlerverband — rapid register breaks between chest voice and falsetto on nonsense syllables (holadi, jo-hu), phrases built on the natural harmonic series over a slow tonic-dominant harmonic tread, sung solo over pasture distance or in three- to four-part male and mixed clubs.
items.description: Alpine yodeling is the pan-Alpine practice of leaping between chest and head register on vocables, developed for calling cattle and communicating across valleys before being formalized into club repertoire and competition in the 19th and 20th centuries. Its defining sound is the audible glottal break, harmonic-series melodic contours that favour the natural seventh and the so-called alphorn fa, and slow triadic part-singing beneath the leading voice. It is broader and more harmonized than the wordless Swiss Naturjodel, and unlike American cowboy or country yodeling it stays inside a strophic, triad-based club idiom without blues inflection.

items.name: Naturjodel
items.lineage: Wordless yodel of central and eastern Switzerland — Appenzell Innerrhoden's Ruggusserli and Zäuerli, Muotathal's Juuz, Toggenburg's Johlen — carried orally by herding families and documented by researchers from Alfred Leonz Gassmann to Hanny Christen; slow free-metred phrases in a small group of male voices, built on natural-harmonic intervals including the flattened seventh, with a low held drone voice (Grundbass) beneath two or three yodelling parts and no instruments.
items.description: Naturjodel is the textless yodel of the central Swiss alpine cantons, sung by two to five voices with no accompaniment and no fixed pulse, its phrases beginning and ending as the singers breathe. Tuning follows the natural harmonic series rather than equal temperament, so the seventh and eleventh degrees sit noticeably low and beat against the sustained bass voice. It differs from club yodeling in having no composed song frame, no verse text and no accordion or brass underneath — the material is a shared body of short melodic formulas varied in performance.

items.name: Schwyzerörgeli Ländlermusik
items.lineage: Central Swiss dance-band idiom that took its modern shape after the 1880s adoption of the Schwyzerörgeli, a small diatonic bisonoric accordion in Helvetic tuning, and was standardized in the 1920s-1950s by Kapellen around Rees Gwerder, Kasi Geisser and the Ländlerkapelle format — one or two Örgeli plus B-flat clarinet and slap double bass playing Ländler, Schottisch, Mazurka and Polka at brisk 3/4 and 2/4, with the bass on beat one and the left hand supplying oom-pah chords.
items.description: Schwyzerörgeli music is the Swiss inn-and-wedding dance repertoire built around a small diatonic accordion whose vibrato-rich Helvetic tuning gives the style its immediately identifiable shimmer. The classic trio pairs the Örgeli with clarinet doubling or answering the tune and a double bass playing a rooted, slightly percussive downbeat under alternating oom-pah. Compared with Bavarian Blaskapelle the ensemble is small and stringed rather than brass-led, and compared with Oberkrainer it lacks trumpet lead and the light swing of the Slovenian idiom.

items.name: Alphorn Music
items.lineage: Repertoire of the Swiss and Austrian wooden alphorn, a valveless 3-4 metre conical natural horn documented from the 16th century, revived from near-extinction in the 1820s by Ferdinand Fürchtegott Huber and the Unspunnen festivals and standardized to F-sharp and G-flat instruments in the 20th century — slow ceremonial Betruf and Kuhreihen melodies restricted to harmonics 2-12, including the characteristic eleventh partial (alphorn fa) sitting between F and F-sharp, often played in two- and three-horn consorts.
items.description: Alphorn music is the ceremonial and pastoral repertoire of the long valveless wooden horn of the Swiss and Austrian Alps, revived as a national emblem in the nineteenth century after herding use declined. Because the instrument can only sound its natural harmonics, its melodies are broad and stepwise only in the upper register and include the out-of-tune-sounding eleventh partial that gives the idiom its signature raised fourth. Its slow open-air phrasing, long decay against valley reflections and consort part-writing set it apart from valved brass folk music such as Blaskapelle.

items.name: Ländler
items.lineage: Rural couple dance of Austria, Bavaria and German-speaking Switzerland attested from the late 18th century as the ancestor of the waltz — slow to moderate 3/4 at roughly 100-150 BPM with a heavy, foot-stamping first beat, played by fiddle and hammered dulcimer (Hackbrett) ensembles before diatonic accordion took the lead in the 19th century, frequently interrupted by sung Gstanzln verses and yodel refrains, with turning and clapping figures cueing repeats.
items.description: The Ländler is the Alpine triple-time couple dance from which the Viennese waltz descends, still performed in Austria, Bavaria and Switzerland at village dances and weddings. It is slower and heavier than the waltz, with a stamped downbeat, short repeated eight-bar strains, and frequent interpolated sung Gstanzln or yodel refrains that stop the instruments cold. Its historic roster of fiddle, Hackbrett and zither survives beside the accordion-led Ländlerkapelle, and it is distinguished from Polka-based Blaskapelle repertoire by triple metre and small string-and-reed instrumentation.

items.name: Oberkrainer
items.lineage: Slovenian-Alpine dance-band style created by Slavko Avsenik and his Ansambel bratov Avsenik in Begunje in 1953 and spread across Austria and Germany as Oberkrainer Musik — a fixed quintet of diatonic accordion, B-flat trumpet, clarinet, baritone horn and guitar with bass, playing brisk polkas at 120-150 BPM and lilting waltzes, with the trumpet and clarinet in parallel thirds over the baritone's counter-melody and an off-beat guitar chop.
items.description: Oberkrainer is the Slovenian polka-and-waltz ensemble style invented by Slavko Avsenik in the early 1950s and exported through German-language television and records as the sound of the Alps. Its fixed instrumentation and voicing are the defining trait: diatonic accordion driving the harmony, trumpet and clarinet locked in thirds on the tune, and a baritone horn weaving a mobile counter-line that no neighbouring style uses the same way. Against Czech dechovka it is smaller, faster and lighter, and against Swiss Ländlermusik it is brass-fronted and tightly arranged rather than string-led.

items.name: Guggenmusik
items.lineage: Swiss carnival brass practice formalized in Basel and Lucerne in the 1930s and expanded through post-war Fasnacht and Fasnet cliques in Switzerland, Alsace and southwest Germany — massed trumpets, trombones, sousaphones and percussion marching at roughly 100-130 BPM playing familiar pop and march tunes deliberately out of tune, with smeared attacks, scooped entries and blown-out fortissimo, driven by bass drum and snare in simple duple patterns.
items.description: Guggenmusik is the carnival brass tradition of Basel, Lucerne and the wider Alemannic Fasnacht region, in which costumed cliques of twenty to fifty players parade through streets playing pop hits and marches with intentional dissonance and roaring volume. Deliberate detuning, glissando entries and overblown tone are the aesthetic point rather than a failure of technique, and the drum section keeps a plain marching duple beat that anchors the noise. It is distinct from the disciplined Blaskapelle and from Basel's own piccolo-and-drum Cliquen, both of which prize precision and clean intonation.

items.name: Blaskapelle
items.lineage: Bavarian and Austrian village wind band tradition that took its modern form in the 19th century out of military and church wind ensembles and was standardized by Ernst Mosch's Egerländer model after 1956 — flugelhorn and clarinet leads in parallel thirds, trombone and tenor horn counterlines, tuba with off-beat tenor horns on oom-pah, playing polkas at 110-130 BPM, waltzes and processional marches in civic halls, church festivals and beer tents.
items.description: Blaskapelle is the German-language village and civic wind band tradition of Bavaria, Austria and the Egerland, playing from written parts at church feasts, funerals, parades and Oktoberfest tents. The sound is defined by mellow flugelhorn rather than bright trumpet on the melody, clarinets doubling above, and a tuba-and-tenor-horn oom-pah bed that never swings. It is more notated and formally arranged than Swiss Ländlermusik, and unlike Guggenmusik it treats intonation and blend as the whole point.
exemplars: Ernst Mosch und seine Original Egerländer Musikanten

items.name: Dechovka
items.lineage: Czech brass band music consolidated in Bohemia in the second half of the 19th century out of military bands and the polka craze, with František Kmoch of Kolín as its 1880s codifier and Václav Bláha and Ladislav Kubeš carrying it through the state-label era — E-flat and B-flat clarinets and flugelhorns in thirds, tenor horn counter-melody, tuba and off-beat horns under polkas at 110-125 BPM, plus waltzes and marches, commonly with a sung couplet verse.
items.description: Dechovka is the Czech and Moravian brass band idiom, built on the polka and disseminated nationally through Supraphon and Panton recordings and Czechoslovak radio from the 1950s onward. Its arrangements favour paired clarinets and flugelhorns in thirds over a tuba oom-pah, with a lyrical tenor horn line and a sung strophe in the middle of most polkas. Compared with Bavarian Blaskapelle, which it heavily influenced, dechovka tends toward a lighter clarinet-forward top end and a stronger vocal presence.

items.name: Cimbálová Muzika
items.lineage: Moravian and Slovak string band form that displaced older bagpipe ensembles in the 19th century and was fixed in its modern shape by 20th-century Slovácko and Wallachian bands and Supraphon recordings — a lead prim violin, second violins on chordal seconds, clarinet, concert cimbalom playing tremolo fills and harmonic filler, and double bass, accompanying rubato table songs (táhlé písně) that break into fast čardáš and sedlácká dances.
items.description: Cimbálová muzika is the cimbalom-and-strings band of Moravia and western Slovakia, playing at weddings, wine cellars and folklore festivals with a lead violinist who shapes tempo freely around a singer. The concert cimbalom, struck with soft beaters, supplies both a shimmering tremolo cushion and rapid ornamental runs between vocal phrases, while inner violins hold chordal seconds and the bass anchors the shift from free rubato into driving čardáš. It shares the Hungarian gypsy band's instrumentation but keeps Moravian modal tunes, heavier vocal leadership and less virtuoso cadenza display.

items.name: Moravian Folk Song
items.lineage: Song tradition of Moravia's Slovácko, Horňácko, Wallachia and Haná regions, collected systematically by František Sušil in the 1830s-1860s and by Leoš Janáček and Pavel Váša around 1900 — modal melodies using Lydian and Mixolydian inflections, unaccompanied or lightly cimbalom-backed strophic songs, slow rubato table songs with wide ornamented leaps giving way to duple dance songs, and two-part women's singing in thirds at village festivals and harvest work.
items.description: Moravian folk song is the eastern Czech vocal tradition documented by Sušil and later by Janáček, whose speech-melody theories drew directly on it. The music is markedly more modal and ornamented than Bohemian folk song, with raised fourths, free rubato in the long table songs, and dense melismatic turns on cadences that singers vary from verse to verse. Where cimbálová muzika presents this material in a full band setting, the core tradition is unaccompanied or minimally supported voice, often two women's parts moving in parallel thirds.

items.name: Góralski
items.lineage: Highlander music of the Polish Tatras (Podhale), documented from the 19th century and shaped by Skalne Podhale village bands and post-war state ensembles — a lead prym violin improvising on inherited nuta melodic cycles, two or three sekund violins scraping harmonic seconds on offbeats, and a three-string basy cello marking the beat, supporting shouted high-register wierchowa singing and a free, non-metric couple dance with the Lydian raised fourth as its harmonic signature.
items.description: Góralski is the string-band music of the Polish Tatra highlanders around Zakopane and the Podhale villages, played for the improvised couple dance of the same name at weddings and mountain inns. Its sound is unmistakable: a single lead violin varying a short nuta cycle at the top of the register, two or three seconding violins grinding harmonic seconds behind it, and a bowed basy marking hard downbeats, all under piercing shouted singing that sits above the instruments. Unlike Moravian cimbalom bands there is no cimbalom and no rubato lyricism — the texture is loud, deliberately rough, and locked to the dancers' calls.

items.name: Polish folk (wiejska muzyka taneczna)
items.lineage: Polish village dance music of the Mazovia, Radom and Rzeszów lowlands as documented from the 1920s by Oskar Kolberg's successors and re-collected on tape in the 1970s-90s by Andrzej Bieńkowski, built on a lead fiddle carrying a heavily ornamented melody over a baraban bass drum struck with a beater and a bowed basy drone, playing mazurka, oberek and kujawiak in a lopsided triple metre at 150-200 BPM with the accent thrown onto the second or third beat, plus tight nasal open-throat female singing in the przyśpiewki interludes.
items.description: Village dance music from central and southeastern Poland, played for weddings and Sunday dances by small fiddle-and-drum bands rather than for the stage. The signature is the oberek's driving triple metre with displaced accent, a rasping unequal-tempered fiddle line full of slides and grace notes, and the baraban's dry beater thud doubling a bowed bass drone. Unlike the Tatra góralski repertory it is lowland, duple-and-triple dance music without the highlanders' parallel-fifth string band, and unlike staged Mazowsze-style folklore it keeps rough intonation and irregular phrase lengths.

items.name: Lemko folk (Łemkowszczyzna song tradition)
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Lemko Rusyn communities of the Beskid Niski range on the Polish-Slovak watershed, documented from the late nineteenth century and largely preserved in diaspora after the 1947 Akcja Wisła deportations, centred on unaccompanied or fiddle-and-cimbalom-accompanied strophic lyric and wedding songs in a narrow modal ambitus, sung in tight two- and three-part harmony with parallel thirds, slow parlando-rubato ballads alternating with brisk duple kolomyika dances at roughly 130 BPM.
items.description: The vocal repertory of the Lemkos, a Rusyn population of the Carpathian foothills scattered by postwar resettlement, kept alive through village choirs, church singing and the Vatra festival circuit. It is voice-first: a lead singer and a close second in parallel thirds, plain modal melodies with descending cadential figures, and Church Slavonic liturgical colouring in the harmony. Against neighbouring Polish lowland dance music it is far less instrumental and less drum-driven, and against Ukrainian steppe song it keeps a narrow range and mountain kolomyika rhythms.

items.name: Rusyn folk (Carpatho-Rusyn village music)
items.lineage: Village music of the Carpatho-Rusyns of Transcarpathian Ukraine, eastern Slovakia and the Prešov region, collected systematically from the 1930s and later channelled through state folk ensembles, combining unaccompanied polyphonic women's song with a fiddle-cimbalom-bass band playing kolomyjka in fast duple metre near 140 BPM, shepherd signalling on the long wooden trembita and sopilka duct-flute solos, and a lyric verbunk-style parlando ballad style with strong ornamental grace-note clusters.
items.description: The Carpathian mountain repertory of the Rusyn communities straddling the Ukraine-Slovakia-Poland borders, spanning pastoral signal instruments, wedding fiddle bands and layered women's song. Its markers are the trembita's open harmonic-series calls across valleys, the cimbalom's tremolo cushion beneath a sliding fiddle, and hard-edged chest singing in kolomyjka couplets. It shares repertory with Lemko song but is more instrument-driven and retains the highland shepherd layer that the resettled Lemko tradition largely lost.

items.name: Hungarian folk (népzene, Bartók-Kodály collected repertory)
items.lineage: The Magyar peasant repertory systematically recorded on wax cylinder by Béla Bartók and Zoltán Kodály from 1905 and revived by the Budapest táncház movement after 1972, divided between the old-style pentatonic parlando-rubato long songs with descending fifth-shift structure and the new-style tempo giusto strophic songs, and performed instrumentally by a Transylvanian string band of prímás violin, chordal three-string kontra viola and gardon or double bass, with cimbalom and clarinet in lowland bands.
items.description: The village music of the Hungarian-speaking Carpathian Basin as classified by Bartók and Kodály and reactivated by the táncház revival, which learned directly from surviving Transylvanian village bands. Its defining sounds are the pentatonic descending-fifth melodic architecture, the rubato flexibility of the old-style songs, and the grinding rhythmic chords of the kontra viola with flattened bridge that make the Hungarian string band unmistakable. It is not the urban magyar nóta of the restaurant Gypsy orchestra, nor the recruiting-dance verbunkos, though both draw on its melodies.
exemplars: Béla Bartók's Hungarian Folk Music cylinder collection

items.name: Csárdás
items.lineage: Hungarian couple dance codified in the 1830s-40s out of verbunkos recruiting music and named for the roadside csárda tavern, built as a paired form of slow lassú in moderate duple metre followed by an accelerating friss reaching 180-200 BPM, played by Roma-led restaurant bands of prímás violin, cimbalom, kontra and bass with a heavy dotted 'Hungarian' rhythm, augmented-second Gypsy-scale inflections, cadenza-like violin flourishes and huge accelerandi.
items.description: The tavern and ballroom couple dance of nineteenth-century Hungary, spread across Europe by Roma restaurant orchestras and absorbed into concert repertory by Liszt, Brahms and Monti. Its architecture is the slow-fast pair: a rubato, heavily ornamented lassú in which the prímás bends every phrase, then a friss that accelerates relentlessly over cimbalom tremolo and off-beat kontra chords. It differs from collected village népzene in being an urban professional idiom with harmonised chromatic accompaniment and virtuoso display rather than a functional peasant dance.

items.name: Muzică lăutărească
items.lineage: Professional Romanian Roma wedding-musician repertory carried by the lăutari guilds of Wallachia and Moldavia since the eighteenth century and passed patrilineally within families such as the Gore and Neacșu lines, played by taraf ensembles of violin, cobza or guitar, țambal cimbalom, nai panpipe, accordion and double bass, mixing free-rhythm doina preludes, Ottoman-derived modal manele and hard-driving 2/4 sârba and 7/16 geampara dances above 160 BPM under declaimed, ornament-saturated solo singing.
items.description: The hereditary trade music of Romania's Roma lăutari, played for weddings, baptisms and restaurant patrons rather than for the state or the concert hall, and circulated for decades on hand-dubbed wedding cassettes. Its texture is a virtuoso violin or nai line over cimbalom tremolo and cobza strumming, with abrupt shifts from rubato lament to breakneck aksak dance and improvised sung praise addressed to paying guests. Where muzică populară smooths the same tunes into tempered ensemble arrangements, lăutărească keeps microtonal Ottoman inflection, harsh nasal delivery and on-the-spot improvisation.

items.name: Muzică populară
items.lineage: Romanian state-sanctioned folkloric popular music built at Electrecord and the national radio orchestras from the late 1940s under the Barbu Lăutaru and Ciocârlia ensembles, arranging regional village tunes for a tempered orchestra of massed violins, țambal, nai, accordion, clarinet and bass, with trained soloists delivering doina-derived free-rhythm openings followed by neatly metred hora and sârba at 120-150 BPM, everything transcribed, conducted and stripped of microtonal drift.
items.description: The orchestrated national folklore of socialist Romania, made for radio, television and Electrecord LPs by conservatory-trained soloists fronting large folk orchestras. It is clean, tempered and arranged: unison violin sections, a bright nai lead, cimbalom filigree and cadenced hora sections, with vocal delivery projected and vibrato-rich rather than raw. It draws on the same regional tunes as lăutărească but replaces improvisation and Ottoman intonation with fixed arrangements and equal temperament, and it stands apart from post-1990 etno by being entirely acoustic.

items.name: Muzică etno
items.lineage: Romanian folk-pop hybrid that emerged on private television and cable radio after 1995 and consolidated around 2000-2010, taking muzică populară melodies and doina-style nai and fluier lines and setting them over programmed four-on-the-floor and 2/4 hora beats at 125-140 BPM with synth pads, sampled cimbalom, sequenced bass and heavily tuned pop-belt vocals, arranged in verse-chorus pop form for playback performance in sequinned costume.
items.description: A post-communist Romanian commercial genre that repackages folkloric melody as synthesised dance-pop for television channels like Etno TV and Favorit. The sound is programmed drums, wide synth pads and sampled or MIDI cimbalom and panpipe hooks under retuned, compressed pop vocals, with the folk material reduced to a recognisable topline. It is distinct from acoustic muzică populară by being fully studio-constructed, and from manele by keeping Carpathian rather than Balkan-Oriental melodic material and avoiding manele's chalga rhythm section.

items.name: Doina
items.lineage: Romanian and Moldovan free-rhythm improvised song type documented across Oltenia, Maramureș and Moldavia and inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, sung or played parlando-rubato with no fixed metre, opening on a held high pitch and descending in long ornamented arcs over a static drone, cadencing on descending sighs and interjected calls, typically solo voice with fiddle, cobza or nai shadowing the line, and used as the improvised prelude before metred dance sets.
items.description: A pan-Romanian genre of unmeasured lyric improvisation, sung alone in the fields or played as an instrumental taksim-like prelude by lăutari. It is defined by the absence of pulse: long breath-length phrases over a held drone, elaborate mordents and glides, recitation formulas and non-lexical cries such as 'of, of' punctuating the descent. Unlike a strophic ballad it has no fixed melody or stanza scheme, and unlike the metred hora that usually follows it, the performer alone controls duration and phrase shape.
exemplars: Fănică Luca doina de jale recordings

items.name: Kaba gaida (Rhodope low bagpipe)
items.lineage: Low-pitched bagpipe tradition of Bulgaria's Rhodope mountains, played on the kaba gaida whose chanter sounds roughly a fourth below the northern djura gaida, documented from the early twentieth century and institutionalised through the Shiroka Laka music school and the 100 Kaba Gaidi mass ensemble founded in 1961, characterised by slow rubato bavna pesen accompaniment, dense flick-ornament kavals of grace notes, a continuous low drone and slow Rhodope horo in 2/4 or 7/8 under wide open-throat female singing.
items.description: The deep-voiced bagpipe music of the Rhodope range in southern Bulgaria, slower and darker than the higher-pitched pipe traditions of Thrace and the northwest. Its identity rests on the kaba's heavy continuous drone, the chanter's percussive finger-flick ornaments that substitute for tonguing, and the long unmeasured Rhodope songs it accompanies. Massed kaba gaida ensembles produce a beating, slightly detuned wall of drones that is unlike any other European pipe tradition.

items.name: Bulgarian folk (narodna muzika ensemble tradition)
items.lineage: Bulgarian national folk idiom codified after 1944 by Filip Kutev's State Ensemble and the Radio Sofia folk orchestras, which arranged village repertory for gaida, kaval, gadulka, tambura and tapan alongside written four-part women's choral settings, keeping regional aksak metres of 7/8, 9/8 and 11/16 and the sharply attacked open-throat vocal timbre while adding functional harmony, second-interval clusters and precise sectional arrangement for broadcast and export.
items.description: The arranged national folk music of Bulgaria as built by state ensembles and radio orchestras from the late 1940s, and exported worldwide through the Le Mystère des Voix Bulgares releases. It combines the village instrumentarium of drone bagpipe, end-blown kaval, bowed gadulka and long-necked tambura with composed choral writing full of deliberate major seconds, over asymmetric aksak metres played with machine precision. It differs from raw village horo recordings by being notated, conducted and studio-balanced, and from Rhodope kaba gaida music by favouring bright northern and Thracian instruments and fast virtuoso tempi.

items.name: Narodna muzika (Yugoslav folk-pop)
items.lineage: Yugoslav commercial folk-pop consolidated in the 1960s-70s on the Jugoton and PGP-RTB labels, in which Serbian, Bosnian and Macedonian village and sevdah melodies were fitted to studio arrangements of lead accordion, clarinet, tamburica and later electric bass and drum kit, mostly in 4/4 kolo or slow ballad tempo with 7/8 excursions, over trained solo voices using wide vibrato, Ottoman-derived augmented-second inflections and melismatic cadence turns.
items.description: The mass-market folk song of socialist Yugoslavia, sold on 7-inch singles and played nightly in kafanas across Serbia and Bosnia. Its sound is a virtuoso accordion or clarinet intro answering a big, vibrato-heavy solo voice, backed by tamburica and a light rhythm section, in short verse-refrain songs about love and exile. It sits between rural izvorna performance and the later synth-driven turbo-folk of the 1990s: professionally arranged and studio-recorded, but still acoustic-led and modally Ottoman rather than beat-driven.

items.name: Izvorna muzika (Bosnian source music)
items.lineage: Rural dance-song style of northeastern Bosnia around Tuzla, Zvornik and Posavina, commercialised on cassette from the 1970s and named 'source music' to claim village authenticity, driven by fretted šargija long-necked lutes strumming in fast even 2/4 or 4/4 at 140-170 BPM with violin doubling, and sung by two or three male voices in shouted narrow-interval seconds derived from ganga and putnička polyphony, with unresolved harsh dissonance at the cadence.
items.description: A northeastern Bosnian village style built on relentless strummed šargija ostinato and multi-voice shouted singing in clashing seconds, sold on cheap cassettes and cheaply pressed CDs through market kiosks and diaspora shops. The vocal parts move in tight, deliberately dissonant parallel motion and end on an unresolved beating interval, an aesthetic inherited from ganga rather than from tempered harmony. Unlike polished narodna muzika it uses no keyboard, no arranger and little dynamic shaping, and unlike sevdalinka it is fast, collective and dance-functional rather than slow and lyrical.

items.name: Starogradska Muzika
items.lineage: Serbian and Vojvodinian urban 'old town' song codified in the kafanas of Belgrade, Novi Sad and Subotica between the 1880s and the 1930s and preserved on Jugoton and PGP-RTB records after 1945 — moderate rubato duple and 3/4 verses in harmonic minor, sung by a single lyric voice with heavy portamento over a tamburica string band or accordion-violin-clarinet kafana quartet, each strophe accelerating into a faster kolo-like coda
items.description: Starogradska muzika is the sentimental urban song repertoire of late-Habsburg and interwar Serbian towns, sung in kafanas and formalised on Yugoslav state-label recordings from the 1950s onward. Its sound is a lyric solo voice with wide portamento and rubato over tamburica strings, accordion, violin and clarinet, cadencing in harmonic minor with a characteristic accelerando into a dance coda. Unlike sevdalinka it is tonally Central European rather than makam-inflected, and unlike turbofolk it uses no drum machine, synthesizer or amplified rhythm section.

items.name: Sevdah (modern Bosnian revival)
items.lineage: The contemporary concert reworking of Bosnian sevdalinka, developed in Sarajevo and the Bosnian diaspora after the 1992-95 war by Damir Imamović, Amira Medunjanin and Božo Vrećo — slow free-tempo openings on saz over sustained drone, melismatic makam-inflected melody with quarter-tone inflection, minimal jazz-informed double bass and violin accompaniment, and long unmetered melodic paragraphs that only occasionally settle into a slow 4/4
items.description: Sevdah in its post-1995 revival form takes the Ottoman-era Bosnian love-song repertoire out of the kafana and onto the concert and festival stage, stripped to saz, voice, bass and violin. The defining traits are unmetered rubato phrasing, dense melisma with neutral seconds and quarter-tone inflection inherited from makam practice, and long-held drones under a single confessional voice. It differs from mid-century recorded sevdalinka, which used a full radio orchestra with accordion and tempered harmonisation, and from Balkan folk-pop by its refusal of a fixed dance pulse.

items.name: Klapa
items.lineage: Dalmatian coastal a cappella harmony singing formalised at the Omiš festival from 1967 out of nineteenth-century church and confraternity practice — four to eight male voices in close homophonic chords, a high first tenor carrying the melody above two inner parts and a bass, with unmetered rubato opening lines, wide crescendos, and long fermatas at cadence, recognised by UNESCO in 2012
items.description: Klapa is the male close-harmony song of the Croatian Adriatic coast and islands, sung unaccompanied or with light mandolin and guitar and codified through the annual Omiš klapa festival since 1967. It is defined by chordal homophony under a soaring first tenor, rubato phrase openings, dynamic swells to a held final chord, and texts about the sea, wine and departure. Unlike Dinaric ojkanje it is fully tempered, harmonised in thirds and sixths, and consciously polished for stage and record.

items.name: Ojkanje
items.lineage: Two-voice shouted singing of the Dinaric hinterland of Croatia, Bosnia and western Herzegovina, documented ethnographically from the early twentieth century and inscribed by UNESCO in 2010 — a lead voice sustaining a tone with a fast pulsating tremolo on the syllable 'oj' while a second voice holds a major or minor second below, unmetered, at maximum chest volume, cadencing on a unison after a prolonged shake
items.description: Ojkanje is the open-air shouted polyphony of the Dinaric karst, sung by two or more voices in narrow non-tempered intervals, most characteristically the dissonant second held until the closing unison. Its signature is the throat-driven tremolo on the vowel 'oj', produced at extreme volume so it carries across valleys, and the total absence of metre or instrumental accompaniment. It is the rural, dissonant counterpart to coastal klapa harmony, and unlike gusle epic it is collective and non-narrative.
exemplars: Croatian Institute of Ethnology archive recordings

items.name: Tamburica Orchestra Music
items.lineage: Pannonian plucked-string ensemble tradition of Vojvodina, Slavonia and Bačka, organised into standardised orchestras from the 1840s Osijek and Zagreb societies onward — prim leading fast tremolo melody, brač and bugarija filling chords on the offbeat, and a berde bass on the downbeat, playing 2/4 kolo dances and strophic urban songs with abrupt tempo steps
items.description: Tamburica orchestra music is the plucked-string ensemble practice of the Pannonian plain, in which a family of long-necked lutes from the tiny prim to the bass berde is arranged like a string orchestra. Its sound is continuous mandolin-like tremolo melody over offbeat chordal strumming and a walking bass, alternating fast 2/4 kolo instrumentals with accompaniments to strophic song. Distinct from Hungarian gypsy-band csárdás, which is violin and cimbalom led, and from Bulgarian village bands, which favour aerophones and additive metres.

items.name: Kolo (Serbo-Croatian circle dance)
items.lineage: The chain and circle dance repertoire of Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia, standardised on record and radio from the 1930s and especially in the Yugoslav 1950s-70s — brisk 2/4 at roughly 130-160 BPM, an accordion or tamburica prim leading continuous sixteenth-note melody in harmonic minor, offbeat brač chords, a stamping bass on the downbeat, and paired repeated eight-bar strains driving the dancers' step cycle
items.description: Kolo is the instrumental circle-dance music of the South Slavic lands, danced in an open chain and recorded prolifically by Yugoslav state labels from the 1950s. Musically it is fast duple metre with unbroken sixteenth-note accordion or prim melody over offbeat chords and a stamped bass, built from short repeated strains that cycle indefinitely so dancers can hold the step pattern. It differs from Bulgarian horo mainly in metre: kolo stays in even 2/4 where horo routinely uses additive 7/8, 9/8 and 11/16.

items.name: Horo (Bulgarian dance music)
items.lineage: Bulgarian village and state-ensemble chain-dance repertoire, systematised after 1951 by Philip Koutev's national ensemble and issued on Balkanton — additive aksak metres (7/8 ruchenitsa, 9/8 daichovo, 11/16 kopanitsa) at high tempo, gaida drone under kaval and gadulka heterophony, tambura offbeat strumming, and a tupan stick-and-beater pattern marking the long and short beats
items.description: Horo is the Bulgarian chain-dance music, played in villages for weddings and fairs and codified for stage and record by the post-war state folk ensembles. Its identity rests on additive aksak metres counted in uneven long-short groups, gaida bagpipe drone with piercing ornamented melody doubled heterophonically by kaval and bowed gadulka, and the tupan's asymmetric bass-and-rim pattern. Against Serbian kolo it is metrically irregular and drone-based; against Greek nisiotika it is inland, aerophone-led and untempered.

items.name: Këngë Popullore e Jugut (South Albanian)
items.lineage: The lyric song and iso-polyphony of Toskëria and Labëria in southern Albania, documented from the 1930s and canonised through the Gjirokastër national folklore festival from 1968 — a taker soloist and turner second voice above a continuous held iso drone sung by the group, unmetered or slow duple, joined in urban saze ensembles by clarinet and violin trading heavily ornamented answering phrases
items.description: South Albanian popular song is built on iso-polyphony: a lead voice and a decorating second voice float over an unbroken vocal drone held by the rest of the group, an arrangement UNESCO recognised in 2005. In its urban saze form the drone role passes to clarinet, violin, llautë and def, with the clarinet answering the singer in dense chromatic ornament and long slides. It is distinct from northern Albanian çifteli epic song, which is monophonic and lute-accompanied, and from Greek Epirot polyphony chiefly by language and repertoire rather than technique.

items.name: Çifteli Song (North Albanian)
items.lineage: Northern Albanian and Kosovar song accompanied by the two-string long-necked çifteli, carried by the Gheg highlands of Malësia and Dukagjin and spread on cassette through the 1970s-90s Kosovo and diaspora market — one string plucked as a fast melodic line, the second sounding a fixed drone, under a nasal declamatory tenor singing strophic heroic and wedding texts in free rhythm or a steady 2/4 with def frame drum
items.description: Çifteli song is the solo lute-and-voice tradition of the Gheg-speaking north of Albania and of Kosovo, where a small two-course lute supplies melody on one string and an unchanging drone on the other. The texture is deliberately bare — one voice, one lute, sometimes a def — with nasal high-tessitura delivery, long strophes of narrative or wedding text, and micro-ornamented melodic turns around a small ambitus. Where southern Albanian song is polyphonic and drone-choral, çifteli song is monophonic, portable and closely tied to solo epic recitation.

items.name: Éntekhno
items.lineage: Greek art-popular song created in Athens from 1958-60 by Manos Hadjidakis and Mikis Theodorakis, who set major poets — Seferis, Elytis, Ritsos — to composed song cycles scored for bouzouki orchestra with strings and santouri, keeping rebetiko modal dromoi and 9/8 zeibekiko and 2/4 hasapiko rhythms but writing the parts out for trained arrangers and recording them at Columbia's Rizoupoli plant
items.description: Éntekhno is the composed art-song branch of Greek popular music, launched around 1960 when Theodorakis and Hadjidakis wedded literary poetry to bouzouki-led orchestration in through-composed cycles such as Epitaphios and Axion Esti. Its markers are notated arrangements for bouzouki, santouri, strings and piano, rebetiko dromoi and zeibekiko or hasapiko metres retained but disciplined, and declamatory baritone or dramatic contralto delivery of literary text. It differs from laïkó by its notated orchestration and poetic sources, and from rebetiko by its concert-hall ambition and absence of improvised taximia.

items.name: Néo Kýma
items.lineage: Short-lived Athenian movement of 1960-67 centred on the Plaka boîtes, combining French chanson phrasing with éntekhno lyricism — soft mid-range voices, nylon-string guitar as the primary accompaniment with double bass and occasional string quartet, tempered Western harmony rather than dromoi, slow to moderate 4/4 and 3/4, and intimate close-miked delivery to small seated audiences
items.description: Néo Kýma was the Greek 'new wave' of the early 1960s, performed in the small Plaka boîtes where singer-guitarists delivered literate lyrics in a hushed, conversational register. Its sound is deliberately spare — nylon guitar, upright bass, a light string or piano pad — in Western tempered harmony with chanson-like verse forms, avoiding both bouzouki timbre and Eastern modality. That avoidance is what separates it from éntekhno and laïkó, whose orchestrations and dromoi it consciously set aside before the 1967 junta dispersed the scene.

items.name: Nisiótika
items.lineage: Song and dance repertoire of the Aegean islands — Cyclades, Dodecanese, Ikaria — carried orally through panigyria and commercialised on Athenian labels from the 1950s by the Konitopoulos family of Naxos — violi leading ornamented melody with laouto strumming a driving offbeat, santouri fills and tsampouna drone in older village practice, brisk syrtos and ballos in 2/4 and 7/8 kalamatianos, with bright open-throat unison singing
items.description: Nisiótika is the island music of the Aegean, played at village festivals and issued commercially from Athens since the 1950s. It is violin-led, with the laouto supplying a percussive offbeat strum, santouri answering phrases, and bright unison singing over fast syrtos, ballos and kalamatianos dance rhythms. Compared with Cretan lyra music it is violin- rather than lyra-based and lighter in texture, and compared with mainland dimotiká it dispenses with clarinet and zurna-daouli heaviness in favour of a quick, sunlit string sound.

items.name: Pontian Folk Music
items.lineage: Music of the Pontic Greeks of the Black Sea coast, transplanted to northern Greece and the diaspora after the 1923 population exchange and sustained at diaspora associations and panigyria — the three-string bowed kemenche (Pontian lyra) playing continuous fast double-stopped melody with a droning lower string, driving the tik, omal and serra dances in 5/8 and 7/8 at high tempo, doubled at open-air events by zurna and davul, with strophic distich singing
items.description: Pontian folk music is the surviving dance and song tradition of Greeks from the Black Sea littoral, now centred on Thessaloniki, Macedonia and the diaspora. It is dominated by the kemenche or Pontian lyra, a narrow box fiddle bowed across two strings at once so melody and drone sound continuously, driving relentless additive-metre dances such as tik and the war-dance serra, with shouted distich singing and, outdoors, zurna and davul. Its narrow melodic ambitus, unbroken tremolo bowing and non-tempered intonation set it apart from both Aegean violin music and mainland clarinet-led dimotiká.

items.name: Greek Clarinet (Klarino)
items.lineage: Epirot and Macedonian folk instrumental tradition formed after the Albanian-Greek Ottoman clarinet trade of the 1830s-1870s and codified on disc by Kitsos Harisiadis, Vasilis Soukas and Petroloukas Chalkias, in which a B-flat or C klarino plays free-rhythm miroloi laments and then aksak dance suites (tsamiko 3/4, syrtos 2/4, beratis 8/8) at 60-130 BPM over a laouto strum-drone with heterophonic violi, using chalumeau-register smears, microtonal bends and long circular-breathed phrases.
items.description: The klarino tradition of northwestern Greece, dominant since Ottoman-era clarinets reached Epirus in the mid-nineteenth century and preserved on Greek Columbia and Minos recordings from the 1930s onward. Its signature is the alternation of an unmeasured, sobbing miroloi introduction with tightly metered village dances, the clarinet bending pitches below equal temperament and sliding between registers while the laouto supplies rhythmic drone rather than functional harmony. Unlike rebetiko it is instrumental and rural rather than urban-song-based, and unlike Turkish makam clarinet it favors Epirot pentatonic-with-flattened-third laments over full makam modulation.

items.name: Georgian Polyphony
items.lineage: Three-voice Caucasian vocal polyphony documented across Guria, Svaneti, Kakheti and Samegrelo, transcribed from the 1880s by Zakaria Paliashvili and Dimitri Arakishvili and recorded on wax cylinder from 1901, built on a bass drone or moving bass with two upper parts colliding in seconds and fourths, non-tempered intervals near neutral thirds, sharp cadences resolving to open fifths, Gurian krimanchuli yodel breaks, and the extended supra table-song and Kakhetian long-song forms sung a cappella by male ensembles.
items.description: An indigenous three-part vocal polyphony of the Georgian highlands and lowlands, continuously practiced since at least the medieval period and inscribed by UNESCO in 2001. Its defining sound is a non-tempered tuning system in which upper voices dwell on seconds and fourths against a sustained bass, cadencing on bare fifths, with regional dialects ranging from the dense yodelled krimanchuli of Guria to the slow melismatic table songs of Kakheti. Distinguished from Balkan diaphonic singing by its three independent parts rather than drone-plus-melody, and from Orthodox chant by its secular supra and work-song repertoire.

items.name: Duduk (Armenian Apricot-Wood Reed)
items.lineage: Armenian double-reed tradition centered on the apricot-wood duduk, formalized in the twentieth century by Vache Hovsepyan, Levon Madoyan and Djivan Gasparyan at the Yerevan conservatory, in which a lead player spins slow rubato modal laments and dance tunes over a second duduk sustaining an unbroken circular-breathed dam drone, with dense finger-slide ornament, breathy subtone attacks and a narrow one-and-a-half-octave nasal-warm range.
items.description: The duduk repertoire of Armenia, an ancient cylindrical-bore double reed given its modern concert form under Soviet-era Yerevan institutions and carried worldwide by Djivan Gasparyan from the 1980s. Its sonic signature is the pairing of a soloist with a dam player whose circular-breathed drone never stops, over which the lead executes microtonal slides, mordents and a heavy vocalized vibrato that mimics Armenian lament singing. Unlike the zurna it is soft, indoor and elegiac rather than piercing and processional, and unlike the Turkish mey it carries a distinct Armenian modal and repertoire identity tied to Komitas's collected village melodies.

items.name: Armenian Folk Music
items.lineage: Village song and dance repertoire of the Armenian highlands, collected and transcribed from roughly 1899 by Komitas Vardapet who separated it from Ottoman-Turkish urban style, featuring modal melodies in narrow-range diatonic and neutral-second modes, plough songs and antuni laments in free rhythm, kochari and shalakho line dances in 6/8 and 2/4 driven by dhol at 100-140 BPM, and heterophonic accompaniment from duduk, zurna, shvi and kanun behind a nasal chest-voiced solo singer.
items.description: The rural song and dance tradition of Armenia and historic Western Armenia, systematized by Komitas Vardapet's ethnographic transcriptions around 1900 and sustained after 1915 by diaspora and Soviet Armenian ensembles. It is characterized by monophonic or heterophonic textures, narrow-range modal melodies with neutral intervals, unmeasured agricultural and exile laments set beside sharply metered dhol-driven circle dances, and a dry chest-forward vocal delivery with restrained ornament. It differs from the duduk concert tradition by being song- and dance-led rather than instrumental-solo, and from Anatolian Turkish folk by its distinct modal cadences and Armenian-language strophic texts.

items.name: Meyxana
items.lineage: Azerbaijani improvised rhyming-duel form from the Baku-Absheron villages, attested from the early twentieth century and commercialized on cassette and wedding video from the 1980s through Aghamirze, Namiq Qaraçuxurlu and Rəşad Dağlı, in which two or more performers trade rhymed couplets on a set theme over a fixed short rhythmic loop from nagara or a cheap drum-machine pattern at 90-120 BPM, delivered in a nasal shouted half-sung cadence with the crowd marking the rhyme landing.
items.description: A competitive improvised-verse genre from the Absheron peninsula around Baku, performed at weddings and street gatherings and spread nationally by cassette and later YouTube video from the 1990s onward. Performers alternate rhymed couplets on an assigned rhyme word and topic over an unchanging short percussion loop, the delivery a loud nasal chant closer to speech than song, judged by the crowd on wit and rhyme accuracy. It shares the battle logic of hip-hop freestyle but predates it locally, and it differs from mugham by abandoning modal melodic development entirely in favor of metered verbal contest.

items.name: Azerbaijani Traditional Music
items.lineage: Umbrella village and ashiq repertoire of Azerbaijan and Iranian Azerbaijan, transmitted by saz-playing ashiq bards and by wedding zurna-nagara duos and codified in transcription by Uzeyir Hajibeyov from the 1920s, spanning strophic ashiq epics in 6/8 declaimed over strummed drone chords, yalli line dances in 6/8 at 120-150 BPM, and Absheron wedding music where paired zurna trade a piercing lead over an unbroken circular-breathed drone and interlocking nagara.
items.description: The non-courtly traditional music of Azerbaijan: ashiq bardic song accompanied by the long-necked saz, communal yalli line dances, and the outdoor zurna-and-nagara wedding ensemble of the Absheron and Karabakh regions. Its markers are drone-anchored modal melody, additive 6/8 dance meters, and an extremely loud open-air double-reed timbre with continuous circular breathing against interlocking cylindrical drums. It sits below mugham in formality, lacking the graded dastgah architecture, and differs from Anatolian ashik traditions by its Azerbaijani modal vocabulary and its heavy nagara-driven dance function.
exemplars: Azerbaijani State Song and Dance Ensemble

items.name: Lezginka
items.lineage: North Caucasian couple-and-solo dance genre of the Lezgin, Avar, Chechen and Circassian peoples, standardized as stage repertoire by Soviet ensembles from the 1930s and by Igor Moiseyev's choreography, played at 140-180 BPM in a driving 6/8 with a constant dotted accent on the first and fourth eighths, led by zurna or accordion over relentless doubli, doira and hand-clap patterns, the melody a rapid ornamented modal line repeated in ever-tightening cycles as the dancer accelerates.
items.description: The signature fast dance music of the North Caucasus, shared across Dagestani, Chechen, Ingush and Circassian communities and turned into a pan-Soviet stage genre by state folk ensembles from the 1930s. It runs in a hard-driving 6/8 at high tempo, with a fixed dotted rhythmic cell hammered by frame and cylindrical drums and clapping while zurna or button accordion loops a short ornamented modal phrase that accelerates toward the dancer's climax. Unlike Georgian dance music it is drone-free and almost entirely instrumental, and unlike Azerbaijani yalli it is a solo-virtuoso showpiece rather than a communal line dance.
exemplars: Lezginka State Dance Ensemble of Dagestan

items.name: Circassian (Adyghe) Folk Music
items.lineage: Adyghe and Kabardian song tradition of the Northwest Caucasus, carried into Ottoman exile after the 1864 expulsion and collected in the Soviet period by Vladimir Baragunov and the Nalchik ethnographers, built on pshinatl heroic narrative songs delivered by a soloist over a wordless male choral drone in seconds and fourths, the shichepshin bowed fiddle scraping a heterophonic second line, and pshine accordion dance tunes in 6/8 marked by hardwood clapper and hand-clap accompaniment.
items.description: The song tradition of the Circassian peoples of the Northwest Caucasus and their large Turkish, Jordanian and Syrian diaspora, sustained orally after the mass deportations of 1864 and documented by Kabardino-Balkarian folklorists in the twentieth century. Its core is the pshinatl, a narrative or lament sung by a soloist against a sustained wordless male chorus that moves in seconds and fourths, joined by the horsehair-strung shichepshin fiddle and, in dance repertoire, the diatonic pshine accordion with rhythmic clapping. It shares Caucasian drone polyphony with Georgian singing but keeps the chorus subordinate to a narrating soloist, and its dance strand overlaps with lezginka while remaining more song-centered.

items.name: Caucasian Folk Music (Regional Composite)
items.lineage: Regional composite of the mountain traditions between the Black and Caspian seas, recorded ethnographically from wax cylinder in the 1900s through Melodiya's Soviet republic series, characterized by drone-anchored vocal polyphony in Georgia, narrow-range modal solo song and lament in Armenia and Dagestan, double-reed and accordion dance music in fast 6/8 at 130-180 BPM, and heterophonic plucked and bowed accompaniment on panduri, tar and kamancha with frame and cylinder drums.
items.description: An umbrella category for the village musics of the Caucasus isthmus, spanning Georgian, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Dagestani, Chechen and Circassian practice as documented by Russian and Soviet ethnographers from the 1900s onward. Common threads are drone-based rather than chordal accompaniment, non-tempered modal intonation, sharply metered 6/8 dance repertoire alongside unmeasured lament, and outdoor double-reed-and-drum ensembles for weddings. It is broader than any single national tradition here and should be treated as the shared substrate from which Georgian polyphony, Armenian folk and lezginka each specialize.

items.name: Russian Folk Music
items.lineage: Village song tradition of the Russian north and south, collected from the 1860s by Yuli Melgunov and Yevgeniya Linyova's phonograph work and later staged by Mitrofan Pyatnitsky's 1911 choir, built on podgoloski heterophonic multipart singing where a zapevala's line is branched by lower voices into open fifths and octaves, protyazhnaya long songs in free rhythm, and metered chastushka and dance tunes at 120-160 BPM over balalaika, gusli, garmon and clacking spoons.
items.description: The rural song repertoire of ethnic Russian villages, first captured on phonograph by Yevgeniya Linyova around 1900 and institutionalized through Soviet state folk choirs after Pyatnitsky's 1911 ensemble. Its defining feature is podgoloski heterophony, in which subsidiary voices split off from a lead melody into open fifths and octaves rather than triadic harmony, set against slow melismatic protyazhnaya laments and fast strophic chastushka couplets over balalaika and garmon. It differs from Ukrainian and Balkan village singing in its open-fifth branching texture, and from Russian Orthodox chant in being secular, strophic and often instrumentally accompanied.

items.name: Russian Romance
items.lineage: Urban Russian art-song genre formed in the 1810s-1840s salons through Alexander Alyabyev, Alexander Varlamov and Pyotr Bulakhov and carried onto disc by Anastasia Vyaltseva and Alexander Vertinsky before 1917, setting sentimental lyric poetry as strophic ballads in slow 3/4 or 4/4 minor with harmonic-minor melodic turns, guitar or piano arpeggio accompaniment, rubato phrase endings and a wide portamento-heavy vocal delivery aimed at intimate rather than operatic projection.
items.description: The Russian urban romance, a nineteenth-century salon song form that fused Italianate melody with Russian minor-mode inflection and gypsy-choir performance style, then survived into Soviet Melodiya recordings and emigre cabaret. It is characterized by strophic sentimental verse, harmonic minor with raised sevenths and diminished passing chords, seven-string guitar or piano arpeggios, and a highly rubato, sob-inflected delivery that privileges diction over vocal power. Distinguished from Russian folk song by its notated authorship and functional harmony, and from Soviet estrada by its pre-revolutionary poetic register and chamber scale.

items.name: Russian Chanson (Blatnyak)
items.lineage: Soviet and post-Soviet outlaw-song genre grown from prison and Odessa blatnaya pesnya, circulated on magnitizdat reel tapes from the late 1950s through Arkady Severny and Vladimir Vysotsky and commercialized by Radio Chanson from 1998 with Mikhail Krug and Alexander Novikov, using strophic minor-key verses at 90-130 BPM over strummed seven-string guitar, bayan and later cheap synth-and-drum-machine backing, sung in a hoarse chest-voiced criminal-argot narration.
items.description: Russian chanson, the commercial descendant of Soviet-era criminal and prison song, spread illicitly on home-taped magnitizdat reels from the late 1950s and turned into a mass radio format after 1998. Its sound is deliberately plain: minor-key strophic verses over strummed guitar and bayan, later padded with budget synthesizers and drum machines, delivered in a rasping conversational baritone whose value lies in narrative detail and thieves' slang rather than melody. It differs from the bard song of Okudzhava and Vysotsky by its commercial packaging and criminal-milieu subject matter, and from Russian romance by rejecting salon refinement for street realism.

items.name: Bandura kobzar tradition
items.lineage: Ukrainian epic-singing tradition of the blind itinerant kobzari and lirnyky of the 17th-19th-century Cossack Hetmanate, who sang duma — unrhymed recitative laments in free irregular verse, half-declaimed in a strained chest voice over sparse plucked figuration on the asymmetric multi-string bandura — codified in the 20th century by Hnat Khotkevych's Kharkiv playing method and by the Soviet-era chromatic concert bandura and state bandurist capellas that replaced the older diatonic Chernihiv/Kyiv instruments.
items.description: A Ukrainian sung-epic practice carried by blind mendicant bandurists from the Cossack era until the tradition's near-destruction under Stalin, then rebuilt as a conservatory and capella art. Its signature is the duma: free-metered recitative on a narrow, ornamented modal core, punctuated by rolled arpeggios and short instrumental interludes on the bandura's fanned treble strings. Unlike Russian balalaika-orchestra repertoire, which is metrically square and ensemble-driven, the kobzar style is speech-paced, soloistic and elegiac.

items.name: Ukrainian village folk song
items.lineage: The calendar-and-life-cycle song repertoire of Ukrainian villages — koliadky and shchedrivky at midwinter, vesnianky in spring, Kupala songs at midsummer, wedding cycles and harvest songs — sung in open-throated 'bili holos' white-voice chest register in two- and three-part heterophony with a high solo 'vyvodchyk' line above a held lower part, transcribed from the 1900s by Mykola Lysenko, Filaret Kolessa and Klyment Kvitka and revived from the 1980s by ethnographic ensembles like Drevo.
items.description: The unaccompanied and lightly accompanied song tradition of rural Ukraine, organized around the agrarian calendar and the wedding rite rather than around staged performance. The sound is a piercing, non-vibrato chest voice in loose parallel-and-drone polyphony, with strophic melodies whose lines are re-decorated on each repetition. It differs from the professionalized bandura repertoire in being collective, metrically ritual-bound and transmitted entirely by ear within the village.

items.name: Russian balalaika orchestra
items.lineage: The Russian folk-instrument orchestra invented in St Petersburg in 1887-1896 when Vasily Andreyev standardized the triangular balalaika into a chromatic fretted family (prima through kontrabass) and added the reconstructed domra and the chromatic bayan, playing quick 2/4 and 4/4 dance sets, chastushka tunes and arranged art music with tremolo-sustained melody lines, strummed rhythm chords and a bowed-bass-substitute kontrabass balalaika pulse.
items.description: A late-19th-century conservatory reworking of Russian village plucked-string playing into a fully notated, chromatic orchestral idiom, then institutionalized across the Soviet period by state ensembles and Melodiya recordings. Its identity rests on massed tremolo on prima balalaikas and domras, hard offbeat strums, accelerating dance sets, and bayan doubling. Against genuine village practice it is metrically rigid, harmonized in functional tonality and read from parts rather than learned by ear.

items.name: Sutartinės
items.lineage: Northeast Lithuanian (Aukštaitija) multipart singing documented from the 17th century and recorded intensively from the 1900s by Jonas Basanavičius and later Zenonas Slaviūnas — two, three or four women singing canonically offset lines that collide in sustained major seconds, in syncopated duple meter over nonsense refrain syllables (sodauto, lylio, tititi), often doubled by skudučiai panpipe sets, birbynė reeds or wooden trumpets where each player sounds a single pitch in interlocking hocket.
items.description: A UNESCO-listed Lithuanian polyphony whose defining sound is the deliberate, sustained dissonance of the major second held between two staggered voices, cycled over short interlocking phrases until the pattern closes. Panpipe and horn versions distribute one note per player, making the melody exist only in the ensemble. This distinguishes sutartinės sharply from the drone-plus-melody polyphony of the southern Baltic and from Balkan second-based singing, which is far more ornamented and metrically freer.

items.name: Lithuanian folk music
items.lineage: The wider Lithuanian village repertoire outside sutartinės — dainos (lyric, war-and-orphan, wedding and work songs) in narrow-range modal melody, raudos laments, and the instrumental dance layer of polkas, valses and suktinis played on kanklės box zither, birbynė single-reed pipe, skudučiai panpipes and, from the later 19th century, the button accordion and fiddle; collected by Basanavičius and Niemi and standardized in the Soviet-era state ensemble and Skamba Skamba Kankliai revival.
items.description: The everyday song and dance music of Lithuanian villages, dominated by monophonic or drone-supported narrow-range dainos and by square-metered couple dances taken up on accordion and fiddle after 1850. Kanklės playing is soft, plucked and arpeggiated, historically a solitary and semi-ritual practice. It sits between the strict canonic dissonance of Aukštaitija sutartinės and the more homophonic, harmonized Latvian daina style.

items.name: Latvian folk music
items.lineage: Latvian village tradition built on the daina — a terse four-line trochaic quatrain, over a million of which Krišjānis Barons catalogued between 1878 and 1915 — sung to short recitative-like tunes with a burdon drone in the eastern regions, alongside the plucked kokle box zither, fiddle-and-accordion dance sets, and, from the first Song Festival in 1873, a massed harmonized choral repertoire that became the national performance form.
items.description: A song culture organized around the daina quatrain and the agrarian/wedding calendar, whose oldest layer is drone-supported group singing from Latgale and Suiti country and whose modern face is the enormous Song and Dance Celebration choir. Melodies are short, repeated across hundreds of verses, and the kokle provides a soft plucked halo rather than chordal accompaniment. Compared with Lithuanian practice it favours drone-over-melody texture and, in its national form, tonal four-part harmony.

items.name: Estonian folk music
items.lineage: Estonian village music divided between the archaic regilaul — Kalevala-meter runic song in eight-syllable trochaic lines with a lead singer and echoing chorus over a narrow four-or-five-note range, preserved longest among the Setu and on the western islands — and the newer end-rhymed strophic songs and dance repertoire played on torupill bagpipe, kannel zither, fiddle and, after 1850, the accordion; documented by Jakob Hurt's mass collection from 1888 and by the Estonian Folklore Archives from 1927.
items.description: Estonia's tradition holds two strata side by side: the pre-rhyme regilaul, delivered as call-and-response over a tiny melodic ambitus and an insistent trochaic pulse, and a later European-influenced dance layer voiced by the droning torupill bagpipe and the accordion. The kannel is played with damped plucking on open modal tunings. Where Latvian and Lithuanian traditions build polyphony from drones or canon, Estonian regilaul is essentially monophonic and text-driven, with variation carried by the leader's line.

items.name: Kantele music
items.lineage: Finnish and Karelian plucked box-zither tradition, originally a five-string instrument tuned to a pentachord and played resting on the lap to accompany Kalevala-meter rune-singing, expanded in the 19th century to ten and fifteen strings and in 1920s-1930s Finland to the large chromatic concert kantele with switchable levers built by Paul Salminen — repertoire ranges from short cyclic drone-and-tremolo improvisations to notated concert works and pelimanni dance tunes.
items.description: The plucked zither idiom of Finland and Karelia, whose small-kantele playing is built from continuously ringing open strings, damped with the free hand to carve short cyclic figures out of a standing chord. Traditional performance is quiet, close and repetitive, tied to rune-song accompaniment; the 20th-century concert kantele adds chromatic levers and a notated virtuoso literature. Its texture is drone-plus-figuration rather than melody-plus-chords, which separates it from Baltic kokle and kanklės ensemble playing.

items.name: Karelian folk music
items.lineage: The song culture of Karelia on both sides of the Finnish-Russian border, centred on Kalevala-meter runic singing in a narrow five-note range with a persistent trochaic tetrameter and a two-singer hand-clasp delivery, alongside itkuvirsi laments improvised by trained women wailers at weddings and funerals in free rhythm with sobbing glottal breaks; recorded by Elias Lönnrot's 1830s collecting journeys and by 20th-century Soviet Karelian and Finnish Literature Society field expeditions.
items.description: Karelian tradition preserved the archaic Finnic layer longest: runic epic sung in unbroken trochaic tetrameter over a handful of pitches, and the lament, a semi-improvised, metaphor-coded wailing genre with descending phrases, audible breath and voiced sobbing. Accompaniment, where present, is a small kantele or bowed jouhikko sustaining the same narrow mode. Against Finnish pelimanni dance music it is unmetered or ritually metered, monophonic and functionally tied to mourning and epic recitation.

items.name: Finnish tango
items.lineage: Finland's national dance-hall genre, arriving from Argentina in the 1910s and reshaped after 1945 by Toivo Kärki and Unto Mononen into a minor-key, 4/4, moderately slow form with a heavy first-beat accent, plain accordion and string-led arrangements, no bandoneón, and lyrics of yearning for an unreachable homeland — Mononen's 'Satumaa' (1955) and Olavi Virta's recordings fixed the style, sustained since 1985 by the annual Seinäjoki Tangomarkkinat contest.
items.description: A distinctly Finnish transformation of Argentine tango into a slower, squarer, overwhelmingly minor-key popular song, sung in an unironic, wide-vibrato baritone or contralto. Arrangements lean on accordion and strings with a marked downbeat, and the harmonic language stays close to simple minor-key cadences rather than tango's chromatic voice-leading. It is far more melancholy and less rhythmically elastic than Rioplatense tango, and more formal than the lighter iskelmä that surrounds it on Finnish radio.

items.name: Iskelmä
items.lineage: Finnish mainstream popular song descending from German schlager and Finnish humppa/tango, professionalized from the late 1940s at Fazer and Scandia by composer Toivo Kärki and lyricist Reino Helismaa — moderate-tempo 4/4 or waltz strophic songs with accordion or piano lead, orchestral strings and later a small rhythm section, plain diatonic harmony, and a clear front-of-mix Finnish-language vocal delivered with wide vibrato and full sentiment.
items.description: The broad category of Finnish-language commercial popular song from the late 1940s onward, covering everything schlager-adjacent that is neither rock nor art music. It is defined by unambiguous strophic form, diatonic harmony, accordion or string sweetening, and a vocal that carries the lyric plainly with no blues inflection.
