It differs from Afrobeat in keeping jazz solo form and shorter arrangements rather than Fela's twenty-minute two-chord structures, and from American hard bop in its cyclic, non-modulating harmonic ground.
exemplars: Guy Warren — Africa Speaks, America Answers

items.name: South African Jazz
items.lineage: Formed in Sophiatown and Cape Town from the 1940s marabi and kwela lineage and codified by the Jazz Epistles, Abdullah Ibrahim, Chris McGregor's Blue Notes and the exile generation after 1964 — a rolling I-IV-V or three-chord marabi cycle at mid tempo, hymn-derived voicings, sung-tone alto and tenor saxophone, muted or open trumpet and trombone, and township-jive backbeat under long collective vamps.
items.description: South African jazz took shape in Johannesburg's Sophiatown and Cape Town's District Six, joining the marabi shebeen cycle and kwela penny-whistle music to American swing and bebop; the Jazz Epistles' 1959 record is its founding statement and the Blue Notes carried it into London exile. Its identity is the repeating three-chord marabi ground, hymn-like church harmony under the horns, and a broad singing saxophone tone rather than bebop's rapid articulation. Against American hard bop it is more cyclic and less harmonically mobile, and against township jive it foregrounds extended improvisation and jazz instrumentation over pop song form.

items.name: Swing Revival
items.lineage: A mid-1990s Californian and American club movement led by Royal Crown Revue, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy, the Brian Setzer Orchestra and Squirrel Nut Zippers, reviving 1930s-40s jump blues and big-band swing for Lindy Hop dancers — shuffle and jump grooves near 180 BPM, riffing brass sections, honking tenor solos, slap upright bass, hollow-body archtop rhythm guitar and shouted crooner vocals, cut with modern rock-level drum recording.
items.description: Swing revival was a 1993-2000 American club phenomenon tied to the Lindy Hop dance resurgence, centred on Los Angeles and popularized by Zoot Suit-styled bands on film soundtracks and beer commercials. Musically it is jump blues and small big-band swing at fast dance tempos: riffing horn sections, honking tenor breaks, slapped upright bass and archtop rhythm guitar, topped by a shouting crooner. It differs from the original swing era in production — close-miked modern drums, compressed rock-loud mixes — and from trad-jazz revivalism in taking Louis Jordan and Louis Prima rather than New Orleans polyphony as its model.
exemplars: Brian Setzer Orchestra — The Dirty Boogie
Cherry Poppin' Daddies — Zoot Suit Riot

items.name: Vintage swing (retro-swing revival)
items.lineage: Mid-1990s Los Angeles and New York revival of 1930s-40s small-group swing and jump blues, codified by Royal Crown Revue, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy and the Squirrel Nut Zippers out of the Derby and Brown Derby dance scene — 170-210 BPM shuffle-swing on ride cymbal and slapped upright bass, riff-based horn sections of trumpet, trombone and tenor sax, hollowbody archtop comping in four, and megaphone-bright crooner or shouter vocals delivered for Lindy Hop dancers.
items.description: Vintage swing is the 1990s-onward revivalist practice of playing 1930s-40s small-band swing and jump blues as living dance music, centred on Los Angeles clubs and the international Lindy Hop circuit before crossing over commercially around 1997-99. Its sound is deliberately period-costumed: slapped upright bass and hi-hat-and-ride shuffle at fast dance tempos, tight riffing horn trios, four-to-the-bar archtop guitar, and vocals sung in a hard-consonant shouter or crooner register, usually cut with vintage ribbon mics and tube gear to court the era's timbre. It differs from the historical Swing-era jazz orchestra in scale and intent — small combos rather than 16-piece books, and revival rather than continuity — and from Western swing by its urban jump-blues and rockabilly borrowings rather than fiddle-and-steel string band roots.
exemplars: Lavay Smith and Her Red Hot Skillet Lickers

items.name: M-Base (odd-metre Brooklyn jazz language)
items.lineage: Mid-1980s Brooklyn collective language codified by alto saxophonist Steve Coleman with Greg Osby, Cassandra Wilson, Gary Thomas and Geri Allen — built on Macro-Basic Array of Structured Extemporization: interlocking asymmetrical rhythmic cells in 11, 13 and 15, funk-derived electric bass and drum-kit backbeats displaced across the cycle, angular chromatic heads doubled by alto and tenor, and a cool, non-vibrato vocal delivery placed as another rhythmic voice.
items.description: M-Base emerged among young musicians rehearsing in Brooklyn lofts around 1983-85 and became the defining alternative to the neo-traditionalist jazz mainstream of the same decade. Its signature is metric: long asymmetrical cycles subdivided into interlocking cells, so that a funk backbeat and a chromatic melodic line sit at different phase positions within the same loop, played with dry articulation and little vibrato over electric bass and kit. Unlike free jazz it is tightly composed and pulse-locked, and unlike fusion it subordinates virtuoso soloing and rock timbre to the structural rhythm concept.

items.name: Contemporary post-bop
items.lineage: Post-1995 New York small-group idiom codified at Smalls and the Village Vanguard by Brad Mehldau, Mark Turner, Kurt Rosenwinkel and Chris Potter — extended-form originals with slow-moving upper-structure harmony, long asymmetric phrase groupings over 4/4 or shifting 5/4 and 7/4, elastic ride-cymbal time and conversational drum interaction, and a soft-attack tenor and nylon-clean guitar timbre far from hard bop's blues declamation.
items.description: Contemporary post-bop is the acoustic small-group mainstream that consolidated in New York from the mid-1990s onward, descending from the Miles Davis mid-1960s quintet and Wayne Shorter's compositional model rather than from Blue Note hard bop. It is marked by originals with irregular phrase lengths, harmony built from slash voicings and pedal-anchored upper structures, drummers who imply rather than state the pulse, and a deliberately unforced, high-resolution recorded tone. It differs from hard bop by rejecting blues-and-gospel vocabulary as the default rhetoric, and from ECM-school jazz by keeping American swing feel and bebop line-construction at the centre rather than open Nordic space.

items.name: Chicago bop
items.lineage: South Side Chicago tenor-and-rhythm bop lineage of the 1950s-70s carried by Von Freeman, Johnny Griffin, Clifford Jordan, Ira Sullivan and drummer Wilbur Campbell in clubs such as the Sutherland Lounge and the New Apartment — hard-driving medium-up 4/4 swing, blues-saturated changes, an intentionally wide-pitched and vocalized tenor tone with slurred altissimo, and long cutting-contest solo forms over organ or piano trio.
items.description: Chicago bop names the distinct South Side strain of bebop and hard bop that developed largely outside the New York recording economy, sustained in neighbourhood lounges through the 1950s to the 1970s. Its hallmarks are an aggressively vocalized tenor saxophone sound with deliberately unstable intonation and altissimo cries, blues form treated as an endlessly reharmonizable vehicle, propulsive brush-and-ride swing, and marathon jam-session structures shaped by cutting contests rather than album programming. It is rougher and more blues-anchored than East Coast hard bop of the same years, and unrelated to the earlier 1920s Chicago jazz of the Austin High Gang.

items.name: Jazz metal
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward fusion of extreme metal with post-bop harmony, crystallized by Florida's Atheist and Cynic and continued in Europe by Ephel Duath, Shining (Norway) and Panzerballett — palm-muted downtuned riffing recast in 7/8 and 5/4, chromatic altered-dominant and diminished harmony under blast-beat and jazz-ride alternation, fretless-inflected bass counterlines, and saxophone or clean vocal passages interleaved with death-metal growls.
items.description: Jazz metal is the technically maximalist meeting of extreme metal instrumentation with jazz harmony and metre, first realized on Atheist's Unquestionable Presence (1991) and Cynic's Focus (1993) and later pursued by European bands adding actual horn sections. The music keeps metal's distorted rhythm guitar, double-kick drumming and growled vocals while replacing power-chord modality with altered-dominant, diminished and quartal voicings, and replacing steady 4/4 with constantly shifting odd metres. Unlike progressive metal it derives its harmonic language specifically from bebop and fusion rather than classical or symphonic sources, and unlike jazzcore it remains composed and precision-tracked rather than improvised and abrasive.

items.name: Jazzcore
items.lineage: Mid-1980s downtown New York and Chicago collision of hardcore punk speed with free-jazz improvisation, codified by John Zorn's Naked City, Last Exit and later The Flying Luttenbachers and Zu — sub-minute compositions of jump-cut blocks, blast-tempo drumming under squealing alto saxophone, detuned or noise-processed guitar, and screamed vocal bursts used as percussive punctuation rather than lyric line.
items.description: Jazzcore grew out of the Lower East Side improvised-music scene of the mid-1980s, where players moved freely between hardcore bands and free-jazz sessions, and was consolidated by Naked City's file-card compositions and the Zorn/Laswell orbit. It is defined by extreme dynamic and stylistic jump-cutting, hardcore tempos and distortion carrying saxophone-led free improvisation, and structures measured in seconds rather than choruses. It sits closer to noise rock and grindcore than to jazz metal, which is comparatively composed and harmonically systematic, and it foregrounds abrupt discontinuity where no-wave jazz favoured sustained atonal texture.

items.name: Jazztronica
items.lineage: Late-1990s Scandinavian and British hybrid of live jazz improvisation with programmed electronics, codified by Nils Petter Molvær's Khmer (1997), Bugge Wesseltoft's New Conception of Jazz and Jaga Jazzist — 90-140 BPM broken-beat and drum-and-bass programming under long modal trumpet or saxophone lines, dub-scale delay and granular processing on horns, Rhodes and analogue synth pads, and post-production editing treated as a compositional stage equal to the take.
items.description: Jazztronica names the studio-constructed strand of jazz-electronic hybrid that emerged around Oslo and London from about 1996, where improvising horn players worked over programmed beats and effect chains rather than a rhythm section alone. Its sonic identity comes from static modal harmony, heavily processed and spatialized lead instruments, dub-derived delay and filtering, and loop-based cyclic form assembled in the DAW. It differs from 1970s fusion by placing the producer and editing desk at the centre instead of live band virtuosity, and from acid jazz by favouring ambient and drum-and-bass textures over dancefloor funk and rare-groove sampling.

items.name: Musique acadienne (Maritime Acadian tradition)
items.lineage: French-language traditional music of the Acadian Maritimes — southeast New Brunswick, southwest Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and the Îles-de-la-Madeleine — carried orally since the eighteenth century and revived from the 1970s by Édith Butler, 1755 and later Barachois and Vishtèn: crooked-metre fiddle reels with irregular bar counts, seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and spoons, and unaccompanied complainte and chanson à répondre call-and-response singing in Acadian French.
items.description: Musique acadienne is the surviving French-language folk tradition of the Maritime provinces, distinct from the Louisiana Cajun music that descends from the same 1755 deportation. Its markers are fiddle tunes with 'crooked' asymmetrical phrase lengths preserved from oral transmission, foot-tapped podorythmie supplying the percussion, button accordion and spoons, and a large ballad repertoire of complaintes and answer-back drinking songs sung in Acadian French with sparse or no accompaniment. Compared with Cajun it lacks the accordion-and-triangle two-step dance-hall format and blues inflection, and compared with Québécois trad it is more song-driven and less reel-band oriented.

items.name: Musique traditionnelle québécoise
items.lineage: Québec's French-Canadian dance and song tradition of the Saint Lawrence valley, documented from the nineteenth century, professionalized by La Bolduc and fiddler Jean Carignan and revived from the 1970s by La Bottine Souriante and Le Vent du Nord — crooked reels and gigues at 110-130 BPM driven by seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and fiddle in unison, ragtime-inflected piano backing, and chansons à répondre with turlutte mouth-music refrains.
items.description: Traditional Québécois music is the kitchen-party and veillée repertoire of French Canada, built on fiddle-and-accordion dance tunes and responsorial song, and continuously performed rather than reconstructed. Its unmistakable features are podorythmie — the fiddler's own seated foot-tapping as the rhythm section — irregular 'crooked' tune structures with added or dropped beats, a piano accompaniment style borrowed from ragtime and vaudeville, and turlutte vocal mouth-music standing in for instruments. It shares Celtic modal tune shapes with Irish and Cape Breton traditions but is distinguished by the foot-percussion drive, the French song layer, and the tolerance for asymmetrical bar counts that Scottish and Irish repertoires largely regularized away.

items.name: Métis fiddle
items.lineage: Red River Valley fiddle tradition of the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and North Dakota Métis, formed in the early nineteenth-century fur trade from Scottish, French-Canadian and Orcadian tunes crossed with Cree and Anishinaabe rhythmic sensibility, and codified on record by Andy De Jarlis and Reg Bouvette — crooked jigs and Red River jigs with beats added or dropped mid-phrase, bow-driven melodic-rhythmic accent instead of vibrato, clogging or foot-tap percussion, and guitar or piano vamp accompaniment for the changing-steps dance.
items.description: Métis fiddling is the distinctive dance-fiddle style of the Red River Métis, developed in fur-trade communities where European settler tunes were reshaped by Indigenous rhythmic practice and transmitted entirely by ear. Its defining traits are the crooked tune — phrases of irregular length that the dancers know and follow — heavy rhythmic bowing with double-stop drones, foot percussion or clogging, and the Red River Jig's alternation between high and low parts governing the changing steps. Against Cape Breton or Québécois fiddling it is sparser, less ornamented with grace-note filigree, and far freer with bar counts, and its accompaniment stays a simple vamp rather than a driving piano tradition.

items.name: Cape Breton fiddle and piano tradition
items.lineage: Gaelic Scottish fiddle repertoire carried to Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia by Highland Clearance emigrants after 1800 and preserved there in older form than in Scotland, codified on record by Winston 'Scotty' Fitzgerald and Buddy MacMaster — strathspey-reel medleys driven at square-dance tempo with pronounced Scotch-snap dotting, cuts and grace notes bowed rather than fingered, foot-tapping, and a percussive chordal piano accompaniment unique to the island.
items.description: The Cape Breton tradition is the Scottish Gaelic fiddle and dance music of northeastern Nova Scotia, retained through nineteenth-century isolation and now regarded as preserving eighteenth-century Highland bowing and repertoire more faithfully than mainland Scotland. Its signatures are the strathspey-to-reel medley built for square sets, dotted Scotch-snap rhythm and bow-driven ornament, insistent foot-tapping, and an off-beat, chordally dense piano backing developed locally rather than imported. Compared with Irish session music it is squarer and less legato-ornamented, and compared with the island's own Gaelic milling-frolic songs it is instrumental and dance-functional rather than work-song vocal.

items.name: Newfoundland traditional song and dance music
items.lineage: Anglo-Irish and French-Newfoundland repertoire of the island's outports, transmitted orally since eighteenth-century West Country and Waterford settlement, collected by Maud Karpeles and Kenneth Peacock and revived from the 1970s by Figgy Duff and Ryan's Fancy — unaccompanied ballad singing in a high nasal outport delivery, single and double jigs for the kitchen set dance played on accordion and crooked-tuned fiddle, and accordion-led 'lancers' with bodhrán or ugly-stick percussion.
items.description: Newfoundland traditional music is the outport repertoire of ballads, dance tunes and recitations that survived on the island through isolation from mainland Canada until 1949, drawing on English West Country, Irish and French-Newfoundland sources. It is characterized by long unaccompanied narrative ballads sung in a tight, high, ornamented outport voice, button-accordion-led single jigs for kitchen sets and lancers, fiddle playing full of crooked bars and idiosyncratic tunings, and improvised percussion on spoons and ugly stick. It is broader than the island's sea-shanty and work-song layer, which is occupational and shipboard, and differs from Irish session music by its accordion-first instrumentation and the persistence of English-language broadside ballads as core repertoire.

items.name: Contra dance band music
items.lineage: New England grange-hall dance music descended from English country dance and French contredanse, sustained in Vermont, New Hampshire and Massachusetts and reshaped from the 1970s by Rodney Miller, Bob McQuillen and Wild Asparagus — 112-124 BPM reels and jigs played in 64-bar tune medleys matched exactly to the caller's figures, fiddle lead with piano and guitar supplying a swung, syncopated chordal drive, and modulating tune sets escalating in energy across the dance.
items.description: Contra dance music is the living New England dance-band idiom that accompanies called longways set dances in grange halls and town halls, continuous since colonial times and substantially revitalized during the 1970s folk revival. Musically it is defined by strict 64-bar AABB tune structure locked to the caller's 32-count figures, a driving syncopated piano-and-guitar rhythm section that swings the beat rather than marching it, and medleys that shift key and tune mid-dance to lift the room. It draws on Irish, Scottish, Québécois and old-time repertoire but is distinguished from all of them by the caller's architecture, the fixed phrase length, and a harmonically adventurous backup style that would be foreign to an Irish session.

items.name: Shanty (Shipboard Work Song)
items.lineage: The functional labour song of Atlantic deep-water merchant sail, consolidated roughly 1815-1875 on packet and clipper crews out of Liverpool, London, Mobile and New York and first systematically transcribed by Richard Runciman Terry, Cecil Sharp, W.B. Whall and later Stan Hugill, whose Shanties from the Seven Seas remains the codifying text; a shantyman improvised solo lines against a fixed crew refrain, with the pull or push of the work fixing the metre - short-drag shanties with two hauls per verse, halyard shanties with a longer chorus, capstan shanties in continuous rolling 6/8 or 4/4 for windlass work - sung unaccompanied at moderate tempo in open chest voice.
items.description: The working shanty is not a song genre so much as a labour tool of Atlantic square-rig merchant sail between roughly 1815 and the 1870s, sung to coordinate hauling, heaving and pumping. Its sound is unaccompanied and strictly functional: a shantyman leading with improvised, often bawdy or topical couplets drawn from a floating stock of verses, and the whole crew answering on a short fixed refrain timed to the pull, with the ship's own gear - chain, capstan pawls, stamping feet - supplying the percussion. It is distinguished from the later revival repertoire by having no instruments, no fixed text and no audience, and from forecastle songs and ballads by its metre being dictated by work rather than by narrative.

items.name: Sea Shanty (Revival Repertoire)
items.lineage: The post-1950s folk-club and festival performance form of maritime song, shaped in Britain by A.L. Lloyd and Ewan MacColl's 1956 Blow Boys Blow, by Stan Hugill's residencies at the Falmouth and Mystic Seaport shanty festivals from the 1970s, and by the Fisherman's Friends and Sea Shanty TikTok waves of 2010 and 2021; performed at fixed brisk tempos in strophic verse-and-chorus form with strong unison male chorus on the refrain, frequently with concertina, melodeon, fiddle or guitar accompaniment that the working original never had.
items.description: The revival sea shanty is the concert-hall and folk-club descendant of shipboard work song, established through the British folk revival of the 1950s-60s and sustained by Cornish and New England maritime festivals into the twenty-first century. Texts are fixed rather than improvised, tempos are steady and singable rather than governed by a hauling rhythm, and instrumental accompaniment - anglo concertina, melodeon, fiddle, occasionally guitar - is standard, with the mass chorus refrain as the emotional centre. It differs from the working shanty in being audience-facing, text-stable and accompanied, and from the broadside ballad tradition in its call-and-response chorus architecture and maritime subject matter.
exemplars: Ewan MacColl and A.L. Lloyd, Blow Boys Blow

items.name: Szanty
items.lineage: The Polish sailor-song movement that emerged from Baltic yacht clubs and student sailing culture in the 1970s-80s, institutionalised by the Shanties festival in Krakow (from 1981) and by groups such as Stare Dzwony, Mechanicy Shanty, Perły i Łotry and Ryczące Dwudziestki; sung in Polish - part translated Anglo-American repertoire, part newly composed - at driving 4/4 or 6/8 tempos with strummed acoustic guitars, accordion, fiddle and a shouted unison male chorus, closer to campfire student song (piosenka turystyczna) than to shipboard labour practice.
items.description: Szanty is the Polish maritime song scene that grew out of Baltic and inland sailing clubs in the late 1970s and became a mass festival culture centred on Krakow, Gdynia and Wrocław. Its sound is guitar-driven and rousing: fast strummed chord cycles, accordion and fiddle counterlines, an upright bass or bass guitar underneath, and a loud shouted male chorus on every refrain, with Polish-language lyrics that are frequently original compositions rather than translations. Unlike Anglo revival shanty it is fully instrumental-accompanied and songwriter-driven, and unlike the German Seemannslieder tradition it is amateur, participatory and festival-based rather than orchestrated commercial schlager.

items.name: Seemannslieder
items.lineage: German-language sailor song as a commercial and choral genre, rooted in nineteenth-century Hamburg and Bremen harbour repertoire and in the 1930s-40s Hans Albers film songs (La Paloma, Auf der Reeperbahn nachts um halb eins), then dominated by Freddy Quinn's Polydor recordings from 1956 onward; typically moderate 3/4 or 4/4, orchestrated with strings, accordion and light rhythm section, sung in a warm baritone with a nostalgic Fernweh lyric and an anthemic male-chorus refrain, alongside an amateur Shanty-Chor branch singing the same material a cappella in four parts.
items.description: Seemannslieder is the German maritime song repertoire as it crystallised commercially in the mid-twentieth century, moving from Hamburg harbour and Reeperbahn cabaret into film song and postwar schlager. The archetypal record is a tube-warm baritone lead over strings, accordion and discreet rhythm section, resolving into a broad male-chorus refrain, with texts of longing for distant ports and home. It differs from Anglo shanty in being through-composed popular song with fixed harmony and orchestration rather than call-and-response labour music, and from Dutch shantykoren in being a soloist-and-studio tradition rather than an amateur choral one.

items.name: Shantykoren
items.lineage: The Dutch and Flemish amateur shanty-choir movement, launched by Rotterdam's Rotterdam Shantykoor and Urk's Crescendo in the late 1970s-80s and now numbering several hundred choirs across the Low Countries; forty to eighty older male singers in unison and simple two- or three-part harmony, accompanied by a front line of accordions with occasional banjo-family strings and bass, performing Dutch, English and German maritime songs at steady march-like 4/4 or lilting 6/8 tempos in harbour-festival and community-hall settings.
items.description: Shantykoren are the amateur male shanty choirs of the Netherlands and Flanders, a community-music phenomenon that expanded rapidly from the 1980s around harbour towns such as Urk, Volendam, Rotterdam and Antwerp. The sound is a large, unforced massed male unison thickened by simple harmony, carried by a bank of accordions rather than a rhythm section, with tempo held steady by a conductor and repertoire mixing Dutch-language originals with translated Anglo shanties. It is distinguished from Anglo revival shanty by choir scale and accordion-front accompaniment, and from German Seemannslieder by its participatory amateur basis rather than a commercial soloist tradition.

items.name: Military Cadence (Jody Call)
items.lineage: The chanted running and marching call of the United States armed forces, conventionally traced to Private Willie Duckworth at Fort Slocum in 1944 whose Sound Off became the model, thereafter standardised across Army, Marine Corps and Navy basic training; a drill instructor calls a two- or four-bar line on a narrow two- or three-note contour and the formation answers in unison on the left-foot strike, locked to a 4/4 march at roughly 110-120 steps per minute or a faster double-time run cadence, with boot-fall and hand-clap as the only percussion.
items.description: The military cadence, or jody call, is a functional American armed-forces chant developed during and after the Second World War to synchronise marching and running formations. Its music is minimal by design: a leader's improvised or stock rhymed line on a narrow declamatory contour, answered by mass unison response, with the downbeat pinned to the left foot and the ambient percussion of boots on pavement or dirt. It is distinguished from work song by its ambulatory rather than task-cycle metre, and from drum-and-bugle traditions by having no melodic instruments at all - the formation itself is the instrument.
exemplars: US Marine Corps recruit depot cadence recordings
Yo Left! Marine Corps cadence collections

items.name: Marching Band
items.lineage: The American outdoor wind-and-percussion ensemble that fused European military band instrumentation with post-Civil-War town-band culture, professionalised by Patrick Gilmore and John Philip Sousa in the 1880s-90s and reinvented in the twentieth century by university and HBCU programs - Florida A&M's Marching 100 under William P. Foster from 1946 - which added dance-derived body movement, R&B and funk arrangements and a heavily amplified sousaphone bass line; standard scoring is trumpets and mellophones over trombones, baritones and sousaphones with a battery of snares, tenors and bass drums plus a front pit, playing at 120-180 beats per minute in strict cut time.
items.description: The marching band is the American stadium and parade ensemble of brass, woodwinds and marching percussion, descended from nineteenth-century military and town bands and codified through Sousa's touring band and, in the twentieth century, through school, university and HBCU programs. Its sonic signature is high-register trumpet and mellophone scoring over a sousaphone bass, a battery drumline whose snare rudiments carry the groove, and enormous outdoor dynamic range with almost no reverberant support. It differs from the concert band in being memorised, mobile and visually choreographed, and from drum corps in retaining woodwinds and a full brass complement rather than a bugle-derived brass line.
exemplars: Jackson State Sonic Boom of the South

items.name: Brass Band (British)
items.lineage: The all-brass amateur ensemble that formed around northern English and Welsh mills, collieries and ironworks in the 1830s-50s - Black Dyke Mills from 1855, Besses o' th' Barn, Foden's - and was standardised by the Belle Vue and National contests into a fixed roster of soprano and solo cornets, flugelhorn, tenor horns, baritones, euphoniums, trombones and E-flat and B-flat basses plus percussion, all reading from transposed treble-clef parts; repertoire runs from marches and hymn settings to purpose-written contest test pieces, played with wide vibrato and a homogeneous conical-bore blend.
items.description: The British brass band is a fixed-instrumentation amateur ensemble born of industrial northern England and south Wales in the mid-nineteenth century and sustained ever since by a rigorous contest circuit. Its defining sound is the homogeneous, dark and vibrato-rich blend of conical-bore cornets, tenor horns, baritones and euphoniums, banded together with trombones and E-flat/B-flat basses and a small percussion section, recorded in resonant halls with minimal spot miking. It is separated from the American marching band by its seated, notation-heavy contest practice and absence of woodwinds, and from the concert band by its exclusively brass and percussion roster.

items.name: Balkan Brass Band
items.lineage: The Ottoman-military-band inheritance of the southern Balkans as remade by Roma musicians in Serbia, North Macedonia and southern Romania from the mid-nineteenth century, focused since 1961 on the Guča trumpet festival and the Vranje and Leskovac orkestars of Boban Marković and the Bakić and Mladenović lineages, and paralleled by Romanian Muntenian fanfare such as Fanfare Ciocărlia; ornamented trumpet and flugelhorn leads over an off-beat tuba-and-horn accompaniment, driven by tapan and snare in fast čoček 2/4 or aksak 7/8, 9/8 and 11/8, at tempos that in the Romanian branch exceed 200 beats per minute.
items.description: Balkan brass is the Roma-led wedding, funeral and festival brass music of Serbia, North Macedonia and southern Romania, descended from Ottoman and Habsburg military bands and taken over by village orkestars during the nineteenth century. Its hallmarks are heavily ornamented, makam-inflected trumpet and flugelhorn lines with rapid grace-note figuration, a tuba pumping the downbeat against off-beat horn chords, and tapan and snare driving čoček and asymmetric aksak metres at ferocious tempo and volume. It differs from British brass banding in being memorised, ornamented and improvisatory rather than notated, and from Western marching bands in its modal melodic language and irregular metres.
exemplars: Goran Bregović Wedding and Funeral Band

items.name: Fife and Drum Corps
items.lineage: The martial signalling ensemble of eighteenth-century European and colonial American armies, preserved after its battlefield obsolescence by New England ancient corps from the 1880s onward and by the Company of Fifers and Drummers founded in Ivoryton, Connecticut in 1965; a section of six-hole keyless B-flat fifes plays two-part duty tunes and quicksteps in D and G over rope-tension snare drums beating rudimental long rolls, flams and drags with a bass drum on the march beat, all outdoors, unamplified and at roughly 110-120 steps per minute.
items.description: Fife and drum is the martial field music of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century armies, kept alive as a living tradition by the ancient corps of Connecticut, Massachusetts and the Hudson Valley. The sound is deliberately piercing and narrow-band: keyless fifes doubling a two-part tune in the top octave with no harmonic filling, over rope-tension snares whose gut snare-beds and rudimental sticking supply all the rhythmic detail, plus a march-beat bass drum. It is distinguished from the marching band by its tiny instrumentation and lack of brass, and from drum corps by its pre-industrial fife rather than valved bugle melody line.
exemplars: The Company of Fifers and Drummers
Ancient Mariners Fife and Drum Corps

items.name: Concert Band
items.lineage: The seated indoor wind-and-percussion ensemble that grew from nineteenth-century military and municipal bands, professionalised by Patrick Gilmore, John Philip Sousa and the Goldman Band, and given a serious concert repertoire by Holst's Suites in E-flat and F (1909, 1911), Vaughan Williams's Folk Song Suite (1923) and the American school-band literature of Persichetti, Grainger and Frank Ticheli; large doubled sections of flutes, clarinets, saxophones, cornets, horns, trombones, euphoniums and tubas with full percussion, reading fully notated scores at conventional concert tempos.
items.description: The concert band is the seated symphonic wind ensemble in its large, section-doubled form, established as a civic and school institution across the United States and Britain from the late nineteenth century onward. Its texture is dense and blended: multiple clarinets carrying the string-substitute middle voice, saxophones filling the tenor register, cornets and trumpets on top, and a tuba-euphonium foundation, all notated and conducted with no improvisation. It differs from the marching band in being stationary, seated and score-read rather than memorised and choreographed, and from the wind ensemble in doubling parts heavily rather than assigning one player per line.
exemplars: Royal Northern College of Music Wind Orchestra
Gustav Holst, First Suite in E-flat

items.name: Wind Ensemble
items.lineage: The one-player-per-part symphonic wind medium founded by Frederick Fennell with the Eastman Wind Ensemble in 1952 as a deliberate reform of the doubled concert band, giving composers a transparent chamber-scaled wind palette exploited by Schoenberg, Stravinsky's Symphonies of Wind Instruments as ancestor, and by Husa, Karel Husa's Music for Prague 1968, Dahl, Maslanka and Joan Tower; variable instrumentation drawn from the full woodwind, brass and percussion families, fully notated, often in extended tonality or serial and aleatoric idioms with mixed and shifting metres.
items.description: The wind ensemble is the transparent, one-per-part symphonic wind medium created by Frederick Fennell at Eastman in 1952 and adopted worldwide as the vehicle for serious contemporary wind writing. Because parts are single rather than doubled, individual timbres stay audible, allowing composers to write chamber-textured counterpoint, extended techniques, complex metric shifts and dissonant harmonic language impossible in a massed band. It differs from the concert band chiefly in scoring philosophy and repertoire - modernist and commissioned rather than march-and-transcription - while sharing the same instrument families and notation-bound practice.
exemplars: Eastman Wind Ensemble under Frederick Fennell

items.name: Drum and Bugle Corps
items.lineage: The American competitive field ensemble that grew out of post-First-World-War American Legion and VFW veterans' units using surplus valveless bugles, reorganised under Drum Corps International from 1972 and progressively liberalised to three-valve brass in 2000 and any-key brass in 2014; a brass line of trumpets, mellophones, baritones, euphoniums and contrabass bugles plus a marching battery of snares, tenors and basses and an amplified front-ensemble pit of mallet keyboards and synthesisers, performing eleven-minute memorised competitive programs with extreme dynamic contrast and metric complexity.
items.description: Drum and bugle corps is the competitive American field-show idiom that evolved from veterans' bugle units into the Drum Corps International circuit after 1972. Its sound is an all-brass line with no woodwinds - trumpets, mellophones, baritones and contrabasses - paired with a virtuosic marching battery and an amplified front pit of mallet percussion and electronics, performing memorised through-composed programs with wide dynamic swings and frequent metric modulation. It differs from the marching band in excluding woodwinds and in its competitive, through-composed show format, and from the concert band in being memorised, mobile and heavily arranged from orchestral and contemporary sources.

items.name: Afro drill
items.lineage: Formed in London and Lagos circa 2019-2021 when UK drill producers and Nigerian-Ghanaian diaspora artists fused the 138-142 BPM sliding 808 drill pattern with Afrobeats' 3-2 log-drum and shaker feel, codified by Kwengface, Tion Wayne, Odumodublvck and producers like Ghosty and Gotcha, marked by triplet hats, a melodic Afro guitar or log-drum loop over the drill bass slide, and pidgin/Yoruba-inflected melodic hooks alternating with flat-affect road rap verses.
items.description: Afro drill emerged around 2019 in London's Nigerian and Ghanaian diaspora scenes and quickly reflected back into Lagos and Accra. It keeps UK drill's sliding, portamento 808 bass and skittering triplet hi-hats at roughly 140 BPM but replaces the grey minor-key piano and glide-bass menace with warm Afrobeats material: log-drum and talking-drum figures, plucked nylon guitar loops, and sung pidgin hooks. Against straight UK drill it is brighter and more melodic; against Afrobeats proper it is far darker, sparser and rhythmically stiffer.

items.name: Drill'n'bass
items.lineage: Mid-1990s British studio-bound offshoot of jungle, named by the UK press and codified by Aphex Twin, Squarepusher, Luke Vibert and µ-Ziq on Rephlex and Warp circa 1995-1998, defined by Amen and Think breakbeats chopped to 1/32-note resolution and machine-gunned at 160-190 BPM, jazz-fusion fretless bass lines, sweet detuned analogue-synth melodies, and an explicitly non-danceable, through-edited arrangement with no MC and no DJ function.
items.description: Drill'n'bass is the mid-1990s bedroom-studio mutation of jungle made by British electronic producers who wanted the Amen break's velocity without the rave's floor obligations. Breakbeats are sliced to impossible densities and re-triggered in stuttering non-repeating figures, over which sit warm Rhodes-ish pads, fretless bass and childlike synth melodies, giving a violent-but-tender contrast. It differs from jungle in having no MC, no dubplate culture and no consistent dance groove, and from later breakcore in its melodic sweetness and comparatively clean production.
exemplars: Luke Vibert / Plug — Drum 'n' Bass for Papa

items.name: Memphis rap (Bluff City lineage)
items.lineage: Developed in Memphis, Tennessee between roughly 1989 and 1999 on locally dubbed cassettes by DJ Spanish Fly, DJ Squeeky, Tommy Wright III, Playa Fly and Three 6 Mafia, built on slow 70-90 BPM half-time patterns, distorted overdriven 808 kicks, minor-key organ, harpsichord or horror-film sample loops, hissing four-track tape ambience and chanted double-time occult-tinged hooks delivered in a flat, threatening Southern drawl.
items.description: Memphis rap is the cassette-economy hip-hop of Tennessee's Bluff City, circulated hand-to-hand on dubbed tapes through the 1990s before any of it reached national distribution. The sound is deliberately degraded: overdriven 808 kicks clipping into tape saturation, murky minor-key keyboard or horror-soundtrack loops, and chanted, often occult or gang-referencing hooks that anticipate crunk's call structure. It is slower and far lo-fi-er than contemporaneous Atlanta bass music, and its tape hiss and clipping later became the explicit aesthetic subject of phonk.

items.name: ATL trap (Atlanta canon)
items.lineage: Codified in Atlanta between 2003 and 2012 by T.I., Young Jeezy and Gucci Mane with producers Shawty Redd, Zaytoven, Drumma Boy, Lex Luger and Metro Boomin, defined by 130-150 BPM half-time feel, long-decay tuned 808 kick-bass, machine-rolled 32nd and triplet hi-hats, tightly gated layered claps and snares, minor-key orchestral or Zaytoven organ/piano loops, and drawled ad-lib-saturated first-person street narrative.
items.description: Atlanta trap is the specific production dialect that turned regional Southern rap into the default grammar of American pop rhythm. Its signature is the tuned, long-decaying 808 doubling as kick and bassline, hi-hats rolled into 32nd and triplet subdivisions, and a sparse minor-key melodic loop, cut at studios like Patchwerk with Avalon-channel vocal chains and heavy ad-lib stacking. It is distinguished from earlier Southern bounce and crunk by its half-time feel and melodic austerity, and from later plugg or drill by its clean commercial mix and rhythmic squareness.
exemplars: Young Jeezy — Let's Get It: Thug Motivation 101

items.name: Detroit trap
items.lineage: Emerged on Detroit's east and west sides circa 2015-2019 through Sada Baby, Tee Grizzley, 42 Dugg, Babyface Ray and producers Helluva and Antt Beatz, using 95-110 BPM double-time-feel beats with a swung shuffled hi-hat, dry punchy kick and clap rather than long 808 slides, chopped soul or eerie synth loops, and a conversational, off-kilter, punchline-dense flow that lands deliberately behind and around the grid.
items.description: Detroit trap is a late-2010s regional rewrite of Atlanta's template that swaps the sliding 808 for dry, shuffling drums and a nervous swung hi-hat pattern, often built by producers like Helluva around a looped soul or synth fragment and a signature bell or vocal tag. Rappers ride the beat conversationally, crowding syllables and landing behind the grid in a way that reads as almost comic-aggressive. Compared with Atlanta trap it is faster-feeling, less bass-dominated and much rougher in mix; compared with Michigan's older hip-hop it is far more melodically minimal.

items.name: Bay Area hip-hop (mobb music lineage)
items.lineage: Developed in Oakland, Vallejo and Richmond from the mid-1980s through the 1990s by Too $hort, E-40, Spice 1, Mac Dre, Digital Underground and producers Khayree and Ant Banks, built on 85-100 BPM funk-derived grooves with live-feel slap electric bass, P-funk synth leads and talkbox, sparse gated drums, and pimp-narrative or rapid-fire regional-slang vocal delivery cut for independent trunk-oriented mixes.
items.description: Bay Area hip-hop, often called mobb music, grew out of Oakland and Vallejo's independent tape-and-trunk economy from the mid-1980s onward, largely outside major-label systems. Its beats favour slapping live or sampled electric bass, greasy P-funk synth leads and talkbox over hard breakbeats, with vocals ranging from Too $hort's laconic drawl to E-40's elastic, slang-inventing cadences. It is looser and more bass-forward than Los Angeles G-funk, which it partly prefigured, and its later hyphy phase pushed the same funk lineage into faster, more manic territory.

items.name: Jazz rap
items.lineage: Formed in New York and London between 1988 and 1994 through the Native Tongues collective — A Tribe Called Quest, De La Soul, Gang Starr, Digable Planets and Guru's Jazzmatazz — built on 88-96 BPM boom-bap breakbeats layered with sampled or live upright bass, muted trumpet, Rhodes and vibraphone from Blue Note and CTI records, swung MPC-quantised drums, and a relaxed, conversational, often abstract or Afrocentric lyric.
items.description: Jazz rap took shape at the turn of the 1990s when New York producers began building boom-bap tracks from hard-bop and soul-jazz records rather than funk breaks alone, sometimes replaying the material with live players. The result pairs warm walking upright bass, Rhodes chords and muted horn fragments with swung, deliberately un-quantised MPC drums and low-key conversational rapping. Against gangsta rap of the same years it is harmonically far richer and dynamically softer; against the later lo-fi hip-hop it descends from, it retains full-length verses and a real MC-centred structure.
exemplars: A Tribe Called Quest — The Low End Theory
De La Soul — 3 Feet High and Rising

items.name: Narco rap
items.lineage: Emerged circa 2010 in Reynosa, Matamoros and the Tamaulipas border corridor of northeastern Mexico, spread by Cartel de Santa's precedent and artists such as Rowsty, Dan Sanchez and El Komander-adjacent rap crews, built on 70-90 BPM half-time trap and boom-bap beats with dark minor synth pads, heavy 808s, occasional sampled accordion or bajo sexto quotes, and blunt first-person cartel narrative delivered in a hard Norteño Spanish over YouTube-distributed, home-mixed audio.
items.description: Narco rap is the Spanish-language border-corridor rap that grew up around Reynosa and Matamoros from about 2010, functioning as a hip-hop parallel to the narcocorrido: commissioned or self-authored chronicles of cartel figures, operations and rivalries. Musically it is stripped-down Mexican trap — dark synth pads, heavy 808s, half-time drums — produced on home DAW rigs and distributed almost entirely through YouTube and social channels rather than labels. What separates it from other Mexican trap is documentary lyrical function and its acoustic-corrido citations; what separates it from the corrido tumbado is that the instrumentation stays electronic.

items.name: Trap Latino (pan-Hispanic trap)
items.lineage: Coalesced across San Juan, Medellín and Miami between 2014 and 2017 through Bad Bunny, Anuel AA, Bryant Myers, Ozuna and producers DJ Luian, Mambo Kingz and Hi Music Hi Flow, taking Atlanta trap's 130-150 BPM half-time 808 template and adding sung Spanish melodic hooks, heavy Auto-Tune, reggaeton-adjacent dembow fills, minor-key pad and plucked-synth loops, and romantic or street lyric in Caribbean Spanish.
items.description: Trap Latino is the Spanish-language wave that displaced classic reggaeton as Caribbean urbano's dominant mode between roughly 2015 and 2018, centred on Puerto Rico and Colombia. It uses the Atlanta half-time 808 and rolled-hat grammar but is far more sung than rapped, with Auto-Tuned melodic hooks, lush minor pads and frequent dembow-inflected transitions back toward the dance floor. Against US trap it is more melodic and romantic; against reggaeton it drops the continuous dembow pulse in favour of half-time space.

items.name: Trap Brasileiro
items.lineage: Formed in São Paulo and Rio between 2016 and 2019 out of the rap-battle and YouTube-cypher circuit, codified by Matuê, Teto, Derek, WIU and producers Papatinho and Sidoka's circle, applying 130-150 BPM half-time 808 trap production with dark plucked-synth and piano loops to Brazilian Portuguese flows, plus periodic funk-carioca tamborzão or samba percussion inserts and sung Auto-Tuned refrains.
items.description: Trap Brasileiro is the late-2010s Brazilian assimilation of Atlanta trap, driven less by radio than by YouTube cyphers, battle-rap alumni and independent collectives like 30PRAUM. Production keeps the tuned 808, triplet hats and sparse minor loop, but the Portuguese cadences sit differently on the grid and tracks frequently splice in tamborzão or samba-derived percussion breaks. It is distinct from funk carioca, which stays on a fast continuous dembow-derived pulse, and from Brazilian boom-bap rap nacional, which is verse-heavy and sample-based rather than melodic and 808-driven.

items.name: Phonk Brasileiro
items.lineage: Emerged online around 2020-2022 as Brazilian producers on SoundCloud and TikTok fused drift-phonk's cowbell-driven 130-150 BPM template with funk carioca's tamborzão and beat-mandela rhythms, codified by producers such as MXZI, Yzomandias-adjacent Brazilian circles, Kordhell imitators and the 'funk phonk' / 'brazilian phonk' YouTube channel economy, marked by distorted 808 cowbell melodies, sidechained subs, chopped Memphis-style vocal samples and Portuguese shouted or pitched vocal chops.
items.description: Phonk Brasileiro is a fully platform-native genre that appeared around 2020 when Brazilian bedroom producers grafted drift phonk's distorted cowbell riffs and heavy sidechain onto funk carioca's tamborzão and 'beat bruxaria' rhythmic vocabulary. Tracks are short, loud, mono-dense and mixed to survive phone speakers, built from clipped 808 cowbells, sub-bass pumping against the kick, and chopped Memphis or Portuguese vocal fragments. It is faster, more percussive and less nostalgic than US drift phonk, and unlike mainstream funk carioca it foregrounds melodic cowbell riffing over vocal MCs.

items.name: Dark plugg
items.lineage: Split off from plugg around 2018-2021 in the SoundCloud producer diaspora around MexikoDro's Plugg tradition, codified by producers such as Yung Icey, Ptolemy and StoopidXool with rappers like SosMula-adjacent underground figures, keeping plugg's 130-150 BPM bell and glassy-pad palette but shifting to minor-second dissonance, detuned brass or choir stabs, sparse distorted 808s with long glides, and heavily reverbed, murky vocals mixed low into the beat.
items.description: Dark plugg is the menacing branch of the plugg beat tradition that developed on SoundCloud and YouTube type-beat channels around 2018, retaining the parent style's FL Studio bell leads, glassy pads and loose swung hats while replacing its pastel prettiness with dissonant intervals, detuned choir or brass stabs and heavy reverb tails. Vocals are often buried, drenched and half-improvised rather than mixed forward. Compared with plugg or pluggnb it is harmonically darker and sparser; compared with Atlanta trap it is far looser rhythmically and made almost entirely by teenage producers working alone in DAWs.

items.name: Dream Plugg
items.lineage: Internet-native offshoot of Atlanta plugg formed circa 2018-2020 on SoundCloud and YouTube type-beat channels, codified by producers MexikoDro, StoopidXool, Nept and Kankan-adjacent rappers, built on 130-145 BPM half-time 808 patterns with long glide-tuned sub bass, sparse triplet hi-hat rolls, and washed reverb-drenched bell, music-box and detuned pad presets under heavily Auto-Tuned melodic mumble delivery.
items.description: Dream plugg emerged around 2018 in the SoundCloud and type-beat economy as the softest branch of Atlanta's plugg sound, trading plugg's brittle brightness for hazy, heavily reverbed bell and pad textures. Beats sit at half-time over long pitch-sliding 808s with minimal drum fills, and vocals are saturated with Auto-Tune to the point of becoming another synth layer. It differs from mainstream trap in its deliberately thin, low-energy mix and from cloud rap in its rigid 808-glide rhythmic grammar.

items.name: Emo Rap
items.lineage: Formed on SoundCloud between 2015 and 2018 in Florida and the wider US internet underground, codified by Lil Peep, XXXTENTACION, Juice WRLD and producers Smokeasac and Nick Mira, marrying looped clean or distorted emo/pop-punk guitar samples to 70-90 BPM half-time 808 trap drums under confessional, Auto-Tuned sung-rapped delivery about depression, addiction and heartbreak.
items.description: Emo rap crystallised on SoundCloud around 2015-2018, when Florida and internet-underground artists looped guitar figures lifted from 2000s emo and pop-punk over trap 808 programming. The sound is defined by lo-fi guitar sampling, clipped and distorted mixes, and vocals that slide between rapping and Auto-Tuned singing with unguarded first-person lyrics. Unlike conscious rap it foregrounds interior emotional collapse rather than narrative, and unlike rap-rock it keeps the trap rhythmic grid intact rather than using a live band.
exemplars: Lil Uzi Vert - Luv Is Rage 2

items.name: Reggaeton Mexicano
items.lineage: Mexican regional adaptation of Puerto Rican reggaeton that broke nationally around 2019-2022 out of Monterrey, Guadalajara and Mexico City through Yeri Mua, El Bogueto, Uzielito Mix and the 'guaracha/reggaeton mexa' DJ circuit, keeping the 90-100 BPM dembow kick-snare pattern but adding sharper Mexican Spanish diction, cumbia-derived keyboard riffs and sequenced brass or requinto stabs over hard-clipped 808s.
items.description: Reggaeton mexicano is the Mexican strain of urbano that went mainstream domestically after 2019, driven by Veracruz and Monterrey artists and by the club-DJ 'mexa' remix circuit. It retains the dembow skeleton and clipped 808 sub of Caribbean reggaeton but layers in cumbia-style keyboard hooks, regional brass or plucked-string stabs, and explicitly Mexican slang and vocal cadence. It is distinguished from Puerto Rican reggaeton by that melodic vocabulary and from corridos tumbados by its programmed rather than acoustic rhythm section.

items.name: Reggaeton Chileno
items.lineage: Santiago-based urbano scene that consolidated between 2016 and 2022 around Pablo Chill-E, Polimá Westcoast, Cris Mj, Standly and the Shishigang/Gran Rah orbit, taking the dembow at roughly 90-100 BPM but slowing and darkening it with minor-key detuned synth pads, heavy sub, minimal percussion layering and a distinctly Chilean drawled, slang-dense vocal delivery often blurred by Auto-Tune.
items.description: Reggaeton chileno grew out of Santiago's poblacion rap and trap scenes in the late 2010s, reaching global charts with Cris Mj and Standly around 2022. Its productions are sparser and darker than Caribbean reggaeton: fewer percussion layers, prominent minor-mode pads, and a lazy behind-the-beat vocal phrasing thick with Chilean slang. Compared to reggaeton mexicano it is more trap-inflected and less melodically ornamented.

items.name: Salsa Venezolana
items.lineage: Caracas salsa style codified from the late 1960s through the 1970s by Federico y su Combo, Dimensión Latina and Oscar D'León, built on Cuban son montuno clave with a trombone-forward front line rather than trumpets, fast aggressive tempos, extended sonero improvisation in the montuno, and a bass-and-piano tumbao driven by D'León's own bass playing and stage showmanship.
items.description: Venezuelan salsa formed in Caracas in the late 1960s and 70s, running parallel to the New York Fania sound but with its own accent: trombone-heavy horn writing inherited from Dimension Latina, unusually fast tempos, and an emphatic slap-and-drive electric bass tumbao popularised by Oscar D'Leon. Vocal sections lean hard on inspired sonero improvisation against tight coro responses. It is more brass-lean and more explicitly Cuban-revivalist than Colombian salsa and less arrangement-dense than the Fania orchestral style.

items.name: Salsa Peruana
items.lineage: Lima salsa scene that took shape from the mid-1970s in the coastal barrios and boomed commercially in the 1990s through Antonio Cartagena, Willie Rivera, Bembé and later Los Hermanos Yaipén, applying Cuban 2-3 son clave and a piano-bass tumbao to romantic 'salsa sensual' repertoire with softer horn voicings, string-pad sweetening and slower 85-95 BPM tempos than Caribbean models.
items.description: Salsa peruana developed in Lima from the mid-1970s and became a mass-market style in the 1990s, dominated by the romantic 'salsa sensual' idiom rather than the aggressive brass of Caracas or New York. Arrangements favour smooth two-horn voicings, keyboard string pads and a foregrounded lead singer, with the montuno section shortened and the ballad-like verse expanded. It is markedly softer and more vocal-centred than salsa venezolana, and distinct from Peruvian chicha, which uses electric guitar over cumbia rather than clave.

items.name: Cumbia Argentina
items.lineage: Argentine reworking of Colombian cumbia that spread from Santa Fe and Greater Buenos Aires in the 1960s-80s and hardened into cumbia villera around 1999-2002 with Pibes Chorros, Damas Gratis and Yerba Brava, built on a 4/4 cumbia paseo with güiro and timbal, cheap preset-heavy synthesizer riffs, a bouncing electric bass line and shouted, socially raw barrio Spanish lyrics.
items.description: Cumbia in Argentina took root through Santa Fe orchestras in the 1960s and 70s and became a dominant working-class pop form in Buenos Aires, culminating in the cumbia villera boom at the turn of the 2000s. The sound is built from a güiro-and-timbal cumbia pulse, a springy electric bass, and cheap keyboard leads playing short repeated hooks, with vocals shouted more than sung. Against Colombian cumbia it is faster, thinner and synth-based rather than accordion-and-brass, and against Peruvian chicha it substitutes keyboards for the psychedelic electric guitar.

items.name: Tecnocumbia
items.lineage: Andean-Amazonian electronic cumbia that emerged in Peru and Ecuador in the early-to-mid 1990s, popularised by Rossy War, Ana Kohler, Agua Marina and Grupo Néctar, replacing chicha's electric guitars with FM and preset polysynths, drum-machine and MIDI percussion over a 4/4 cumbia paseo at 100-115 BPM, topped by bright, slightly nasal female lead vocals and rapid keyboard countermelodies.
items.description: Tecnocumbia arose in Peru and Ecuador in the 1990s as the synthesizer-era successor to chicha, carried by touring provincial groups and cassette distribution. Its signature is glossy FM keyboard timbres and programmed percussion locked to a cumbia paseo, with ornamented keyboard fills answering a bright female lead voice. Unlike chicha it abandons surf-reverb electric guitar, and unlike Argentine cumbia villera its lyrics are romantic rather than confrontational.

items.name: Merengue de Calle
items.lineage: Santo Domingo street style that emerged around 2003-2008 through Omega y su Mambo Violento, Silvio Mora, El Sujeto and Fulanito's orbit, accelerating merengue's tambora-and-güira 2/4 to 140-170 BPM, replacing the horn section with sampled synth stabs and 808 kick reinforcement, and swapping sung verses for shouted, chanted, call-and-response urban vocals.
items.description: Merengue de calle, also called mambo urbano, came out of Santo Domingo's barrios in the mid-2000s as merengue collided with reggaeton and hip-hop production. Live tambora and güira remain the rhythmic core but are pushed to extreme tempos and glued to programmed 808 kicks and looped synth stabs in place of the traditional saxophone-and-brass jaleo. Its shouted, hook-driven vocals and abrupt beat-drop arrangements separate it from orchestral merengue and from Dominican dembow, which uses a slower reggaeton pattern.

items.name: New York Garage House
items.lineage: Named for the Paradise Garage, where Larry Levan DJed from 1977 to 1987, and codified on record in the mid-1980s by Tony Humphries at Newark's Zanzibar and producers Timmy Regisford, Blaze and Masters at Work — 118-124 BPM four-on-the-floor built on live-feel drum programming and Roland TR-909, gospel-rooted full-voiced lead singing, real piano and organ chords, and long dub-style breakdowns on the twelve-inch mix.
items.description: Garage house is the New York/New Jersey branch of house that grew directly out of the Paradise Garage's disco and soul programming in the late 1970s and 80s. It is the most song-oriented and most vocally demanding house dialect: gospel-trained singers, real piano and organ voicings, warm bass lines, and extended twelve-inch arrangements with dub-influenced breakdowns. Against Chicago house it is less raw and more harmonically rich; against UK speed garage it keeps a straight four-four kick rather than a shuffled, chopped one.

items.name: German Techno
items.lineage: Techno as it was rebuilt in Frankfurt and post-Wall Berlin between 1989 and 1995 by Sven Väth, Hardfloor, Westbam, Marusha, Dr. Motte and the Tresor/Harthouse labels, taking Detroit's template toward 135-150 BPM, hard TR-909 kicks and open hats, TB-303 acid lines, sequenced hoover and stab riffs, and long linear arrangements engineered for warehouse and Love Parade sound systems.
items.description: German techno is the early-1990s Frankfurt and Berlin reworking of Detroit techno into a harder, faster, rave-scaled form, spread through Tresor, Harthouse, Low Spirit and the Love Parade. It is defined by punishing 909 kicks, acid 303 sequences, hoover and stab riffs, and arrangements that unfold as long linear builds rather than song structures. It is more aggressive and less soulful than Detroit techno, and denser and more anthem-driven than the Berlin minimal sound that followed it.

items.name: Berlin Minimal Techno
items.lineage: Berlin techno's reductionist turn from 1993 onward, codified by Basic Channel/Chain Reaction (Moritz von Oswald and Mark Ernestus), Monolake, and later the Perlon and Berghain/Ostgut orbit — 125-132 BPM, muted 909 or sampled kicks, single evolving chord stabs washed in tape delay and reverb, deep sub bass, and arrangements built from slow parameter automation over eight-to-twelve-minute durations.
items.description: Berlin minimal techno began in the mid-1990s with Basic Channel and the Chain Reaction label, applying dub studio technique — tape delay, spring reverb, filtered feedback — to a stripped four-four techno frame. Tracks are built from one or two elements whose timbre slowly mutates across very long durations, with sub bass carrying the weight and almost no melodic or vocal material. It is far sparser and slower-moving than the Frankfurt hard-techno of the same years, and more dub-saturated and less funk-derived than Detroit or Hawtin-style minimal.

items.name: Birmingham Techno
items.lineage: UK industrial-techno strain forged in Birmingham between 1993 and 1999 around Karl O'Connor's Downwards label with Regis, Surgeon, Female and Anthony Child, running 130-140 BPM loops of distorted, heavily compressed drum machine hits, feedback-driven metallic percussion, no melodic content and post-punk/industrial sonic references drawn from Whitehouse and early Throbbing Gristle.
items.description: Birmingham techno emerged in the mid-1990s from the Downwards label and the city's post-industrial club scene, taking techno toward noise and industrial music rather than dance-floor euphoria. Tracks are short distorted loops of overdriven drum machines and feedback, mixed with deliberate harshness and almost no harmonic material, often assembled live from hardware in single takes. It is drier and more abrasive than Berlin minimal and less anthem-oriented than German rave techno, sitting closer to power electronics than to house.

items.name: South African house (SA house)
items.lineage: Johannesburg and Durban house variant that emerged in the mid-1990s as kwaito's faster sibling and was codified through Oskido, DJ Christos, Black Coffee and the Soulistic/Soul Candi label network — four-on-the-floor at 118-125 BPM, deep Rhodes-and-pad chords over rolling shaker and conga layers, gospel-inflected lead vocals in isiZulu, Sesotho and English, and extended 7-9 minute arrangements built for taxi-rank and club sound systems.
items.description: South African house formed in mid-1990s Johannesburg when local producers took Chicago and New York deep house at full tempo instead of slowing it to kwaito's 100 BPM, and it became the country's dominant popular music through the 2000s. Its signature is a chord-rich, warm-pad deep-house bed layered with live-feel percussion (shakers, congas, cowbell) and a full sung vocal delivered with gospel phrasing rather than a chanted hook. It is distinguished from kwaito by tempo and four-on-the-floor regularity, from gqom by its melodic harmonic content and unbroken kick, and from American deep house by the density of its percussion overlay and the vernacular-language lead vocal.

items.name: Kenyan drill
items.lineage: Nairobi drill scene that formed around 2019-2021 as Eastlands and Kayole crews absorbed UK/Brooklyn drill via YouTube — sliding 808 glides at 138-145 BPM over sparse triplet hi-hat rolls and dark minor-key piano or flute loops, with deadpan half-sung Sheng-language delivery, gang-affiliated collective posses (Wakadinali, Buruklyn Boyz) and low-budget handheld video culture driving distribution.
items.description: Kenyan drill emerged in Nairobi around 2019 when Eastlands collectives fused imported UK and Brooklyn drill production with Sheng, the Swahili-English street argot of the city. The beats keep drill's sliding 808 bass and skittering triplet hats but frequently sit on Kenyan-inflected melodic loops and slightly brighter mixes than UK drill, and vocals are delivered in dense, rapid Sheng with heavy crew ad-libs. It differs from gengetone, its immediate local rival, by its darker minor tonality and slower conversational cadence rather than gengetone's shouted call-and-response party chants.

items.name: Naija old school
items.lineage: Nigerian urban pop of roughly 1995-2008, formed in Lagos and Ajegunle out of galala, reggae-dancehall and imported hip-hop and codified by Daddy Showkey, Plantashun Boiz, Tony Tetuila, P-Square and Kennis Music radio — mid-tempo 100-115 BPM keyboard-and-drum-machine tracks with dancehall-derived bounce, talking-drum accents, sung Pidgin choruses over rapped verses, and thin bright General MIDI-era synth timbres.
items.description: Naija old school covers the first generation of Nigerian home-grown urban pop, roughly from the mid-1990s Ajegunle galala scene through the Kennis Music radio boom of the early 2000s. It is built on cheap workstation keyboards and drum machines rather than live bands, carrying dancehall bounce and hip-hop cadence under Pidgin hooks, with a characteristically thin, bright, midrange-heavy mix reflecting limited Lagos studio budgets. It precedes and directly feeds Afrobeats, from which it is separated by its coarser production, stronger reggae-dancehall skeleton and heavier reliance on rapped verses.

items.name: Afro R&B
items.lineage: Continental and diasporic African R&B consolidated from the mid-2000s onward in Lagos, Accra and London through artists such as Banky W, Wizkid's slower material, Bisa Kdei and Tems — 85-105 BPM programmed grooves marrying American contemporary-R&B chord vocabulary and stacked melisma-light harmonies to shaker-and-log-drum Afrobeats percussion, with lead vocals moving between English, Pidgin, Twi and Yoruba.
items.description: Afro R&B is the slow-lane branch of modern African popular music, taking shape in Lagos, Accra and the London diaspora during the 2000s as producers applied contemporary-R&B harmony and vocal stacking to an African rhythmic bed. Tracks sit well below Afrobeats tempo, foreground sustained pads and Rhodes-style keys, and use dense multi-tracked backing vocals with restrained rather than gospel-heavy melisma. It differs from American contemporary R&B by keeping shaker, log drum and clave-adjacent percussion audible under the ballad, and from alté by its cleaner commercial production and conventional song forms.

items.name: Afro soul
items.lineage: Band-based African soul that formed in the late 1960s-1970s across Johannesburg, Lagos, Nairobi and the diaspora — Letta Mbulu, Miriam Makeba's later work, Hugh Masekela and later Thandiswa Mazwai and Vusi Mahlasela — coupling American soul horn charts, Rhodes and gospel-derived vocal harmony with mbaqanga guitar figures, conga-and-shaker layers and mid-tempo 90-110 BPM grooves sung in Xhosa, Zulu, Yoruba or Swahili.
items.description: Afro soul names the live-band tradition, strongest in South Africa and West Africa from the late 1960s, in which African vocalists and arrangers absorbed American soul and gospel while retaining indigenous language, harmony and guitar idiom. Its sound is a full rhythm section with Rhodes or organ, horn punches, high-tuned mbaqanga-style guitar and layered call-and-response backing voices, recorded to analogue tape with a warm, mid-forward balance. It differs from Afro R&B by being performed rather than programmed, and from mbaqanga by its slower tempos, soul chord changes and prominence of a single expressive lead singer.

items.name: Coladeira
items.lineage: Cape Verdean urban dance genre that crystallised on São Vicente and in Mindelo in the 1930s-40s as morna's up-tempo counterpart and was carried to Lisbon, Rotterdam and Boston diaspora studios from the 1960s — brisk duple-time 120-160 BPM guitar-and-cavaquinho strumming with an offbeat accompaniment stroke, walking bass, satirical or topical Kriolu lyrics, and later horn sections and drum machines in the funaná-adjacent coladeira-zouk hybrid.
items.description: Coladeira developed in Mindelo, São Vicente in the 1930s and 40s as the fast, sardonic dance partner to the slow lyric morna, sharing its harmonic language of major-minor cadences and chromatic bass motion but doubling the tempo. The texture is guitar and cavaquinho in a springy offbeat strum with a walking bass and often violin or clarinet obbligato, over topical, mocking or socially critical Kriolu texts. It is distinguished from morna by tempo and satirical register, and from funaná by its European-derived harmony and guitar basis rather than funaná's accordion-and-ferrinho ostinato.

items.name: Mbube
items.lineage: Zulu male-choral style named for Solomon Linda's 1939 Gallo recording 'Mbube', formed among Natal migrant workers in Johannesburg hostels — a loud, full-throated four-part bass-led homophonic choir with a soaring solo falsetto or high tenor over cycling I-IV-I-V harmony, sung in isiZulu at moderate walking tempo and staged in all-night competitive hostel contests.
items.description: Mbube is the loud, unaccompanied Zulu male choral style that took its name from Solomon Linda and the Evening Birds' 1939 Gallo recording, developed among migrant hostel workers in Johannesburg. It sets a powerful bass-dominated four-part homophonic block against a high solo line, cycling a short mission-hymn-derived chord progression through many repetitions with steadily rising intensity. Its immediate descendant isicathamiya, popularised by Ladysmith Black Mambazo, is quieter and more choreographed — mbube is defined precisely by the full-volume, unrestrained delivery isicathamiya softened.
exemplars: Solomon Linda and the Evening Birds

items.name: Bristol trip hop
items.lineage: Bristol sound that grew out of the Wild Bunch sound-system crew and was codified 1991-1998 by Massive Attack, Portishead, Tricky and Smith & Mighty — 65-95 BPM dub-weighted breakbeats, minor-key vinyl-noise loops of soundtrack strings and organ, deep sub bass borrowed from reggae sound-system practice, and murmured, close-miked vocals alternating between soul singing and near-whispered rap.
items.description: Bristol trip hop formed in the early 1990s among musicians from the city's Wild Bunch sound-system network, fusing Jamaican dub bass weight, hip-hop sampling method and British post-punk melancholy. The music runs at half hip-hop tempo, layers dusty sampled or deliberately degraded live breaks under filmic minor-key strings, Rhodes and theremin-like leads, and keeps vocals intimate and dry against a wide, reverberant instrumental field. It differs from American boom-bap in its slower tempo and harmonic gloom, and from downtempo or chillout in its sound-system-derived sub-bass and confrontational lyrical content.

items.name: Sheffield bleep techno
items.lineage: Northern English techno variant codified 1988-1991 around Warp Records in Sheffield by LFO, Unique 3, Nightmares on Wax and Forgemasters — 118-130 BPM tracks built from pure sine or FM 'bleep' motifs over enormous sound-system sub-bass, sparse 808/909 programming, dub-derived delay drops, and almost no chord content, deliberately mixed for the low end of West Yorkshire and South Yorkshire warehouse rigs.
items.description: Bleep techno, also called bleep-and-bass, appeared in Sheffield and Leeds in 1988-1990 and was the first distinctly British answer to Detroit techno, released chiefly by the young Warp Records. Its formula is extreme reduction: a handful of clean synthetic bleep tones, a hard drum-machine pattern, and a sub-bass line so low it functions as physical pressure on a sound system, with reggae-derived echo and dropouts structuring the track. It differs from Detroit techno by discarding chordal pads and string washes entirely, and from acid house by using pure tones rather than resonant 303 filter sweeps.

items.name: Kosmische Musik
items.lineage: West German electronic-psychedelic practice of roughly 1969-1978, centred on Berlin and Cologne around Tangerine Dream, Klaus Schulze, Ash Ra Tempel, Popol Vuh and producer Conny Plank — long-form sequencer and modular-synthesiser pieces over static or slowly shifting drones, minimal or absent vocals, tape-delay guitar washes, and either free-floating pulseless expanses or steady motorik eighth-note drumming.
items.description: Kosmische Musik is the electronic and drone-oriented wing of the German post-1968 experimental scene, distinct from the rock-band core of krautrock. Its records favour side-long durations, sequencer arpeggios and modular timbres evolving through filter movement, Mellotron and organ beds, echo-saturated guitar, and a near-total absence of song form or lead vocal. Where krautrock proper keeps drums, riffs and a band identity, kosmische often abandons the pulse altogether or reduces it to a hypnotic ostinato, and it directly seeds later ambient and Berlin-school electronic music.

items.name: Zamrock
items.lineage: Zambian fuzz-rock movement of roughly 1972-1979 that arose in Lusaka and the Copperbelt under Kaunda-era radio quotas favouring local content, codified by WITCH, Amanaz, Ngozi Family and Musi-O-Tunya — heavily fuzzed and wah-inflected guitar over garage-grade drum kit, mid-tempo 4/4 grooves inflected by kalindula and Congolese rumba guitar figures, and English or Bemba vocals recorded fast to modest local tape facilities.
items.description: Zamrock is the psychedelic hard-rock scene that flourished in Zambia through the 1970s, encouraged by state broadcasting rules that required a large share of Zambian music on the radio after independence. Bands built on Hendrix, Black Sabbath and Cream fuzz vocabulary but grounded it in local kalindula bass figures and Congolese rumba guitar interlock, recorded with saturated, distorted and often overloaded signal paths at small Lusaka studios. It is separated from Nigerian Afro-rock of the same decade by its heavier, doomier guitar tone and sparser horn use, and the scene collapsed with the late-1970s copper crash and the AIDS epidemic.

items.name: Turkish psychedelic (Anadolu psych)
items.lineage: Istanbul and Ankara studio movement of roughly 1968-1980 that set Anatolian türkü melodies against Western rock instrumentation — Erkin Koray, Selda Bağcan, Barış Manço, Moğollar and Ersen — using fuzz guitar and electrified bağlama tuned to makam-derived modes, aksak 9/8 and 7/8 grooves alongside straight 4/4, combo organ and early synth, darbuka doubling the kit, and declamatory folk-poetic Turkish vocals cut to Unkapanı 45s.
items.description: Turkish psychedelic rock, known locally within the wider Anadolu rock movement, developed from the mid-1960s Altın Mikrofon competitions that encouraged setting Anatolian folk repertoire to Western instruments, peaking in the 1970s. Its distinctive sound comes from makam intervals and long ornamented melismas played on fuzz guitar or amplified bağlama, aksak additive metres pushed through a rock rhythm section, and the compressed, bright cut of Unkapanı's fast 45 rpm production. Compared with Anadolu rock generally it leans further into fuzz, wah, tape echo and extended instrumental sections rather than tight verse-chorus pop settings.

items.name: Indonesian Psychedelia
items.lineage: Late-1960s/70s Indonesian guitar-band psychedelia formed in Jakarta, Bandung and Surabaya as bands like Koes Bersaudara, AKA, Panbers and Dara Puspita absorbed British beat and fuzz rock through radio and cassette, welding tremolo-drenched single-coil guitars, farfisa-style combo organ and 4/4 backbeat drum kit to Malay/kroncong melodic contours, minor-pentatonic vocal lines sung in Bahasa at 100-140 BPM, with heavy plate reverb and tape saturation from small Jakarta studios.
items.description: Indonesian psychedelia crystallized in Jakarta and Bandung between roughly 1967 and 1976, when local beat groups rebuilt imported fuzz-and-organ rock around Malay song form. Its signature is a bright single-coil guitar soaked in spring reverb and tremolo, cheap combo organ, tight backbeat kit occasionally shadowed by kendang, and close-harmony Bahasa vocals over minor-pentatonic melodies. Unlike Thai psych's molam-driven modal loops, the Indonesian strain keeps verse-chorus pop architecture and vocal-group harmony inherited from kroncong and Koes Bersaudara.

items.name: Thai Psychedelic
items.lineage: Thai psychedelic rock of the late 1960s-70s, formed in Bangkok and the Isan northeast when luk thung and mor lam singers were backed by electric string bands — Plearn Promdan, Dao Bandon and later reissue-canonized groups — pairing khaen-derived modal riffs and free-reed drone with fuzz guitar, farfisa organ, driving 4/4 kit at 110-150 BPM and nasal Thai vocal delivery cut to raw mono singles.
items.description: Thai psychedelic rock emerged in Bangkok and Isan in the late 1960s as electric bands absorbed mor lam and luk thung repertoire. The sound is a cyclic modal vamp derived from khaen playing, fuzzed guitar doubling the vocal line, wheezing combo organ, and hard-swung kit with ching timekeeping under nasal, heavily inflected Thai singing. It differs from Indonesian psychedelia by staying riff-cyclic and near-heptatonic rather than pop-harmonic, and from Cambodian rock by its Isan free-reed grounding.

items.name: Group Sounds
items.lineage: Japanese Group Sounds (GS), Tokyo 1965-1969, codified by the Spiders, the Tigers, the Blue Comets and Ox under producers at Nippon Columbia and Toshiba — Ventures-derived twangy single-coil guitars, combo organ, 4/4 beat-group backbeat at 120-150 BPM, tight Japanese-language unison-and-harmony vocals, brass sweetening on ballads, all cut fast to two- and four-track for the kayokyoku singles market.
items.description: Group Sounds was Japan's 1965-69 beat-band boom, launched by the Ventures' and Beatles' tours and channelled through the domestic kayokyoku hit machine. Records combine reverbed single-coil guitar hooks, cheap combo organ, disciplined backbeat and tambourine, and matinee-idol Japanese vocals in close harmony, often with orchestral or brass overdubs. It is more song-factory and less improvisatory than the Western garage rock it borrows from, and it predates the heavier, underground Japanese psych of Flower Travellin' Band.

items.name: J-Core
items.lineage: Japanese hardcore-techno lineage that formed in late-1990s Tokyo doujin and Comiket circles around HARDCORE TANO*C, Betwixt & Between and m1dy, running 175-190 BPM distorted gabber/happy-hardcore kicks under sampled anime and vocaloid vocal chops, supersaw hoover leads, breakcore-fast amen edits and rapid-fire chiptune melodic writing, produced entirely in-the-box and pressed to self-released CDs.
items.description: J-core is the Japanese branch of hardcore techno, consolidated from the late 1990s onward in Tokyo's doujin-music economy and the HARDCORE TANO*C label circle. It runs at 175-190 BPM on clipped distorted kicks, with hyper-bright supersaw and FM leads, sped-up anime or vocaloid vocal samples, and maximalist loudness-war mastering. Compared with Dutch gabber it is far more melodic and pop-referential, and compared with speedcore it keeps hook-driven chorus structure.

items.name: Hokkien Pop (Taiyu)
