items.lineage: Taiwanese-Hokkien language popular song, formed in 1930s Taipei under Japanese rule with Columbia label recordings and revived commercially from the 1970s-90s by Chiang Hui, Ye Chi-tien and Wu Bai — pentatonic-leaning melodies with heavy vibrato and enka-style bending, backed first by moon lute and small orchestra, later by electric organ, saxophone obbligato, electric bass and shuffle or ballad kit at 70-110 BPM.
items.description: Hokkien pop (Taiyu gequ) is Taiwanese-language popular song, begun with 1930s Columbia recordings in Taipei and reaching mass audiences again after martial-law-era restrictions eased in the 1980s. Its markers are wide-vibrato, heavily ornamented vocal delivery descending from enka and local folk song, sentimental minor-pentatonic melody, and arrangements that pair Chinese strings or moon lute with saxophone and electric backing. It is distinguished from Mandopop by language, its blue-collar lyric world, and a rougher, more melismatic vocal style.

items.name: Taiwan Campus Folk
items.lineage: Taiwanese campus folk song movement (xiaoyuan minge), Taipei 1975-1985, launched by Li Shuang-tse's 'sing our own songs' call and codified by Yang Hsien and Hou Te-chien on the Sing Your Own Songs and Golden Melody compilations — moderate-tempo acoustic guitar strumming with fingerpicked accompaniment, unaffected clear Mandarin vocals, literary lyrics, simple diatonic harmony and light string or flute overdubs.
items.description: Taiwan's campus folk movement ran from the mid-1970s through the mid-1980s, when university students, spurred by nativist cultural debate, wrote Mandarin songs to acoustic guitar rather than covering Anglo-American folk. Recordings are deliberately plain: strummed or fingerpicked steel-string guitar, light bass and flute or piano coloring, and clean, vibrato-light vocals foregrounding poetic text. It is quieter and more literary than contemporaneous Hokkien pop, and less politically confrontational than later Taiwanese indie and protest song.

items.name: Skramz
items.lineage: North American and European term-of-record for 1990s emotional hardcore as practiced by Orchid, Pg. 99 and Jeromes Dream, played in basements and DIY spaces at 160-250 BPM with trebly overdriven guitars, blast-and-stop drumming, dissonant open-string chords, sub-two-minute songs and a wholly shrieked vocal, self-released on 7-inches recorded live to cheap digital or eight-track.
items.description: Skramz is the DIY scene's own name for chaotic 1990s screamo, used to separate the basement lineage from the 2000s major-label 'screamo' marketing tag. The music is short, fast and dissonant: thin distorted guitars playing chromatic open-voiced figures, abrupt tempo cuts, and unrelenting screamed vocals, usually captured live with minimal isolation. Relative to melodic emo it abandons singing entirely, and relative to powerviolence it keeps dissonant chordal writing rather than pure grind riffing.

items.name: Screamo
items.lineage: San Diego, 1991-94, codified by Gravity Records bands Heroin and Antioch Arrow and carried east by Moss Icon and Rites of Spring's example — hardcore punk restructured around dynamic quiet-loud shifts, arpeggiated clean interludes and sudden 180-220 BPM bursts, with the vocal moving from spoken murmur to full-throat scream and guitars using dissonant suspended voicings rather than power-chord blocks.
items.description: Screamo took shape in San Diego in the early 1990s around the Gravity Records roster, extending DC emotional hardcore with extreme dynamic contrast. Songs pivot between chiming clean arpeggios and sudden distorted eruptions, with vocals that break into screaming at the peaks and drumming that shifts meter mid-phrase. Compared with skramz it is somewhat better produced and more willing to hold a melodic passage; compared with 2000s post-hardcore it is far less chorus-oriented.

items.name: Emoviolence
items.lineage: Coined by In/Humanity in mid-1990s Columbia, South Carolina and realized by Orchid, Usurp Synapso and Jeromes Dream — the fusion of powerviolence's blast-beat/slow-crawl whiplash with screamo's dissonant chordal guitar, songs typically 30-90 seconds, tempos alternating 240+ BPM blasts with half-time sludge, vocals uniformly shrieked, recorded cheap and mastered hot on split 7-inches.
items.description: Emoviolence is the powerviolence-screamo hybrid named half-jokingly by In/Humanity around 1995 and made canonical by Orchid and Jeromes Dream. Tracks are extremely short and structurally violent, cutting without warning between blast beats and crawling half-time passages while guitars grind dissonant, often chordally ambiguous figures under continuous screaming. It is faster, briefer and more percussion-dominated than screamo proper, and unlike grindcore it retains emo's dissonant open-string harmony and emotive lyric stance.

items.name: Street Punk
items.lineage: British working-class punk of 1979-84 — the Exploited, GBH, Discharge and Blitz — stripping first-wave punk to a 180-220 BPM d-beat or straight-eighths pulse, buzzsaw distorted downstroked guitars in root-fifth power chords, gang-shouted terrace-chant choruses, barked hoarse lead vocal and cheap fast recordings for Secret, Clay and No Future.
items.description: Street punk (UK82, Oi!-adjacent) is the second British punk wave of 1979-84, built by and for working-class audiences after the first wave went art-school. Records are fast, mid-forward and abrasive: relentless downstroked distorted guitar, simple I-IV-V or minor-third riffing, a shouted lead over massed gang vocals, and drumming that leans on the d-beat. It is less musically ambitious than the Clash-style first wave and less politically anarcho-doctrinaire than Crass, favouring chantable choruses and immediacy.

items.name: Ska Punk
items.lineage: American third-wave ska-punk of 1987-98, formed in Orange County and Boston by Operation Ivy, the Mighty Mighty Bosstones and Less Than Jake — alternating upstroke offbeat ska verses at 150-190 BPM with distorted straight-eighth punk choruses, a two-to-four-piece horn section riffing behind, walking or pumping electric bass, and shouted-melodic vocals cut in mid-budget US indie studios.
items.description: Ska punk is the North American third wave that welded Jamaican offbeat guitar and horn arrangements to hardcore punk tempo and distortion, running from Operation Ivy in 1987 to the mid-1990s mainstream breakout. The defining move is the switch between clean skanking upstrokes on the verse and full-distortion punk on the chorus, with horns carrying countermelody rather than the melody. It is faster and more distorted than 2 Tone, and unlike traditional ska it centers punk vocal delivery and song structure.

items.name: Dancehall
items.lineage: Kingston, Jamaica, late 1970s onward: sound-system deejay music codified by Henry 'Junjo' Lawes, Volcano and Jammy's, turning fully digital with Wayne Smith's 'Under Mi Sleng Teng' in 1985 — 90-110 BPM riddim tracks with drum-machine kick/rim patterns, dominant sub-bass ostinato, one-drop or steppers derivatives, sparse synth stabs and chatted or half-sung patois vocals voiced by many artists over one shared riddim.
items.description: Dancehall emerged in Kingston in the late 1970s as sound-system deejays took over from roots reggae's band-and-message model, then became fully machine-based after the 1985 Sleng Teng riddim. Tracks are sparse and bass-heavy, built on a reusable riddim of programmed drums and synth bass at 90-110 BPM, with the vocal — chatted patois toasting or melodic singjay — carrying nearly all the information. It is faster, drier and more percussive than roots reggae, and unlike dub it foregrounds the voice rather than the mixing desk.
exemplars: Wayne Smith — Under Mi Sleng Teng

items.name: UK Dancehall (Bashment)
items.lineage: British-Caribbean dancehall descendant formed in London, Birmingham and Luton sound-system circuits from the late 1990s and consolidated in the 2010s around Stylo G, Gappy Ranks and Riko Dan, built on digitally sequenced one-drop and steppers riddims at 95-105 BPM, 808 sub-bass and sparse hi-hat rolls, riddim-versioning where many MCs voice the same instrumental, and a Jamaican-patois-over-London-inflection deejay delivery pitched between toasting and grime bars.
items.description: UK dancehall, or bashment, is the British diaspora branch of Jamaican dancehall that hardened into its own scene through London pirate radio and community studios from the late 1990s onward. It keeps the riddim-and-version economy and patois deejay delivery of Kingston dancehall but takes its low end and drum programming from UK sound-system culture — heavier 808 sub, drier snares, and frequent tempo and cadence borrowings from grime and UK funky. It is distinguished from Jamaican dancehall by production locale and the code-switched London-patois register, and from grime by riddim-based Caribbean rhythmic architecture rather than 140 BPM square-wave eski patterns.

items.name: Traphall
items.lineage: Kingston and Atlanta hybrid formed circa 2013-2016 through producers and deejays including Vybz Kartel, Alkaline, Popcaan and Rvssian, replacing dancehall's one-drop riddim with Southern trap architecture — booming long-decay 808 kicks, triplet hi-hat rolls at 70-75 BPM half-time (140 double-time), sparse minor-key synth motifs, and patois deejay vocals heavily doubled, Auto-Tuned and stacked in ad-lib layers.
items.description: Traphall emerged around 2013 as Jamaican deejays absorbed Atlanta trap's drum programming wholesale while keeping dancehall's vocal grammar, riddim-versioning and patois lyricism. Its signature is the collision of a long-tailed tuned 808 kick and triplet hi-hat subdivision with dancehall phrasing and melodic Auto-Tuned patois hooks, usually in dark minor modes with minimal chordal movement. It differs from mainstream trap in vocal language and phrasing, and from conventional dancehall in that the skeletal one-drop or steppers drum pattern has been discarded entirely.

items.name: Basshall
items.lineage: Producer-driven club hybrid codified around 2016-2018 by Jillionaire, Major Lazer affiliates and European festival DJs, welding dancehall's 100-105 BPM skank and Caribbean vocal chops onto EDM drop architecture — sidechained saw and pluck leads, big-room build-and-release form, heavily compressed sub-bass, and chopped, pitched vocal samples used as instrumental hooks rather than continuous toasting.
items.description: Basshall is a late-2010s club genre built by European and North American dance producers who took dancehall's skank and vocal texture and rebuilt it inside EDM's drop-oriented structure. It is defined by chopped and pitch-shifted Caribbean vocal samples treated as melodic hooks, aggressive sidechain pumping, sub-bass tuned for large-format PA, and eight- or sixteen-bar build-drop cycles that dancehall itself does not use. It is distinguished from actual dancehall by the absence of a full sung or toasted lead performance and by its festival-mix loudness, and from moombahton by faster tempo and dancehall rather than reggaeton dembow phrasing.

items.name: Neo Soul
items.lineage: Philadelphia, New York and Detroit R&B movement of 1995-2005 centered on D'Angelo, Erykah Badu, the Soulquarians and producers James Poyser and J Dilla, marked by live Rhodes-and-bass rhythm sections playing deliberately behind the beat, extended jazz voicings over hip-hop-derived boom-bap drum feels at 70-95 BPM, warm analog tracking, and a conversational, melismatic gospel-rooted vocal delivery layered into dense close-harmony stacks.
items.description: Neo soul crystallized in the mid-1990s as a reaction against the programmed gloss of contemporary R&B, restoring live band tracking, analog tape warmth and jazz-level harmony while retaining hip-hop's rhythmic sensibility. Its defining sound is the drunk, dragging pocket — drums and bass placed audibly late against the click — over Rhodes and Wurlitzer voicings with ninths, elevenths and passing chromatic movement, topped by intimate, heavily stacked lead vocals. It differs from classic 1970s soul in its hip-hop drum feel and studio-loop construction, and from mainstream 1990s R&B in its refusal of quantized grids and its harmonic ambition.

items.name: Motown Sound
items.lineage: Detroit label style codified 1959-1972 by Berry Gordy at Hitsville U.S.A., with Holland-Dozier-Holland writing and the Funk Brothers house band, defined by four-on-the-floor tambourine-and-handclap backbeats, James Jamerson's melodically active syncopated electric bass, doubled guitars and vibes, layered horn and string sweetening, gospel-trained lead vocals with call-and-response backing groups, and 8-track basement tracking mixed for AM car radio.
items.description: The Motown Sound is the house style of Berry Gordy's Detroit label between 1959 and its 1972 move to Los Angeles, produced almost entirely in the Hitsville basement studio known as the Snakepit. It is identifiable by an insistent four-on-the-floor pulse reinforced with tambourine and handclaps, an unusually melodic and forward electric bass line, bright doubled rhythm guitars, orchestral and horn sweetening added later, and gospel-derived lead singing answered by tight backing vocal groups. It differs from Stax's Memphis soul in its pop-orchestral polish, arranged-rather-than-jammed construction, and mixes deliberately voiced for small transistor and car speakers.
exemplars: The Supremes — Where Did Our Love Go
Marvin Gaye — I Heard It Through the Grapevine
Martha and the Vandellas — Dancing in the Street

items.name: Kansas City Jazz
items.lineage: Territory-band jazz that matured in Kansas City, Missouri during the Pendergast era of roughly 1928-1942 through Bennie Moten, Count Basie, Andy Kirk and Jay McShann, defined by relaxed evenly weighted four-beat walking bass and brush-driven swing, riff-based head arrangements traded antiphonally between reed and brass sections, twelve-bar blues form as primary vehicle, extended jam-session soloing led by Lester Young's light-vibrato tenor, and blues-shouting vocals.
items.description: Kansas City jazz developed in the wide-open nightclub economy of Prohibition-era Missouri, where all-night jam sessions favored improvisation over written arrangement. Its hallmarks are a smoothed-out four-to-the-bar rhythmic feel with walking bass and closed hi-hat, head arrangements assembled from repeated call-and-response section riffs rather than notated charts, a deep reliance on blues form, and long solo statements in a lighter, more linear saxophone idiom than the East Coast norm. It is distinguished from New York swing by its riff-and-blues basis and looser rhythmic weight, and from later bebop by its danceable tempos and sectional writing.
exemplars: Count Basie Orchestra — One O'Clock Jump
Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

items.name: Indie Rock
items.lineage: American and British guitar-band idiom that formed on independent labels — SST, Homestead, Twin/Tone, Rough Trade, Creation — between roughly 1983 and 1994 through R.E.M., Hüsker Dü, the Pixies, Pavement and Sonic Youth, defined by jangly or fuzzed single-coil guitars over unadorned drum-kit-bass rhythm sections at mid tempos, verse-chorus songwriting with quiet-loud dynamic swings, unpolished conversational vocals mixed level with the band, and cheap fast tracking in regional commercial studios.
items.description: Indie rock names the guitar-band music that circulated through independent distribution networks and college radio in the United States and Britain from the early 1980s, defined as much by its economics and recording budgets as by any single sound. Common markers are bright or fuzz-toned electric guitars carrying the melodic weight, a plain unsyncopated rhythm section, deliberately untreated and often flat-affect vocals sitting inside rather than above the mix, and quick low-budget analog tracking that leaves room noise and amp buzz audible. It is distinguished from mainstream alternative rock by production scale and refusal of vocal polish, and from punk by wider harmonic and dynamic range and slower average tempos.

items.name: Nu Jazz
items.lineage: European studio idiom of roughly 1996-2006 developed by Jazzanova and Bugge Wesseltoft in Berlin and Oslo, St Germain in Paris and Nils Petter Molvær in Norway, laying live jazz soloing — trumpet, Rhodes, upright bass, saxophone — over programmed broken-beat and deep-house drum grids at 100-125 BPM, with modal static harmony, sampled and re-edited acoustic fragments, dub-style spatial effects, and arrangement decided at the sequencer rather than in performance.
items.description: Nu jazz is the late-1990s European convergence of jazz improvisation with club electronic production, made largely in project studios by musicians who edited and sequenced as much as they played. Its consistent traits are looped programmed drums borrowed from deep house and broken beat, largely static modal harmony over a repeating bass figure, live horn and Rhodes solos recorded and then cut into the grid, and heavy use of delay, filtering and spatial processing. It differs from acid jazz in being sequencer-built rather than band-performed, and from jazz fusion in relinquishing virtuoso metric complexity for a fixed dance-floor pulse.
exemplars: Bugge Wesseltoft — New Conception of Jazz

items.name: J-Ska
items.lineage: Japanese ska scene founded in Tokyo in 1985 by Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra and extended through the 1990s by Kemuri and Ska Flames, combining a full horn section of trumpets, trombones and saxophones with offbeat upstroke guitar and walking bass at 160-200 BPM, Jamaican first-wave and 2 Tone rhythmic phrasing, instrumental-forward arrangements drawing on jazz and Showa-era kayokyoku melody, and bright close-miked studio tracking.
items.description: J-ska is the Japanese branch of ska, launched by the large-format Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra in 1985 and broadened in the 1990s by ska-punk bands playing faster and louder. It keeps the offbeat guitar-and-organ skank and walking bass of Jamaican ska but pushes the horn section to the front as the main melodic voice, writes instrumental heads with jazz and Japanese pop-melody contours, and records with the tight, bright, heavily arranged clarity of Tokyo commercial studios. It is distinguished from British 2 Tone by its big-band instrumental focus rather than vocal social commentary, and from Jamaican original ska by tempo, precision and studio polish.

items.name: J-Punk
items.lineage: Japanese punk lineage running from Tokyo's 1978-1983 first wave — the Stalin, INU, Gauze, the Star Club — through the 1987-1995 melodic era of the Blue Hearts and Hi-Standard, characterized by fast downstroke barre-chord guitar at 180-240 BPM, driving eighth-note bass, hardcore d-beat or straight-eight drumming, Japanese-language shouted or strained-melodic vocals, and abrasive fast tracking in small Tokyo and Osaka studios and live houses.
items.description: J-punk covers Japanese punk and hardcore from the late-1970s Tokyo underground onward, a scene shaped by the live-house circuit and by independent labels rather than by major-label distribution. Early J-punk and the related Japanese hardcore of Gauze and G.I.S.M. is faster, noisier and more distorted than its Western models, with saturated guitar recorded to tape hot enough to break up; the later melodic wave retained the tempo and downstroke attack while adding singable major-key choruses. It differs from Western hardcore chiefly in the phrasing and syllabic density of Japanese-language vocals and in its intensely local live-house economy, and from J-ska in the absence of horns and offbeat skank.

items.name: European Free Jazz
items.lineage: Continental improvised-music movement formed 1965-1975 around Peter Brötzmann and the FMP label in Berlin, Han Bennink and Misha Mengelberg's Instant Composers Pool in Amsterdam, and Derek Bailey and Evan Parker's Incus circle in London, abandoning tune, changes and steady pulse in favor of collective free improvisation, extended saxophone multiphonics and overblowing, non-idiomatic prepared guitar, percussion played as noise and theater, and dry direct-to-tape documentation at concerts and small studios.
items.description: European free jazz separated from its American antecedents in the second half of the 1960s, when players in Germany, the Netherlands and Britain built a self-organized network of labels, festivals and musician collectives around fully improvised music. Its sound is defined by dense collective playing without a governing pulse or key, saxophone technique pushed into overblown multiphonics and split tones, percussion treated as a field of timbre and physical gesture rather than timekeeping, and a recording aesthetic that captures the raw room with minimal editing. It is distinguished from American free jazz by its detachment from blues and gospel vocabulary and from swing-based rhythmic residue, and from composed avant-garde music by the total absence of a score.
exemplars: Alexander von Schlippenbach — Globe Unity Orchestra

items.name: C-Pop (Chinese-Language Popular Song)
items.lineage: Umbrella tradition of Chinese-language popular song running from 1930s Shanghai shidaiqu through Hong Kong Cantopop of the 1970s-90s and Taipei-centered Mandopop from the 1980s, codified by Teresa Teng, Sam Hui, Jonathan Lee and Jay Chou, and marked by pentatonically inflected melody set to lush ballad arrangements, verse-prechorus-chorus form built for lyric intelligibility across tonal Chinese, string-and-synth orchestration, and close, heavily compressed lead vocals tracked in Hong Kong and Taipei hit-factory studios.
items.description: C-pop is the collective term for commercial popular song in Chinese languages across the mainland, Hong Kong, Taiwan and the diaspora, descending from prewar Shanghai shidaiqu and consolidating in the Cantopop and Mandopop industries of the 1970s onward. Its central form is the mid-tempo or slow ballad with sustained, clearly enunciated vocal melody carrying the lyric, backed by strings, piano and synth pads, with occasional erhu, guzheng or pentatonic melodic coloring signaling Chinese identity within a Western pop harmonic frame. It is distinguished from J-pop and K-pop by its ballad-and-lyric centrality rather than rhythm-track and choreography focus, and from Chinese traditional music by fully tempered Western harmony and studio-constructed arrangement.

items.name: T-Pop
items.lineage: Thai idol-and-boyband pop industry consolidated in Bangkok from the late 2010s onward — building on GMM Grammy's 1990s-2000s string-pop lineage and codified by 4EVE, BUS, PROXIE and above all BAMBAM and the group 4MIX, plus the breakout of Milli and F.HERO into rap-pop crossover — defined by 100-128 BPM programmed four-on-the-floor or half-time trap hybrids, sidechained synth-and-808 beds, English-Thai code-switching hooks, choreographed multi-member vocal splits with heavy pitch-correction and stacked doubles, and K-pop-derived A&R structure (title track, dance break, rap verse) applied to Thai tonal-language prosody.
items.description: T-Pop is the Thai idol-pop industry that consolidated in Bangkok from roughly 2018, deliberately importing K-pop's trainee, title-track and dance-break format while retaining GMM Grammy's older Thai string-pop melodic instincts. Sonically it runs on programmed 808 and synth-bass beds, tight sidechained pads, glossy multitracked group vocals with audible retuning, and hooks that alternate Thai and English phrases. It is distinguished from K-pop by Thai tonal-language phrasing that flattens melodic leaps into speech-contour lines, from luk thung by the total absence of rural instrumentation and khaen-derived ornament, and from earlier Thai string by its choreography-first group format.
exemplars: BUS Because of You I Shine

items.name: Funk BH (Belo Horizonte funk)
items.lineage: Belo Horizonte regional strain of Brazilian funk that emerged in Minas Gerais baile circuits from the mid-2010s, codified by DJ Win, MC Neguinho do Kaxeta's BH collaborators and the 'beat de BH' producers — running 130-150 BPM over a hard, dry tamborzão-derived kick-and-clap montagem, aggressive detuned lead stabs and sampled vocal snips looped into the beat, with MCs rapping in fast, percussive, heavily regional-accented delivery and a mix built for cheap PA horn stacks rather than club subwoofers.
items.description: Funk BH is the Belo Horizonte dialect of Brazilian funk, built in home DAW setups across Minas Gerais from around 2015 and circulated through YouTube and WhatsApp rather than physical release. Its signature is a dry, clipped montagem: short sampled vocal fragments and stabs chopped into a fast 130-150 BPM tamborzão grid with almost no sustained harmony, mixed loud and lossy for portable speakers. It differs from Rio funk carioca by tempo and by the montagem's collage density, from funk paulista by rejecting ostentação's melodic hooks and polished bass, and from funk 150 by its stab-and-sample texture over pure kick pressure.

items.name: Funk RJ (Rio proibidão and tamborzão lineage)
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro's own funk lineage from the 1990s favela bailes onward, codified by DJ Marlboro's Volume series, then the tamborzão beat built by DJ Luciano Oliveira circa 1998 from sampled atabaque, timbal and repique hits, and carried by Cidinho e Doca, MC Cidinho, Bonde do Tigrão and the proibidão MCs — 125-135 BPM in a syncopated non-four-on-floor pattern, minimal or absent harmony, call-and-response chanted refrains, and lyrics reporting favela life and command territory, recorded fast and pressed straight to CD or sound-system playback.
items.description: Funk RJ is the Rio-specific stream of Brazilian funk, running from Miami-bass-derived 1990s bailes into the tamborzão era after 1998, when producers replaced imported drum-machine loops with sampled Brazilian hand-percussion hits. The result is a syncopated, mid-tempo, harmonically empty beat carrying chanted call-and-response vocals, often documenting favela and militia realities in the proibidão strand. It is separated from funk paulista by its percussion-sample foundation rather than melodic ostentação synths, from funk BH by slower tempo and sparser montagem, and from Miami bass by Portuguese chant phrasing and community sound-system distribution.

items.name: Nuevo Folklore Argentino
items.lineage: Argentine folk-renewal movement running from the late 1960s Nuevo Cancionero manifesto (Mendoza, Armando Tejada Gómez and Oscar Matus, with Mercedes Sosa as its voice) through the 1970s Cuchi Leguizamón and Gustavo 'Cuchi' circle and the 1990s-2010s revisionists Dino Saluzzi, Juan Falú, Liliana Herrero and Carlos Aguirre — retaining chacarera hemiola and zamba 6/8 but opening them to jazz-derived extended chords, through-composed forms, bandoneón and piano colour, rubato vocal declamation and chamber-quiet dynamics rather than peña ensemble drive.
items.description: Nuevo folklore argentino is the art-music renovation of Argentine folk forms, rooted in the 1963 Nuevo Cancionero declaration and extended by later composer-performers who treated the chacarera, zamba and vidala as material rather than repertoire. Its markers are extended and modal harmony on piano and guitar, bandoneón as a lyric rather than tango voice, elastic rubato around the 6/8 hemiola, and an intimate, close-miked chamber dynamic. It differs from classic folklore argentino by harmonic ambition and through-composed form, and from tango nuevo by keeping the rural bombo legüero pulse and provincial song texts at the centre.

items.name: Chinese Opera (xiqu regional traditions)
items.lineage: Umbrella tradition of some three hundred Chinese sung-theatre forms descending from Yuan zaju and Ming kunqu, standardized regionally from the eighteenth century onward — jingju in Beijing after the 1790 Anhui troupes, yueju in Shanghai and Guangdong, chuanju in Sichuan, yuju in Henan — built on role-type vocal production (sheng, dan, jing, chou), a percussion-led ensemble whose bangu clapper-drum leader cues every entrance and gesture, bowed jinghu or erhu carrying the melodic line in fixed banqiang metrical types, and highly ornamented, nasal-forward, non-vibrato singing over pentatonic gong-based modes.
items.description: Chinese opera, or xiqu, is the family of regional sung-theatre traditions that crystallized between the Yuan dynasty and the nineteenth century, of which Beijing jingju is the best-known but by no means the only branch. Every performance is governed by percussion: the bangu clapper-drum player conducts entrances, fight scenes and speech rhythm, while gongs and cymbals punctuate gesture and bowed jinghu or erhu doubles the singer in heterophony. The singing is role-typed and strongly ornamented, with piercing falsetto dan lines and declamatory jing roles, and melodies are assembled from fixed banqiang metrical patterns rather than composed anew — the feature that separates xiqu from Western opera and from later staged Chinese art song.
exemplars: The Legend of the White Snake

items.name: P-Funk
items.lineage: Detroit-and-Plainfield funk collective universe built by George Clinton around Parliament and Funkadelic from 1970 to 1981, recorded largely at United Sound Systems Detroit, with Bootsy Collins, Bernie Worrell, Eddie Hazel, Michael Hampton, Fred Wesley and Maceo Parker — slow-to-mid 95-110 BPM one-drop grooves with the emphasis violently on the One, Worrell's Minimoog portamento bass lines doubling or replacing electric bass, envelope-filtered Bootsy bass, layered gospel-shout and cartoon-character group vocals, extended acid-rock guitar solos, and a full JB-derived horn section over multi-album mythology.
items.description: P-Funk is the interlocking Parliament-Funkadelic body of work George Clinton assembled in the 1970s, splitting a single pool of players between Funkadelic's psychedelic guitar-rock albums and Parliament's horn-driven, synthesizer-heavy dance records. Its defining sounds are Bernie Worrell's Minimoog bass and clavinet, Bootsy Collins's envelope-filtered space-bass, stacked chorus vocals shifting between gospel shout and cartoon voice, talkbox leads, and grooves that hang on a single vamp for eight minutes. Against James Brown's lean, dry funk it is maximalist, harmonically static but timbrally enormous, and against Earth Wind and Fire it trades polish and jazz voicings for science-fiction narrative and distortion.
exemplars: Funkadelic One Nation Under a Groove

items.name: Appalachian Black Metal
items.lineage: American regional black-metal strain from the southern Appalachian mountains, emerging late 2000s through Panopticon (Austin Lunn, Kentucky, 2012), Nechochwen and Twilight Fauna — grafting tremolo-picked minor-modal riffing, blast beats at 180-240 BPM and shrieked vocals onto banjo, fiddle and mountain-dulcimer passages and old-time modal tunes, with lyrics on coal extraction, union violence and land loss, and long tracks alternating full-band assault with unaccompanied acoustic string interludes.
items.description: Appalachian black metal formed in the late 2000s and early 2010s as a mostly one-person, home-studio American answer to Scandinavian black metal, most fully realized on Panopticon's Kentucky (2012). It keeps the tremolo tremolo-picked chord walls, blast beats and rasped vocals of the parent genre but interleaves them with genuine old-time material played on clawhammer banjo and fiddle, and takes its subject matter from coal mining, labor struggle and mountain ecology rather than occultism. Compared with Cascadian black metal it is more explicitly rooted in a documented regional folk repertoire, and compared with folk metal it uses those acoustic sections as structural contrast rather than as riff decoration.

items.name: Nu Disco
items.lineage: European and American dance-production style consolidating in the mid-2000s from the Norwegian space-disco scene (Lindstrøm, Prins Thomas, Todd Terje) and French filter-house lineage, codified through labels Permanent Vacation, Eskimo and Feedelity — 100-120 BPM four-on-the-floor with live-feel or sampled disco drums, chorused electric-bass or synth-bass octave lines, Rhodes and string-machine chord pads, long linear arrangements with slow filter and delay builds, and mostly instrumental or lightly-sung vocal treatment.
items.description: Nu disco is the mid-2000s revival strand of house that rebuilt 1970s and early-80s disco and Italo textures with modern production rather than sampling them wholesale. Its hallmarks are relaxed 100-120 BPM tempos, real or convincingly played bass guitar and Rhodes over a 909-derived kit, string-machine pads, and long cosmic arrangements that unfold over eight or ten minutes with gradual filter opening. It differs from disco house by playing parts instead of looping a filtered break, from French touch by its slower, warmer, less compressed feel, and from Italo disco by being a retrospective construction rather than a period style.

items.name: Jazz Fusion (electric jazz-rock idiom)
items.lineage: Electric jazz idiom formed 1969-1976 out of Miles Davis's In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew sessions at Columbia 30th Street and CBS Studio B and carried by his sidemen — Weather Report (Zawinul, Shorter, Jaco Pastorius), Mahavishnu Orchestra (John McLaughlin), Return to Forever (Chick Corea), Herbie Hancock's Head Hunters — defined by Rhodes and ARP/Moog keyboards, distorted guitar, fretless electric bass, straight-eighth rock and funk backbeats or fast odd meters, static modal vamps replacing bebop changes, and virtuoso extended solos over multitrack studio construction.
items.description: Jazz fusion is the electric jazz-rock idiom that crystallized around Miles Davis's 1969-70 sessions and dominated jazz recording through the 1970s. It replaced walking bass and swung eighths with straight-eighth rock and funk backbeats or fast asymmetric meters, replaced piano and acoustic bass with Rhodes, synthesizers and electric or fretless bass, and replaced bebop chord cycles with long static modal vamps that host virtuoso improvisation. Against hard bop it is louder, denser and studio-assembled through editing and overdub; against jazz-funk and smooth jazz it prioritizes instrumental complexity and odd meter over groove-and-hook accessibility.
exemplars: Mahavishnu Orchestra The Inner Mounting Flame

items.name: Japanese City Pop
items.lineage: Tokyo studio-pop idiom of roughly 1976-1986 grown out of Happy End's members and the Alfa and Canyon label rosters — Tatsuro Yamashita, Mariya Takeuchi, Taeko Onuki, Anri, Toshiki Kadomatsu, arranged by Haruomi Hosono and Masataka Matsutoya — built on AOR and Philly-soul harmony with major-seventh and altered chords, session players from the Tin Pan Alley and Parachute bands, Rhodes and DX7 keyboards, clean chorused guitar, brass and string overdubs, 100-120 BPM shuffled or straight backbeats, and pristine 24-track mixes cut for urban consumer-electronics playback.
items.description: City pop is the affluent-Tokyo studio pop of the late 1970s and 1980s, made by first-call session musicians for a bubble-era audience with good stereos and cars. It borrows AOR, Philly soul and Brazilian harmony — major sevenths, chromatic ii-V motion, lush brass and string overdubs — and delivers it with immaculate 24-track separation, clean chorused guitar, Rhodes and later DX7 electric piano, and unforced Japanese vocals about coastlines, night driving and romantic distance. It is distinguished from kayokyoku by its Western harmonic vocabulary and session-band production, and from later Japanese AOR revivals by being a period commercial style rather than a stylistic homage.

items.name: Korean City Pop
items.lineage: Seoul urban-pop strain of roughly 1983-1992, running from Kim Hyun-sik and Lee Moon-sae through Kim Wan-sun, Bit-gwa Sogeum, Sanullim's late records and arranger Kim Myung-gon — Korean-language songwriting set to imported AOR and funk-pop harmony, played by Seoul session bands on Rhodes, DX7, slap electric bass and gated LinnDrum or acoustic kit at 95-115 BPM, with saxophone obbligati, chorused clean guitar and a slightly drier, more mid-forward mix than its Tokyo counterpart because of smaller domestic studios and cassette-first distribution.
items.description: Korean city pop is the 1980s Seoul urban-pop idiom that paralleled Japan's city pop, absorbing AOR, funk and light disco harmony into Korean-language songwriting during the country's rapid urbanization. Its markers are Rhodes and DX7 pads, slap or fingered electric bass, gated drum-machine and live-kit hybrids, saxophone fills and clean chorused guitar, sung with a warmer, more balladic vocal delivery than Japanese equivalents. It differs from Japanese city pop in its drier, mid-forward mixes and stronger trot-and-ballad melodic residue, and from later K-pop by being band-and-songwriter driven rather than agency-produced.
exemplars: Yoo Jae-ha Because I Love You

items.name: Ambient country
items.lineage: Late-2010s onward instrumental country-ambient convergence represented by New York group SUSS: sustained pedal steel and resonator-guitar traces against synthesizer beds, with country timbre retained while dance pulse and verse-chorus singing recede. The selected three-instrument arrangement and clean digital recording chain are authored models, not a reconstruction of a documented studio session.
items.description: Ambient country retains the sliding steel and resonator colors of Americana while organizing them as sustained instrumental space. SUSS combines those strings with loops and synthesizers, with harmonica or fiddle on some recordings. Country harmony and Western imagery remain points of reference, but a dance backbeat and lead singer are optional. Distinct from alt-country by its foregrounded drone and from ambient guitar by steel-led pitch glides. The default is a deliberately compact steel, resonator, and synth ensemble; it is not a universal roster.

items.name: Ambient folk
items.lineage: 2000s onward intersection of intimate acoustic songwriting and ambient/noise recording practice, represented by Grouper: quiet guitar-and-voice songs blurred by repeat recording, softened attacks, and low-fidelity space. This recipe selects the acoustic-song branch rather than piano-only or pure-drone work; domestic four-track texture is an authored model informed by firsthand accounts.
items.description: Ambient folk carries quiet acoustic song through the recording practices of ambient and experimental music. In the Grouper branch selected here, voice and strummed guitar remain recognizable while doubling, tape wear, and reverberant overlap soften their boundaries. It differs from conventional singer-songwriter folk by the compositional importance of recorded atmosphere, and from beatless ambient guitar by sung song fragments. A two-card acoustic and vocal default represents that branch, not every acoustic ambient artist.
exemplars: Grouper — Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill
Grouper — The Man Who Died in His Boat

items.name: Ambient guitar
items.lineage: 1990s onward guitar-centered ambient practice represented by Windy & Carl: extended electric-string tones, bass foundation, and occasional keyboard sustain shape pieces without a conventional drum rhythm section. Their firsthand account emphasizes played textures through pedals and rack delays rather than computer transformation; this beatless guitar-bass-keyboard recipe uses an authored domestic tape model.
items.description: Ambient guitar makes extended electric-string sound the principal material. Windy & Carl describe performances shaped by pedals and rack delays, a largely drummerless approach, and spontaneous layers of guitar, bass, and keyboard. The chosen model sustains feedback guitar over muted bass and a held keyboard tone. It differs from ambient country by lacking steel-led Americana vocabulary, from ambient folk by instrumental foreground, and from ambient post-rock by avoiding a drum-driven dynamic arc. Occasional vocals in the wider practice are outside this default.

items.name: Ambient pop
items.lineage: 2010s vocal pop branch in which sustained ambience surrounds recurring songs and intimate sung melody, represented here by Cigarettes After Sex and the Brooklyn-recorded Apocalypse. This slow band model combines restrained drums and bass with clean guitar, keyboard pads, and an undersung vocal; microphones, processing, instrument construction, and room are authored choices, not claims about the actual session.
items.description: Ambient pop preserves recurring melodic songs while making surrounding space and subdued delivery central to the sound. The Cigarettes After Sex branch places a low-effort lead vocal over guitar, keyboard, bass, and drums; Apocalypse credits that roster and a December 2015 Brooklyn recording. The default models a sparse slow pulse with clean arpeggios and sustained keyboard color. Compared with the existing dream-pop default it has fewer electronic colors, a single undersung lead, and restrained rim clicks; compared with ambient folk it retains a pop-band rhythm foundation.
exemplars: Cigarettes After Sex — Cigarettes After Sex

items.name: Ambient post-rock
items.lineage: 2000s onward meeting of post-rock ensemble dynamics and ambient sustain, represented by Nashville duo Hammock. Their guitar-rooted work moves between atmospheric passages and fuller rhythmic arrivals; Everything and Nothing documents a guitar-based return, beats, vocals, and cello. This instrumental guitar-bass-drum-cello branch and modern multitrack chain are authored models rather than a session-equipment inventory.
items.description: Ambient post-rock joins long guitar sustain to the evolving ensemble form of post-rock. Hammock provides a Nashville anchor: its official account calls Everything and Nothing a return to guitar roots, and its release notes identify intricate melodies, beats, and cello. This default selects the instrumental band-and-cello branch, with tremolo guitar and soft bowed sustain expanding around rock drums and bass. It differs from ambient guitar through an active rhythm section and fuller dynamic arrivals; sung tracks and more orchestral releases remain adjacent possibilities.
exemplars: Hammock — Raising Your Voice... Trying to Stop an Echo

items.name: Action rock
items.lineage: Scandinavian high-energy rock-and-roll and garage-punk continuum, represented by the Swedish Hellacopters. The action-rock label foregrounds immediate riff attack, melodic guitar leads and a driving band backbeat. This contemporary studio model selects the guitar-bass-drums core rather than prescribing every keyboard or percussion overdub heard across the repertoire.
items.description: High-energy rock-and-roll built on compact riffs, overdriven lead guitar, assertive sung vocals and a hard backbeat. The Scandinavian action-rock repertoire links garage-punk urgency to classic hard-rock lead playing. Unlike the catalog’s 1960s garage-rock model, this selected arrangement has no organ and uses a contemporary overdub chain; unlike broader hard rock, it emphasizes punk drumming and immediate melodic attack. Material and processing pins are production choices rather than measured historical attributes.

items.name: Alternative metal
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward metal and alternative-rock crossover, represented here by Faith No More and the 1989 album The Real Thing. Heavy guitar riffing shares the arrangement with a rhythmically active bass, keyboards and an elastic sung vocal. The selected model emphasizes contrasts of riff, keyboard color and vocal register; funk bass and rap delivery are possible influences, not requirements of the entire genre.
items.description: Broad crossover of metal weight with alternative-rock experimentation in vocal delivery, rhythm and timbral contrast. This Faith No More-oriented model adds a keyboard pad and register-shifting sung vocal to muted guitar and a fingerstyle bass pulse. It differs from the catalog’s funk-metal model by not mandating slap bass, and from speed metal by prioritizing contrasting textures over continuous fast attack. Drop-D, octave doubling and the modern chain are authored choices for this arrangement, not session claims.
exemplars: Faith No More — The Real Thing
Faith No More — From Out of Nowhere

items.name: Black speed metal
items.lineage: Black-metal and speed/thrash-metal intersection represented by the Scottish solo recording project Hellripper, whose own account identifies black/speed metal and documents DIY recording of Coagulating Darkness in 2016-2017. Fast riffs, active lead guitar and harsh vocal attack retain the forward motion and compact song orientation of speed metal. The modern chain below is a reproducible authored model, not the equipment of that session.
items.description: Speed/thrash riff propulsion and solo guitar combined with a rough black-metal vocal and tonal attack. Hellripper’s DIY releases anchor this selected contemporary solo-production model. Unlike the catalog’s speed-metal configuration it selects a rough saturated vocal rather than a melodic belt; unlike atmospheric black metal it keeps the ensemble compact and effect space dry. Tremolo picking, standard tuning and the chain are selected modeling controls rather than an equipment transcription.

items.name: Atmospheric post-metal
items.lineage: Atmosphere-centered strand of post-metal represented by Cult of Luna, extending heavy guitar-bass-drums writing with keyboards, long dynamic arcs and passages of reduced density. The Long Road North documents an Umeå-centered recording and writing practice. This selected arrangement places clean arpeggiation and sustained electronic texture beside distorted peaks and a textural harsh vocal, rather than treating the label as a separate universal origin story.
items.description: Post-metal composition that foregrounds spacious texture, long ebbs and flows, and contrast between heavy guitar sections and reduced-density passages. Cult of Luna’s guitar-bass-drums-keyboard ensemble and The Long Road North provide the anchor. Unlike the catalog’s generic post-metal recipe, this model explicitly adds a sustained synth and pins clean arpeggiation with delay and hall space; unlike atmospheric black metal it does not center tremolo-picked blast-beat continuity. Drop-C and synth settings are authored controls, not documentary measurements.
exemplars: Cult of Luna — The Long Road North

items.name: Ambient black metal
items.lineage: Ambient and black-metal intersection represented by the Swiss trio Darkspace, founded in Berne in 1999; its 2003 debut Dark Space I combines heavy guitar with electronic samples and extended immersive pieces. This configuration models a drone-and-sample-dominant passage with guitar, bass and distant harsh voice. It omits a percussion card for that passage without claiming the wider recordings are beatless.
items.description: Ambient-black-metal intersection in which sustained electronic space and guitar mass can dominate perception more than a foreground riff or lyric. Darkspace’s cosmic, sample-enriched recordings anchor this selected drone passage. Unlike the catalog’s atmospheric-black-metal model it explicitly includes a layered sampler and omits a percussion card for the passage; unlike dark ambient it retains amplified guitar, electric bass and harsh voice. The omission does not describe the complete albums, and the digital processing choices are an authored contemporary realization.

items.name: Abstract hip hop
items.lineage: Late-1990s and 2000s independent hip-hop emphasizing associative imagery and densely constructed MC writing. Aesop Rock and Blockhead’s Labor Days (2001), issued through Definitive Jux, anchors the selected New York sample-based strand. Abstract describes the writing and approach, rather than a single production technology; this authored studio recipe selects an articulate solo flow and chopped sample bed.
items.description: Abstract hip hop foregrounds associative language, unusual images and densely woven rhyme rather than a compulsory lyric topic. The selected sample-based solo-MC model follows the Aesop Rock / Blockhead collaboration on Labor Days. It differs from conscious hip-hop, which is organized around social or political content, and from instrumental hip-hop, which need not have an MC. It overlaps alternative hip-hop, but the latter is a wider category covering many departures from dominant conventions. Chopped samples and a clear solo lead are selected here, without claiming that abstraction requires those sounds.

items.name: Alternative hip hop
items.lineage: A broad alternative hip-hop designation encompassing departures from dominant rap conventions in subject matter, sample selection and song form. This recipe selects the late-1980s Long Island / New York sample-collage strand of De La Soul and Prince Paul’s 3 Feet High and Rising (1989), with playful MC exchanges, layered breaks and interludes. The selected configuration is not a sonic definition of every alternative hip-hop artist.
items.description: Alternative hip hop is a broad category for rap that departs from dominant musical and persona conventions. This recipe deliberately chooses one historical strand: De La Soul and Prince Paul’s layered sample construction, playful vocal exchanges and skits on 3 Feet High and Rising. It is broader than abstract hip-hop’s emphasis on associative MC writing, and need not be socially didactic like conscious hip-hop. The selected collage configuration also differs from the narrower boom-bap production designation; later alternative recordings may use live bands or electronic production instead. Its sample resolution, swing and studio chain are authored choices, not a reconstruction of the original session.
exemplars: De La Soul — 3 Feet High and Rising (1989)
De La Soul / Prince Paul — The Magic Number (1989)

items.name: Comedy rap
items.lineage: Rap in which comic narrative, character, incongruity or parody is the organizing purpose. The selected 2000s studio model takes The Lonely Island’s Lazy Sunday (2005) and the rap tracks on Incredibad (2009) as recording anchors: emphatic rhythmic speech, sharply timed exchanges and a programmed beat. The wider category includes other eras and production styles; humorous interludes alone do not make a rap album comedy rap.
items.description: Comedy rap makes jokes, character performance and comic incongruity central to the song. This selected studio model uses the tightly timed rhythmic speech and exchanged lines of The Lonely Island’s Lazy Sunday and Incredibad rap repertoire. It retains a programmed hip-hop beat and forward vocal clarity; the wider category has no unique drum sound. It differs from stand-up comedy by the rhythmic song form and from alternative hip-hop by comic purpose rather than musical nonconformity. A comic skit between otherwise serious rap songs does not define the whole recording as comedy rap.
exemplars: The Lonely Island / Chris Parnell — Lazy Sunday (2005)

items.name: Dark trap
items.lineage: 2010s internet-circulated trap with an ominous atmosphere, weighty bass and dark vocal presentation. This selected model is anchored to Ottawa rapper-producer Night Lovell’s self-released Concept Vague (2014) and his baritone delivery, documented in a 2016 studio performance and interview. It selects a low speech-derived lead, sustained synth texture and 808-derived rhythm; it does not prescribe horror narratives, shouted metal vocals or a single birthplace for the wider label.
items.description: Dark trap is an atmospheric trap designation, selected here through Night Lovell’s Concept Vague and documented baritone studio performance. The authored model combines a low speech-derived MC lead, a restrained sustained synth bed and foreground 808-derived bass rhythm. It overlaps cloud rap and Memphis-influenced internet rap, but this model foregrounds an ominous low vocal and bass pulse rather than cloud rap’s weightless wash. It differs from the historical Memphis cassette tradition by its selected 2010s digital production, and from rage rap by its restrained vocal and pad texture rather than a screaming lead-synth and high-energy delivery. Dark atmosphere does not imply that every lyric is horrorcore.
exemplars: Night Lovell — Contraband, Kinda Neat studio performance (2016)

items.name: Christian trap
items.lineage: A trap-production strand within Christian hip-hop, joining 808-derived beats and melodic rap delivery to faith and hope testimony. The selected East Atlanta model is anchored to 1K Phew’s Never Too Late (2017), What’s Understood 2 (2019) and Church House Trap House (2022) on Reach Records. The label describes his music as trap rooted in East Atlanta and his message as faith and hope; this is a production-specific subset of Christian hip-hop, not a template for every Christian rap recording.
items.description: Christian trap selects trap production and rap delivery within faith-centered hip-hop. 1K Phew’s Reach Records work anchors the East Atlanta strand: his label describes a trap sound and a message of faith and hope, while Church House Trap House makes the church/street relationship explicit. This authored recipe selects an 808-derived rhythm, short synth notes and a punctuated melodic-rap vocal lane. It differs from Christian hip-hop’s broad thematic category by choosing a specific trap production vocabulary; it differs from congregational gospel by using a studio rap arrangement rather than prescribing choir, organ or worship-service performance. The selected retuning speed, room and chain are authoring choices, not documented session settings.
exemplars: 1K Phew / 1K Pson — Church House Trap House (2022)

items.name: Bass house
items.lineage: Mid-2010s international house-and-bass-music convergence represented by Jauz, Habstrakt and Dustycloud: club kick patterns meet mobile, distorted bass sound design and short vocal cuts. This seed selects the bass-led club-single strand rather than the full catalog of any artist.
items.description: Bass house brings house pulse into the bass-music sound-design world of the mid-2010s. Habstrakt describes his transition from dubstep through a 128-BPM remix and a renewed connection to house and techno; Jauz explicitly resists reducing his whole identity to this label. This selected club recipe uses a forceful kick-and-clap grid, layered sampled drums, animated saturated bass and cut-up vocal material, leaving harmonic accompaniment sparse. Its emphasis on a moving bass timbre separates it from the broad electro-house record and from future house's more chordal bounce. Compared with fidget house, bass sound design carries more weight than restless sample rearrangement; G-house instead puts hip-hop attitude and a more restrained rolling groove at the center. The synth architecture, effects and numerical axes are authored models, not transcriptions of a named session.
exemplars: Jauz and Ephwurd — Rock the Party

items.name: G-house
items.lineage: Early-2010s G-house associated with Marseille duo Amine Edge & DANCE and their CUFF network; their hip-hop and R&B backgrounds shaped a heavy-bass house groove and fragmentary rap attitude, disseminated through online tracks and international club sets.
items.description: G-house took shape around Amine Edge & DANCE in the early 2010s, bringing gangsta-rap attitude and hip-hop/R&B listening histories to house grooves. Their own account places the collaboration in 2011 and identifies Going To Heaven With The Goodie-Goodies as an early breakthrough. The recipe foregrounds a rounded monophonic bass figure, a subtly swung synthesized kit and looped rap fragments; a sampler represents those recorded voices rather than prescribing a fresh sung lead. Compared with late-1980s hip house, this is a producer-and-DJ groove built around brief vocal hooks instead of a full MC verse. Compared with bass house, the bass is more stable and the arrangement less dependent on aggressively changing digital timbres. Marseille is a lineage anchor for the duo, while CUFF and their club circulation make the practice international. Exact instruments and chain settings are an authored contemporary arrangement.
exemplars: Amine Edge & DANCE — Going To Heaven With The Goodie-Goodies
Amine Edge & DANCE — Our G-House Sauce EP

items.name: Ambient dub techno
items.lineage: Ambient-facing extension of dub techno represented by Detroit producer Deepchord and Soma releases such as Sommer (2012) and Campfire EP (2017). Field-recording atmospheres, submerged pulses and echo space carry the arrangement beyond the compact chord-and-kick dub-techno tool.
items.description: Ambient dub techno emphasizes the atmospheric edge of techno's dub-processing lineage. Deepchord's Sommer is a reference for field-recording layers and gently shifting rhythm inside a warm, immersive soundfield; Campfire EP supplies a later recorded reference from the same producer. This seed gives sustained polyphonic synthesis and environmental samples priority over a soft synthesized pulse, with spreading reverb and recirculating echoes. It differs from the existing dub-techno record by making electroacoustic atmosphere a principal voice, and from the existing ambient-dub record by retaining a techno-derived pulse rather than a reggae riddim, melodica and live bass ensemble. It is narrower than ambient techno, selecting dub space and field recordings rather than the whole listening-techno continuum. Detroit is a Deepchord recording-lineage anchor, not a claim that the international genre has a single birthplace. The microphone, synth models, room and chain are authored equivalents, not verified Sommer session equipment.

items.name: Hypnotic techno
items.lineage: Deep and psychedelic techno continuum represented by Donato Dozzy, Luigi Tozzi and Hypnus Records, founded near Stockholm in 2013. The selected model emphasizes rolling percussion, interlocking cyclic figures and gradual atmospheric transformation rather than festival breakdowns.
items.description: Hypnotic techno organizes a dancefloor journey around cyclic percussion, interlocking figures and slowly changing depth. Hypnus founder Michel Iseneld describes a meeting of cinematic atmosphere, Prologue-style deep techno and psychedelia; Donato Dozzy's Parola rework offers a concrete example of repeating vocal material over supple rolling drums. This seed uses a sequenced, densely modulated synthesizer, a steady synthesized kit and environmental sampling, with offset echoes creating movement without a large drop. It differs from minimal techno by allowing a layered atmospheric field rather than pursuing maximum subtraction. Ambient dub techno places the soundfield above the beat; this record keeps percussion prominent. Modular techno is defined here by patch-performance method, while hypnotic techno is a listening and arrangement aesthetic that can be made with hardware or software. Stockholm marks the documented Hypnus label network, alongside important Italian producers; neither anchor is exclusive. The chosen modular architecture and chain are authored, not claims about every producer's studio.
exemplars: Donato Dozzy and Anna Caragnano — Parola (Rework)

items.name: Modular techno
items.lineage: Patch-centered techno practice developed across contemporary hardware scenes, represented here by Surgeon's live modular work and From Farthest Known Objects (2016). Voltage sequencing, synthesized percussion and hands-on timbral intervention distinguish the selected performance workflow.
items.description: Modular techno describes techno made through patchable synthesis, voltage sequencing and direct manipulation of a live signal path. Surgeon's modular performances and From Farthest Known Objects anchor this selected model; its spontaneous composition is documented by the Superbooth performance program. The recipe separates the patch voice from synthesized drum voices as editable catalog chairs, although a real system can generate both inside one rack. Sequenced gates, timbral percussion, resonant plucks and ring modulation supply change; preserving dynamics replaces the strongly pumped bass-house chain. Compared with industrial techno, distorted timbre is optional rather than the defining requirement. Compared with hypnotic techno, the distinction is the hands-on patch workflow and high improvisational scope, not a requirement for one particular mood. Birmingham anchors the documented artist and recording example, while modular techno remains an international method. The Eurorack variant, percussion partition and digital capture path are authored modeling choices, not a module-by-module reconstruction of the album.

items.name: Afghan pop
items.lineage: Selected 2010s Dari-language commercial pop shared between Kabul television and Afghan diaspora circuits, represented by Aryana Sayeed and the keyboard-and-tabla pop practice documented in European Afghan communities. This is a vocal song-and-dance branch, not a national summary or a replacement for Kabuli klasik, regional folk repertoires, Pashto pop or every diaspora production.
items.description: Selected 2010s Dari-language pop: a foreground melodic singer, keyboard hooks, tabla articulation and a Western rhythm-section vocabulary. European fieldwork documents keyboard, electric guitar and drum kit alongside tabla in Afghan pop practice, while Aryana Sayeed supplies a commercial vocal and transnational-media anchor. The default is an authored compact band reduction with tempered backing and vocal slides; it is not a transcription of Anar or an assertion that every Afghan pop record uses this roster. Distinct from afghan_traditional by concise commercial song form and electric backing, and from Tehrangeles Persian pop by the selected Afghan repertoire and tabla layer. Contemporary tracking choices model the practice; source pages do not establish microphone or console models.

items.name: Albanian pop
items.lineage: Selected late-2010s Albanian-language electronic commercial pop represented by Elvana Gjata and the producer-led Me tana release of 2019, circulating through Festivali i Kenges and digital singles. This compact dance-song branch coexists with Kosovo and diaspora pop scenes, ballads and acoustic repertoire; Albanian language or nationality alone does not define one sound.
items.description: Selected late-2010s Albanian-language producer-led dance pop, anchored by Elvana Gjata’s Me tana and UNIK’s own writing, production and mixing credits. A direct lead, short electronic hook, sampled percussion, sub-layered bass and answering vocal lane form the authored reduction. This record covers a commercial single practice rather than all Albanian or Kosovo music. Distinct from Albanian iso-polyphony by harmonic electronic song backing and individual studio lead; distinct from dasma and the catalog’s Balkan pop by avoiding an assumed wedding clarinet-and-accordion ensemble. The distributed-production room and contemporary digital chain are reusable recording choices, not verified session locations or hardware.

items.name: Armenian pop
items.lineage: Selected Yerevan-centered 2008-2012 folk-inflected dance pop associated with Sirusho, connecting her pop-and-folk recordings and international Qele Qele and PreGomesh singles with contemporary electronic song production. This is one crossover branch among Armenian-language and diaspora pop practices, distinct from liturgical chant, acoustic folk ensembles and the wider rabiz scene.
items.description: Selected 2008-2012 Armenian folk-and-pop crossover centered on Sirusho’s Yerevan practice and international singles. EBU documents her Armenian folk and original Armenian/English recordings; her production company describes traditional instruments in modern compositions. The default authors an ornamented duduk answer against an arpeggiated synth, layered sample beat, bass and a strong harmonized lead. It does not claim that all of these instruments appear on every exemplar or that the registered Punjabi dhol represents an Armenian drum. Distinct from Armenian folk and liturgical traditions through dance-song production and electronically constructed backing; wider rabiz, acoustic pop and diaspora styles require their own selections. Gear and vocal-processing settings are a contemporary model rather than documented session facts.

items.name: Azeri pop
items.lineage: Selected 2010 international studio pop-ballad branch of Azerbaijani popular music, represented by Safura and Drip Drop through the Ictimai/Eurovision platform and Swedish songwriting partnership. The English-language crossover is one documented branch rather than a definition of all Azerbaijani-language pop, regional dance music, mugham or ashig practice.
items.description: Selected Azerbaijani international pop-ballad practice around Safura’s Drip Drop (2010), documented by the EBU with Swedish songwriting credits and the Azerbaijani talent-show pathway. The default is an authored piano-arpeggio and orchestral-keyboard arrangement over a sampled beat and muted bass, with a light lead opening into sustained phrasing. This English-language crossover does not stand for all Azerbaijani-language pop. It is distinct from azeri_traditional through fixed commercial song sections and contemporary harmonic backing rather than a mugham ensemble or ashig performance; unlike the Armenian crossover default it does not require a folk instrument. Exact keyboard, microphone, compression and reverberation selections are design choices, not claims about the original session.

items.name: Burmese pop
items.lineage: Selected 2000s-2010s Burmese-language dramatic vocal pop and pop-rock represented by Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein, with her 2003-onward stage career, A Girl is Broken-hearted album and later official singles as anchors. The authored band configuration represents this melodic branch and does not collapse Myanmar's ethnic-language scenes, hip-hop, mahagita, hsaing waing or all copy-song practices into one tradition.
items.description: Selected 2000s-2010s Burmese-language dramatic melodic pop, anchored by Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein’s 2003-onward career and 2012 album A Girl is Broken-hearted, discussed in her firsthand interview. The default authors a single forceful lead with clean arpeggiated electric guitar, block-chord piano, locked bass and stick-played backbeat. Her official releases provide song anchors; this small band is a reusable pop-rock reduction, not a claim to a particular recorded personnel list. Distinct from mahagita and hsaing waing by commercial song sections and Western backline, and from Burmese hip-hop by sung melodic foreground. Myanmar contains many languages and regional practices; this selection does not define their common sound. The generic treated studio and digital chain are authored recording choices.
exemplars: Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein — A Girl is Broken-hearted (2012)
Phyu Phyu Kyaw Thein — A Shone Htet Po Thaw (2019)

items.name: Ambient IDM
items.lineage: The atmospheric, lower-intensity branch of listening-oriented IDM, represented here by Arovane’s Tides (2000): intricate sample-built rhythm, environmental recordings and edited guitar fragments arranged around quiet melodic space. Later Arovane/Porya Hatami collaborations extend the electronics/environmental-sound intersection. This is a selected calm, broken-beat branch rather than all IDM or all Arovane releases.
items.description: Ambient IDM retains carefully edited rhythmic events while giving atmospheric harmony and negative space more weight than percussion. Arovane’s Tides supplies a concrete sample-based branch: small jazz-record fragments, field recordings and edited improvised guitar coexist with downbeat grooves. The default uses one sampler for detailed beat/texture editing, a gently moving pad and clean guitar fragments; this is a reusable reduction rather than the album’s complete instrument inventory. Compared with IDM, percussion and intensity recede; compared with ambient techno, broken-beat detail replaces a regular techno machine pulse. Unlike beatless space ambient, discrete rhythmic edits remain audible. Synth construction and recording equipment are authored choices.

items.name: Ambient fusion
items.lineage: Ambient-oriented electric improvisation and studio montage, represented by Jon Hassell and Maarifa Street’s Last Night the Moon Came Dropping Its Clothes in the Street (2009). Trumpet, bass, violin and live sampling dissolve the boundary between ensemble performance and electronic soundscape. Hassell’s Fourth World practice is a formative branch of this wider jazz/electronic intersection, not a synonym for every ambient-fusion recording.
items.description: Ambient fusion places improvised instrumental gestures inside a continuously reworked electronic environment. The selected Hassell/Maarifa Street branch keeps a breath-led trumpet, subdued electric bass, bowed violin and live-sampling layer, with motifs overlapping instead of a solo succession over a driving rock backline. The credited 2009 album combines studio material, live recordings and subsequent montage; this reduced ensemble captures that practice without reproducing every credit. Unlike conventional jazz fusion, percussion and virtuosic attack are secondary; unlike ambient IDM, live melodic improvisation is central. The trumpet articulation, fretless setup and spatial chain are proposed defaults, not documented artist equipment.
exemplars: Jon Hassell — Last Night the Moon Came Dropping Its Clothes in the Street (2009)

items.name: Ambient psychill
items.lineage: The spacious, predominantly instrumental synthesizer branch of psychedelic chillout represented by Carbon Based Lifeforms’ Hydroponic Garden (2003) and World of Sleepers (2006), on Ultimae. Slow electronic rhythms, resonant bass, environmental samples and layered harmony sustain an ambient listening space. This narrower branch does not stand for the entire psychill festival repertoire or presume its acoustic-instrument and vocal collage.
items.description: Ambient psychill selects the unhurried, spacious electronic end of psychedelic chillout: slowly developing pads and melodic bass carry the track while programmed percussion stays recessed and environmental samples add depth. Carbon Based Lifeforms’ credited Ultimae albums and firsthand account of melody/bass relationships, added drums and field-recording practice anchor this model. The roster deliberately omits generic flute, didgeridoo and sung-vocal defaults from the broader psychill entry. Compared with ambient IDM, its underlying loop is more stable and its bass/filter motion less chopped; compared with space ambient, it retains a quiet beat and resonant bass sequence. It is a narrower ambient branch of existing psychill, with an authored synth/sampler configuration.
exemplars: Carbon Based Lifeforms — World of Sleepers (2006)

items.name: Ambient synth
items.lineage: Synthesizer-led ambient in which articulated patterns and changing electronic timbres remain recognizable, represented by Steve Hauschildt’s solo work around Strands (2016). A harmonic bed can give rise to arpeggios and aleatoric sequences, then be shaped through processing and editing. This selected pattern-oriented branch differs from beatless, steady-state space ambient and from the historically specific Berlin School.
items.description: Ambient synth centers the synthesizer as a played or programmed sound source: slowly changing harmony, gently articulated figures and interacting electronic voices create the space without requiring drums or acoustic instruments. The selected Hauschildt branch combines arpeggiated motion with flexible timing and detailed processing, rather than treating every synth part as an undifferentiated drone. The default pairs a soft short-envelope triangle figure with harmonic FM tones; these are authored ways to achieve the sourced practice, not claims about Strands’ instruments. Unlike space ambient, repeated note attacks remain a compositional foreground; unlike Berlin School, neither a 1970s tape ensemble nor a fixed ostinato defines the scope.
exemplars: Steve Hauschildt — Where All Is Fled (2015)

items.name: Space ambient
items.lineage: Beatless spatial electronic ambient, represented here by Steve Roach’s long-form steady-state Immersion work. Sustained polyphonic tones, slow timbral change and deep artificial space make duration and immersion more prominent than melody or sequence. This entry models the non-pulsed branch; space-oriented music also includes more rhythmic or dramatic forms that are not its default.
items.description: Space ambient is represented by a beatless, sustained-tone branch of space music, with slow changes in register and spectral color creating an enveloping field rather than a foreground beat or a repeating note sequence. Projekt’s Immersion: One release describes a continuous, minimal steady-state zone designed for extended low-volume listening; Roach’s firsthand synthesis account supports held chords and electronic sound construction. The default uses a stable sine tone and slowly morphing polyphonic wavetable layer with deep stereo reverberation. Unlike ambient synth’s articulated pattern branch, note attacks recede; unlike new age, a melodic tune or acoustic ensemble is not required. The modern two-synth chain is an authored reusable model.

items.name: Detroit house
items.lineage: Detroit producer-led house associated with Theo Parrish, Moodymann and Sound Signature: disco and soul sampling, jazz-informed keyboard movement, elastic groove and independent record culture. This selection follows the sample-and-keyboard strand rather than equating all Detroit electronic music with techno.
items.description: Selected Detroit sample-and-keyboard house: a swung programmed pulse supports soul/disco fragments, rounded synth bass and repeating jazz-informed electric-piano figures. Theo Parrish discusses sampling as musicianship and the relation between jazz, Chicago house and Detroit techno; his label records provide the concrete repertoire anchor. This does not prescribe a single sound for Detroit or classify his entire work as house. Unlike the Chicago-house seed, keyboard movement and elastic sample texture lead rather than an acid-bass template; unlike Detroit techno, soul/disco material and harmonic pocket outweigh mechanical synthesis. The small ensemble, equipment, bit depths and 13 axes are authored operational models, not inventories of Parallel Dimensions sessions.

items.name: Piano house
items.lineage: Transatlantic piano-led house vocabulary carried from 1990s club records into contemporary productions by Mark Knight, ATFC and Gene Farris: a recurring piano riff supplies the principal harmonic hook above kick, clap, offbeat hats and bass. This is an arrangement practice rather than the historical Italian Italo-house scene.
items.description: Piano house names a piano-riff-led arrangement practice spanning early house, 1990s anthems and current club production. Toolroom documents Mark Knight’s reworking of a 1995 Mr Roy record with piano, chopped vocals, clap snares and offbeat hats; ATFC describes played piano arpeggios and chords in The Spirit of House. This selected contemporary instrumental-led model foregrounds a ringing piano figure against tightly programmed percussion, bass and sampled hook texture. The catalog’s Italo-house record specifically represents the late-1980s/early-1990s Italian production scene and diva-vocal lineage, whereas this entry covers a broader transatlantic technique and its later revival. The grand piano is an editable timbral equivalent for acoustic, sampled or keyboard piano sounds; its brand, tracking setup and numeric axes are authored choices.
exemplars: Mark Knight vs Mr Roy — Something About U
ATFC and Gene Farris — The Spirit of House

items.name: Organic house
items.lineage: International emotive house network represented by All Day I Dream, Lee Burridge, Lost Desert and Pippi Ciez. Understated pulse, detailed melodic textures and hand-played or hand-like percussion support gradual development; organic here describes an aesthetic that can use substantial synthesis.
items.description: Selected All Day I Dream organic-house strand: detailed melodic sequences and layered textures develop over an understated groove, with percussion that feels played rather than merely rigid. Burridge identifies emotion as the label’s core and describes the organic-house name as a later category for music initially spread across genres. Lost Desert describes hybrid analog/software production; Pippi Ciez documents synth sequences and hand-played electronic percussion. Organic therefore does not require an acoustic-only ensemble or an invented ethnic-instrument palette. The three chairs model synthesis, hand-like sampled rhythm and looped textures; they are catalog equivalents, not the exact equipment on Melt. Compared with tropical house, extended instrumental development replaces a radio-pop vocal/drop template; compared with melodic house, the selected seed gives softer rhythmic weight and more intimate texture. Gear, room and axes remain authored.
exemplars: Lee Burridge and Lost Desert — Melt (2019)

items.name: Speed house
items.lineage: Late-2010s and 2020s international rave-house strand developed around Haus of Panda, Speed House Movement and CHYL, joining bass-house sound design with speed-garage and hard-house energy. Rapid club pulse and compact, forceful bass-led sections define this selected recipe.
items.description: Speed house combines rapid house pulse with bass-house timbral movement and speed-garage/hard-house rave energy. Monstercat’s Haus of Panda biography identifies that hybrid explicitly, and CHYL’s biography documents fast, bass-heavy production; Ignite provides a credited collaborative release. This selected instrumental drop model uses a rigid layered drum grid, animated speech-like synthesized bass and short sampled cuts, commonly in the roughly 140–160 BPM zone. Tempo is a descriptive target rather than a parameter encoded by the 13-axis schema. Distinct from bass house through the rapid rave context, and from UK hard house through bass-music sound design rather than making Hoover stabs compulsory; speed garage retains its own swung garage rhythmic identity. Wavetable architecture, limiter and exact sample settings are authored defaults, not documented Ignite gear.
exemplars: CHYL and Haus of Panda feat. MYLK — Ignite (2023)

items.name: Deep disco house
items.lineage: Disco-informed deep-house intersection represented by COEO and the Toy Tonics network: sample-based funk, soul and disco material joins a rounded bass pocket and chordal accompaniment. This selected strand uses the deeper harmonic groove rather than requiring the heavy filter-sweep arrangement of the broad disco-house record.
items.description: Selected disco-flavoured deep house within the COEO/Toy Tonics network: disco and funk sampling meets soulful chord movement, rounded bass and an elastic house pocket. The label describes COEO’s sample-based funk and its connection to deep-house charts, French touch and early Masters at Work; the artist’s Back In The Days release supplies repertoire and Munich practice context. This is an overlapping stylistic intersection rather than a separate birthplace claim.
