items.lineage: Finnish jazz connects local performers and composers with international improvising traditions. Solo piano, small ensembles and other approaches explore modern jazz harmony, songlike melody and individual rhythmic languages.
items.description: In the reflective piano strand, sustained arpeggios and melodic variations alternate with resonant lower-register responses. Flexible phrasing and changes of density connect composed themes with improvisation.

items.name: Jazz accordion
items.lineage: Accordion-centered jazz practice, represented by Richard Galliano’s drummerless Mare Nostrum collaboration with Paolo Fresu and Jan Lundgren. Accordion, trumpet and piano share melodic and harmonic roles.
items.description: The authored arrangement uses dry-tuned chromatic accordion lead and chordal responses, lyrical unmuted trumpet and spacious piano. It selects accordion and trumpet from documented instrumental doublings rather than stacking bandoneon, accordina and flugelhorn as simultaneous extra players. Reed configuration and cassotto are representative timbral choices, not a claim about the exact recording instrument.

items.name: Australian jazz
items.lineage: Australian jazz developed through local performance communities, recordings and international exchange. Its varied practices encompass small-group jazz, contemporary composition, solo improvisation and collaborations across musical traditions.
items.description: The solo-piano strand moves between lyrical statements, dense chord voicings and freer transitions. Melodic counterlines, changes of register and a flexible pulse provide contrast within the instrument’s broad dynamic range.

items.name: Italian jazz
items.lineage: Italian jazz encompasses lyrical modern-jazz improvisation, exploratory ensemble playing and composition across local and international networks. Small groups bring together acoustic rhythm sections, brass, reeds, keyboards and amplified instruments in varied combinations.
items.description: Spacious trumpet phrases develop into quicker improvised lines above restrained guitar harmonies, plucked bass and mobile percussion. Responsive accompaniment and changing density shape the exchanges between composed themes and open interaction.

items.name: French jazz
items.lineage: French jazz scenes; selected Galliano New Musette quartet branch
items.description: The authored quartet sets a chromatic accordion line against clean hollow-body guitar, plucked bass and light drums. It represents the jazz-oriented New Musette collaboration rather than making a waltz rhythm compulsory for all French jazz. The guitarist’s credited role is realized with an authored archtop model; no exact Catherine guitar construction is claimed. Dry reed tuning, cassotto and materials are representative settings, not a reconstruction of Galliano’s instrument.
exemplars: Richard Galliano — New Musette (1991), with Philip Catherine, Pierre Michelot and Aldo Romano

items.name: Israeli jazz
items.lineage: Israeli jazz connects local composers and improvisers with international jazz networks. Contemporary ensembles explore melodic composition, rhythmic complexity and close interaction between bass, keyboards, percussion and other instrumental voices.
items.description: Foreground bass melodies and repeated figures interlock with piano harmonies and detailed drum responses. Shifting phrase lengths and accents create momentum while leaving space for expansive improvisation and lyrical contrast.
exemplars: Avishai Cohen — Gently Disturbed (2008), with Shai Maestro and Mark Guiliana

items.name: Jazz blues
items.lineage: Jazz blues develops blues melodies and recurring harmonic forms through jazz improvisation, reharmonization and ensemble interplay. Small instrumental groups and vocal-led ensembles explore the relationship between repeated choruses, swing and expressive melodic variation.
items.description: Blues-derived piano phrases unfold over a steady plucked-bass foundation and responsive swung percussion. Repeated harmonic cycles support contrasting solos, rhythmic displacement and exchanges between melody and accompaniment.
exemplars: Oscar Peterson Trio — Night Train (1963 release; 1962 recording), title-track branch

items.name: Canadian modern jazz
items.lineage: Canadian modern jazz draws together contemporary composition, improvisation and international collaboration. Small ensembles often combine extended harmonies and distinctive melodic themes with flexible rhythmic and collective interplay.
items.description: Trumpet and tenor saxophone exchange lines above piano, plucked bass and drums. Written figures open into responsive improvisation, with shifting roles and dynamics allowing the group to move between clear themes and denser interaction.
exemplars: Ingrid Jensen & Steve Treseler — Invisible Sounds: For Kenny Wheeler (2018), live Foxy Trot quintet

items.name: Contemporary vocal jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary vocal jazz reinterprets songs through flexible phrasing, harmonic invention and expressive storytelling. Singers work in formats from intimate duos to larger ensembles, using timbre, rhythm and improvisation to reshape familiar and original material.
items.description: An exposed vocal line interacts with responsive piano harmonies, stretching time and varying melodic emphasis. Space between phrases, changing dynamics and subtle rhythmic placement foreground the singer’s interpretation and the accompanist’s replies.
exemplars: Cécile McLorin Salvant with Sullivan Fortner — The Window (2018)

items.name: Faroese jazz
items.lineage: Faroe Islands jazz scenes; selected Yggdrasil drummerless mixed ensemble
items.description: The authored Duologues branch combines piano, tenor saxophone, flute, electric guitar and double bass, with occasional non-lexical vocal expression by the pianist. The voice is a doubling rather than a sixth permanent player. Soprano saxophone and bass flute are alternatives in the credited practice; the default chooses one size of each. No kit is inserted into the documented drummerless personnel. Vocal mechanism remains unspecified; the model does not recast experimental wordless sounds as throat singing or a named Indigenous tradition.
exemplars: Kristian Blak & Yggdrasil — Duologues (2009), selected Don Quixote and the Horned Beast branch

items.name: Jazz guitar trio
items.lineage: Jazz guitar trio centres guitar within a three-part improvising ensemble, commonly alongside bass and drums. The format ranges from swinging chord-melody interplay to spacious contemporary textures and varied drummerless combinations.
items.description: Clean guitar supplies melodic and harmonic movement while plucked bass and delicate percussion respond around it. Open voicings, sustained fragments and shifts in rhythmic emphasis create space for close three-way interaction.
exemplars: Jakob Bro, Thomas Morgan and Jon Christensen — Gefion (2015; recorded 2013)

items.name: Jazz trio
items.lineage: Jazz trio is a small-ensemble format built around the interaction of three performers. Piano, bass and drums form a widely established configuration, alongside guitar-led, organ-led and other combinations with their own balances of melody, harmony and rhythm.
items.description: Piano phrases and chordal responses meet plucked bass and a responsive drum pulse. Shared time, improvised exchanges and changes in accompaniment allow each instrument to move between supporting and foreground roles.
exemplars: Oscar Peterson, Ray Brown and Ed Thigpen — Night Train (1962 sessions)

items.name: Jazz quartet
items.lineage: Jazz quartet brings four instrumental voices into a compact improvising ensemble. A horn with piano, bass and drums is a common configuration, while guitar, organ and other combinations support different approaches to melodic and rhythmic interaction.
items.description: A tenor saxophone line unfolds over flexible piano harmonies, plucked bass and acoustic drums. Themes lead into improvisation, with changing accompaniment and dynamic responses giving the four parts room to converse.
exemplars: Nubya Garcia — Source (2020), documented four-player core

items.name: Jazz guitar
items.lineage: Jazz guitar encompasses melodic improvisation, chordal accompaniment and solo approaches across acoustic and amplified instruments. Chord-melody playing lets a single guitarist combine bass movement, harmony and a singing upper line.
items.description: Fingerstyle voicings and melodic variations unfold over independently shaped bass notes. Nylon-string attack and resonant decay support an intimate solo texture, with flexible time and harmonic colour guiding the improvisation.

items.name: Jazz clarinet
items.lineage: Jazz clarinet developed through early ensemble jazz, swing and later improvising practices. Its flexible register, articulated attack and sustained tone support both melodic leadership and conversational small-group playing.
items.description: Clarinet phrases alternate with piano harmonies and rhythmic replies. Connected melodic lines, clear note beginnings and changes in register create contrast, while flexible accompaniment leaves space for improvisation.
exemplars: Anat Cohen & Fred Hersch — Live in Healdsburg (2018; recorded 2016)

items.name: Jazz harp
items.lineage: Jazz harp brings plucked resonance, flowing voicings and melodic improvisation into jazz ensemble and solo practice. Pedal-harp harmony supports interpretations of standards, contemporary compositions and connections with soul and other song traditions.
items.description: Ringing harp chords and melodic figures meet a flexible plucked-bass line. Clear attacks and overlapping decay create an intimate dialogue, with harmonic colour and rhythmic placement carrying the movement.
exemplars: Dezron Douglas & Brandee Younger — Force Majeure (2020), instrumental acoustic duet branch

items.name: Jazz organ
items.lineage: Hammond-organ jazz; selected Goldings/Bernstein/Stewart organ trio
items.description: The authored trio uses drawbar organ for harmony and the low-register foundation, supported by clean jazz guitar and drums. It does not add a separate bass player. Goldings’s primary interview establishes the real Hammond B-3 practice; slow Leslie rotation, short harmonic percussion and jazz drawbars are authored registration choices rather than a transcription of every tune. Guitar construction, amplifier and drum materials also remain representative.
exemplars: Larry Goldings, Peter Bernstein & Bill Stewart — Perpetual Pendulum (2022)

items.name: Jazz drums
items.lineage: Jazz drums combines timekeeping, interactive accompaniment and melodic-rhythmic improvisation across the drum kit. Drummer-led groups foreground composition and ensemble dialogue, with rhythmic decisions shaping the unfolding form.
items.description: Contrasting cymbal and drum attacks converse with tenor saxophone and plucked bass. In this chordless texture, mobile accents, brush-and-stick colour and changing density guide the interplay while leaving harmonic space open.
exemplars: Bill Stewart, Walter Smith III & Larry Grenadier — Live at the Village Vanguard (2025; recorded 2023)

items.name: Jazz chileno
items.lineage: Jazz chileno encompasses Chilean musicians, local scenes and diaspora collaborations working in jazz composition and improvisation. Modern small-group approaches connect melodic development with rhythmic dialogue and international exchange.
items.description: Tenor saxophone motifs develop over plucked bass and responsive drums. The open harmonic space of a chordless trio encourages interaction, with articulate runs, contrasting dynamics and flexible accompaniment shaping the improvisation.
exemplars: Melissa Aldana & Crash Trio — Melissa Aldana & Crash Trio (2014)

items.name: Jazz puertorriqueño
items.lineage: Puerto Rican jazz connects improvisation and modern harmony with the island’s musicians, song traditions and wider Caribbean exchanges. Reinterpreting bolero melody is one strand within a diverse instrumental and ensemble practice.
items.description: Lyrical alto saxophone and responsive piano transform song melodies through flexible phrasing and harmonic variation. Sustained lines and subtle rhythmic changes retain the expressive shape of song while opening space for improvisation.
exemplars: Miguel Zenón & Luis Perdomo — El Arte del Bolero (2021)

items.name: Jazz dominicano
items.lineage: Dominican jazz musicians; selected Michel Camilo solo piano
items.description: The selected What’s Up? branch is unaccompanied acoustic piano, balancing rhythmic drive, chordal color and lyrical passages. Dominican and wider Afro-Caribbean influences inform the music without implying a separate conga, tambora or bass player. The model’s full-size piano, materials, jazz articulation and clean room/chain are authored settings rather than claims about the Carriage House session’s exact instrument.

items.name: Jazz venezolano
items.lineage: Venezuelan jazz musicians and diaspora; selected Edward Simon songbook trio
items.description: The selected 2016 Latin American Songbook trio interprets song melodies through piano, bass and drums. Broader Latin American repertoire is part of this Venezuelan musician’s practice; it is not relabeled as exclusively Venezuelan composition. Cuatro, maracas, singers and additional percussion from Simon’s other projects are not inserted into this three-player recording. Exact constructions, articulations and recording environment are authored defaults.
exemplars: Edward Simon, Joe Martin and Adam Cruz — Latin American Songbook (2016)

items.name: Modern jazz piano
items.lineage: Modern jazz piano explores harmony, rhythm and melodic invention through composition and improvisation. Solo and ensemble practices draw on jazz vocabulary while expanding texture, register and rhythmic organization.
items.description: Compact motifs develop through chordal variation, counterlines and changes of register. Contrasting articulation and dynamic range connect lyrical passages with denser improvisation, allowing melody, harmony and pulse to interact within the keyboard.

items.name: Modern jazz trio
items.lineage: Modern jazz trio develops close three-way interaction through contemporary composition and improvisation. Piano, bass and drums form a prominent configuration, with other instrumental combinations offering different balances of melody, harmony and rhythm.
items.description: A melodic bass line interlocks with recurring piano figures and responsive drums. Shifting accents, phrase lengths and instrumental roles turn repeated material into a flexible framework for improvisation.
exemplars: Avishai Cohen, Shai Maestro and Mark Guiliana — Gently Disturbed (2008)

items.name: Progressive jazz fusion
items.lineage: Progressive jazz fusion combines jazz improvisation and extended harmony with amplified rock energy and compositionally intricate forms. Electric ensembles explore changing meters, contrasting sections and tightly coordinated instrumental figures.
items.description: Piano attack and sustained guitar lead trade prominence above electric bass and emphatic drums. Irregular phrase lengths, dynamic contrasts and coordinated rhythmic shifts frame expansive solos and ensemble exchanges.

items.name: Norwegian jazz
items.lineage: Norwegian jazz developed through local ensembles and international collaborations, exploring both melodic composition and open improvisation. Acoustic small groups form an important strand, with sustained instrumental voices and responsive rhythmic interplay.
items.description: Tenor saxophone melody moves through spacious piano harmonies above plucked bass and flexible drums. Long phrases, changing density and close ensemble responses connect composed themes with improvisation.
exemplars: Jan Garbarek/Bobo Stenson Quartet — Witchi-Tai-To (1974; recorded 1973)

items.name: Norwegian contemporary jazz
items.lineage: Norwegian contemporary jazz encompasses composition-led ensembles, exploratory improvisation and varied acoustic and electronic approaches. Lyrical small-group practice often brings songlike melody and resonant harmony into flexible, open structures.
items.description: Concise piano themes develop through sustained voicings, melodic bass and restrained percussion. Subtle dynamic changes and attentive use of silence support intimate ensemble dialogue, with chorale-like harmony informing some branches.
exemplars: Tord Gustavsen, Harald Johnsen and Jarle Vespestad — Changing Places (2003)

items.name: Jazz violin
items.lineage: Violin-centered jazz improvisation; selected Carter/Barron duet
items.description: The authored duet gives a single acoustic violin room for sustained lines and phrased responses to piano harmony. Freefall’s two credited musicians justify omitting rhythm section. The existing orchestral-violin body model represents an ordinary modern four-string violin here, not an orchestra or classical repertoire requirement. Synthetic-core strings, carbon-fiber bow and modern varnish are explicitly authored alternatives, not claims about Carter’s personal instrument.

items.name: Polish jazz
items.lineage: Polish jazz developed through local scenes, composition and international exchange, spanning lyrical modern-jazz writing and freer improvisation. Small ensembles have cultivated distinctive melodic voices and a close relationship between written themes and collective response.
items.description: Restrained trumpet melody and piano harmony unfold above plucked bass and responsive drums. Gradual variations of phrase, density and intensity create a reflective texture that can open into more expansive improvisation.
exemplars: Tomasz Stańko Quartet — Soul of Things (2002)

items.name: Polish modern jazz
items.lineage: Polish modern jazz brings contemporary composition, reinterpretation of repertoire and collective improvisation into dialogue. Piano-led ensembles are one important strand within a scene that moves between lyrical detail and freer interaction.
items.description: Resonant piano phrases, mobile bass and nuanced percussion share the development of each idea. Changing roles and dynamics allow written material and spontaneously formed passages to flow into one another.

items.name: Polish free jazz
items.lineage: Polish free jazz connects the country’s exploratory improvisers with international avant-garde jazz. Open interaction, expanded instrumental colour and flexible form coexist with composed themes and recurring melodic ideas.
items.description: Trumpet and saxophone exchange angular phrases and rougher overblown colours above mobile bass and drums. Without a chordal instrument fixing every harmony, density, register and rhythmic response help shape the collective flow.
exemplars: Tomasz Stańko, Tomasz Szukalski, Dave Holland and Edward Vesala — Balladyna (1976)

items.name: NZ jazz
items.lineage: New Zealand jazz encompasses local scenes and diaspora musicians working across modern composition and improvisation. Acoustic small-group playing is one strand within a varied field shaped by international exchange and individual musical languages.
items.description: Open piano harmonies and melodic bass counterlines interact with flexible drum pulses. Shared motifs, changing dynamics and responsive accompaniment let the ensemble move between clear themes and more exploratory passages.
exemplars: Mike Nock, Eddie Gomez and Jon Christensen — Ondas (1982)

items.name: Portuguese jazz
items.lineage: Portuguese jazz brings local composers and improvisers into dialogue with international jazz and varied musical influences. Contemporary small ensembles explore harmonic colour, melodic development and rhythmically responsive group playing.
items.description: Original piano themes meet mobile double-bass lines and detailed drum responses. Contrasting textures and accents connect lyrical passages with more rhythmically animated improvisation.
exemplars: Mário Laginha, Bernardo Moreira and Alexandre Frazão — Jangada (2022)

items.name: Korean jazz
items.lineage: Korean jazz connects local musicians and international collaborators across instrumental and vocal practices. Song interpretation, modern harmony and improvisation support formats ranging from intimate duos to larger ensembles.
items.description: In the vocal-piano strand, expressive singing meets flexible chordal accompaniment and rhythmic replies. Changes of tone, phrasing and harmonic emphasis reshape songs while leaving space for the voice and piano to interact.
exemplars: Youn Sun Nah with Éric Legnini — Sisteron, July 30, 2024; acoustic-piano branch of the live duo

items.name: Scottish jazz
items.lineage: Scottish jazz encompasses contemporary composition and improvisation alongside exchanges with local folk traditions and international jazz. Folk-informed melodic figures are one strand of a wider scene of ensembles and individual instrumental voices.
items.description: Recurring piano patterns combine with active double bass and responsive drums. Folk-like melodic contours and strong dynamic expansion develop into improvisation, balancing clear motifs with flexible rhythmic interplay.

items.name: Jazz cubano
items.lineage: Cuban jazz brings Cuban musicians and diaspora communities into dialogue with jazz harmony, improvisation and Afro-Caribbean musical languages. Solo, small-group and larger-ensemble practices balance rhythmic invention with melodic and harmonic exploration.
items.description: In the solo-piano strand, flowing arpeggios, rhythmic figures and sustained harmonies create contrasting textures. Dynamic shifts and melodic variation connect reflective passages with more animated improvisation.

items.name: Jazz català
items.lineage: Jazz català encompasses musicians and scenes associated with Catalonia, shaped by local performance culture and international jazz exchange. Bebop-derived improvisation and solo-piano practice form part of a wider field of ensembles and contemporary approaches.
items.description: A moving left-hand bass line supports agile upper-register melody and changing chord voicings. Rhythmic independence, accents and harmonic substitutions create a full solo texture, balancing song form with improvisation.

items.name: Belgian drum and bass
items.lineage: Belgian drum and bass developed through local producers, clubs, labels and festival networks connected with the wider international scene. Melodic liquid-derived production and crossover songs form an influential strand alongside other approaches.
items.description: Rolling edited drum breaks and a controlled sub-bass foundation support layered melodic samples and a sung topline. Smooth sustained tones contrast with quick rhythmic detail, while builds and changes in texture give the arrangement direction.

items.name: Stateside drum and bass
items.lineage: Stateside drum and bass connects producers, DJs, labels and touring networks across the United States. Its varied practices include forceful dancefloor production built on the rhythmic and bass vocabulary of the international drum-and-bass scene.
items.description: Fast cut-up drum patterns meet moving synthesized bass riffs and atmospheric sample layers. Darker timbres, rhythmic tension and changes in density drive an energetic club-oriented arrangement.

items.name: UK drum and bass
items.lineage: UK drum and bass emerged from British jungle and breakbeat production, developing through clubs, pirate radio, labels and studio collaborations. Its broad field includes atmospheric, melodic and harder dancefloor approaches.
items.description: Finely edited percussion loops and a sustained low-frequency foundation support extended atmospheric sample phrases. Small changes in break placement, layering and effects develop the arrangement around recurring rhythmic and melodic ideas.

items.name: Brazilian bass
items.lineage: Brazilian bass emerged in the 2010s around Brazilian producers and house-music networks, including Alok, Illusionize and Liu. The contested name identifies a bass-forward house-derived scene rather than the entirety of Brazilian bass music.
items.description: A firm four-on-the-floor kick and clap pattern underpins short, resonant synthesized bass notes. Sampled hooks, layered percussion and changes in texture build momentum around a prominent low end.

items.name: Classic garage rock
items.lineage: Classic garage rock centres on the raw 1960s guitar-band tradition, with groups such as Tacoma’s Sonics linking rhythm and blues, early rock and forceful amateur-band energy. Its recordings helped shape later punk and garage revivals.
items.description: Abrasive electric-guitar riffs, emphatic bass and a hard backbeat drive forceful singing. Honking tenor saxophone and percussive piano add rhythm-and-blues colour to the rough-edged band sound.

items.name: Garage pop
items.lineage: Garage pop combines the rough attack of garage rock with concise, melodic pop songwriting. Independent guitar-band scenes have renewed this combination through catchy songs, fuzzed textures and direct performances.
items.description: Compact guitar riffs, assertive bass and a straightforward drum backbeat support melodic vocal hooks. Fuzz and tape-like colour roughen the edges while short phrases and recurring choruses keep the songs immediate.

items.name: Indie garage rock
items.lineage: Indie garage rock grows through independent labels, local guitar-band scenes and home-recording networks. Musicians such as Ty Segall connect garage-rock directness with contemporary alternative-rock songwriting and production.
items.description: Distorted guitar figures, driving bass and brisk drums support sharp melodic singing. Raw amplifier colour and an energetic rhythm section coexist with articulate hooks and a controlled mix.

items.name: Garage psych
items.lineage: Garage-rooted psychedelic guitar-band practice associated with the late 2000s West Coast scene including Ty Segall, Oh Sees and White Fence. This model selects the fuzzed guitar-band branch rather than later piano/orchestral experiments.
items.description: An overlapping garage/psychedelic rock discovery field. The authored default uses sustained fuzzed guitar figures, a more open drum-and-bass backing and doubled melodic singing, with delay for depth. Psychedelic here describes arrangement and timbre; it does not imply a compulsory sitar, exotic tuning or uniform studio rig.

items.name: Trance
items.lineage: A broad electronic-dance discovery label encompassing multiple trance scenes. The representative theme-led branch is documented by Armin van Buuren’s studio account: recurring synthesized musical phrases, programmed drums and bass, and extended tension-building arrangements.
items.description: An umbrella trance discovery entry. This authored default chooses a melodic club-studio branch with an unfolding synthesizer theme, firm electronic percussion and layered phrases shaped around a long build and release. The branch is intentionally narrower than the full roster, which spans eras and substyles; vocals, orchestral players and any one synthesizer brand are not mandatory.

items.name: Russian trance
items.lineage: Russian-origin trance producers represented here by ARTY/ALPHA 9. The selected progressive branch follows his first-person description of 128–132 BPM sets with large breakdowns and gradual transitions; it does not impose this tempo or arrangement on every Russian trance artist.
items.description: A geographic producer-origin cluster spanning trance styles. This authored ALPHA 9-informed branch places short melodic synth gestures and layered harmonic textures over controlled programmed percussion, with spacious breakdowns and patient transitions. Russian origin does not imply a unique national instrument, and the photograph depicts ARTY, whose work also extends beyond trance.

items.name: Jazzy drum and bass
items.lineage: Jazz- and soul-inflected drum-and-bass production represented by LTJ Bukem and the Good Looking network. His first-person production account documents chopped original breaks, synthesizer/sample-CD atmospheres, Rhodes keyboards and extended sectional composition.
items.description: A drum-and-bass discovery field emphasizing jazz/soul harmony, phrasing and textures. The authored default combines a rolling sliced drum pattern, bell-like electric-piano comping, sustained low bass and layered sampled atmospheres. It selects a keyboard-and-sample branch; jazzy does not require a live saxophone section, acoustic jazz quartet or one fixed key/tempo.

items.name: Electric bass
items.lineage: Electric-bass-led music spans solo performance and ensembles across jazz, funk and related styles. Players such as Victor Wooten expand the instrument’s rhythmic and melodic roles through slap, harmonics, tapping and thumb techniques.
items.description: Percussive thumb-and-pop attacks articulate bass lines and upper-register melodic figures on a single instrument. Clear direct amplification preserves the contrast between ringing notes, muted accents and rapid rhythmic gestures.

items.name: Classic dubstep
items.lineage: A historical dubstep discovery cluster spanning more than one era. Skream’s first-person 2006 account anchors this selected early Croydon branch in instrumental dark garage, bass-led stripped-down programming and occasional background samples.
items.description: A historical dubstep discovery entry. The authored early-Croydon branch combines sparse programmed drums, long low synthesized bass and intermittent sampled atmospheres. It preserves space around the rhythm rather than prescribing continuous midrange growls. The broad classifier also contains later artists; the chosen branch is not a date boundary imposed on its entire membership.

items.name: Canadian garage rock
items.lineage: Canadian garage rock connects local guitar-band scenes with garage, punk and melodic rock traditions. Vancouver’s Japandroids exemplify a forceful guitar-and-drums approach within this wider field.
items.description: Distorted chordal guitar, direct singing and a hard acoustic-drum backbeat create a dense, energetic sound. Broad amplifier tone gives the guitar rhythmic weight and a substantial low end alongside ringing upper-register chords.

items.name: French garage rock
items.lineage: French garage-rock scenes, represented by The Limiñanas’ Perpignan-based, self-recorded riff-led practice. Direct interviews describe garage-punk roots, played repeating figures, acoustic drums, voice and small percussion, with selective guest instruments and arrangement changes.
items.description: A French garage-rock discovery field modeled here through The Limiñanas’ repeating riffs and home-recorded guitar, bass, acoustic drums, voice and tambourine. The authored branch centers played repetition and changing timbral layers rather than a compulsory verse/chorus form. Their oud, bouzouki and Moroccan bass collaborations are real optional branches, not requirements for every French garage band.

items.name: Breakbeat
items.lineage: A broad break-led electronic dance discovery field. The selected early Prodigy branch is grounded in Liam Howlett’s direct account of reconstructing snippets of live drum breaks, reinforcing them with drum-machine hits and building sampled and synthesized hooks.
items.description: Break-led dance production spanning multiple tempos and scenes. This authored early-rave branch slices and recombines drum breaks, reinforces attacks, and sets forceful synthesizer gestures against short sampled motifs. It reflects one documented Prodigy-era production approach rather than requiring every breakbeat track to be rave, distorted or produced with vintage hardware.

items.name: Instrumental grime
items.lineage: Instrumental production within grime, represented by the independent rhythmic and melodic tracks circulated to DJs and later voiced by MCs. Wiley’s primary account documents module melodies, string-like sounds, sampling and deliberate removal of drums in an optional bass-mix branch.
items.description: Grime production foregrounded as instrumental music, with clipped percussion, keyboard/module melodies, low bass weight and sampled textures. The authored default selects a rhythm-bearing string-preset branch with no compulsory vocal card. It also acknowledges drumless bass mixes; a tune may have both instrumental and subsequently voiced versions, so the label does not imply that its producers never rap.

items.name: Australian garage punk
items.lineage: Australian garage punk develops through local DIY guitar-band scenes, combining garage-rock roughness with punk’s direct songwriting and performance energy. Groups such as Queensland’s Chats favour brief songs, economical riffs and an unpolished attack.
items.description: Short overdriven guitar figures, picked electric bass and a firm kit backbeat support direct singing. Limited chord changes, sharp accents and a live-room feel keep the arrangement punchy without requiring maximum guitar saturation.

items.name: Garage punk blues
items.lineage: Garage punk blues joins amplified blues and roots music with garage rock’s rough attack and punk’s economy. Stripped-down groups, one-person bands and acts such as the Jon Spencer Blues Explosion use forceful rhythms and unruly guitar textures.
items.description: Fuzzed riffs, low-register guitar weight and cleaner answering figures interact with a driving drum kit and direct singing. Repetition, sharp accents and flexible rhythmic phrasing give the lean ensemble a raw, physical energy.

items.name: Garage rock mexicano

items.name: Australian black metal
items.lineage: Australian black metal developed through underground recording and rehearsal scenes, including exchanges with thrash and other extreme-metal forms. Melbourne-origin Deströyer 666 exemplify a raw, riff-driven crossover that later extended through international membership and touring.
items.description: Rapid repeated guitar notes and dense distorted lines ride over picked bass and double-kick drumming. Forceful vocals and an abrasive ensemble attack sustain intensity, while shifting riffs give shape to the continuous guitar texture.

items.name: Australian thrash metal
items.lineage: Australian scene-origin scope, represented by the documented Melbourne beginnings of Deströyer 666 and their black/thrash crossover. Later membership and residence are multinational.
items.description: An Australian-origin thrash discovery field. The authored Deströyer 666-informed crossover branch favors clipped guitar riff articulation and a driving bass-and-kit pulse in a controlled studio capture. Its blackened lineage is acknowledged while the default foregrounds rhythmic riff attack rather than the sustained rapid-picking branch used for Australian black metal.

items.name: Canadian death metal
items.lineage: Canadian death metal includes a prominent technical current associated with Montreal bands such as Cryptopsy. Elaborate rhythmic coordination and contrasts between dissonant, melodic and groove-based passages shape this strand of the wider extreme-metal scene.
items.description: Rapid electric-guitar articulation and tightly coordinated bass and drums build dense, changing sections beneath harsh vocals. Double-kick patterns and sudden accents intensify the attack, while more spacious grooves interrupt the busiest passages.

items.name: Canadian metal
items.lineage: Canadian metal encompasses diverse regional scenes and styles, including the technically elaborate extreme-metal work associated with Montreal. Cryptopsy provide one example of the interaction between dense riff writing, rhythmic variation and a powerful band foundation.
items.description: Amplified guitar, electric bass, acoustic drums and voice form a flexible heavy ensemble. Recurring muted riffs and low-register weight can alternate with melodic lines, dissonant passages and more open grooves, with contrasting intensity shaping the arrangement.

items.name: Austrian black metal
items.lineage: Austrian black metal includes raw underground approaches and developed black/death crossovers. Salzburg’s Belphegor exemplify a low-tuned, riff-centered strand combining rapid guitar lines with the weight and attack of death metal.
items.description: Fast repeated guitar notes build a dense distorted surface over bass and forceful double-kick drumming. Harsh vocal delivery and strongly articulated accents reinforce the tension, while guitar melodies and sectional contrasts give the texture direction.

items.name: Austrian metal
items.lineage: Austrian metal encompasses multiple heavy styles and regional scenes, including the black/death crossover associated with Salzburg’s Belphegor. Low-tuned guitar writing and forceful ensemble attack form one prominent extreme-metal strand.
items.description: Weighty distorted chords and recurring bass-and-drum accents support intense vocals. Contrasts between sustained guitar mass and sharply defined rhythmic figures give the arrangement shape, with tuning and density varying across the wider field.

items.name: British power metal
items.lineage: British scene-origin power metal represented by London-founded DragonForce. The authored historical keyboard-and-guitar branch combines rapid lead exchange, melodic choruses and a full rhythm section.
items.description: A British power-metal discovery field, represented by DragonForce’s London-origin melodic high-speed branch. The authored model combines virtuosic electric-guitar lead work, melodic vocal display, bass and acoustic drums with a PCM workstation lead. It selects the documented historical keyboard era; it does not claim that every current touring lineup contains that keyboardist or that every British power-metal band shares this setup.

items.name: Argentine heavy metal
items.lineage: Argentine heavy metal connects guitar-led hard rock, virtuosic playing and melodic songcraft. Rata Blanca exemplify a keyboard-supported strand whose repertoire combines forceful riffs, expressive leads and widely heard ballads.
items.description: Overdriven guitar lines and sustained keyboard support sit above electric bass and driving acoustic drums. Connected melodic singing and dynamic changes give the songs breadth, balancing instrumental display with strong vocal hooks.

items.name: Argentine metal
items.lineage: Argentine metal spans heavy, melodic and more extreme scenes connected through local bands and recording networks. Rata Blanca exemplify one established guitar-and-keyboard tradition within this broader field.
items.description: Amplified guitar riffs, electric bass, drums and voice provide a flexible heavy-band foundation, with keyboard layers adding harmonic depth. Forceful chord attacks and melodic passages alternate; quieter ballads remain part of the repertoire alongside heavier songs.

items.name: Boston metal
items.lineage: Boston-area metal includes a strong exchange with hardcore and experimental heavy music. Andover-founded Converge exemplify a rhythmically intricate strand shaped through band interaction and self-produced recording practice.
items.description: Clipped distorted guitar figures and forceful bass meet irregularly accented acoustic drums and abrasive vocals. Abrupt shifts, dense attacks and spaces between gestures create tension, with the guitar and drum parts developing closely together.

items.name: American melodeath
items.lineage: American melodic death metal combines extreme-metal attack with shaped guitar melodies and prominent lead phrasing. Michigan’s Black Dahlia Murder exemplify a riff-centered approach in which melodic detail remains clear within an aggressive band sound.
items.description: Singing distorted guitar lines rise above a distinct picked-bass foundation, fast acoustic drums and harsh vocals. Low tuning and boosted amplification add weight, while rhythmic definition and contrasting lead contours keep the texture articulate.

items.name: Canadian metalcore
items.lineage: Canadian metalcore connects heavy guitar writing with hardcore song and rhythmic traditions. Montreal’s Despised Icon illustrate its overlap with deathcore and grind through direct hardcore pulses, dense riffs and alternating vocal attacks.
items.description: Muted guitar chugs and picked bass lock to forceful drum-kit patterns. Contrasting harsh vocal parts can trade or combine above the rhythm, while breaks and recurring accents emphasize the physical drive of the ensemble.

items.name: Belgian death metal
items.lineage: Belgian-origin scene scope represented by Aborted’s multinational death/grind lineage and its documented contrast of speed with groove. Historic instrumental practice is not a current-personnel claim.
items.description: A Belgian death-metal discovery field, with an Aborted-informed high-intensity branch. Rapid repeated guitar lines and explicit alternating blast-pattern drumming drive a bass-and-harsh-voice core. The selected single-stroke blast is a documented general technique implemented as an authored pattern; it is not confused with the physical presence of a double pedal.

items.name: Belgian metal
items.lineage: Belgian metal encompasses multiple regional and international heavy-music networks. Aborted provide one extreme-metal example within the broader field, linking intense death/grind passages with recurring heavy grooves.
items.description: Distorted guitar, electric bass, acoustic drums and voice supply a flexible heavy-band foundation. Short muted riffs and strongly marked accents can build a weighty pulse, with density, melody and tempo varying across the wider repertoire.

items.name: British death metal
items.lineage: British death metal grew through underground scenes with connections to grind and other extreme forms. Liverpool’s Carcass exemplify a strand where low guitar tuning and harsh, rhythmically emphatic vocals coexist with melodic guitar writing.
items.description: Sharply picked low-register riffs and harmonized guitar lines work against electric bass and forceful acoustic drums. The voice adds percussive weight while the guitars carry much of the melodic contour, combining blunt attacks with connected instrumental phrases.

items.name: British grindcore
items.lineage: British grindcore emerged from underground punk and extreme-metal exchanges, with Birmingham’s Napalm Death central to its early development. Very short songs, distorted ensemble attack and explosive drumming became defining resources of the style.
items.description: Rapid guitar and bass figures collide with single-stroke blast patterns and harsh vocals. Compressed song forms, sudden changes and raw instrumental energy create an intense texture, with heavily driven strings and sharply marked drum attacks.

items.name: American grindcore
items.lineage: American grindcore connects extreme-metal technique with compressed song forms and underground punk intensity. Virginia’s Pig Destroyer illustrate its changing ensemble practices, from an early guitar-and-drums core to expanded bass and noise arrangements.
items.description: Rapid distorted guitar figures, electric bass, acoustic blast drumming and harsh vocals create short, forceful bursts. Abrupt rhythmic changes and dense attacks dominate, while some groups use sparse lineups or add electronic noise and samples for contrast.

items.name: Buffalo NY metal
items.lineage: Buffalo’s metal scene includes a strong exchange with hardcore and riff-driven heavy rock. Every Time I Die exemplify a locally rooted approach combining disruptive accents, collaborative guitar writing and occasional cleaner or more melodic passages.
items.description: Broad distorted guitar chords and active electric bass support a forceful acoustic kit and harsh vocals. Contrasting riffs and abrupt accents keep the rhythm unsettled, balancing dense attacks with more open stretches of groove.

items.name: Brutal deathcore
items.lineage: Brutal deathcore emphasizes low-register impact and rhythmic precision within the intersection of death metal and hardcore. Groups such as Fit For An Autopsy connect extended-range guitar writing with melodic, heavy-groove and slow crushing passages.
items.description: Tightly damped seven-string guitar figures lock with electric bass and double-kick drums beneath harsh vocals. Low tuning, dense attacks and strongly spaced accents create weight, with sharply coordinated changes between rapid motion and breakdowns.

items.name: British black metal
items.lineage: British black metal includes the first-wave legacy of Newcastle’s Venom and later developments across the underground. Its early heavy- and speed-metal roots combined abrasive guitar, heavily driven bass and theatrical harsh singing.
items.description: Forceful guitar chords and an overdriven bass foundation press against hard acoustic drums and harsh vocals. Raw amplified texture and direct rhythmic attack characterize the early strand, while the wider field also includes more sustained and atmospheric approaches.

items.name: Brazilian death metal
items.lineage: Brazilian death metal developed through underground bands and international extreme-metal networks. Ijuí’s Krisiun exemplify a tightly interacting guitar, singing-bass and drum trio whose intense playing also makes room for thrash-derived rhythms and grooves.
items.description: Sharply articulated guitar riffs, aggressive electric bass and forceful acoustic drums support harsh vocals. Fast passages alternate with more measured accents and skank-like rhythmic drive, keeping ensemble interaction and dynamics central to the weight.

items.name: Arab metal
items.lineage: Arab-world metal discovery scope represented by Myrath’s specifically Tunisian melodic/progressive branch. Primary musicians distinguish their Tunisian tunes, quarter-step vocal inflection and guitar/bass/drum/keyboard core from generic exotic-instrument accumulation.
items.description: An Arab-world metal discovery field, with an explicitly Tunisian Myrath branch rather than a uniform regional formula. The authored setup combines extended-range guitar leads, bass, acoustic drums and orchestral-color keyboards with connected, melismatic voice and quarter-step inflection. It keeps the tempered instrumental framework separate from aurally adjusted vocal pitch; no single maqam or exact quarter-tone scale is attributed to every song.

items.name: Blackened deathcore
items.lineage: Blackened deathcore connects deathcore’s low-register rhythmic impact with black-metal atmosphere and, in some bands, elaborate symphonic writing. Lorna Shore exemplify a composition-driven strand where orchestral layers are developed alongside the distorted band material.
items.description: Low, tightly damped guitar figures and electric bass lock with forceful acoustic drums beneath harsh vocals. Sustained sampled orchestral layers broaden the harmonic space, contrasting sweeping textures with abrupt attacks and heavy rhythmic breaks.

items.name: Baltic black metal
items.lineage: Baltic black metal connects regional underground scenes with local historical and folk interests. Latvia’s Skyforger illustrate a path from early black-metal influence toward a broader mixture of folk, pagan and heavy-metal writing.
items.description: Rapid repeated guitar lines, electric bass and acoustic drums support harsh singing and band chants. Guitar-centered passages can alternate with folk-derived melodic material, with strong ensemble accents carrying the regional repertoire into amplified arrangements.

items.name: Canadian black metal
items.lineage: Canadian black metal spans regional underground scenes and differing raw or atmospheric approaches. Vancouver’s Blasphemy exemplify an early extreme strand grounded in rehearsal-driven guitar, bass, drum and vocal interaction.
items.description: Rapidly articulated distorted guitars and electric bass build a dense surface around forceful acoustic drums and harsh vocals. Dry vocal attacks and rough-edged recording color heighten the directness, with compact riffs and persistent rhythmic intensity shaping the ensemble.

items.name: Brazilian black metal
items.lineage: Brazilian black metal developed through underground scenes with varied raw, atmospheric and melodic approaches. Salvador’s Mystifier exemplify an evolving practice built around amplified guitars, bass, drums and voice, with keyboards adding further color in part of the repertoire.
items.description: Rapid distorted guitar lines and a heavy bass-and-drum foundation support harsh vocals. Sustained keyboard tones can deepen the harmonic background, while differences in density and vocal treatment provide contrast within the intense band texture.

items.name: Brazilian metalcore
items.lineage: Brazilian metalcore connects heavy guitar riffs and hardcore-derived rhythm with local independent production. São Paulo’s Project46 exemplify Portuguese-language performance and collaborative riff writing that also incorporates melody and groove.
items.description: Tight low guitar figures and active bass lock to a forceful acoustic-kit pulse beneath harsh vocals. Repeated accents and spaces between attacks give the riffs weight, while melodic passages contrast with the most compressed and rhythmically direct sections.

items.name: Bolivian metal
items.lineage: Bolivian metal includes locally rooted heavy bands and experiments combining amplified rock with other production approaches. La Paz’s Alcoholika La Christo illustrate a development from heavy metal toward industrial influences and Altiplano melodic material.
items.description: Distorted electric-guitar chords, bass, acoustic drums and voice provide a central heavy-band foundation. Repetition and strong rhythmic accents emphasize weight, with electronic production and locally rooted melodic ideas enriching some strands of the wider repertoire.

items.name: Belgian black metal
items.lineage: Belgian black metal spans fast, raw playing and more elaborate atmospheric or progressive writing. Namur-origin Enthroned exemplify a repertoire moving between ferocious blast passages, oppressive mid-tempos and changing guitar-led structures.
items.description: Dense distorted guitar chords and electric bass press against an acoustic kit and harsh voice. Deliberate accents can create a heavy, constrained pulse, contrasting with faster passages and more extended guitar figures elsewhere in the repertoire.

items.name: Belgian jazz
items.lineage: Belgian jazz connects local scenes with international improvising traditions. Brussels-born Toots Thielemans made the chromatic harmonica a distinctive melodic voice in this history, bringing lyrical phrasing to small-group jazz and collaborations abroad.
items.description: Flexible harmonica lines interact with spacious piano chords, plucked acoustic bass and light drum-kit textures. Improvised phrases develop over a shared harmonic frame, balancing clear melodic direction with responsive rhythm-section interplay.

items.name: Harmonica jazz
items.lineage: Harmonica jazz foregrounds the instrument as an improvising melodic voice, notably through the chromatic-harmonica tradition associated with Toots Thielemans. Its repertoire ranges from intimate duets to larger jazz ensembles.
items.description: Sustained chromatic lines and flexible phrasing respond to changing piano harmony. Breath-shaped attacks and connected melodic contours can lead a spacious dialogue, with timing shared between soloist and accompanist rather than dependent on a constant drum pulse.

items.name: Jazz vibraphone
items.lineage: Jazz vibraphone combines pitched metal-bar resonance with melodic improvisation and chordal playing. Gary Burton’s four-mallet approach expanded its harmonic possibilities, including a long-running chamber-jazz dialogue with pianist Chick Corea.
items.description: Clear mallet attacks open into sustained metallic tones, allowing single lines and voiced chords to overlap. Piano and vibraphone can exchange accompaniment and melody in a responsive duet, with pedal control and articulation shaping the space between phrases.

items.name: Jazz trombone
items.lineage: Jazz trombone spans ensemble brass writing and agile solo improvisation. Modern players such as Steve Turre carry the instrument’s broad vocal-like tone into small groups with other horns and a responsive rhythm section.
items.description: Open tenor-trombone lines combine sustained notes, articulated runs and expressive phrasing. Saxophone, piano, plucked bass and drums answer or support the lead, balancing a strong brass presence with harmonic movement and rhythmic flexibility.

items.name: Jazz tuba
items.lineage: Jazz tuba brings a low brass voice into both bass-line and melodic roles. Contemporary players such as Theon Cross connect that history with London’s rhythmically forceful small-group jazz scene.
items.description: Punchy low-register tuba figures provide a moving foundation while leaving room for melodic variation. Tenor saxophone and drums trade accents around the brass pulse, creating a compact ensemble whose low end is carried by breath and valves rather than a separate bass guitar.

items.name: Roots Americana
items.lineage: Roots Americana connects contemporary performers working with multiple older American song and instrumental traditions. Charlie Parr’s documented blues/folk twelve-string work provides one branch of this broad recording network.
items.description: Narrative singing and fingerpicked twelve-string guitar emphasize paired-string resonance and a clear rhythmic contour. This selected compact model follows Parr’s documented roles while leaving his resonator and other collaborators outside this particular configuration.

items.name: Southern Americana
items.lineage: Southern Americana encompasses roots-oriented recording and performance networks across the southern United States. Margo Price’s Nashville sessions provide one documented contemporary country-soul branch.
items.description: Lead voice, acoustic guitar, steel-guitar color and a rhythm section form a recorded-song arrangement grounded in the credited Price session. Exact equipment and room remain authored production choices, and the selected branch is not a complete definition of Southern roots music. Open-G steel tuning and sliding song accompaniment are authored choices, not a claim about Price’s exact tuning.

items.name: UK Americana
items.lineage: UK Americana connects UK-rooted artists with transatlantic country, soul and roots-song practice. Yola’s Bristol-to-Nashville Walk Through Fire sessions supply one documented country-soul branch.
items.description: Lead voice, Wurlitzer piano and fiddle are supported by steel guitar, bass and drums. The label’s personnel establish these roles; pedal-steel E9 tuning, electric-bass construction and the reduced ensemble are authored choices within a much larger album palette.

items.name: Yorkshire folk
items.lineage: Yorkshire folk encompasses local inherited songs and contemporary folk performers. Kate Rusby’s South Yorkshire recording practice supplies a documented voice, fiddle and diatonic-accordion branch.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices are answered by fiddle and diatonic accordion over plucked double bass. Blooming Heather credits establish these roles; the compact configuration leaves out the record’s electric guitar and orchestral strings, and D/G melodeon rows are an authored choice.

items.name: Medieval folk
items.lineage: The discovery roster centers modern medieval-inspired ensembles such as FAUN, OMNIA and Blackmore’s Night. It denotes contemporary revival/fusion practice, not proof that these recordings reconstruct medieval performance unchanged.
items.description: Layered voices and hurdy-gurdy melody/drone interlock with harp and Irish bouzouki. This selected acoustic branch follows FAUN’s documented quieter concert format and musicians’ actual instruments; it leaves electronic festival production optional rather than pretending it did not exist or making it compulsory.

items.name: Italian folk
items.lineage: Italian folk encompasses diverse local song, dance and instrumental traditions. Sicilian performer Alfio Antico exemplifies a text-centered voice-and-frame-drum practice connected to dialect song, memory and the craft of hand-built instruments.
items.description: Narrative singing and a hand-played jingled frame drum exchange pulse, flourishes and silence. Vocal phrasing and changing percussion attacks shape the story, with the drum supplying both rhythmic grounding and expressive color.

items.name: New England Americana
items.lineage: New England Americana connects roots-song performers, venues and recording networks. David Wax Museum’s rural Maine sessions and Newport appearances offer one documented, Mexican-rooted branch of that regional network.
items.description: Harmony voices, strummed jarana, twin fiddle lines and jawbone percussion form a compact arrangement drawn from the documented Unfruitful session. This authored subset leaves out the record’s additional horsehead fiddle, organs and other colors rather than pretending those instruments were absent.

items.name: Macedonian folk
items.lineage: Macedonian folk encompasses local vocal repertories and instrumental dance traditions. The gajda has longstanding ties to shepherding and community celebrations; Radio Skopje and players such as Pece Atanasovski helped circulate the Prilep lineage during the twentieth century.
items.description: A continuous bagpipe drone supports a richly ornamented chanter melody. Closed-finger embellishments and register changes animate repeated dance figures; solo playing and drum-accompanied performance coexist with larger modern ensembles.

items.name: Indie folk argentino
items.lineage: Indie folk argentino is a discovery network including Mía Maestro and other Argentine-connected performers. Maestro’s Si Agua combines bilingual songwriting with acoustic, keyboard and arranged string parts in an international recording context.
items.description: Lead voice, acoustic guitar, Wurlitzer electric piano and cello create a compact chamber-song texture. Si Agua credits establish these roles; using one cello is an authored reduction of a larger string section, with programming and brass left outside this selected configuration.

items.name: Midwest Americana
items.lineage: Midwest Americana draws together regional roots songwriting, folk and blues performance across the American Midwest. Minnesota songwriter Charlie Parr exemplifies its connection to vernacular storytelling and resonant fingerpicked guitar, with both solo and ensemble approaches circulating through independent labels and venues.
items.description: A direct lead voice carries the narrative over interlocking twelve-string guitar patterns. Paired strings add shimmer and rhythmic weight to the bass-and-treble movement, leaving space for the words and the instrument’s natural decay.

items.name: Bhojpuri folk
items.lineage: Bhojpuri folk in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar includes migration songs, birha, seasonal repertories and music for life-cycle occasions. Singers and community ensembles sustain these text-centered practices through oral transmission, public performance and contemporary recording.
items.description: Lead and responding voices unfold stories and expressive phrases over hand-pumped harmonium. Dholak patterns and small manjira cymbals articulate the pulse, with vocal exchanges and rhythmic accents shaping the song’s unfolding narrative.

items.name: Folk siciliana
items.lineage: Sicilian folk carries local dialect song, narrative repertories and varied instrumental traditions. Alfio Antico’s singing and hand-built frame drums connect contemporary performance with shepherding memories and oral storytelling.
items.description: A narrative voice and jingled frame drum alternate steady pulse, short flourishes and expressive pauses. Shifts in vocal delivery and hand attack make the drum an answering voice as well as a rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Indian singer-songwriter
items.lineage: India’s independent performer-songwriters work in multiple languages and modern acoustic/electronic formats. Prateek Kuhad, present in the exact roster, supplies the selected Hindi-and-English guitar-based song branch.
items.description: A close lead voice and fingerpicked acoustic guitar create a sparse melodic setting. The model follows Kuhad’s documented acoustic songwriting roots while recognizing his later electronic and band releases; it does not import tabla, sitar or classical vocal training merely from the national label.

items.name: Greek folk
items.lineage: Greek folk includes distinct regional traditions of narrative song, dance and instrumental performance. Cretan musicians such as Psarantonis and Giorgos Xylouris sustain a particularly expressive interaction between singing, bowed lyra and accompanying laouto.
items.description: Inflected vocal phrases alternate with ornamented lyra melody above the rhythmic support of the plucked laouto. Sustained bowing, ringing strings and responsive phrasing link narrative delivery with the movement of the instrumental line.

items.name: Irish singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Irish performer-songwriters span acoustic storytelling, rock and studio experimentation. Glen Hansard’s documented Dublin-to-international career supplies the selected acoustic-song branch.
items.description: Lead voice and acoustic guitar carry the main narrative, with restrained bowed-string responses. ANTI’s specific track credits document Hansard’s voice/guitar and Rob Moose’s strings; choosing a single violin here is an authored reduction of that credited string role, not a claim about its entire overdubbed arrangement.
exemplars: Glen Hansard — Song of Good Hope

items.name: NL folk
items.lineage: The exact discovery roster resolves NL to Newfoundland and Labrador, with Great Big Sea, Alan Doyle and the Irish Descendants; it is not an abbreviation for the Netherlands. The selected branch follows Doyle’s modern Newfoundland kitchen-party folk-rock practice.
items.description: Group-friendly lead singing is driven by acoustic guitar, fiddle and accordion over bass and drums. Doyle’s own band descriptions document these roles and mixtures of new songs, Great Big Sea repertoire and traditional Newfoundland material; the recording setup is an authored contemporary band model.

items.name: Kurdish folk
items.lineage: Kurdish folk connects regional and linguistic traditions across Kurdish communities and diaspora. Bardic song, ornamented vocal delivery and long-necked lute accompaniment remain important resources for contemporary performers such as Aynur.
items.description: A sustained lead voice shapes melismatic phrases above plucked bağlama, leaving space for answering melodic figures. Flexible intonation, ringing strings and expressive ornament keep the text and vocal contour at the center of the arrangement.

items.name: Malagasy folk
items.lineage: Malagasy folk encompasses the varied song and instrumental traditions of Madagascar. Rajery’s singing and bamboo-tube valiha connect highland song with contemporary collaboration and regional musical exchange.
items.description: Bright plucked zither figures interlock beneath smoothly connected singing. Overlapping string resonance, clear attacks and responsive vocal phrasing create a light, mobile texture in which the valiha carries both melodic movement and accompaniment.

items.name: Malawian folk
items.lineage: Malawian folk includes local song traditions and a longstanding vernacular guitar-song practice. Giddes Chalamanda’s career exemplifies a direct, rhythmically animated relationship between narrative singing and acoustic guitar that also extends into ensemble performance.
items.description: Lead singing and fingerpicked acoustic patterns interlock in a compact texture. Repeated bass figures and treble responses support the words, while changes in accent and phrasing create motion without requiring a separate rhythm section.

items.name: Indonesian folk
items.lineage: This label’s actual discovery roster includes contemporary Indonesian acoustic folk acts. Endah N Rhesa’s documented guitar-bass-vocal duo is the selected branch, not a proxy for Indonesia’s many regional traditional ensembles.
items.description: Acoustic-guitar figures and vocal phrasing interlock with a distinct electric-bass part rather than simply doubling the guitar root. The compact arrangement follows the duo’s stated instrumentation; exact bass strings, guitar body and studio are authored production choices.

items.name: Indonesian singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Indonesian performer-songwriters work in solo and collaborative formats. Endah Widiastuti’s documented own-song work with bassist Rhesa Aditya supplies the selected independent acoustic branch.
items.description: Acoustic-guitar figures and vocal phrasing interlock with a distinct electric-bass part rather than simply doubling the guitar root. The compact arrangement follows the duo’s stated instrumentation; exact bass strings, guitar body and studio are authored production choices.

items.name: Korean indie folk
items.lineage: Korean independent folk includes small song-led ensembles and solo performers in the Hongdae scene. Kim Sawol and Kim Haewon supply a documented guitar-and-vocal branch.
items.description: Lead and answering vocals unfold over rhythmically articulated acoustic guitar. The authored setting retains the documented relationship between two independent songwriters’ voices and guitar; it does not impose gayageum, pansori technique or a single traditional Korean scale on contemporary authored songs.
exemplars: Kim Sawol X Kim Haewon — Secret

items.name: Korean singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Korean performer-songwriters span folk, pop and band formats. Kim Sawol’s first-person account of writing and performing songs supplies the selected intimate acoustic branch.
items.description: Lead and answering vocals unfold over rhythmically articulated acoustic guitar. The authored setting retains the documented relationship between two independent songwriters’ voices and guitar; it does not impose gayageum, pansori technique or a single traditional Korean scale on contemporary authored songs.
exemplars: Kim Sawol X Kim Haewon — Secret

items.name: NZ folk
items.lineage: New Zealand folk includes contemporary acoustic songwriting alongside inherited repertories. Tiny Ruins’ Hollie Fullbrook is documented by an artist interview and local label as part of the folk resurgence.
items.description: Lightly picked acoustic guitar and a lead voice are supported by spare bass and brushed percussion. The model follows Tiny Ruins’ documented band and acoustic core; it is an authored reduction of recordings that can also include organ, brass and additional electric guitar.

items.name: NZ singer-songwriter
items.lineage: New Zealand performer-songwriters work across solo and band recordings. Hollie Fullbrook’s Tiny Ruins began as solo authored songs and developed into an Auckland-based ensemble.
items.description: Lightly picked acoustic guitar and a lead voice are supported by spare bass and brushed percussion. The model follows Tiny Ruins’ documented band and acoustic core; it is an authored reduction of recordings that can also include organ, brass and additional electric guitar.

items.name: Japanese indie folk
items.lineage: The exact roster includes Shugo Tokumaru and other contemporary Japanese acoustic/independent acts. Tokumaru’s richly layered songcraft provides a documented branch that does not reduce indie folk to voice and guitar alone.
items.description: Acoustic-guitar picking and lead voice are surrounded by short toy-piano and wooden-xylophone figures. The selected palette follows instruments identified around In Focus? and its song Decorate; it is an authored playable reduction of dense home-studio layering, not a claim to reproduce every one of the many recorded parts.

items.name: Japanese singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Japanese performer-songwriters span several generations of popular song. Yumi Matsutoya’s documented composition, lyric writing, singing and piano practice supplies the selected piano-led branch.
items.description: A single lead voice is supported by piano chords and connecting melodic fills. This authored small-ensemble setting presents the song-writing core and does not claim that Matsutoya’s expansive album and concert productions are piano-only.

items.name: Norwegian americana
items.lineage: Norwegian Americana connects local songwriting and roots ensembles with transatlantic recording practice. Malin Pettersen, named in the exact roster, supplies a documented country-leaning band branch.
items.description: Lead and harmony vocals sit over acoustic guitar, piano, pedal-steel responses and a bass/drum foundation. Pettersen’s own Hometown credits identify all these roles; this authored subset of the full session leaves its extra electric/baritone guitar and banjo layers optional rather than inventing a national instrument formula.

items.name: Norwegian country
items.lineage: Norwegian country spans local-language country-rock bands and transatlantic country influences. Hellbillies’ documented blend of Norwegian and American musical traditions provides the selected electric-band branch.
items.description: Lead and supporting voices ride acoustic/electric guitars, keyboard chords, bass and drums. The source identifies the band’s real performance roles; exact guitar pickup, piano substitution for general keyboards and drum attack are authored choices rather than equipment claims.

items.name: Norwegian singer-songwriter
items.lineage: Norwegian performer-songwriters work across jazz-inflected pop, acoustic song and studio arrangements. Sondre Lerche’s explicit solo nylon-string-guitar programme supplies the selected intimate branch.
items.description: A direct lead voice moves over articulated nylon-string guitar chords and short connecting lines. Lerche describes touring solo with this instrument; the authored recipe preserves nylon-string construction and a chord-melody role without claiming a classical recital or duplicating his full band records.

items.name: Nashville americana
items.lineage: Nashville Americana links contemporary roots songwriters and bands through local stages and studios. Margo Price, in the exact roster, supplies the selected country-rooted band branch.
items.description: Narrative lead singing and acoustic guitar are supported by electric guitar, lap steel, bass and drums. A documented Price concert identifies these actual roles; the authored modern recording model keeps the slide instrument distinct and does not replace it with a generic guitar texture.

items.name: New americana
items.lineage: New Americana brings contemporary roots songwriters and bands into conversation with country, folk, blues and rock. Artists such as Margo Price connect narrative writing with expressive ensemble playing and a renewed interest in roots-music traditions.
items.description: Lead singing and ringing acoustic strums ride a steady bass-and-drum pulse. Clean electric-guitar responses and sliding lap-steel lines add melodic detail between verses, balancing direct storytelling with the energy of a working band.

items.name: Michigan folk
items.lineage: Michigan folk includes local acoustic-song communities and contemporary songwriter bands. May Erlewine’s documented Michigan roots and Traverse City recording identity supply the selected authored-song branch.
items.description: Lead voice and piano share the melody, supported by acoustic-guitar accents, bass and understated drums. Erlewine’s own release credits establish these roles; the piano-led emphasis and compact texture are authored selections within a broader band record.

items.name: New Orleans americana
items.lineage: New Orleans Americana connects roots songwriting with the city’s multilingual and Afro-diasporic musical exchanges. Leyla McCalla’s work brings cello-led song into this varied field alongside guitar, banjo and other acoustic traditions.
items.description: Intimate singing and bowed cello share a close, conversational texture. Sustained low notes, short melodic responses and rhythmic bow gestures support the text while leaving space for flexible vocal phrasing.

items.name: Indie anthem-folk

items.description: Lead and supporting voices build a singable melodic line above picked acoustic guitar, banjo and a restrained bass/drum foundation. The Paper Kites provide the documented branch; the authored arrangement preserves acoustic detail rather than reading anthem as an instruction to erase the quieter textures.

items.name: Modern indie folk

items.name: Manitoba country

items.name: Okinawan folk
items.lineage: Okinawan folk song joins expressive singing with the distinctive sound of the sanshin. Island repertoires and varied social settings sustain songs of memory, everyday life and feeling, with local traditions distinct from those of mainland Japan.
items.description: A flexible sung melody is answered and supported by the bright, plucked tone of a three-string sanshin. Short figures, recurring melodic shapes and the instrument’s resonant attack frame the words while leaving space for expressive vocal phrasing.

items.name: Danish folk

items.name: Croatian folk
items.lineage: Croatian folk encompasses regionally distinct song, dance and instrumental traditions. Northeastern tamburica ensembles form one important branch, alongside northwestern string-and-dulcimer groups and varied Adriatic practices preserved and renewed by ensembles such as LADO.
items.description: Group singing rests above interlocking plucked strings: bright prim melody, middle-register brač responses, bugarija chords and berda bass. Tremolo sustains the upper voices while chordal accents and alternating bass notes keep a clear rhythmic foundation.

items.name: Finnish folk

items.name: Cape Verdean folk

items.name: Rap chrétien
items.lineage: Rap chrétien connects French-language Christian testimony with hip-hop performance and production. Manou Bolomik exemplifies its movement between rap, electronic music, church networks and concert audiences.
